title: Ophthal Notes GenX – core eye diseases

topics.PEI: Penetrating eye injury & intraocular foreign body
topics.AION: Anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (NAION vs arteritic)

cards.q: What is strabismus, and what are its two main clinical classes?
cards.a:
• **Strabismus (squint)** = misalignment of the two eyes (visual axes not directed at the same object)
• **Concomitant / non-paralytic**: angle of deviation the SAME in all directions of gaze (typical childhood squint)
• **Inconcomitant / paralytic or restrictive**: angle VARIES with direction of gaze (nerve palsy, muscle disease or mechanical restriction)
• Further described as **intermittent, constant or alternating**
cards.m: Concomitant = Constant angle in every gaze; Inconcomitant = Inconsistent angle.

cards.q: Define eso-, exo-, hyper- and hypo-deviations, and the difference between a -tropia and a -phoria.
cards.a:
• **Eso** = eye turned IN; **exo** = OUT; **hyper** = UP; **hypo** = DOWN (named by the deviating eye)
• **-tropia** = MANIFEST deviation, present with both eyes open
• **-phoria** = LATENT deviation, held straight by fusion and seen only when fusion is broken (one eye covered)
• Small phorias are normal; tropias in children are always abnormal
cards.m: Tropia = True squint you can see; Phoria = Phantom squint that hides until you cover an eye.

cards.q: What are the typical features of a concomitant (non-paralytic) squint?
cards.a:
• **Childhood onset** in the majority
• **Family history** of squint is a risk factor
• Angle of misalignment **equal in all directions of gaze**; full eye movements
• **No neurological signs**
• Child suppresses the deviating eye -> **no diplopia** but risk of **strabismic amblyopia**
• Can occur in adults after loss of vision in one eye (intraocular or optic nerve disease) — 'sensory' squint
cards.m: Child squint: Suppress -> no double vision -> but lazy eye.

cards.q: What are the features and causes of an inconcomitant (paralytic/restrictive) squint?
cards.a:
• Usually **late (adult) onset**
• Angle **varies with direction of gaze** — largest when looking in the direction of action of the weak muscle
• **Diplopia** in adults (mature visual system cannot suppress); may adopt a compensatory head posture
• Causes: **cranial nerve palsy** (e.g. CN3 paresis — serious neurological disease), **trauma**, **thyroid eye disease** (restrictive), **orbital floor blow-out fracture** (inferior rectus entrapment)
cards.m: Adult + double vision + angle changes with gaze = look for a nerve, a muscle or a fracture.

cards.q: List the examination of a patient presenting with a squint.
cards.a:
• **Visual acuity** each eye (age-appropriate chart) — screen for amblyopia
• **External examination**: ptosis, head posture, facial asymmetry, proptosis
• **Tests of alignment**: **cover-uncover test**, **Hirschberg** corneal reflex test
• **Ocular motility** in the 9 positions of gaze
• **Fundus examination** (dilated) and **red reflex**
• **Cycloplegic refraction**
• **Tests of binocularity and fusion** (e.g. stereopsis)
cards.m: V-E-A-M-F-R-B: Vision, External, Alignment, Motility, Fundus, Refraction, Binocularity.

cards.q: Which cover test detects a tropia and which detects a phoria?
cards.a:
• **Cover test** (cover one eye, watch the OTHER eye): if the uncovered eye moves to take up fixation = **tropia** (manifest)
• **Uncover / alternate cover test** (watch the eye as the cover is REMOVED or switched): eye moving back to straight = **phoria** (latent)
• Direction of re-fixation movement tells the type: eye moves OUT to fixate = it was turned in = **eso**
• Test at **near (33 cm) and distance (6 m)**, using an accommodative target
cards.m: Cover reveals the Tropia (watch the other eye); Uncover unmasks the Phoria (watch the covered eye).

cards.q: A mother brings her 1-year-old with a broad nasal bridge who 'looks cross-eyed'. How do you confirm a pseudosquint, and how is the Hirschberg test read?
cards.a:
• **Pseudosquint**: broad **epicanthic folds** hide the nasal sclera, so the eyes look turned in
• **Hirschberg**: pen-torch at 33 cm — corneal light reflexes **symmetrical and central** in both eyes = no true squint
• **Cover test**: no re-fixation movement
• Reading: each **1 mm decentration ≈ 7° (≈ 15 prism dioptres)**; reflex displaced **temporally = esotropia**, **nasally = exotropia**
• Reassure, but re-check if parental concern persists (true squint can still develop)
cards.m: Light reflex goes the opposite way to the eye: eye turns in, reflex sits out.

cards.q: Why must every child with a new squint have a red reflex and dilated fundus examination?
cards.a:
• Squint may be the presenting sign of poor vision in one eye (sensory squint)
• Must exclude **retinoblastoma** (squint is the 2nd commonest presentation after **leukocoria**), **congenital cataract**, optic nerve or macular disease
• Absent/white/asymmetric red reflex -> **urgent ophthalmology referral** (retinoblastoma is life-threatening)
• Also do **cycloplegic refraction** at the same visit
cards.m: Squint + white reflex = cancer until proven otherwise.

cards.q: A 2.5-year-old develops an intermittent esotropia, worse when looking at toys close up. What is the likely diagnosis and first-line management?
cards.a:
• **Refractive accommodative esotropia** — child is **hyperopic**; extra accommodation to focus drives extra **convergence** (accommodation-convergence link)
• Typical onset **2-3 years**, often intermittent at first, worse at near
• First step: **cycloplegic refraction** (cyclopentolate 1%, or atropine in very young/dark irides) and **FULL hyperopic correction with glasses** worn all day
• Glasses alone often straighten the eyes — **surgery is NOT first-line**
• Treat any associated amblyopia
cards.m: Long-sighted toddler focuses hard -> eyes cross: give the glasses, not the knife.

cards.q: How do third, fourth and sixth cranial nerve palsies present, and which needs emergency imaging?
cards.a:
• **CN3**: eye **'down and out'**, **ptosis**, ± **dilated pupil**. **Pupil-involving CN3 = posterior communicating artery aneurysm until proven otherwise** -> **emergency CT/CT angiography**. Pupil-sparing is often microvascular (DM, HTN)
• **CN4** (superior oblique): vertical diplopia worse looking **down and in** (reading, stairs); **head tilt to the OPPOSITE side**
• **CN6** (lateral rectus): **esotropia**, horizontal diplopia worse at **distance** and on gaze to the affected side; can be a **false-localising sign of raised ICP**
cards.m: LR6 SO4, rest 3. Blown pupil = blown aneurysm risk.

cards.q: What are the complications of strabismus?
cards.a:
• **Diplopia** — mainly in adults (same object seen in two places)
• **Confusion** — two DIFFERENT objects seen superimposed in the same place (each fovea looks at a different target)
• **Amblyopia** — in children, from suppression of the deviating eye
• Loss of **binocular single vision and stereopsis**
• **Adverse psychosocial and vocational consequences** (appearance, teasing, job limitations)
cards.m: Diplopia = one thing twice; Confusion = two things in one spot.

cards.q: What are the aims and options of strabismus management, and what do recession and resection do?
cards.a:
• **Aims**: best vision in each eye (treat amblyopia), **ocular alignment**, and **binocularity (including stereopsis)**
• **Glasses** (full refractive correction) ± amblyopia treatment first
• **Surgery**: **recession** = muscle insertion moved back -> **WEAKENS**; **resection** = muscle shortened -> **STRENGTHENS**
• Lecturer add-on: prisms or botulinum toxin for selected adult diplopia; treat the cause in paralytic squint
cards.m: Recession = Retreat (weaker); Resection = Reef it tight (stronger).

cards.q: Define amblyopia ('lazy eye').
cards.a:
• **Reduced best-corrected visual acuity** caused by **form vision deprivation and/or abnormal binocular interaction**
• **No structural pathology** of the eye or visual pathway to explain it (or loss is out of proportion to it)
• Usually unilateral; working threshold = **2 or more Snellen lines difference** between the eyes
• It is a **cortical** developmental problem — the eye itself looks normal
cards.m: Amblyopia = a normal eye with an untrained brain.

cards.q: Why is amblyopia age-dependent, and up to what age can it be reversed?
cards.a:
• The visual cortex needs a **clear, aligned image from each eye** during the **critical (sensitive) period** of visual development
• Plasticity is greatest in the first months to years and declines with age — **the earlier the treatment, the better the result**
• Per notes: reversible up to **7-8 years in strabismic** and **11-12 years in anisometropic** amblyopia
• So an older anisometropic child (e.g. 9 years) is still worth treating
cards.m: The brain's wiring sets like cement: pour early, shape early.

cards.q: What is strabismic amblyopia and how common is it?
cards.a:
• Commonest type (**~50%**)
• Results from **abnormal binocular interaction**: continued **monocular suppression of the deviating eye** to avoid diplopia/confusion
• A constant unilateral squint is most amblyogenic; a freely **alternating** squint usually spares both eyes
cards.m: The brain switches off the wandering eye — and if it stays off, it forgets how to see.

cards.q: What is anisometropic (refractive) amblyopia, and why is it often detected late?
cards.a:
• **~20%** of amblyopia; caused by a **difference in refractive error** between the eyes, most commonly **hyperopic**
• Abnormal binocular interaction from **superimposition of a large (clear) and small (blurred) image** (aniseikonia)
• Why hyperopes: accommodation is equal in both eyes and set by the better eye, so the more hyperopic eye is **never in focus**
• Detected **at an older age** because the eyes look **straight — no obvious squint**; found at vision screening
cards.m: Straight eyes, hidden blur: the quiet amblyopia found only by screening.

cards.q: What is deprivational amblyopia, and give examples of causes.
cards.a:
• **Least common (~5%) but MOST SEVERE** type
• Structural abnormality **obscures the incoming image** (form deprivation)
• Causes: **congenital cataract**, **ptosis** covering the pupil, **congenital corneal opacity**, **vitreous haemorrhage**, very severe refractive error
• Treat the obstruction urgently, then optical correction and occlusion
cards.m: Deprivation = Dark eye: no image at all is the worst teacher.

cards.q: What are meridional and bilateral isoametropic amblyopia?
cards.a:
• **Meridional (astigmatic)**: uncorrected high **astigmatism** blurs one meridian -> reduced acuity in that orientation
• **Bilateral isoametropic**: high but **equal** refractive error in both eyes (usually **high hyperopia** or astigmatism) -> **both eyes** reduced
• Both usually improve with **full-time glasses** alone over months
cards.m: Both eyes blurred equally -> both eyes lazy equally.

cards.q: A baby has a dense unilateral congenital cataract. Why is surgery urgent, and when should it be done?
cards.a:
• Deprivation is the **most amblyogenic** stimulus; a dense opacity in early infancy causes profound, often permanent amblyopia and nystagmus
• Operate within the **first 6-8 weeks of life**
• Then **optical correction** (contact lens/glasses/IOL) and **occlusion** of the good eye
• Every newborn needs a **red reflex check** to detect it
cards.m: Congenital cataract: six weeks, not six months.

cards.q: How is amblyopia detected, and what is the crowding phenomenon?
cards.a:
• **Pre-school vision screening** (around 4-5 years) and school screening; red reflex in infants
• Test each eye separately with an **age-appropriate chart** (pictures, logMAR/Snellen); look for squint and refractive error
• **Crowding phenomenon**: an amblyopic eye reads **single letters better than letters in a line**
• So use **crowded (linear) optotypes** — single letters overestimate vision
cards.m: Lazy eyes read alone, but get lost in a crowd.

cards.q: What is ALWAYS the first step in treating amblyopia?
cards.a:
• **Cycloplegic refraction** and **full refractive correction with glasses**
• Glasses alone improve VA in many children (**refractive adaptation**) — continue for several months until VA plateaus
• Only then add **occlusion or atropine penalisation** if a residual difference remains
• Remove any cause of deprivation first (e.g. cataract, ptosis)
cards.m: Focus first, force later: glasses before patches.

cards.q: How does occlusion therapy work, and which eye is patched?
cards.a:
• Patch the **NORMAL (good) eye** to force the brain to use the amblyopic eye and redevelop its vision
• Dose-titrated: commonly **2 hours/day** for moderate and **~6 hours/day** for severe amblyopia, with near activities during patching (lecturer pearl)
• Adhesive patch on the skin (not over glasses) gives better compliance
• Review VA every 6-12 weeks
cards.m: Patch the hero so the lazy one has to work.

cards.q: What is atropine penalisation and when is it useful?
cards.a:
• **Atropine 1%** drops instilled in the **GOOD eye** — cycloplegia blurs its near vision, so the amblyopic eye is preferred
• Daily or weekend dosing; as effective as patching for **moderate amblyopia**
• Useful when **patching compliance is poor**; works best if the good eye is **hyperopic**
• Side effects: photophobia, light sensitivity; rarely systemic toxicity (flushing, fever)
cards.m: Atropine = a 'chemical patch' on the good eye.

cards.q: What are the complications and causes of failure of amblyopia treatment?
cards.a:
• **Poor compliance** is the main cause of failure — counsel and involve parents/school
• **Occlusion (reverse) amblyopia** in the patched good eye -> check **VA of BOTH eyes** at each visit; stop/reduce patching if the good eye drops (usually recovers)
• **Recurrence** after stopping treatment -> taper rather than stop abruptly
• Older age at start and dense deprivation give the worst outcomes
cards.m: Every patch visit: test both eyes, not just the lazy one.

cards.q: What is central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO), and why is it called an 'ocular stroke'?
cards.a:
• Occlusion of the **central retinal artery** (first branch of the ophthalmic artery, from the internal carotid) -> **oxygen starvation of the inner retina** and cell death
• The CRA supplies the **inner retina**; the outer retina is fed by the **choroid** (posterior ciliary arteries)
• It is an **ophthalmic emergency** and the retinal equivalent of a **cerebral stroke** — same causes, same risk of further stroke
cards.m: The retina is brain tissue: CRAO = a stroke you can see with an ophthalmoscope.

cards.q: Who typically gets CRAO? Give the epidemiology and main associations.
cards.a:
• **Elderly**, more often **men**
• Cardiovascular risk factors: **hypertension (~60%)**, **diabetes (~25%)**, **hypercholesterolaemia**, **smoking**
• **Carotid artery disease**, cardiac disease (arrhythmia, valve disease)
• Young patient with CRAO -> think **cardiac emboli, coagulopathy, vasculitis, sickle cell**
cards.m: Same patient as a stroke ward: old, hypertensive, diabetic, smoker.

cards.q: What are the causes of CRAO?
cards.a:
• **Emboli** (commonest): **carotid** atheroma, **heart** (AF/arrhythmia, valve disease, endocarditis, atrial myxoma, septal defects)
• **Thrombus / coagulopathy** (antiphospholipid syndrome, hyperhomocysteinaemia, leukaemia/lymphoma)
• **Vasculitis**: **giant cell (temporal) arteritis**, PAN, GPA, SLE
• **Sickle cell** vaso-occlusion; others — OCP, cocaine, trauma, infection (syphilis, mucormycosis)
cards.m: Causes = Clot travelling (embolus), Clot forming (thrombus), Cuffed artery (vasculitis), Clumped cells (sickle).

cards.q: Name the three types of retinal emboli and their usual sources.
cards.a:
• **Cholesterol (Hollenhorst plaque)**: bright, glistening, yellow-orange, at **arteriolar bifurcations** — from **carotid** atheroma; often do not fully block flow
• **Calcific**: white, non-glistening, near the disc — from **heart valves**; more likely to cause complete occlusion
• **Platelet-fibrin**: dull grey, elongated, mobile — from carotid/heart; cause **amaurosis fugax**
cards.m: Yellow = carotid cholesterol; White = valve calcium; Grey = platelet plug.

cards.q: Describe the classic presenting symptoms of CRAO.
cards.a:
• **Sudden, painless, severe and persistent monocular loss of vision**
• White, quiet eye: **no redness, tearing, glare or discharge**
• VA **counting fingers to perception of light** at presentation; may progress to **NPL** if untreated
• Ask about previous **transient episodes (amaurosis fugax)**
cards.m: Painless, sudden, profound, one eye: think artery first.

cards.q: What is amaurosis fugax, and why does it matter?
cards.a:
• **Transient monocular painless loss of vision** (seconds to minutes), often a 'curtain' coming down, then full recovery
• Usually a **platelet-fibrin embolus** passing through the retinal circulation = **retinal TIA**
• May precede CRAO; also a warning of **GCA** in the elderly
• Needs **urgent stroke/TIA work-up** (carotid imaging, ECG) and ESR/CRP if over 50
cards.m: Amaurosis fugax is the retina's warning shot.

cards.q: What pupil finding is expected in CRAO, and why?
cards.a:
• **Marked relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD)** in the affected eye
• The ischaemic inner retina (ganglion cells) cannot send a light signal along the optic nerve
• On swinging-light test the affected pupil **dilates** when the light swings to it
• A dense RAPD with a clear media helps separate CRAO from **vitreous haemorrhage** (little or no RAPD)
cards.m: Dead ganglion cells = no afferent signal = big RAPD.

cards.q: What is the cherry-red spot in CRAO, and what causes it?
cards.a:
• **Red spot at the centre of the macula** — the **hallmark** of CRAO
• The surrounding inner retina becomes **opaque and white** (ischaemic oedema of the ganglion cell/nerve fibre layers)
• The **fovea is thin** and has no inner retinal layers, so the **intact, highly vascular choroid** shows through as red
• Fades over ~4-6 weeks, leaving optic atrophy and attenuated arterioles
cards.m: White fog everywhere, but a red window at the fovea where the retina is thinnest.

cards.q: Apart from the cherry-red spot, what fundus signs are seen in CRAO?
cards.a:
• **Retinal pallor / whitening** (posterior pole)
• **Arteriolar attenuation** and **segmentation of the blood column — 'box-carring' / 'cattle-trucking'**
• **Cotton-wool spots** (nerve fibre layer infarcts)
• **Emboli** — cholesterol **Hollenhorst plaques**, usually at **arteriolar bifurcations**
• Red reflex is usually **preserved** (media clear) — the problem is behind the lens
cards.m: Box-cars = blood standing still in the arteries like a train stopped at a station.

cards.q: What is cilioretinal artery sparing, and how does it change the presentation?
cards.a:
• A **cilioretinal artery** (from the **posterior ciliary/choroidal** circulation, not the CRA) is present in roughly **15-30% of eyes**
• It supplies a tongue of retina between disc and macula, including the **papillomacular bundle**
• In CRAO it keeps that area pink and perfused -> **central vision can be relatively preserved** (sometimes 6/12 or better) with a small central island of field
• Conversely, **GCA** can occlude a cilioretinal artery because it arises from the posterior ciliary arteries
cards.m: A back-door artery that keeps the reading spot alive.

cards.q: How does a branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO) differ from CRAO?
cards.a:
• **Sectoral** retinal whitening along the territory of the occluded branch, often with a visible **embolus** at a bifurcation
• **Sectoral/altitudinal field defect**; VA may be normal if the fovea is spared
• RAPD mild or absent
• Mostly **embolic** -> **same urgent stroke work-up** as CRAO
cards.m: One branch blocked = one slice of retina white, one slice of field missing.

cards.q: How do you distinguish CRAO from CRVO on fundoscopy?
cards.a:
• **CRAO**: pale, **white** oedematous retina, **cherry-red spot**, thin attenuated arteries, box-carring, dense RAPD, VA CF-PL
• **CRVO**: **'blood and thunder'** — flame and dot-blot haemorrhages in **all 4 quadrants**, **dilated tortuous veins**, disc swelling, cotton-wool spots; RAPD marked only in ischaemic CRVO
• Other differentials of sudden painless loss: **vitreous haemorrhage** (no fundus view), **retinal detachment**, **AION** (swollen disc)
cards.m: Artery blocked = white and empty; Vein blocked = red and flooded.

cards.q: A 72-year-old with sudden painless loss of vision and a cherry-red spot also reports jaw pain on chewing. What must be done immediately, and why?
cards.a:
• Suspect **arteritic CRAO from giant cell arteritis**
• **Urgent ESR and CRP** (and platelets) in EVERY CRAO patient **over 50**
• If GCA is suspected clinically, **start high-dose steroids the same day** (do not wait for results or biopsy) — protects the **fellow eye**, which can be lost within days
• Arrange temporal artery biopsy later; cross-ref GCA
• Note: the notes list vasculitis as a cause but omit this step — it is mandatory
cards.m: Old eye + artery blocked = check the ESR before you check the carotid.

cards.q: What investigations are needed after a CRAO?
cards.a:
• Mainly to find the **source/risk factors** (diagnosis is clinical)
• **ESR/CRP** (GCA) if over 50; **BP**, **blood glucose/HbA1c**, **lipids**, FBC, coagulation screen (younger patients: thrombophilia, sickle screen)
• **Carotid duplex (Doppler) ultrasound** for carotid stenosis
• **ECG ± Holter** for AF; **echocardiogram** for cardiac/valvular emboli
• Note: the notes say 'Doppler echocardiogram' — these are TWO separate tests: carotid Doppler ultrasound AND echocardiography
cards.m: Look up the pipe: heart (ECG, echo) -> neck (carotid Doppler) -> blood (ESR, sugar, lipids).

cards.q: What is meant by 'time is retina' in CRAO?
cards.a:
• Retinal damage becomes **irreversible after ~90-100 minutes** of complete occlusion (experimental data)
• Aim to restore blood flow within **~2 hours** of onset for any hope of recovery
• Treatment is still attempted in presentations up to **6 (to 24) hours**, as occlusion is often incomplete
• So: **immediate referral** to ophthalmology (and stroke team) — no routine appointment
cards.m: Every minute of a blocked artery costs retinal cells — like a heart attack.

cards.q: What emergency measures are used to try to dislodge the embolus in an early CRAO?
cards.a:
• **Ocular (digital) massage**: compress the closed eye with the heel of the hand **10 s, release 10 s, repeat for ~5 minutes** — pressure swings may push the embolus distally
• **Lower IOP** to raise perfusion pressure: **topical beta-blocker** (timolol 0.5%), **IV acetazolamide 500 mg**, **IV mannitol** (draws fluid from the eye)
• **Anterior chamber paracentesis** — sudden IOP drop; risks **infection** and **lens puncture**
• Lecturer pearl: none of these has proven benefit in trials — used only in very early presenters
cards.m: Massage, Medicines, Mini-tap: lower the pressure, push the clot.

cards.q: What reperfusion and systemic measures are used for CRAO, and what is the evidence?
cards.a:
• **Nd:YAG laser embolysis/embolectomy** of a visible embolus — risk of vitreous haemorrhage
• **Intra-arterial or intravenous thrombolysis** in stroke centres within a few hours — evidence limited; intra-arterial fibrinolysis (EAGLE trial) showed **no benefit and more complications**
• Current practice: treat as acute stroke -> **same-day stroke pathway**; stroke risk is highest in the first weeks
• Secondary prevention: antiplatelet, statin, BP/DM control, anticoagulation for AF, carotid endarterectomy for significant symptomatic stenosis
cards.m: Save the brain and the other eye even if you cannot save this retina.

cards.q: What is the prognosis of CRAO, and what are its late complications?
cards.a:
• **Poor prognosis** — most eyes remain **CF or worse**; better if cilioretinal sparing or incomplete occlusion
• Potentially reversible only within the first hours; late presenters are managed for **prevention (fellow eye, stroke)**
• Late: **optic atrophy**, attenuated arteries, **rubeosis iridis and neovascular glaucoma** (less common than after CRVO; usually within the first ~3 months -> follow up, PRP if new vessels)
• Systemic: increased risk of **stroke and myocardial infarction**
cards.m: CRAO ends badly for the eye — the job is to protect the brain, heart and fellow eye.

cards.q: What is giant cell arteritis (temporal arteritis)?
cards.a:
• **Granulomatous vasculitis of LARGE and MEDIUM-sized arteries**, especially the **extracranial branches of the carotid** (superficial temporal, ophthalmic, posterior ciliary, occipital) and the aorta
• Closely associated with **polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR)**
• A **medical and ophthalmic emergency** — risk of irreversible blindness
• Note: the notes say 'large cerebral arteries' — intracranial involvement is actually rare; it is the extracranial arteries that are affected
cards.m: GCA hits the arteries OUTSIDE the skull — the ones you can feel at the temple.

cards.q: Describe the epidemiology of GCA.
cards.a:
• Almost never under **50**; incidence rises with age, average around **70 years**
• **Women affected 2-3 times more** often than men
• Most frequent systemic vasculitis in older adults in Western populations (North America/Northern Europe); less common but under-recognised in Asia
• Note: the notes give different sex ratios (2:1 on p7, 4:1 on p47) and say '>60 years' — teach 'over 50, women 2-3x'
cards.m: Over 50, mostly women, mostly in their 70s.

cards.q: What are the histological features of GCA on temporal artery biopsy?
cards.a:
• Infiltrates of **CD4+ T lymphocytes, macrophages and multinucleated giant cells** in the vessel wall
• **Granulomatous inflammation of the intima and media**
• **Fragmentation (breaking up) of the internal elastic lamina**
• Giant cells are **not seen in every case** — mononuclear infiltration alone can be diagnostic
• Lesions are **patchy ('skip lesions')**
cards.m: Giant cells chew up the elastic lamina — but they don't always show up for the photo.

cards.q: State the ACR 1990 classification criteria for GCA.
cards.a:
• **Age at onset ≥ 50**
• **New headache** (often temporal)
• **Temporal artery abnormality** — tenderness or reduced pulsation (not due to arteriosclerosis)
• **ESR ≥ 50 mm/h**
• **Abnormal artery biopsy** (mononuclear infiltrate or granulomatous inflammation, usually with giant cells)
• **≥ 3 of 5** -> sensitivity **94%**, specificity **91%**
cards.m: 50-Head-Artery-ESR 50-Biopsy: three out of five makes GCA alive.

cards.q: Describe the headache of GCA and its cause.
cards.a:
• **New-onset headache**, usually **temporal** (sometimes occipital), in a patient over 50
• **Scalp tenderness** — pain when **combing hair** or lying on a pillow
• Due to inflammation of the involved **temporal or occipital arteries**
• Any new headache in an older patient = ask about GCA symptoms and check ESR/CRP
cards.m: Over 50 + new headache + sore scalp when combing = GCA until proven otherwise.

cards.q: What is jaw claudication, and why is it important?
cards.a:
• **Pain in the muscles of mastication on prolonged chewing**, relieved by rest (also tongue claudication)
• Due to ischaemia from **maxillary/facial artery** involvement
• It is the **most specific symptom** of GCA (lecturer pearl) — strongly predicts a positive biopsy and visual risk
• Distinguish from TMJ pain (pain at the first bite, joint clicking)
cards.m: Claudication = 'limping' of a muscle: the jaw limps the way calves do in PVD.

cards.q: How does polymyalgia rheumatica present, and what is its relation to GCA?
cards.a:
• Occurs in about **30% of GCA** patients (and GCA can develop in patients with PMR)
• **Proximal myalgia** with **shoulder and pelvic girdle pain and morning stiffness**
• **Constitutional symptoms**: fever, weight loss, malaise, anorexia
• **Elevated ESR**
• PMR patients must be warned to report headache, jaw pain or visual symptoms at once
cards.m: Can't comb hair (scalp) and can't lift arms to comb it (shoulders) = GCA + PMR.

cards.q: What are the visual symptoms of GCA, and how urgent are they?
cards.a:
• **Sudden, painless loss of vision** — often severe (to PL or worse)
• Often preceded by **amaurosis fugax** (transient obscurations) and sometimes **diplopia**
• Can affect **both eyes**: about **1/3 lose the fellow eye, usually within a week**, if untreated
• Untreated GCA causes **permanent blindness in 20-25%**
• Any visual symptom = **emergency**: steroids today
cards.m: In GCA the first eye is a warning; the second eye is your responsibility.

cards.q: Which artery is responsible for visual loss in GCA, and what does the fundus show?
cards.a:
• Narrowing of the **posterior ciliary arteries (commonest)** or the ophthalmic artery
• **Arteritic AION**: pale, **'chalky white' swollen disc** (cross-ref AION)
• **Central retinal artery occlusion**: cherry-red spot (cross-ref CRAO)
• **Cilioretinal artery occlusion** (it arises from the posterior ciliary circulation)
• Diplopia from ischaemia of extraocular muscles or nerves
cards.m: Posterior Ciliary = Pale Chalky disc.

cards.q: What do you look for when examining the temporal arteries in suspected GCA?
cards.a:
• **Tender, thickened, nodular** ('cord-like') superficial temporal artery
• **Reduced or absent pulsation** (not due to arteriosclerosis)
• Overlying redness occasionally; scalp necrosis in severe cases
• A **normal-feeling artery does NOT exclude GCA**
• Also check BP in both arms and listen for bruits (large-vessel/aortic arch involvement)
cards.m: Feel for a rope, not a pulse.

cards.q: What blood results support a diagnosis of GCA?
cards.a:
• **ESR raised**, usually **50-120 mm/h**
• **CRP very high** (more sensitive than ESR; check both)
• **Normochromic normocytic anaemia** (anaemia of chronic disease)
• **Raised platelets** (thrombocytosis) — lecturer pearl; adds to suspicion
• Liver tests: raised **ALP and GGT** (acute inflammation), low **albumin**
• A normal ESR does not completely exclude GCA
cards.m: Inflamed blood: high ESR, high CRP, high platelets, low Hb, low albumin.

cards.q: A 75-year-old woman has new temporal headache, jaw claudication and ESR 90 mm/h. What is the next step — biopsy or steroids?
cards.a:
• **Start high-dose steroids IMMEDIATELY** on clinical suspicion — **DO NOT WAIT TO TREAT**
• Arrange **temporal artery biopsy within 2 weeks** of starting treatment
• Histology **stays positive for ~2 weeks after steroids** begin, so treatment does not ruin the biopsy
• Same-day referral to ophthalmology/medicine; if any visual symptom -> emergency admission
cards.m: Treat first, prove later: steroids today, biopsy within 2 weeks.

cards.q: How is a temporal artery biopsy performed and interpreted?
cards.a:
• **Definitive diagnostic test**; take from the **symptomatic (affected) side**
• Lesions are **patchy (skip lesions)**, so take a **long segment (> 1 cm; ideally 1.5-2 cm)** and examine its whole length
• **Negative biopsy does not exclude GCA** (false negatives up to ~10% per notes; some series report more)
• If clinical suspicion is high and biopsy negative -> continue treatment; consider contralateral biopsy or ultrasound
cards.m: Skip lesions = the disease can skip the bit you cut.

cards.q: What is the role of temporal artery ultrasound in GCA?
cards.a:
• Colour Doppler ultrasound of temporal (± axillary) arteries is increasingly used first-line in fast-track GCA clinics
• Key sign: **'halo sign'** — dark (hypoechoic) ring of **vessel-wall oedema** around the lumen; **non-compressible** artery ('compression sign')
• Quick, non-invasive; should be done **within days of starting steroids** (halo fades)
• Large-vessel involvement can be assessed with CT/MR angiography or PET-CT
cards.m: Halo around the artery = inflamed wall, not an angel.

cards.q: What steroid regimen is used in GCA, with and without visual involvement?
cards.a:
• **No visual symptoms**: **oral prednisolone 60 mg/day** (about 40-60 mg or 1 mg/kg) started immediately
• **Evolving visual loss or amaurosis fugax**: **IV methylprednisolone** — lecturer pearl dose **500 mg-1 g daily for 3 days**, then oral prednisolone 60 mg/day
• Aim: protect the **fellow eye** and prevent further ischaemia — lost vision rarely recovers
• Steroids are highly effective at preventing blindness, further ischaemic episodes and pain
cards.m: Eyes threatened = IV; eyes safe = oral 60.

cards.q: How are steroids tapered and monitored in GCA, and what steroid-sparing options exist?
cards.a:
• **Reduce gradually once symptoms resolve and ESR/CRP fall**; **increase the dose if symptoms recur**
• Total course typically **1-2 years** (notes: 'a 2-year course' — approximate), some need longer
• Monitor symptoms, ESR/CRP, BP, glucose, weight
• Steroid-sparing (lecturer pearl): **methotrexate**; **tocilizumab** (IL-6 receptor blocker) reduces relapses and steroid exposure — note it suppresses CRP, so CRP is unreliable for monitoring
cards.m: Taper by symptoms and ESR: slow down, never stop suddenly.

cards.q: What must be prescribed alongside long-term steroids in GCA, and why?
cards.a:
• The **main cause of death and morbidity in GCA is long-term steroid treatment** — balance the risks
• **PPI** — gastric protection
• **Bisphosphonate** (e.g. alendronate) + **calcium with colecalciferol (vitamin D)** — bone protection against osteoporosis
• **Consider low-dose aspirin** — reduce ischaemic events (unless contraindicated)
• Also monitor for steroid diabetes, hypertension, infection, cataract and glaucoma
cards.m: Protect the Gut, the Bones and the Vessels: PPI, bisphosphonate + Ca/vit D, aspirin.

cards.q: What are the long-term vascular complications of GCA, and how are they screened?
cards.a:
• **Thoracic aortic aneurysm** and **aortic dissection** (± rupture) — increased risk years later
• **Aortic arch syndrome**: involvement of subclavian/brachial branches -> arm claudication, unequal BP, **'pulseless disease'**
• Screening: **yearly chest X-ray ± abdominal ultrasound** (CT/MR angiography if suspicion)
• Without treatment: **permanent blindness in 20-25%**
cards.m: GCA can return years later through the aorta — keep imaging the chest.

cards.q: What is infective conjunctivitis, and what are the two main types you must tell apart in clinic?
cards.a:
• Inflammation of the **conjunctiva** (bulbar + tarsal) from infection
• **Bacterial**: mucopurulent discharge, **papillae**, often both eyes sticky in the morning
• **Viral**: watery discharge, **follicles**, tender pre-auricular node, very contagious
• Both: diffuse redness, gritty irritation, **normal VA**, normal pupil, clear cornea
cards.m: Bacteria make pus, viruses make tears.

cards.q: Name the usual organisms of acute bacterial conjunctivitis.
cards.a:
• **Staphylococcus** (S. aureus)
• **Streptococcus**
• **Pneumococcus** (S. pneumoniae)
• **Haemophilus** influenzae — especially in children
• Hyperacute copious pus in an adult -> think **N. gonorrhoeae** (separate, urgent)
cards.m: 'SSPH' — Staph, Strep, Pneumo, Haemophilus.

cards.q: What is the commonest cause of viral conjunctivitis, and which other viruses cause it?
cards.a:
• **Adenovirus** — commonest by far
• **Coxsackie** and other **picornaviruses** (enterovirus) — outbreaks
• Herpes simplex — usually unilateral with lid vesicles (look for dendrites)
cards.m: Red eye after a sore throat = adenovirus until proven otherwise.

cards.q: How does the redness and discharge differ between bacterial and viral conjunctivitis?
cards.a:
• Bacterial: diffuse redness including the **palpebral/tarsal** conjunctiva; **mucopurulent** discharge; lids stuck together on waking
• Viral: diffuse redness; **watery** discharge with little pus; **lid oedema** and excessive lacrimation
• Both are irritating/gritty rather than truly painful
cards.m: Glued lids = bacteria; streaming tears = virus.

cards.q: Papillae vs follicles — what do you see on the slit lamp and what does each mean?
cards.a:
• **Papillae**: raised lesions with a **central vascular core**, mostly **upper tarsus**; **non-specific** sign of inflammation (bacterial, allergic, contact lens)
• **Follicles**: pale, gelatinous lymphoid aggregates with vessels around the edge, mostly **lower tarsus/fornix**; **specific** for **viral** and **chlamydial** infection (also some drug reactions)
cards.m: Papilla = vessel in the middle; Follicle = vessels round the edge.

cards.q: A tender pre-auricular lymph node in a red eye points to which causes?
cards.a:
• **Viral** conjunctivitis (adenovirus) — classic
• **Chlamydial** (adult inclusion) conjunctivitis
• Also HSV primary infection and severe gonococcal disease
• **Note:** the notes place 'pre-auricular LN enlarged' between the bacterial and viral columns; it is a **VIRAL (and chlamydial)** sign, not typical of simple bacterial conjunctivitis
cards.m: Follicles + node = virus or chlamydia.

cards.q: Which red-eye red flags tell you it is NOT simple conjunctivitis and needs same-day eye referral?
cards.a:
• **Reduced VA** (not clearing with blinking)
• **Photophobia** and real **pain** (not just grittiness)
• **Ciliary (circumcorneal) flush**
• **Abnormal pupil** — small (uveitis) or fixed mid-dilated (acute angle closure)
• **Corneal staining/opacity** or hypopyon
• **Raised IOP**; contact lens wearer; recent trauma or surgery
cards.m: Conjunctivitis leaves vision, pupil and cornea alone — if any is abnormal, refer.

cards.q: Describe epidemic keratoconjunctivitis and pharyngoconjunctival fever.
cards.a:
• Both are **adenovirus** syndromes
• **Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC)**: severe follicular conjunctivitis, ± pseudomembranes; **subepithelial infiltrates** appear 1-2 weeks later -> **glare/blurred vision** for weeks-months
• **Pharyngoconjunctival fever**: children, **fever + sore throat + follicular conjunctivitis**, spread in families/swimming pools
• Both are contagious for about **2 weeks**
cards.m: EKC leaves 'coins' under the epithelium that cause glare.

cards.q: What is acute haemorrhagic conjunctivitis and why does it matter in Malaysia?
cards.a:
• Picornavirus: **enterovirus 70** or **coxsackie A24**
• Very rapid onset, watery discharge, follicles, **petechial/subconjunctival haemorrhages**
• Causes **explosive outbreaks** in schools, hostels and communities in tropical countries
• Self-limiting in ~1 week; management is hygiene and isolation
cards.m: Coxsackie = 'blood-shot epidemic'.

cards.q: A sexually active adult has hyperacute conjunctivitis with copious pus and lid swelling. What is it and how is it managed?
cards.a:
• **Gonococcal** conjunctivitis (N. gonorrhoeae) until proven otherwise
• Danger: **corneal ulceration and perforation** within days
• Same-day referral; **Gram stain + culture** of discharge
• **Systemic ceftriaxone** (e.g. 1 g IM/IV) + frequent saline irrigation ± topical antibiotic
• Screen/treat for chlamydia; refer to STD clinic with partner tracing
cards.m: Hyperacute pus = 'Neisseria needs a needle' (systemic).

cards.q: How is uncomplicated bacterial conjunctivitis treated?
cards.a:
• Usually **self-limiting** in 5-7 days
• A broad-spectrum topical antibiotic speeds resolution: **chloramphenicol** 0.5% drops / 1% ointment, **fusidic acid**, or a **fluoroquinolone** (e.g. ciprofloxacin)
• Clean discharge with cooled boiled water; hand hygiene
• **Note:** the notes list 'ceftazidine'; ceftazidime is **not** a routine topical for simple conjunctivitis (reserved as fortified drops for keratitis/endophthalmitis)
cards.m: First-line trio: Chloramphenicol, Fusidic acid, Fluoroquinolone.

cards.q: When should you take a conjunctival swab for culture in conjunctivitis?
cards.a:
• Bacterial conjunctivitis that **fails to resolve** with treatment
• **Hyperacute** purulent discharge (suspect gonococcus)
• **Neonates** (ophthalmia neonatorum — mandatory)
• Chronic follicular conjunctivitis (chlamydia — Giemsa/PCR)
• Contact lens wearers and immunocompromised patients
cards.m: Swab the stubborn, the severe and the small.

cards.q: How do you manage viral conjunctivitis and stop it spreading?
cards.a:
• **Self-limiting**; antibiotics unnecessary unless secondary bacterial infection
• Symptomatic: cold compress, lubricants
• **Highly contagious** for ~2 weeks: frequent **hand washing**, **separate towels/pillowcases**, no eye make-up sharing
• Consider time off school/work while eyes are discharging
• Clinic: disinfect **tonometer** tips and slit lamp, wash hands between patients
cards.m: Treat the community, not the virus.

cards.q: Why must you avoid prescribing steroid eye drops for an undiagnosed red eye, and what is the contact-lens caveat?
cards.a:
• Steroids worsen **HSV dendritic ulcers** (geographic ulcer), fungal and bacterial keratitis
• They also cause **raised IOP** and cataract with prolonged use
• A **contact lens wearer** with 'conjunctivitis' may have **microbial keratitis** (Pseudomonas, Acanthamoeba) -> stop lens wear, stain the cornea, same-day referral if any staining/infiltrate
• No steroid without slit-lamp examination by an eye doctor
cards.m: Steroid + herpes = disaster.

cards.q: Define ophthalmia neonatorum.
cards.a:
• **Any conjunctivitis in the first 28 days of life**
• Acquired mostly during passage through an **infected birth canal**
• A **notifiable disease**
• Can blind a baby within days (gonococcal corneal perforation) — treat as urgent
cards.m: 28 days = the neonatal month.

cards.q: What three things are MANDATORY in every baby with ophthalmia neonatorum?
cards.a:
• **Swab for culture** (Gram stain, culture, chlamydia PCR/immunofluorescence, viral PCR)
• **Examine the cornea** to exclude ulceration/perforation
• **Notify** (notifiable disease)
• Plus: treat the **mother and her partner** (sexually transmitted organisms)
cards.m: Swab, See the cornea, Send the notification.

cards.q: List the causes of ophthalmia neonatorum.
cards.a:
• **Chemical** (historically silver nitrate prophylaxis)
• **Gram-positive bacteria** (Staph, Strep) — common, mild
• **Neisseria gonorrhoeae** — most dangerous (corneal perforation)
• **Chlamydia trachomatis** — chronic conjunctivitis, corneal scarring
• **Herpes simplex** (HSV-2 > HSV-1) — corneal scarring, systemic disease

cards.q: How does the day of onset help you guess the cause of a sticky eye in a newborn?
cards.a:
• **Day 1** (first 24 h): **chemical** conjunctivitis
• **Day 1-5**: **gonococcal** — hyperacute, copious pus
• **Day 5-14**: **chlamydial** — commonest infective cause in many settings
• **1-2 weeks**: **HSV** — vesicles on lids, dendritic keratitis
• Bacterial (Staph/Strep) can appear any time in the first weeks
cards.m: Typical peaks: Chemical day 1, Gonococcus day 3, Chlamydia day 7, Herpes day 10-14.

cards.q: Describe gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum and its main danger.
cards.a:
• Onset **day 1-5**
• **Hyperacute**: profuse, thick purulent discharge, marked **lid swelling** and chemosis
• Gram stain: **Gram-negative intracellular diplococci**
• Neisseria can penetrate intact epithelium -> **corneal ulceration and perforation** within 24-48 h
• May be part of **disseminated** infection (sepsis, arthritis, meningitis)
cards.m: Gonococcus Goes through the cornea.

cards.q: How is gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum treated?
cards.a:
• Admit; **systemic ceftriaxone** single dose **25-50 mg/kg IV/IM (max 125 mg)** (cefotaxime if hyperbilirubinaemia)
• **Frequent saline irrigation** of the discharge (hourly) ± topical antibiotic
• Evaluate for **disseminated** infection; treat for chlamydia co-infection
• Treat **mother and partner**; refer to STD clinic
• **Note:** the notes say topical + systemic penicillin — outdated because of **penicillinase-producing** strains; ceftriaxone is correct
cards.m: Gonococcus gets Ceftriaxone — not penicillin.

cards.q: How does chlamydial ophthalmia neonatorum present?
cards.a:
• Onset **day 5-14**
• Mucopurulent discharge, lid swelling; less violent than gonococcus
• Neonates **cannot form follicles** (lymphoid tissue immature) — papillary/pseudomembranous picture
• Untreated: **chronic conjunctivitis**, conjunctival and **corneal scarring** (micropannus)
• Can be accompanied by **chlamydial pneumonitis** (staccato cough, weeks 3-12)
cards.m: Babies cannot make follicles — immature lymphoid tissue.

cards.q: What is the correct treatment of neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis, and why is topical therapy alone not enough?
cards.a:
• **Oral erythromycin 50 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses for 14 days**
• Systemic therapy eradicates **nasopharyngeal carriage** and treats/prevents **chlamydial pneumonitis**
• Topical tetracycline/erythromycin ointment can be added but is **inadequate alone**
• Treat **both parents** (STD clinic)
• **Note:** the notes list topical tetracycline + systemic erythromycin — the oral course is the essential part
cards.m: Chlamydia lives in the nose and lungs too — treat by mouth.

cards.q: How do you recognise and treat neonatal herpes simplex conjunctivitis?
cards.a:
• Onset ~**1-2 weeks**; usually **HSV-2** from maternal genital herpes
• **Lid/skin vesicles**, watery discharge, **dendritic** or geographic corneal ulcer (fluorescein)
• Risk: **corneal scarring** and **disseminated/CNS** herpes
• Treat: topical antiviral (aciclovir ointment / ganciclovir gel) **plus IV aciclovir** (e.g. 60 mg/kg/day for 14-21 days) with paediatrics
• **Note:** the notes give topical antiviral only; neonates also need **systemic** aciclovir
cards.m: Vesicles on a baby's lid = IV aciclovir.

cards.q: How is ophthalmia neonatorum prevented?
cards.a:
• **Antenatal screening and treatment** of maternal gonorrhoea/chlamydia (best prevention)
• **Ocular prophylaxis at birth** where policy dictates: e.g. **erythromycin 0.5% ointment** or **povidone-iodine 2.5%** drops
• **Silver nitrate 1%** is historical — it causes **chemical conjunctivitis** on day 1
• Caesarean section if active genital herpes at delivery

cards.q: What is the main differential of a sticky eye in a baby, and how do you tell it from ophthalmia neonatorum?
cards.a:
• **Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction** (imperforate membrane at the valve of Hasner)
• **Watering + sticky lashes** from a few weeks of age, but a **white, quiet eye**
• **Reflux** of mucus/pus from the punctum on pressing over the lacrimal sac
• Mx: **lacrimal sac massage**, lid hygiene; most resolve by 12 months; **probing** if persistent
• Red, swollen conjunctiva with pus = conjunctivitis -> swab
cards.m: White eye + wet eye = blocked duct; red eye + pus = infection.

cards.q: Chlamydia trachomatis causes two different eye diseases. Which serotypes cause which?
cards.a:
• **Serotypes A, B, Ba, C** -> **trachoma** (endemic, spread by flies, fingers, fomites)
• **Serotypes D-K** -> **inclusion (adult and neonatal) conjunctivitis** — sexually transmitted
• (L1-L3 cause lymphogranuloma venereum)
cards.m: A-B-C = the ABC of community blindness (trachoma); D-K = genital serotypes.

cards.q: What are the features of adult inclusion keratoconjunctivitis?
cards.a:
• Young sexually active adult; **sexually transmitted** (D-K)
• **Chronic, unilateral or bilateral mucopurulent follicular conjunctivitis** — not settling with ordinary drops
• **Tender pre-auricular node**; **micropannus** (superficial peripheral corneal vascularisation, upper cornea)
• Associated **urethritis or cervicitis** (often silent)
• Chronic course — can persist up to **18 months** untreated
cards.m: 'Conjunctivitis for months in a young adult' = ask about sex.

cards.q: How is adult inclusion conjunctivitis diagnosed and treated?
cards.a:
• Conjunctival swab/scrape: **NAAT/PCR**, **immunofluorescence**, or **Giemsa** stain (intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies)
• **Azithromycin 1 g orally single dose**, or **doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days** (erythromycin in pregnancy)
• Refer to **STD clinic**: screen for gonorrhoea, syphilis, HIV; **partner tracing and treatment**
• **Note:** notes say topical and systemic tetracycline — systemic azithromycin/doxycycline is the modern standard; topical alone fails

cards.q: Why does trachoma cause blindness? Explain the sequence.
cards.a:
• Commonest **infective** cause of blindness worldwide; poverty, overcrowding, poor hygiene, hot dry climate, **flies** as vector
• Repeated **re-infection** -> chronic follicular inflammation (TF/TI)
• -> **Subconjunctival fibrosis** of the upper tarsus (TS, Arlt line)
• -> Lid **entropion and trichiasis** (TT) — lashes abrade the cornea
• -> Recurrent keratitis -> **corneal opacity** (CO) and blindness
cards.m: WHO grades: TF -> TI -> TS -> TT -> CO.

cards.q: What is the WHO SAFE strategy for trachoma?
cards.a:
• **S**urgery for trichiasis (lid rotation)
• **A**ntibiotics: **single-dose oral azithromycin 20 mg/kg (1 g adult)**, mass treatment of the community; topical tetracycline if azithromycin unsuitable
• **F**acial cleanliness (face washing in children)
• **E**nvironmental improvement: water, sanitation, fly control
• **Note:** the notes give oral/topical tetracycline + surgery; SAFE with azithromycin is the current standard
cards.m: SAFE = Surgery, Antibiotics, Face, Environment.

cards.q: What is the immunological mechanism of allergic conjunctivitis?
cards.a:
• **Type I (IgE-mediated) hypersensitivity**
• Allergen binds **IgE on conjunctival mast cells** -> degranulation
• Release of **histamine** (itch, redness, oedema), prostaglandins, leukotrienes
• Chronic forms (vernal, atopic) add **Th2/eosinophil** inflammation -> papillae, corneal damage
cards.m: Mast cell pops -> histamine itch.

cards.q: What is the cardinal symptom of allergic conjunctivitis, and how does it separate allergic from viral and bacterial conjunctivitis?
cards.a:
• **ITCH** — the cardinal symptom; rubbing makes it worse
• Allergic: itch, **watery/stringy** discharge, **papillae**, chemosis, bilateral, atopic history
• Viral: gritty, watery, **follicles**, tender pre-auricular node, contact history
• Bacterial: gritty, **mucopurulent**, lids stuck, no itch
cards.m: If it doesn't itch, it isn't allergy.

cards.q: Describe acute seasonal (hay fever) allergic conjunctivitis.
cards.a:
• **Acute IgE reaction to airborne allergens** — pollen, dust mite, animal dander
• Bilateral **itch**, **lacrimation**, **chemosis**, lid swelling; often with **allergic rhinitis**
• **Chemosis = conjunctival OEDEMA** (jelly-like swelling), which can look dramatic but is benign
• **Note:** the notes define chemosis as 'conjunctival injection and swelling'; chemosis is the **oedema**, injection is the redness
cards.m: Chemosis = conjunctival 'jelly'.

cards.q: Who typically gets vernal keratoconjunctivitis (spring catarrh)?
cards.a:
• **Boys** with **atopy** (asthma, eczema, hay fever) — typically age 5-15
• Usually remits around puberty
• In temperate climates it is seasonal (spring); in **hot climates like Malaysia** it is often **perennial** (all year long)
• Bilateral, chronic and recurrent; IgE- and eosinophil-driven
cards.m: Vernal = Very itchy Young boy.

cards.q: What are the classic tarsal signs of vernal keratoconjunctivitis?
cards.a:
• Evert the **upper lid**: **giant 'cobblestone' papillae** (>1 mm, coalescing, flat-topped)
• **Thick, ropy, stringy white mucus** discharge
• Intense **itch** and **photophobia**
• Lower tarsus is usually spared
cards.m: Always evert the upper lid in an itchy child.

cards.q: What are the limbal and corneal signs of vernal keratoconjunctivitis?
cards.a:
• **Limbal VKC**: gelatinous limbal follicles/papillae with white dots = **Horner-Trantas dots** (aggregates of **eosinophils** and epithelial debris)
• Cornea: **punctate epithelial keratopathy** (upper cornea) -> macroerosion -> **shield ulcer**
• Long term: limbal stem cell deficiency, pseudogerontoxon
• **Note:** the notes call these 'limbal follicles and white spots' — the white spots are **Horner-Trantas dots**
cards.m: Trantas dots = Tiny eosinophil Towers at the limbus.

cards.q: What is a shield ulcer and how urgent is it?
cards.a:
• Sight-threatening complication of **VKC**
• **Oval, shallow, non-infective epithelial defect** in the **upper cornea** with a plaque of mucus/fibrin at the base
• Caused by toxic eosinophil products + mechanical rubbing by giant papillae
• Child has **severe pain, photophobia, reduced VA**
• **Urgent ophthalmology referral**: topical steroid + antibiotic cover, cycloplegic, ± surgical debridement of plaque; amblyopia risk in young children
cards.m: Shield on the top — giant papillae scrape it like sandpaper.

cards.q: What is the first-line drug treatment for allergic conjunctivitis, and what is the timing pitfall?
cards.a:
• Topical **antihistamine** (e.g. antazoline, levocabastine) for rapid itch relief
• **Mast-cell stabilisers**: **sodium cromoglycate**, **nedocromil**, **lodoxamide** — prevent degranulation
• Mast-cell stabilisers take **~2 weeks** to work -> start **before the season** and use regularly
• **Dual-action** drops (**olopatadine**, **ketotifen**) give both effects — convenient first-line
• Oral antihistamine helps if rhinitis co-exists (may dry the eye)
cards.m: Stabilisers are a shield, not a sword — raise them before the attack.

cards.q: What non-drug advice do you give a patient with allergic conjunctivitis?
cards.a:
• **Avoid allergens** (dust mite control, pets out of bedroom, close windows in high-pollen periods)
• **Cold compress** and refrigerated **preservative-free artificial tears** (dilute and wash out allergen)
• **Do NOT rub** the eyes — rubbing worsens mast-cell release and in VKC is linked to **keratoconus**
• Treat associated rhinitis/eczema; avoid contact lens wear during flares
cards.m: Cool it, wash it, don't rub it.

cards.q: When are topical steroids used in allergic conjunctivitis, and what are the risks?
cards.a:
• Only for **severe** disease (VKC flares, shield ulcer, AKC) — **short courses**, then taper
• Prefer low-penetration steroids (e.g. **fluorometholone**, loteprednol)
• Risks: **steroid-induced glaucoma** (IOP rise) and **cataract** (posterior subcapsular) with long use; also herpes/fungal keratitis
• Must be prescribed and **IOP monitored** by an ophthalmologist — VKC children often abuse over-the-counter steroid drops
cards.m: Steroid drops: Short, Supervised, check the pressure.

cards.q: Which steroid-sparing agents are used in chronic vernal or atopic keratoconjunctivitis?
cards.a:
• Topical **ciclosporin** (e.g. 0.1% cationic emulsion) — calcineurin inhibitor, reduces T-cell activation
• Topical **tacrolimus** ointment 0.03-0.1% — for refractory VKC/AKC
• Allow steroid tapering, reducing glaucoma/cataract risk
• Severe disease: supratarsal steroid injection or papillae excision (specialist)

cards.q: Name two other allergic conjunctivitis variants and their typical patients.
cards.a:
• **Atopic keratoconjunctivitis (AKC)**: **adults with atopic eczema**; chronic, perennial; lower tarsal papillae, lid eczema, scarring; risks — keratoconus, **HSV keratitis**, cataract (anterior subcapsular)
• **Giant papillary conjunctivitis (GPC)**: **contact lens** wearers (or ocular prosthesis, exposed sutures); itch, mucus, lens intolerance, giant upper tarsal papillae
• GPC Mx: stop/change lenses (daily disposables), better lens hygiene, mast-cell stabiliser
cards.m: VKC = boys; AKC = Adults with eczema; GPC = Got a contact lens.

cards.q: Define endophthalmitis and explain why it is an ocular emergency.
cards.a:
• **Infection inside the eye** involving the **aqueous and/or vitreous** (bacterial or fungal)
• The vitreous is an avascular gel — an ideal culture medium with poor immune access
• Bacterial toxins and inflammation destroy the **retina within hours**
• Requires **urgent admission**, sampling and intravitreal antibiotics
cards.m: The vitreous is a 'Petri dish' behind the lens.

cards.q: How is endophthalmitis classified?
cards.a:
• **Exogenous** — organism enters from outside:
  – **Post-operative**: **acute** or **delayed-onset (chronic)**
  – **Post-traumatic** (penetrating injury, IOFB)
  – Also bleb-related (after trabeculectomy) and after intravitreal injection
• **Endogenous** — **haematogenous** spread from a distant source (bloodstream infection)
cards.m: Outside-in (exogenous) vs inside-out (endogenous).

cards.q: What are the symptoms and signs of acute endophthalmitis?
cards.a:
• Symptoms: **pain** and **reduced/blurred vision** (the key pair), red eye, lid swelling
• Signs: injected conjunctiva, chemosis, **corneal oedema**
• **Anterior chamber cells/fibrin and hypopyon** (75-85%)
• **Vitritis** -> **loss of red reflex**, no fundal view
• **RAPD** in severe cases; retinal periphlebitis if the view allows
cards.m: Pain + Poor vision + Pus in the AC.

cards.q: Day 3 after cataract surgery: how do you tell endophthalmitis from normal post-operative inflammation?
cards.a:
• Normal: mild discomfort, mild AC cells, VA **improving** day by day
• Endophthalmitis: **increasing pain**, **VA falling** (often to HM/CF), marked lid swelling
• **Hypopyon**, fibrin, **vitritis**, reduced/absent red reflex
• Any post-op eye that is **more painful and seeing worse** than the day before = endophthalmitis until proven otherwise -> same-day ophthalmology
cards.m: Post-op eyes should get better every day — if worse, think infection.

cards.q: When does acute post-operative endophthalmitis usually present?
cards.a:
• **Most within the first week** after surgery
• **MOH CPG**: acute infectious endophthalmitis usually presents **within 2 weeks** of surgery
• **Chronic** (delayed-onset) presents **weeks to months/years** later
• **Note:** the notes say 'within 7 days' — teach 'most within the first week; MOH CPG definition is within 2 weeks' (EVS used 6 weeks)
cards.m: Acute = first fortnight; chronic = after it.

cards.q: What is the commonest organism in acute post-cataract endophthalmitis, and where does it come from?
cards.a:
• **Coagulase-negative staphylococci** — **Staphylococcus epidermidis** (~33-77%)
• Then **S. aureus**, **streptococci**, Gram-negatives (Pseudomonas), rarely fungi
• Source: the patient's own **lid and conjunctival flora** (proven by matching isolates)
• Hence prophylaxis targets the **ocular surface**
cards.m: The bug comes from the patient's own lashes.

cards.q: What are the risk factors for post-operative endophthalmitis?
cards.a:
• **Pre-op**: **blepharitis**, conjunctivitis, **dacryocystitis/NLDO**, contact lens, **DM**, immunosuppression
• **Intra-op**: **posterior capsule rupture / vitreous loss**, anterior vitrectomy, **prolonged surgery**, inadequate povidone-iodine/draping, clear corneal wound, ICCE > ECCE > phaco, secondary IOL
• **Post-op**: **wound leak**, exposed sutures, vitreous wick, filtering bleb, delayed topical antibiotics
cards.m: Dirty lids, broken capsule, leaky wound.

cards.q: What are the evidence-based prophylactic measures against post-operative endophthalmitis?
cards.a:
• **Povidone-iodine 5%** into the **conjunctival sac** before surgery (+ skin prep) — **Grade A**, the best-proven measure
• **Chlorhexidine 0.05%** if allergic to povidone-iodine
• **Intracameral cefuroxime 1 mg in 0.1 mL** at the end of surgery (ESCRS trial ~5-fold reduction)
• Treat blepharitis/NLDO before surgery; careful draping of lashes; watertight wound
• Never use povidone-iodine containing detergent (corneal damage)
cards.m: Iodine in, cefuroxime last.

cards.q: A diagnosis of acute post-operative endophthalmitis is made. What must be done, and how fast?
cards.a:
• **Vitreous tap ± anterior chamber tap within ONE hour** of clinical diagnosis
• Followed immediately by **intravitreal antibiotic injection** in the same sitting ('tap and inject')
• Send samples for **Gram stain, culture and sensitivity** (± PCR)
• Do **not** wait for culture results, and topical drops alone are never enough
• Early vitreoretinal referral
cards.m: Golden hour: Tap and Inject.

cards.q: Which intravitreal antibiotics are used, at what doses, and why that pair?
cards.a:
• **Vancomycin 2 mg in 0.1 mL** — covers **Gram-positives** (incl. MRSA, CoNS)
• PLUS **ceftazidime 2 mg in 0.1 mL** — covers **Gram-negatives** (incl. Pseudomonas)
• Alternative: vancomycin + **amikacin 0.4 mg in 0.1 mL** — ceftazidime preferred because of amikacin **retinal (macular) toxicity**
• Separate syringes; repeat after **48-72 h** if needed
cards.m: 'Vanc and Taz' — 2 and 2.

cards.q: Which investigations are useful in suspected endophthalmitis?
cards.a:
• **Vitreous tap** (best yield) ± **AC tap** — Gram stain, culture & sensitivity, PCR for low-count chronic cases
• **B-scan ultrasound** when the fundus is not visible: degree of vitritis, **retinal detachment**, retained lens fragments, choroidal detachment, IOFB
• **Conjunctival swabs** are listed in the notes but are **usually unhelpful** for the intraocular organism (MOH CPG)
• Endogenous cases: blood cultures, echo, source search

cards.q: According to the Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study, who needs immediate vitrectomy?
cards.a:
• **VA = light perception only** -> **immediate pars plana vitrectomy** (+ intravitreal antibiotics) — substantial benefit
• **VA hand movements or better** -> **tap and inject** is sufficient initially
• Vitrectomy removes the organisms, toxins and inflammatory debris and gives a larger diagnostic sample
• Early vitreoretinal opinion for all; vitrectomy later if not improving
cards.m: LP = PPV; HM or better = tap & inject.

cards.q: What additional antibiotic therapy is given beyond intravitreal injection?
cards.a:
• **Topical fortified antibiotics** (e.g. ceftazidime 5%, vancomycin 5%) **hourly round the clock**, then taper ± subconjunctival antibiotic
• **Systemic IV antibiotics** showed **no benefit in the EVS** — reserve for severe/virulent infection
• Oral option: **moxifloxacin 400 mg OD for 10 days** (good ocular penetration, anti-biofilm vs CoNS) or ciprofloxacin 750 mg BD for 14 days
• **Clarithromycin 500 mg BD for 2 weeks** for culture-negative cases with poor response
• **Note:** the notes spell it 'moxifloxacilin' — the drug is **moxifloxacin**

cards.q: How are steroids used in bacterial endophthalmitis?
cards.a:
• **Topical prednisolone acetate 1% or dexamethasone 1% every 1-2 hours**, started soon after intravitreal antibiotics — controls AC inflammation
• **Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day**, started **24 h after** intravitreal antibiotics, tapered by 10 mg/week (up to 3 weeks) with gastric protection
• Intravitreal dexamethasone reduces early inflammation but does not improve final VA
• **Never** give systemic steroids in **fungal** endophthalmitis
• **Note:** the notes muddle 'oral steroids (topical dexa)' — both routes are used, topical first, oral after antibiotics
cards.m: Antibiotic first, steroid second.

cards.q: Describe delayed-onset (chronic) post-operative endophthalmitis.
cards.a:
• Onset **4 weeks to years** after (often uneventful) cataract surgery
• Typical organism: **Propionibacterium (Cutibacterium) acnes** (anaerobe); also Corynebacterium, fungi
• **Painless/mild** progressive blurring, floaters
• Low-grade granulomatous uveitis (**mutton-fat KPs**), small hypopyon
• Inflammation **responds to steroids then recurs when steroids stop**
• **White plaque on the posterior capsule/IOL** — the organism sequestered in the capsular bag
cards.m: 'Steroid-responsive uveitis that keeps coming back after cataract surgery' = P. acnes.

cards.q: How is P. acnes (chronic) endophthalmitis managed?
cards.a:
• Sample aqueous/vitreous; request **anaerobic culture** (incubate up to 2 weeks) ± PCR
• **Intravitreal antibiotic** (vancomycin) — MOH CPG: given to all chronic cases
• Recurrence is common because organisms hide in the capsular bag -> **pars plana vitrectomy with capsulectomy and removal of the IOL/capsular bag**
• **Note:** the notes start with empirical oral moxifloxacin — oral therapy alone is rarely curative; intravitreal antibiotic ± bag/IOL removal is definitive

cards.q: What are the features of post-traumatic endophthalmitis, and which organism is classic?
cards.a:
• Follows **penetrating injury** — dirty/soil-contaminated wound, lens capsule rupture, **retained IOFB**, delayed repair
• Classic organism: **Bacillus cereus** — fulminant, **corneal ring abscess**, rapid loss of vision, often within 24 h
• Others: S. epidermidis, Streptococcus, Gram-negatives, fungi, mixed
• Always **exclude a retained IOFB** (CT orbit; no MRI if metallic)
• Prophylaxis after open globe: e.g. oral **ciprofloxacin 750 mg BD** or **moxifloxacin 400 mg OD**
cards.m: Soil + metal + Bacillus = blind by tomorrow.

cards.q: Who gets endogenous endophthalmitis and how do you work them up?
cards.a:
• Haematogenous spread — a minority (~2-15%) of all endophthalmitis
• Risk factors: **DM**, HIV, cancer/chemotherapy, **renal failure on dialysis**, **indwelling IV lines**, TPN, IV drug use, prolonged **broad-spectrum antibiotics**/steroids/immunosuppressants, liver abscess (Klebsiella — common in Asia)
• Work-up: **blood cultures**, line tips, urine, **echocardiogram** (endocarditis), CT abdomen for abscess
• Treat source + **systemic** antimicrobials + intravitreal therapy ± vitrectomy
• **Note:** the notes quote '28% of cases' — true figure is far lower (~2-15%)
cards.m: Inside-out: find the source in the body.

cards.q: How does Candida endophthalmitis look and how is it treated?
cards.a:
• Patient with **central line, TPN, IV drug use**, recent abdominal surgery or immunosuppression
• Slow onset; floaters, mild pain
• **Creamy-white chorioretinal lesions** with overlying vitritis; **fluffy 'cotton-ball' / 'string of pearls'** vitreous colonies
• Treat: **systemic antifungal** (**voriconazole** or fluconazole; amphotericin B) **plus intravitreal amphotericin B (5-10 µg) or voriconazole** ± vitrectomy; **no systemic steroid**
• Aspergillus: yellowish retinal/subretinal infiltrates heading for the macula — worse prognosis
• **Note:** notes list 'intravitreal and oral fluoroquinolone' — fluoroquinolones do not treat fungi
cards.m: String of pearls = fungal necklace.

cards.q: Which features predict a poor outcome in endophthalmitis?
cards.a:
• **Virulent organisms**: **Streptococci**, **Bacillus**, Gram-negatives (Pseudomonas), and **H. influenzae/Strep in bleb-related** infection — worse than CoNS
• **Presenting VA of light perception** only
• Rapid onset (within 1-2 days), corneal ring infiltrate, afferent pupil defect
• **Delay** in tap and inject
• Complications: retinal detachment, phthisis bulbi, loss of the eye
cards.m: Fast bug + LP vision + delay = poor outlook.

cards.q: What is a trabeculectomy bleb, and why does it create an infection risk?
cards.a:
• Trabeculectomy = **guarded fistula** from the anterior chamber to the **subconjunctival space** under a partial-thickness scleral flap
• Aqueous collects under the conjunctiva as a **filtering bleb** (usually under the upper lid) and is absorbed
• **Antifibrotics** (**mitomycin C**, 5-FU) are used to stop scarring
• Only a thin conjunctival layer now separates tear-film bacteria from the inside of the eye — a lifelong portal of entry
cards.m: A bleb is a 'window' in the eye wall covered only by conjunctiva.

cards.q: Define blebitis and describe the bleb-related infection spectrum.
cards.a:
• **Blebitis**: presumed infection in/around a filtering bleb **WITHOUT vitreous involvement**
• **Stage 1**: infection confined to the **bleb**
• **Stage 2**: bleb + **anterior chamber** reaction (cells ± hypopyon)
• **Stage 3**: **vitreous** involvement = **bleb-related endophthalmitis**
• Can occur **months to years** after surgery
cards.m: Bleb -> Bleb + AC -> Bleb + vitreous.

cards.q: What are the risk factors for blebitis?
cards.a:
• **Inferior bleb** — **7.8%** risk per patient-year vs **1.3%** for superior blebs (not protected by the upper lid, bathed in tear lake)
• **Bleb leak**
• **Intraoperative mitomycin C**
• Prolonged **antibiotic use** after the post-op period
• **High axial length** (myopia)
• **Conjunctivitis**, blepharitis, **upper respiratory infection**, winter season, contact lens wear
cards.m: Low, Leaky, MMC bleb = Likely infected.

cards.q: Why do antimetabolites such as mitomycin C increase the risk of bleb infection years later?
cards.a:
• MMC kills fibroblasts and vascular cells -> bleb becomes **thin-walled, avascular and cystic**
• Thin avascular conjunctiva is prone to **micro-leaks** and has poor local immune defence
• Bacteria can cross the wall or enter through a leak long after surgery
• This is why late infection can appear **years** after an apparently successful trabeculectomy
cards.m: The more 'successful' (thin, avascular) the bleb, the more fragile it is.

cards.q: What are the clinical features of blebitis, and what is the classic sign?
cards.a:
• **Sudden onset** pain, **photophobia**, **discharge**, redness
• **Mildly reduced vision**
• **Milky-white, opacified bleb** surrounded by intensely **hyperaemic conjunctiva** — the **'white on red'** appearance
• ± anterior chamber reaction / hypopyon (stage 2)
• Vitreous clear (if vitritis -> endophthalmitis)
cards.m: White bleb on a red sea.

cards.q: How do you detect a bleb leak?
cards.a:
• **Seidel test**: apply concentrated **fluorescein** (wet strip) over the bleb and examine with **cobalt blue** light
• Positive = a stream of **dilute (green-bright) fluorescein** where aqueous dilutes the dye
• Also suggestive: low IOP, shallow AC, flat bleb
• A leaking bleb is a major infection risk -> repair or bandage contact lens / autologous blood as advised by glaucoma surgeon
cards.m: Seidel = 'see the aqueous seep'.

cards.q: Which organisms cause bleb-related infection, and how do they differ from post-cataract infection?
cards.a:
• Early (acute) after glaucoma surgery: **coagulase-negative staphylococci**
• Late (chronic) bleb infection: **Streptococcus** species and Gram-negatives, especially **Haemophilus influenzae**
• These are **more virulent** than the CoNS typical of post-cataract endophthalmitis -> faster progression and worse visual outcome
• Source: conjunctival/upper respiratory flora
cards.m: Late bleb bugs = 'Strep and H. flu' — throat bugs.

cards.q: How is blebitis (no vitreous involvement) managed?
cards.a:
• Same-day ophthalmology; **culture** any purulent material/conjunctival swab
• **Intensive topical fortified antibiotics** (e.g. **vancomycin** or **cefazolin** + a Gram-negative agent such as a fluoroquinolone) — **hourly**, day and night initially
• ± oral fluoroquinolone (e.g. moxifloxacin) for good penetration
• **Add topical steroid only after ~24 h of clinical improvement** — to preserve bleb function and limit scarring/fibrosis
• Review closely (daily) for vitreous spread
cards.m: Kill first, calm second.

cards.q: What decides whether a bleb infection is blebitis or bleb-related endophthalmitis, and how does management change?
cards.a:
• The **vitreous**: any **vitritis** (cells, haze, loss of red reflex; B-scan if no view) = **bleb-related endophthalmitis**
• Blebitis -> intensive **topical** antibiotics
• Endophthalmitis -> treat as endophthalmitis: **vitreous tap + intravitreal vancomycin and ceftazidime** urgently ± vitrectomy
• Prognosis is worse than post-cataract endophthalmitis (virulent organisms)
cards.m: Clear vitreous = drops; cloudy vitreous = needle.

cards.q: What lifelong advice do you give a patient after trabeculectomy to protect against bleb infection?
cards.a:
• **RSVP** warning symptoms: **R**edness, **S**ensitivity to light, **V**ision decrease, **P**ain -> attend eye casualty **the same day**
• Do not self-treat a sticky red eye — any 'conjunctivitis' needs prompt review
• Avoid **contact lenses** over/near the bleb; do not rub the eye
• Treat blepharitis and URTI early; keep follow-up for bleb checks (leaks)
cards.m: RSVP — reply to these symptoms immediately.

cards.q: What is orbital cellulitis and why is it treated as an emergency?
cards.a:
• Bacterial infection of the orbital soft tissues **posterior to the orbital septum** (post-septal)
• Both an **ocular and a medical emergency**: it can blind (optic nerve compression/ischaemia) and kill (meningitis, brain abscess, cavernous sinus thrombosis)
• Commonest in **children**, the elderly and the immunocompromised
cards.m: Septum = the fire door. Fire in front of it (preseptal) burns the lid; fire behind it (orbital) reaches the optic nerve and the brain.

cards.q: What is the orbital septum and why does it matter clinically?
cards.a:
• A membranous sheet (palpebral fascia) that forms the **anterior boundary of the orbit**
• Runs from the **periosteum of the orbital rim** into the tarsal plates of the lids
• Acts as a **barrier**: infection in front of it = preseptal cellulitis; infection behind it = orbital cellulitis
• A penetrating lid injury or insect bite that breaches the septum lets infection into the orbit

cards.q: What is the commonest source of orbital cellulitis, and why does it spread so easily?
cards.a:
• **Ethmoid sinusitis** — about **90%**, typically in **children**
• Why: the medial orbital wall (**lamina papyracea**) is paper-thin and perforated by vessels and nerves
• Orbital veins are **valveless**, linking face, sinuses, orbit and **cavernous sinus** in both directions
• So: always look for (and treat with ENT) the sinus behind the swollen eye
cards.m: Child + red swollen eye after a cold = ethmoid until proven otherwise.

cards.q: Apart from ethmoid sinusitis, what are the other routes by which infection reaches the orbit?
cards.a:
• **Extension of preseptal cellulitis** through the septum
• **Local spread** — dacryocystitis, dental infection (via the maxillary sinus)
• **Haematogenous** spread
• **Post-traumatic** — usually within **72 hours** of an injury that penetrates the septum (including insect bites)
• **Post-surgical** — after retinal, lacrimal or orbital surgery
cards.m: Sinus, Skin, Sac, Sore tooth, Spread in blood, Surgery.

cards.q: Which organisms cause orbital cellulitis?
cards.a:
• **Streptococcus pneumoniae**, **Staphylococcus aureus** (including MRSA), **Streptococcus pyogenes**
• **Haemophilus influenzae** — now uncommon in children because of **Hib vaccination**
• Anaerobes with chronic sinus or dental sources (reason for adding metronidazole)
• Think **fungal (mucormycosis, Aspergillus)** in diabetic ketoacidosis or immunosuppression

cards.q: What are the clinical features of orbital cellulitis?
cards.a:
• **Fever**, unwell, marked lid oedema and redness
• **Proptosis** (often down-and-out displacement with ethmoid disease)
• **Pain on eye movement** and **restricted ocular motility** (diplopia)
• **Reduced VA**, **RAPD**, reduced colour vision — optic nerve involvement
• **Chemosis** and conjunctival injection
• **Leukocytosis**, raised ESR

cards.q: A child has a swollen red eyelid. Which findings tell you the infection is orbital (post-septal) rather than preseptal?
cards.a:
• **Proptosis**
• **Pain on eye movement** / **restricted motility** (ophthalmoplegia, diplopia)
• **Reduced VA** or colour vision
• **RAPD**
• Marked chemosis and systemic toxicity
• Preseptal cellulitis has a swollen lid but a **white, quiet, normally moving eye with normal vision and pupils**
cards.m: The 4 Ps of post-septal disease: Proptosis, Pain on movement, Poor vision, Paralysis of eye movement.

cards.q: What may fundoscopy show in orbital cellulitis, and what does it mean?
cards.a:
• **Choroidal folds** — the globe is indented by orbital mass effect/abscess
• **Optic disc swelling** — compression or inflammation of the optic nerve
• Venous congestion; rarely CRAO/CRVO
• Any of these = the optic nerve is threatened → urgent imaging and senior/ENT input

cards.q: What is the Chandler classification of orbital infection?
cards.a:
• **I** — preseptal cellulitis (inflammatory oedema)
• **II** — orbital cellulitis (diffuse post-septal infection)
• **III** — **subperiosteal abscess** (pus between bone and periorbita, usually medial wall)
• **IV** — **orbital abscess** (pus within orbital fat)
• **V** — **cavernous sinus thrombosis**
cards.m: Chandler climbs from the lid to the brain: Lid, Orbit, under Periosteum, Abscess, Brain sinus.

cards.q: How do you recognise cavernous sinus thrombosis complicating orbital cellulitis?
cards.a:
• **Bilateral** involvement — signs spread to the fellow eye
• **Rapidly progressive proptosis** with congestion of **facial, conjunctival and retinal veins**
• Palsies of **CN III, IV, VI** and numbness in **V1/V2** (all run through or beside the sinus)
• Severe headache, high fever, drowsiness, meningism
• Confirm with **MRI/MR or CT venography**; ICU-level care with IV antibiotics
cards.m: One eye = orbit. Two eyes + cranial nerves = cavernous sinus.

cards.q: List the complications of orbital cellulitis.
cards.a:
• **Ocular**: exposure keratopathy, raised IOP, **CRAO/CRVO**, endophthalmitis, **optic neuropathy** (blindness)
• **Orbital**: **subperiosteal abscess**, orbital abscess
• **Intracranial** (rare but extremely serious): **meningitis**, **brain abscess**, **cavernous sinus thrombosis**
• Systemic: septicaemia

cards.q: What investigations do you request for suspected orbital cellulitis?
cards.a:
• **FBC** (white cell count), **blood cultures**, CRP/ESR; check **tetanus** status after trauma
• Nasal/conjunctival swabs, culture of any pus
• **Lumbar puncture** only if meningeal signs (and after imaging excludes raised ICP)
• **Contrast CT orbit, sinuses and brain** — shows opacification posterior to the septum, sinus disease and **subperiosteal abscess**
• Note: the notes file LP under 'biochemistry'; it is CSF analysis for meningitis

cards.q: When is CT of the orbit, sinuses and brain indicated in a patient with periorbital cellulitis?
cards.a:
• **Proptosis**, ophthalmoplegia or pain on eye movement
• **Reduced VA**, reduced colour vision or **RAPD**
• Eye **cannot be assessed** (tense lid swelling, uncooperative young child)
• **No improvement after 24-48 h** of IV antibiotics, or deterioration
• Bilateral oedema or **CNS signs** (headache, drowsiness, vomiting)
• Suspected abscess or retained foreign body

cards.q: What is the initial management of orbital cellulitis?
cards.a:
• **Admit** (joint ophthalmology + **ENT**, paediatrics in children)
• **IV antibiotics** without delay — notes: **IV ceftazidime + oral metronidazole**; **vancomycin** as the alternative in penicillin allergy or MRSA risk
• Many local protocols use IV ceftriaxone or co-amoxiclav + metronidazole — follow the hospital guideline
• Continue IV until afebrile and clearly improving (notes: about 4 days), then step down to oral to complete the course
• Nasal decongestant for sinusitis; analgesia; lubricate exposed cornea
cards.m: Admit, Antibiotics IV, Assess the optic nerve, Ask ENT.

cards.q: How is optic nerve function monitored in orbital cellulitis, and how often?
cards.a:
• Every **4 hours** on the ward
• **Visual acuity**
• **Pupils** — new **RAPD**
• **Colour vision** — Ishihara / red desaturation (often the earliest sign)
• Also proptosis, motility and temperature
• Any deterioration → urgent CT and surgical drainage
cards.m: VA, Pupils, Colour — four-hourly, like neuro obs for the optic nerve.

cards.q: When is surgery needed in orbital cellulitis?
cards.a:
• **Subperiosteal or orbital abscess** with **visual compromise** (falling VA, RAPD, colour loss)
• Large abscess, or **no improvement / worsening after 24-48 h** of IV antibiotics
• Intracranial extension or frontal sinus involvement
• Procedure: **drainage of the abscess** and of the **infected sinuses** (often endoscopic sinus surgery by ENT)
• Small medial subperiosteal abscess in a young child with normal vision may first be managed medically with close monitoring

cards.q: What is the role of corticosteroids in orbital cellulitis?
cards.a:
