• **Oral corticosteroid** may be used as an **adjunct** to IV antibiotics
• Reduces inflammatory oedema and symptoms, with a low risk of worsening infection
• Start only once IV antibiotics are working (clinical improvement) and **fungal infection** has been excluded
• Never a substitute for antibiotics or drainage

cards.q: A man in diabetic ketoacidosis has orbital cellulitis with a black eschar on the palate. What is it and how is it managed?
cards.a:
• **Rhino-orbital(-cerebral) mucormycosis** — Mucor/Rhizopus invading vessels, causing **necrosis**
• Risk: **DKA**, neutropenia, high-dose steroids, transplant
• Signs: **black eschar** on palate/nasal turbinates/skin, ophthalmoplegia, rapid visual loss, CRAO
• Mx: correct the DKA, **IV liposomal amphotericin B**, urgent **surgical debridement** (ENT ± exenteration)
• High mortality — do not wait for culture
cards.m: Black eschar + sugar sky-high = Mucor: debride and amphotericin.

cards.q: What is preseptal cellulitis, and how does it differ anatomically from orbital cellulitis?
cards.a:
• Infection of the eyelid and periorbital soft tissues **anterior to the orbital septum**
• The septum (from the orbital rim periosteum to the tarsal plates) keeps the infection **out of the orbit**
• So the globe, optic nerve and extraocular muscles are **spared**
• Much commoner and milder than orbital cellulitis, especially in **children**
cards.m: Preseptal = PRE (in front of) the septum: the lid is sick, the eye is well.

cards.q: What are the causes and usual organisms of preseptal cellulitis?
cards.a:
• **Skin trauma** — laceration, **insect bite**, infected eczema/impetigo → **S. aureus**, **S. pyogenes**
• **Spread of local infection** — dacryocystitis, sinusitis, stye/chalazion
• **Spread from remote infection** — URTI or **otitis media** via the bloodstream (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae)
• Unvaccinated (Hib) toddlers with haematogenous spread risk bacteraemia and meningitis

cards.q: What are the clinical features of preseptal cellulitis?
cards.a:
• Tender, red, **swollen eyelid** (may close the eye), ± mild fever
• **Normal VA**
• **Normal eye movements**, no pain on eye movement
• **No proptosis**, **no RAPD**, normal colour vision
• **White eye** or only mild conjunctival injection; no or mild chemosis
• Note: the notes list it as a 'painless red eye' — the lid is tender; it is the globe that stays quiet
cards.m: Puffy lid, perfect eye.

cards.q: The lids are too swollen to open. How do you make sure you are not missing orbital cellulitis?
cards.a:
• Gently open the lids (use a **Desmarres lid retractor** if needed, analgesia, help to hold a child)
• Check **VA**, **pupils for RAPD**, **colour vision**, **eye movements** and **proptosis**
• If you **cannot examine** the eye adequately, **treat as orbital** — admit, IV antibiotics and CT
• Document findings to compare at review
cards.m: If you can't see it, you can't clear it.

cards.q: What are the main differential diagnoses of a unilateral swollen eyelid in a child or adult?
cards.a:
• **Allergic lid oedema** / angio-oedema — **itchy**, pale boggy swelling, **non-tender**, no fever, often bilateral
• **Insect bite reaction** — punctum, itch, rapid onset
• **Chalazion / infected hordeolum** — localised lump on the lid margin or tarsus
• **Acute dacryocystitis** — medial canthal swelling
• **Herpes zoster ophthalmicus** — dermatomal vesicles, Hutchinson sign
• **Orbital cellulitis** — proptosis, pain on movement, reduced vision

cards.q: How do you tell acute dacryocystitis from preseptal cellulitis?
cards.a:
• **Dacryocystitis**: tender red swelling centred over the **lacrimal sac**, **below the medial canthal tendon**
• History of **watering** (nasolacrimal duct obstruction); pressure may **reflux pus** from the punctum
• **Preseptal cellulitis**: diffuse lid swelling, not localised to the sac
• Dacryocystitis can itself spread to cause preseptal or orbital cellulitis
cards.m: Below the tendon = the sac.

cards.q: What is the first-line treatment of uncomplicated preseptal cellulitis?
cards.a:
• **Oral co-amoxiclav 500/125 mg 8-hourly** (adult) for about 7-10 days; weight-based dosing in children
• Penicillin allergy: e.g. **clindamycin** (or a macrolide per local protocol)
• Treat the source — warm compresses for a stye, drain any localised abscess
• **Severe infection → IV antibiotics**
• Topical antibiotics alone are not enough
cards.m: Pre = Per oral; Post (septal) = IV.

cards.q: Which patients with preseptal cellulitis should be admitted for IV antibiotics?
cards.a:
• **Children under 1 year**
• Eye **cannot be assessed** properly
• **Systemically unwell** / septic, or immunocompromised
• **Not improving after 24-48 h** of oral antibiotics, or unable to take oral medication
• Any doubt about orbital involvement
• Unvaccinated (Hib) toddler — risk of bacteraemia and meningitis

cards.q: What follow-up and safety-net advice do you give an outpatient with preseptal cellulitis?
cards.a:
• **Review in 24-48 hours**
• Return **immediately** if: **double vision**, **eye bulging**, **pain on moving the eye**, **blurred vision**, worsening fever or drowsiness, swelling spreading despite antibiotics
• Complete the antibiotic course
• Reason: preseptal cellulitis can **progress to orbital cellulitis**
cards.m: Return if it Bulges, Blurs, Doubles or Hurts to move.

cards.q: What is the main complication of preseptal cellulitis and what should prompt a CT scan?
cards.a:
• Main complication: **progression to orbital cellulitis** (treat early to minimise this risk)
• CT orbit, sinuses and brain if: **proptosis**, restricted/painful eye movement, **reduced VA or colour vision**, **RAPD**, cannot examine the eye, or **no response after 24-48 h**
• Otherwise preseptal cellulitis is a **clinical diagnosis** — CT is not routine

cards.q: What is blepharitis and how is it classified?
cards.a:
• Common, **chronic, symptomatic inflammation of the lid margin**
• **Anterior** — around the **lash bases**: **staphylococcal** or **seborrhoeic**
• **Posterior** — **meibomian gland dysfunction (MGD)** / meibomitis
• Anterior and posterior forms often **coexist** in the same lids
• A **clinical diagnosis** made at the slit lamp
cards.m: Anterior = lashes; Posterior = meibomian glands (behind the lashes).

cards.q: What symptoms does a patient with blepharitis typically describe?
cards.a:
• **Bilateral** burning, grittiness, itching and mild redness of the lid margins
• **Crusting** and stuck lashes, **worse in the morning**
• Fluctuating blurred vision that clears on blinking (unstable tear film)
• Chronic, with remissions and exacerbations
• A cause of **painless red eye** — VA, pupil and cornea usually normal

cards.q: What do you see on the slit lamp in staphylococcal anterior blepharitis?
cards.a:
• Hyperaemic, telangiectatic anterior lid margin
• **Hard, brittle yellow crusts** around the lash bases (**collarettes** encircling the lash)
• **Small ulcers** that **bleed when the crusts are removed** (ulcerative blepharitis)
• **Lash abnormalities** — misdirection (trichiasis), whitening (poliosis), loss (madarosis)
• Cause: **Staphylococcus aureus** colonisation and hypersensitivity
cards.m: Staph = hard crusts that bleed.

cards.q: How does seborrhoeic anterior blepharitis differ from staphylococcal blepharitis?
cards.a:
• **Seborrhoeic**: **greasy, soft white scales** ('dandruff') among the lashes; thickened lid margin; **no ulcers**, no bleeding
• Associated with **seborrhoea of the scalp (dandruff)**, eyebrows and nasolabial folds, seborrhoeic dermatitis and rosacea
• **Staphylococcal**: **hard crusts**, ulcers that bleed on removal, lash damage
cards.m: Seborrhoeic = soft and greasy; Staph = hard and bloody.

cards.q: What is meibomian gland dysfunction (posterior blepharitis) and how do you confirm it?
cards.a:
• Improper function of the **meibomian (oil) glands** of the tarsal plate — excessive or abnormal secretion
• **Terminal ducts are obstructed** by squamous debris; the secretion thickens from clear oil to viscous
• Slit lamp: **capping of meibomian orifices** with oil globules, pouting/plugged orifices, foamy tear film
• Simple test: **press on the lid margin** → **toothpaste-like** cloudy, opaque secretion
cards.m: Squeeze the tube: toothpaste out = MGD.

cards.q: Why do the lid secretions become irritating in posterior/seborrhoeic blepharitis?
cards.a:
• Commensal bacteria (**Cutibacterium (Propionibacterium) acnes**, staphylococci) release **lipases**
• These split meibomian lipids into **irritating free fatty acids**
• Result: unstable tear film (**evaporative dry eye**), burning and lid/conjunctival inflammation
• Note: the notes say 'Corynebacterium acne'; the correct organism is **Propionibacterium (Cutibacterium) acnes**

cards.q: Which systemic skin conditions are associated with blepharitis?
cards.a:
• **Acne rosacea** — strongly linked to **posterior blepharitis/MGD** (look for facial flushing, telangiectasia, rhinophyma)
• **Seborrhoeic dermatitis** — scalp dandruff, seborrhoeic anterior blepharitis
• **Atopic dermatitis** — staphylococcal colonisation
• Treating the skin disease (e.g. oral doxycycline for rosacea) helps the lids
cards.m: Red face + red lid margins = rosacea until proven otherwise.

cards.q: A patient has cylindrical sleeves around the lash bases and intense itching. What is the cause and treatment?
cards.a:
• **Demodex** mite infestation (Demodex folliculorum in follicles, D. brevis in glands)
• Sign: **cylindrical dandruff / sleeves** wrapped around the lash base — distinct from the flat staph collarettes
• Itching worse at night; often in the elderly
• Treat with **tea tree oil** lid scrubs (e.g. terpinen-4-ol wipes) for several weeks plus lid hygiene; ivermectin is an option
cards.m: Sleeves on lashes = mites: use tea tree.

cards.q: What is the cornerstone of blepharitis management and how is it done?
cards.a:
• **No permanent cure — the aim is control**; lifelong maintenance
• **Lid hygiene** once or twice daily:
• **Warm compress** 5-10 minutes to soften crusts and melt meibum
• **Lid massage** to express the glands
• **Lid cleaning** with diluted baby shampoo, cotton bud or **impregnated pads** to remove crusts mechanically
• Explain chronicity at the first visit to improve compliance
cards.m: Warm, Massage, Clean — every day, for life.

cards.q: When are topical antibiotics used in blepharitis and which ones?
cards.a:
• For **active staphylococcal folliculitis** or marked anterior blepharitis
• Ointment rubbed into the lid margin after cleaning: **fusidic acid**, **chloramphenicol**, **erythromycin**, bacitracin, or **azithromycin** drops
• Short courses (weeks), then return to lid hygiene alone

cards.q: How are oral tetracyclines used in posterior blepharitis, and who must not take them?
cards.a:
• **Doxycycline 50-100 mg daily** for **6-12 weeks** (or tetracycline/oxytetracycline)
• Work mainly as **anti-inflammatory** and **anti-lipase** agents (reduce free fatty acids), not just by killing bacteria
• **Contraindicated** in **pregnancy**, breastfeeding and **children under 8** (tooth staining, bone growth) → use **oral azithromycin or erythromycin**
• Side effects: photosensitivity, GI upset, oesophagitis (take upright with water)
cards.m: Doxy for the oil glands, not for the bump or the baby.

cards.q: What other treatments help blepharitis besides lid hygiene and antibiotics?
cards.a:
• **Tear substitutes** for associated evaporative dry eye
• **Omega-3 (fish/plant oil) supplements** to improve meibum quality
• **Short-course weak topical steroid** (e.g. fluorometholone) for severe inflammation or marginal keratitis — monitor **IOP**, avoid long-term use
• **Tea tree oil** for Demodex
• Treat associated rosacea or seborrhoeic dermatitis

cards.q: What are the complications of chronic blepharitis?
cards.a:
• **Chalazion** (blocked meibomian gland) and **hordeolum/stye**
• **Marginal keratitis** — staph hypersensitivity: peripheral corneal infiltrate with a **clear zone** from the limbus; treat with weak steroid + lid hygiene
• **Trichiasis**, **madarosis**, poliosis, lid margin scarring
• **Tear film instability / dry eye**, recurrent conjunctivitis, phlyctenulosis

cards.q: An elderly woman has unilateral 'blepharitis' with lash loss that has not responded to months of treatment. What must you exclude?
cards.a:
• **Sebaceous gland carcinoma** — the classic **masquerade** of chronic unilateral blepharitis or recurrent chalazion
• Clues: **unilateral**, **madarosis** (lash loss), thickened lid, **recurrent chalazion** at the same site, failure of treatment
• Next step: **full-thickness lid biopsy** (± conjunctival map biopsies); refer to oculoplastics
• Also consider basal or squamous cell carcinoma
cards.m: Unilateral + lash loss + not getting better = biopsy.

cards.q: What is scleritis?
cards.a:
• A serious, often chronic **inflammation of the sclera** with **oedema and cellular infiltration through its full thickness**
• Hallmark: **deep, severe, boring ocular pain**
• Frequently the eye sign of an **underlying systemic inflammatory disease** — about half have one
• Potentially sight-threatening (thinning, perforation, posterior segment involvement)
cards.m: Episcleritis irritates; scleritis hurts.

cards.q: Which systemic diseases are associated with scleritis?
cards.a:
• **Rheumatoid arthritis** — commonest
• **Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)** — the notes' 'Wegener's granulomatosis'
• **Polyarteritis nodosa** — the notes' 'polyarthritis nodosa' is a slip
• **SLE**, relapsing polychondritis, IBD, ankylosing spondylitis
• Infections: **herpes zoster**, syphilis, TB; also post-surgical scleritis
cards.m: RA, GPA, PAN, SLE — the vasculitis club.

cards.q: How is scleritis classified?
cards.a:
• **Anterior**
• – **Non-necrotising**: **diffuse** or **nodular** — commonest
• – **Necrotising with inflammation** — most severe
• – **Necrotising without inflammation** = **scleromalacia perforans**
• **Posterior** — behind the equator

cards.q: Describe the pain of scleritis.
cards.a:
• **Severe, deep, boring** pain — far worse than the appearance suggests
• **Wakes the patient at night** / early morning
• **Radiates** to the brow, temple, jaw or sinuses
• **Globe tender** to touch; pain worse on eye movement
• Photophobia and watering; VA may fall
cards.m: Pain that keeps you awake = scleritis, not episcleritis.

cards.q: How do you distinguish episcleritis from scleritis?
cards.a:
• **Episcleritis**: mild discomfort, bright red sectoral redness, superficial vessels **move** with a cotton bud, **blanch with phenylephrine 10%**, not tender, self-limiting → reassure, artificial tears ± topical NSAID
• **Scleritis**: severe boring pain, **tender globe**, **deep violaceous/bluish-red** hue, vessels **immobile** and **do not blanch** with phenylephrine
• Scleritis needs a systemic work-up; episcleritis usually does not
cards.m: Phenylephrine test: blanches = episcleritis; stays red = scleritis.

cards.q: What should you look for on examination of a patient with suspected scleritis?
cards.a:
• Look at the sclera in **daylight**: **violaceous hue**, oedema, nodules, **avascular white patches**, **blue thinning** (uvea showing)
• **Cornea**: **peripheral ulcerative keratitis**, stromal keratitis
• **AC**: anterior uveitis; **IOP** (raised)
• **Fundus**: choroidal folds, **exudative RD**, disc oedema (posterior scleritis)
• Systemic: joints, skin, sinuses/nose, lungs, kidneys (urinalysis)

cards.q: What are the features of anterior non-necrotising scleritis?
cards.a:
• **Most common** type of scleritis
• Redness, **moderate to severe pain**, watering
• **Diffuse** — widespread scleral inflammation involving **more than one quadrant**
• **Nodular** — a deep, **immobile, tender nodule** of inflamed sclera
• Generally the most benign form, but can progress to necrotising disease

cards.q: What is anterior necrotising scleritis with inflammation?
cards.a:
• The **most severe** form of scleritis
• Associated with **systemic vasculitis** (RA, GPA, PAN)
• Severe pain, redness, watering
• Signs: intense inflammation with **avascular (white) patches** of **scleral necrosis**; thinning so the **blue uvea shows through**
• Risk of **perforation** and loss of the eye
cards.m: White patch in a red angry eye = dead sclera.

cards.q: What is scleromalacia perforans?
cards.a:
• **Necrotising scleritis WITHOUT inflammation**
• Typically **elderly women** with long-standing **rheumatoid arthritis**; usually **bilateral**
• **Painless**, minimal symptoms, white eye
• Signs: **yellow-white necrotic patches** with scleral thinning through which the **blue/dark uvea** shows
• Note: the notes say 'yellow scleral nodules'; the lesions are necrotic **patches**, not nodules
• Despite the name, spontaneous perforation is rare
cards.m: Scleromalacia = silent melting of the sclera in RA.

cards.q: What are the features of posterior scleritis?
cards.a:
• Inflammation of the sclera **behind the equator**; often **misdiagnosed** because the anterior eye may look white
• **Pain** and **reduced vision**
• Signs/complications: **proptosis**, **ophthalmoplegia**, choroidal folds, **exudative retinal detachment**, **choroidal detachment**, **optic disc oedema**
• Mimics orbital cellulitis, orbital inflammation or a choroidal tumour

cards.q: How do you confirm posterior scleritis?
cards.a:
• **B-scan ultrasonography**: thickened posterior sclera with fluid in **sub-Tenon's space** — the **'T-sign'** (fluid outlines the optic nerve stem and scleral line)
• **CT/MRI orbit**: **thickened posterior sclera** (scleral enhancement)
• Also screen for systemic disease as for anterior scleritis
cards.m: T for Tenon: fluid around the nerve makes a T on B-scan.

cards.q: What systemic work-up do you request in a new case of scleritis?
cards.a:
• **FBC, ESR, CRP**, renal function and **urinalysis** (GPA nephritis)
• **RF / anti-CCP** (RA), **ANCA** (GPA, PAN-type vasculitis), **ANA / dsDNA** (SLE)
• **VDRL/TPHA** (syphilis), **TB screen** (Mantoux/IGRA)
• **Chest X-ray** (GPA, TB, sarcoid)
• Ask about herpes zoster; involve **rheumatology**

cards.q: What is the first-line treatment of anterior non-necrotising scleritis?
cards.a:
• **Oral NSAID** — e.g. **flurbiprofen**, **indomethacin**, naproxen or diclofenac (with gastric protection)
• **Topical steroids** (prednisolone, dexamethasone, fluorometholone) help symptoms but **alone are usually inadequate**
• **Oral steroid** if NSAIDs fail; immunosuppressants for steroid-dependent disease
• Note: the notes list topical steroid first; teach oral NSAID as first-line
cards.m: Scleritis is a systemic disease in the eye — treat it systemically.

cards.q: How is necrotising scleritis treated, and what must you never do?
cards.a:
• **High-dose systemic steroid** — oral prednisolone or **IV methylprednisolone** pulses
• **Systemic immunosuppression**: **cyclophosphamide** or rituximab (vasculitis), ciclosporin, methotrexate — with rheumatology
• Topical steroid only as an adjunct
• **NEVER subconjunctival / periocular steroid injection** — risk of **scleral melting and perforation**
• Note: the notes list subconjunctival steroid under necrotising scleritis — this is wrong
cards.m: Necrotising sclera + needle = perforation.

cards.q: Why is necrotising scleritis in a patient with rheumatoid arthritis a medical red flag?
cards.a:
• It often **heralds active systemic vasculitis** (heart, lungs, kidneys, nerves)
• Untreated, it carries a **raised mortality**
• Needs urgent **systemic immunosuppression** and joint care with **rheumatology**, not just eye drops
• Watch for peripheral ulcerative keratitis — the same vasculitic process in the cornea

cards.q: What are the complications of scleritis and when is surgery needed?
cards.a:
• **Scleral thinning** and **perforation**
• **Peripheral ulcerative keratitis**, anterior uveitis, **cataract** (also steroid-induced), **glaucoma**
• Posterior: exudative RD, macular oedema, optic neuropathy
• **Surgery — scleral grafting** (donor sclera/pericardium patch) for **extensive thinning** or **perforation**, once inflammation is controlled

cards.q: What is infective keratitis (corneal ulcer)?
cards.a:
• **Microbial inflammation of the cornea**
• Hallmark: a **break in the epithelium** (stains with fluorescein) with **stromal infiltrate and necrosis** of the surrounding tissue
• Organisms: **bacteria, viruses, protozoa (Acanthamoeba), fungi**
• Sight-threatening: scarring, perforation, endophthalmitis
cards.m: Ulcer = hole (epithelial defect) + white (infiltrate). Abrasion is a hole without the white.

cards.q: Name the four groups of organisms that cause infective keratitis, with examples.
cards.a:
• **Bacteria**: **Pseudomonas**, Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, Enterobacteriaceae (Klebsiella)
• **Viruses**: **HSV**, VZV, adenovirus
• **Protozoa**: **Acanthamoeba**
• **Fungi**: filamentous (**Fusarium, Aspergillus**) and yeasts (**Candida**)
• In tropical Malaysia, fungi are a **common** cause after vegetative/agricultural trauma
cards.m: B-V-P-F: Bugs, Viruses, Protozoa, Fungi.

cards.q: What predisposes a cornea to bacterial keratitis?
cards.a:
• Healthy epithelium resists most bacteria, so infection needs a **breach**
• **Contact lens wear** (commonest in young adults)
• **Trauma** (corneal abrasion, foreign body) and **ocular surgery**
• **Dry eye** (keratoconjunctivitis sicca), exposure, lid disease
• **Prolonged topical steroids** (local immunosuppression)
cards.m: CL-TraSS: Contact lens, Trauma, Surgery, Sicca, Steroids.

cards.q: What is the classic organism in contact-lens-related bacterial keratitis, and why?
cards.a:
• **Pseudomonas aeruginosa** (Gram-negative rod)
• Forms **biofilm** on lenses and lens cases; adheres to a hypoxic, micro-traumatised epithelium
• Aggressive: rapid **stromal melt**, ring ulcer, heavy mucopurulent discharge, can perforate within 24-48 h
• Also think **Acanthamoeba** in CL wearers
• Note: the notes imply Staphylococcus is the common CL organism; correct is **Pseudomonas**
cards.m: Pseudomonas loves water and plastic: lens + lens case = its home.

cards.q: What are the symptoms and slit-lamp signs of bacterial keratitis?
cards.a:
• Symptoms: **pain**, redness, **photophobia**, tearing, **purulent discharge**, **reduced vision**
• Signs: **ciliary (circumcorneal) injection**
• **White/yellow corneal infiltrate** with overlying **epithelial defect** (fluorescein-positive)
• Stromal oedema, AC reaction, **hypopyon** (usually sterile)
• Lid oedema in severe cases
cards.m: A white spot on a red, painful eye is an ulcer until proven otherwise.

cards.q: A contact lens wearer presents to Klinik Kesihatan with a red, painful, photophobic eye. What is the rule, and what do you do?
cards.a:
• Rule: **any CL wearer with a red painful eye = microbial keratitis until proven otherwise**
• Look for **reduced VA**, ciliary flush, a **white corneal spot**, fluorescein staining
• **Stop CL wear**; keep the **lens and lens case** for culture
• **Same-day referral** to the eye clinic
• Do NOT start topical steroid; do NOT patch
cards.m: Red + painful + lens = refer today.

cards.q: What is the first investigation in suspected bacterial keratitis, and when must it be done?
cards.a:
• **Corneal scrape** at the slit lamp under topical anaesthetic (blade/needle at the ulcer edge and base)
• Send for **Gram stain** and **culture** (blood, chocolate agar; add Sabouraud if fungus suspected)
• Do it **BEFORE starting antibiotics** (otherwise cultures turn negative)
• Also culture **CL, lens case and solution**
• Small peripheral infiltrates may be treated empirically without scraping
cards.m: Scrape first, shoot later.

cards.q: How is bacterial keratitis treated?
cards.a:
• **Intensive topical antibiotics**: **fortified** cephalosporin (cefuroxime or cefazolin 5%) + aminoglycoside (gentamicin ~1.4%)
• **Hourly day and night** for 48 h, then taper by response
• Alternative: **fluoroquinolone monotherapy** (moxifloxacin 0.5%) for small, peripheral ulcers
• **Cycloplegic** (cyclopentolate 1%) for ciliary spasm pain
• Adjust by culture; daily review until improving
• Usually admitted if central/large or poor compliance
cards.m: Fortified pair: a 'cef' for Gram-positives + a 'mycin' for Gram-negatives.

cards.q: In suspected keratitis, what two common GP/ED actions must you AVOID, and why?
cards.a:
• **Topical steroids** in an undiagnosed red eye: worsen **HSV** (geographic ulcer) and **fungal** keratitis, and mask bacterial infection
• **Eye pad / patching** of a **contact-lens-related** abrasion or ulcer: warm, closed, hypoxic eye favours **Pseudomonas**
• Also avoid repeated topical anaesthetic drops for pain (toxic, delay healing)
cards.m: No Steroid, No Pad, No Anaesthetic take-home bottle.

cards.q: What are the complications of severe keratitis and how is perforation managed?
cards.a:
• **Corneal scarring** -> reduced VA, irregular astigmatism
• **Thinning and perforation** -> **cyanoacrylate tissue glue** + bandage contact lens for small perforations
• **Corneal graft (keratoplasty)** for scarring, done **when the inflammation has settled**; therapeutic graft only for uncontrolled infection/large perforation
• Others: **endophthalmitis**, secondary glaucoma, cataract
cards.m: Glue now, graft later (when quiet).

cards.q: What are the features of primary herpes simplex (HSV-1) eye infection?
cards.a:
• Usually **children 6 months - 5 years**; often subclinical
• **Fever**, **vesicular lid lesions** (blepharitis)
• **Follicular conjunctivitis**
• **Pre-auricular lymphadenopathy**
• Keratitis is uncommon in primary disease; virus then lies latent in the **trigeminal ganglion**
cards.m: Primary = skin + conjunctiva; Recurrent = cornea.

cards.q: What is the classic slit-lamp sign of recurrent HSV epithelial keratitis?
cards.a:
• **Dendritic ulcer**: branching linear epithelial ulcer with **terminal bulbs**
• **Stains with fluorescein** (green under cobalt-blue light)
• **Reduced corneal sensation** (test with a cotton wisp before anaesthetic)
• If steroids are used it may enlarge into a **geographic (amoeboid) ulcer**
• May heal without scarring or progress to stromal disease
cards.m: Dendrite = tree branches with buds at the tips.

cards.q: What is HSV disciform (stromal) keratitis?
cards.a:
• **Immune-mediated** reaction to viral antigen in the stroma, not active epithelial infection
• **Disc- or ring-shaped central stromal oedema** with inflammatory infiltration
• Underlying **keratic precipitates**; often with **iritis**
• Epithelium usually intact
• Can lead to stromal scarring and vascularisation
cards.m: Disciform = a disc of swelling; immune, not invasion.

cards.q: How is HSV keratitis treated, and what is the steroid rule?
cards.a:
• Epithelial (dendritic): topical **acyclovir 3% ointment** 5x/day or **ganciclovir 0.15% gel**
• **NO topical steroids** for a dendritic ulcer (extensive geographic ulcer)
• Stromal (disciform): **topical steroid** to suppress the immune response **under antiviral cover**, tapered slowly
• Frequent recurrences: oral acyclovir prophylaxis (400 mg BD)
cards.m: Dendrite: Drug (antiviral) only. Disciform: Drops of steroid + Drug.

cards.q: What is Hutchinson sign in herpes zoster ophthalmicus, and how is HZO treated?
cards.a:
• **Vesicles on the tip/side of the nose** = **nasociliary nerve** (V1) involvement -> high risk of eye involvement (keratitis, uveitis)
• Treat with **oral acyclovir 800 mg 5x/day for 7 days** (or valaciclovir 1 g TDS), ideally **within 72 h** of rash onset
• Refer to the eye clinic for slit-lamp examination
• Complications: keratitis, uveitis with raised IOP, post-herpetic neuralgia
cards.m: Nose tip = eye at risk (same nasociliary branch).

cards.q: Who gets Acanthamoeba keratitis, and what are its clues?
cards.a:
• **Soft contact lens** wearers, especially lenses **rinsed in tap water** or worn **swimming**/showering
• **Pain out of proportion** to the signs
• Early: epithelial irregularity, **radial keratoneuritis** (infiltrates along corneal nerves)
• Late: **ring-shaped stromal infiltrate**
• Often misdiagnosed as HSV and not responding to antivirals
cards.m: Acanthamoeba = Agony + Aqua (tap water) + A ring.

cards.q: How is Acanthamoeba keratitis diagnosed and treated?
cards.a:
• Diagnosis: corneal scrape stained with **periodic acid-Schiff (PAS)**; culture on non-nutrient agar with E. coli overlay
• **In vivo confocal microscopy** shows **amoebic cysts**
• Treatment: **epithelial debridement** (aids drug penetration)
• Topical **chlorhexidine** and/or **PHMB** (polyhexamethylene biguanide) ± **propamidine**
• Continue for **months** because cysts are resistant (prevents relapse)
cards.m: Cysts hide for months, so treat for months.

cards.q: A Malaysian rubber tapper or grass-cutter is hit by a plant twig. Which keratitis do you fear, and what does it look like?
cards.a:
• **Fungal keratitis** (filamentous: **Fusarium, Aspergillus**)
• Hard to tell from bacterial, but: **feathery/fuzzy margins**, dry grey-white raised infiltrate
• **Satellite lesions** around the main infiltrate; hypopyon; slower course
• Candida (yeast) in compromised corneas (steroid use, chronic surface disease)
• Note: the notes call fungal keratitis 'unusual'; correct is that it is **common in tropical climates** after **vegetative trauma**
cards.m: Fungus = Feathery edges + Field (agricultural) injury.

cards.q: How is fungal keratitis confirmed and treated?
cards.a:
• Scrape for **Gram/KOH/calcofluor** and culture on **Sabouraud dextrose agar**
• Topical **natamycin 5%** hourly = first-line for **filamentous** fungi
• **Voriconazole** (topical ± oral) for Aspergillus/yeasts or deep disease
• Treat for weeks; **steroids worsen fungal keratitis** -> stop them
• Deep or non-responding -> therapeutic keratoplasty
cards.m: Fungus loves Steroid; Natamycin for Filaments.

cards.q: Exam revision: match the clinical clue to the likely organism in keratitis.
cards.a:
• **Contact lens + rapid stromal melt + heavy discharge** -> **Pseudomonas**
• **CL rinsed in tap water + severe pain + ring infiltrate** -> **Acanthamoeba**
• **Plant/twig injury + feathery margins + satellites** -> **Fungus**
• **Branching ulcer + reduced corneal sensation** -> **HSV**
• **Nose-tip vesicles** -> **Varicella-zoster (HZO)**
cards.m: Lens-Pseudo, Tap-Amoeba, Twig-Fungus, Tree-HSV, Tip-Zoster.

cards.q: What is uveitis, and what structures make up the uveal tract?
cards.a:
• **Inflammation of the uveal tract**: the vascular, pigmented middle coat of the eye
• **Iris** + **ciliary body** = anterior uvea
• **Choroid** = posterior uvea
• Inflammation often spills into neighbouring structures (cornea endothelium, vitreous, retina)
cards.m: Uvea = 'grape' (Latin): the dark vascular grape skin under the white sclera. I-C-C: Iris, Ciliary body, Choroid.

cards.q: How is uveitis classified anatomically (SUN classification)?
cards.a:
• **Anterior**: primary site **anterior chamber** (iritis, iridocyclitis) — commonest
• **Intermediate**: primary site **vitreous** (pars planitis); floaters
• **Posterior**: **retina/choroid** (retinitis, choroiditis, retinochoroiditis)
• **Panuveitis**: AC + vitreous + retina/choroid
• Also describe onset (sudden/insidious), duration (limited ≤3 months / persistent) and course (acute, recurrent, chronic)
cards.m: Front, Middle, Back, All: A-I-P-Pan.

cards.q: What are the main causes of uveitis?
cards.a:
• **Idiopathic** in a large proportion
• **Infective**: **HSV/VZV**, **syphilis**, **toxoplasmosis**, **CMV**, **tuberculosis** (endemic in Malaysia)
• **Ocular**: **trauma**, **sympathetic ophthalmia**, lens-induced, advanced glaucoma
• **Systemic**: **HLA-B27 disease**, **sarcoidosis**, **IBD**, **psoriasis**, **SLE**, **AIDS**, Behçet
• Note: the notes say 'Acquired Immuno-Deficiency Virus'; correct is **Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome** (caused by HIV)
cards.m: Uveitis causes = I-I-O-S: Idiopathic, Infective, Ocular, Systemic.

cards.q: What is the commonest systemic association of acute anterior uveitis, and which diseases carry it?
cards.a:
• **HLA-B27** (positive in roughly half of acute anterior uveitis)
• **Ankylosing spondylitis** — ask about **morning back stiffness**
• **Reactive arthritis** (urethritis, arthritis, conjunctivitis)
• **Inflammatory bowel disease**, **psoriatic arthritis**
• Typical picture: young adult, **unilateral, recurrent, alternating** eyes, non-granulomatous
cards.m: B27 = Back pain, Bowel, Bladder (reactive), Big toe/skin (psoriatic).

cards.q: What are the symptoms of acute anterior uveitis?
cards.a:
• **Ocular pain** (ciliary spasm), often aching
• **Photophobia** — marked; light in the OTHER eye also hurts (consensual)
• **Blurred vision**
• **Red eye**, watering (no purulent discharge)
• Ask for systemic symptoms: back pain, joint pain, diarrhoea, rash, cough
cards.m: Iritis triad: Pain, Photophobia, Poor vision.

cards.q: What signs of anterior uveitis do you look for on the slit lamp?
cards.a:
• **Reduced VA**
• **Ciliary (circumcorneal) injection** — redness concentrated at the limbus
• **AC cells and flare** (protein) — the key sign
• **Keratic precipitates (KPs)**: inflammatory cells on the corneal endothelium
• **Hypopyon**: layered white cells in the inferior AC
• **Posterior synechiae**: iris stuck to lens -> small, irregular pupil
• Note: the notes group KPs and hypopyon under 'reduced red reflex'; correct is that they are **anterior chamber signs** seen on slit lamp
cards.m: Cells, Flare, KPs, Synechiae: the 'CFKS' of the AC.

cards.q: How do you tell acute anterior uveitis from acute angle-closure glaucoma, keratitis and conjunctivitis?
cards.a:
• **AAU**: **small/irregular pupil**, deep AC with cells/flare, KPs, IOP usually normal or **low** (can be high in HSV/trabeculitis)
• **AACG**: **mid-dilated fixed vertically oval pupil**, **IOP >50**, hazy cornea, **shallow AC**, haloes, vomiting
• **Keratitis**: **white corneal infiltrate** that **stains with fluorescein**
• **Conjunctivitis**: **normal VA and pupil**, conjunctival (not ciliary) injection, discharge, little photophobia
cards.m: Small pupil = iritis; Mid-dilated = angle closure; Stain = keratitis; Sticky with normal VA = conjunctivitis.

cards.q: What is granulomatous uveitis, and when do you investigate uveitis?
cards.a:
• **Granulomatous**: large greasy **mutton-fat KPs**, **iris nodules** (Koeppe at pupil margin, Busacca on iris surface) -> **sarcoidosis, TB, syphilis**, VKH, sympathetic ophthalmia
• **Non-granulomatous**: fine small KPs -> HLA-B27, idiopathic
• A first, unilateral, non-granulomatous AAU needs little work-up
• Investigate if **recurrent, bilateral, granulomatous, posterior or systemic features**
• Tests: FBC, ESR/CRP, **VDRL/TPHA**, **CXR**, **Mantoux/IGRA**, serum **ACE**, **HLA-B27**, HIV, toxoplasma serology
cards.m: Mutton fat = Sarcoid, TB, Syphilis (the 'STS' trio).

cards.q: What are the principles of treating uveitis, and what is the first-line drug for acute anterior uveitis?
cards.a:
• Principles: **reduce inflammation and pain**, **treat any infection**, **treat the underlying systemic cause**
• **Steroids are the mainstay**
• AAU: topical **prednisolone acetate 1%** — hourly when severe, then **taper over weeks** (abrupt stop -> rebound)
• Posterior/bilateral severe: periocular, intravitreal or **systemic** steroid; steroid-sparing immunosuppressants/biologics for chronic disease
• **Exclude infection** (HSV, TB, syphilis, toxoplasma) before high-dose steroids
cards.m: Steroid + Stretch the pupil (cycloplegic) = the two S of iritis.

cards.q: Why is a cycloplegic such as cyclopentolate given in anterior uveitis?
cards.a:
• **Relieves pain** by paralysing the inflamed, spasming **ciliary muscle**
• **Dilates the pupil**, pulling the iris away from the lens -> **prevents (and breaks) posterior synechiae**
• Cyclopentolate 1% for most; **atropine 1%** for severe inflammation or fresh synechiae
• Stabilises the blood-aqueous barrier (less flare)
cards.m: Cycloplegic = Comfort + keeps the iris off the lens.

cards.q: What are the classic infective posterior uveitis pictures of toxoplasmosis and CMV?
cards.a:
• **Toxoplasmosis**: commonest infective posterior uveitis; **focal white retinochoroiditis next to an old pigmented scar** with dense vitritis = **'headlight in the fog'**
• Treat if sight-threatening (near macula/disc) or immunocompromised: pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + folinic acid, or co-trimoxazole; oral steroid only under antimicrobial cover
• **CMV retinitis**: AIDS with **CD4 <50**; haemorrhagic necrotising retinitis along vessels, little vitritis = **'pizza pie'**
• Treat with **ganciclovir/valganciclovir** + antiretroviral therapy
cards.m: Toxo = foggy headlight; CMV = pizza (cheese and ketchup) in a patient with very low CD4.

cards.q: What is sympathetic ophthalmia?
cards.a:
• **Bilateral granulomatous panuveitis** after a **penetrating injury** (or intraocular surgery) to ONE eye
• Mechanism: autoimmune T-cell response to **uveal/retinal antigens** exposed by the wound
• Injured eye = **exciting eye**; fellow eye = **sympathising eye**
• Onset 2 weeks to years (most within the first year)
• Signs: mutton-fat KPs, vitritis, **Dalen-Fuchs nodules**, exudative RD
• Treat with high-dose **systemic steroids** + immunosuppression
• Note: the notes say 'sympathetic ophthalmitis'; correct is **sympathetic ophthalmia**
cards.m: One eye injured, both eyes inflamed: the healthy eye 'sympathises'.

cards.q: Why do children with juvenile idiopathic arthritis need regular slit-lamp screening?
cards.a:
• JIA uveitis is **chronic, bilateral and asymptomatic** — a **white, painless eye**
• Highest risk: **oligoarticular** JIA, **ANA-positive**, **girls**, early onset (<6 years)
• Often found only after **band keratopathy, cataract, glaucoma** or amblyopia have developed
• Screen by slit lamp **every 3-4 months** in high-risk groups
cards.m: JIA eye is White and Quiet: Silent but Sight-threatening.

cards.q: What are the complications of uveitis?
cards.a:
• **Cystoid macular oedema** — commonest cause of visual loss
• **Cataract** (posterior subcapsular; from inflammation and steroids)
• **Glaucoma**: trabeculitis, synechial angle closure, **steroid response**
• **Posterior synechiae** -> 360° (**seclusio pupillae**) -> **iris bombé** -> secondary angle closure
• **Band keratopathy** (chronic, especially JIA)
• **Hypotony / phthisis** from ciliary body shutdown
cards.m: The 4 C + G of uveitis: CMO, Cataract, Calcium (band), Ciliary shutdown, Glaucoma.

cards.q: What are the common causes of penetrating eye injury, and what determines its severity?
cards.a:
• Causes: **assault**, **domestic** accidents, **occupational** accidents (construction, metal work, grass-cutting), **sports**
• Severity depends on the object's **size**, **speed at impact** and **composition** (metal, glass, organic)
• Small high-velocity fragments penetrate; large slow objects tend to cause blunt injury
• Prevention: **polycarbonate protective goggles** at work
cards.m: Size, Speed, Stuff (what it is made of).

cards.q: Which history should make you suspect an intraocular foreign body even when the eye looks almost normal?
cards.a:
• **High-velocity** fragment: **hammering metal on metal**, chiselling, grinding, drilling, grass-cutter/strimmer
• Patient often felt only a 'something hit my eye' sting
• Symptoms: **tearing**, **blurred vision**, **photophobia**; floaters from **vitreous haemorrhage**
• Also record: time, material, protective eyewear, tetanus status, last meal
• Any such history -> **image the orbit** even if the wound is invisible
cards.m: Hammer + chisel = CT the orbit.

cards.q: What examination signs suggest an open globe?
cards.a:
• **Peaked / teardrop pupil** pointing towards the wound
• **Shallow or flat AC** (corneal wound) or unusually deep AC (posterior scleral rupture)
• **Positive Seidel test**: aqueous leak dilutes fluorescein
• **Uveal tissue prolapse** (dark tissue at the wound)
• **360° bullous subconjunctival haemorrhage** with chemosis -> occult scleral rupture
• Hyphaema, vitreous haemorrhage, **soft eye**, marked VA drop
cards.m: The pupil 'points' to the hole.

cards.q: Where do superficial foreign bodies lodge, and what clue points to a subtarsal FB?
cards.a:
• Many are washed out by the **tear film**
• Others impact on the **cornea or conjunctiva**, or stick under the **upper lid (superior tarsal conjunctiva)**
• Some **penetrate the cornea** and lodge deeper
• Clue for subtarsal FB: **vertical linear corneal abrasions** on fluorescein (scratched with each blink)
• Always **evert the upper lid**
cards.m: Vertical scratches = look under the lid.

cards.q: How do you remove a superficial corneal foreign body?
cards.a:
• Instil **topical anaesthetic**; examine with the **slit lamp** to check depth and look for entry/exit wounds
• Try **irrigation with normal saline**, then a **moistened cotton bud**
• Embedded FB: tangential **needle tip** at the slit lamp (trained hands)
• Metallic FB leaves a **rust ring** -> remove with a **burr**
• Afterwards: **topical antibiotic**, analgesia (NSAID), review
• Refer if deep, central, Seidel-positive or not removable
cards.m: Wash, Wipe, then Needle; leave no rust behind.

cards.q: In the emergency department, what are the first-aid steps for a suspected open globe?
cards.a:
• Stop examining once open globe is obvious; apply a **rigid shield** (no pad, no pressure)
• **Do NOT remove a protruding FB**; stabilise it
• Keep **nil by mouth** (theatre); give **antiemetic** and **analgesia** (vomiting raises IOP)
• **Tetanus** prophylaxis; **systemic antibiotics**
• No topical drops or ointment
• **CT orbit** and **urgent** ophthalmology referral for primary repair (ideally <24 h)
cards.m: SHIELD: Shield, Hold NBM, Inject antiemetic/analgesia, Exclude metal (CT), Leave the FB in, Dial ophthalmology.

cards.q: What must you NOT do to an eye with a suspected open globe?
cards.a:
• **No pressure on the globe**: no forced lid opening, no eye pad, no squeezing
• **No tonometry** and **no gonioscopy** (contact lenses press on the eye -> extrusion of contents)
• No B-scan by the inexperienced; **no MRI** if metal is possible
• Fundoscopy only **gently** (or after repair)
• Note: the notes say 'fundoscopy and gonioscopy is a must' for IOFB; correct is that **gonioscopy is contraindicated until the globe is closed**
cards.m: Open globe: Look, don't touch.

cards.q: Which imaging is used for a suspected intraocular foreign body, and which is contraindicated?
cards.a:
• **CT orbit**, thin slice (≤1 mm) axial + coronal = investigation of choice; locates metal, glass, stone
• Plain orbital X-ray if CT unavailable (screens for metal only)
• **MRI is contraindicated** with a possible **metallic (ferromagnetic) FB**: the magnet moves it -> further damage
• Wood/organic FB may be missed on CT (looks like air) -> MRI only after metal is excluded
cards.m: Metal + Magnet = Mayhem: CT first.

cards.q: What is the commonest intraocular foreign body, and what mechanical damage can it cause?
cards.a:
• Commonest: **minute chips of iron and steel**
• Mechanical effects along its track: corneal/scleral wound, iris hole, **traumatic cataract** (lens breach)
• **Vitreous liquefaction** and **vitreous haemorrhage**
• **Retinal haemorrhage, retinal tears** and detachment
• Plus **infection** (endophthalmitis) and **toxic** effects of the metal
cards.m: An IOFB hurts 3 ways: Mechanical, Microbial, Metal toxicity.

cards.q: Compare siderosis and chalcosis.
cards.a:
• **Siderosis** = retained **iron**: rust-brown deposits; **iris heterochromia** (injured eye darker), **poorly reactive dilated pupil**, brown anterior subcapsular cataract, **pigmentary retinopathy**, glaucoma; **ERG progressively reduced** -> remove FB
• **Chalcosis** = retained **copper alloy** (brass/bronze): **Kayser-Fleischer-like ring**, **sunflower cataract**, golden retinal deposits
• **Pure copper** (>85%) causes acute, severe sterile **endophthalmitis-like inflammation** -> urgent removal
• Glass, plastic and stone are relatively inert
cards.m: Siderosis = Steel/iron, Slowly rusts; Chalcosis = Copper, Sunflower.

cards.q: Which prophylactic systemic antibiotic is given after a penetrating eye injury, and why that class?
cards.a:
• **Oral ciprofloxacin 750 mg BD** or **oral moxifloxacin 400 mg OD**
• Fluoroquinolones achieve good **vitreous penetration** after oral dosing
• Many units add IV vancomycin + ceftazidime for high-risk wounds
• Intravitreal antibiotics at surgery if soil contamination or retained IOFB
• Plus **tetanus** cover
cards.m: Quinolones get Quickly into the vitreous.

cards.q: What is the feared infection after penetrating trauma, and who is at highest risk?
cards.a:
• **Post-traumatic endophthalmitis**
• Risk factors: **dirty (soil/rural) wound**, **retained IOFB**, **lens capsule rupture**, delayed repair, older age
• **Bacillus cereus** (soil): fulminant within 24-48 h, **corneal ring abscess**, very poor prognosis
• Others: S. epidermidis, streptococci, Gram-negatives, fungi, mixed
• Signs: severe pain, lid swelling, hypopyon, vitritis, loss of red reflex
cards.m: Bacillus = Bad, Bush (soil), Burns fast.

cards.q: What is the definitive management of an open globe injury with an intraocular foreign body?
cards.a:
• **Urgent primary repair** of the globe under general anaesthesia, ideally **within 24 h**
• Corneal wound suturing (fine nylon); scleral exploration and repair
• **IOFB removal**: anterior segment FB via limbus/magnet; posterior segment FB via **pars plana vitrectomy**
• Lensectomy if traumatic cataract; intravitreal antibiotics if high risk
• Primary enucleation only if the globe cannot be reconstructed
cards.m: Close the hole, take out the metal, guard against bugs.

cards.q: How do you counsel a patient after a severe penetrating eye injury about the risk to the OTHER eye?
cards.a:
• Risk of **sympathetic ophthalmia**: bilateral granulomatous panuveitis (rare, can occur weeks to years later)
• Report **any blurring, photophobia, floaters or pain in the good eye** urgently
• A **blind, painful, non-salvageable** injured eye: enucleation (traditionally within ~2 weeks of injury) is considered to reduce risk
• One-eyed patients: **protective polycarbonate spectacles** for life
cards.m: Protect the precious one: the good eye is now the only eye.

cards.q: What are the classic causes of blunt eye trauma, and how does a blunt blow damage the eye?
cards.a:
• Classic: **squash balls**, **elastic luggage (bungee) straps**, **champagne corks**; locally also shuttlecocks, fists, sepak takraw balls
• Mechanism: sudden **antero-posterior compression** with **equatorial stretching** of the globe
• Force is transmitted from cornea to optic nerve -> damage at any level
• Effects may be **delayed or subtle** (e.g. glaucoma years later)
cards.m: Small, fast ball that fits the orbit = maximum globe damage.

cards.q: How do you assess a patient after blunt eye trauma?
cards.a:
• **Visual acuity** first (medicolegal and prognostic)
• Pupils: shape, reactions, **RAPD** (traumatic optic neuropathy)
• **Slit lamp**: cornea with **fluorescein**, **AC** (hyphaema, cells, depth), iris, lens
• **IOP** only once an open globe is excluded
• Dilated **fundus** examination
• Orbit: eye movements/diplopia, **infraorbital sensation**, enophthalmos
• Always **exclude globe rupture**
cards.m: Front to back: Vision, Pupil, Slit lamp, Pressure, Fundus, Orbit.

cards.q: List the complications of blunt eye trauma from front to back.
cards.a:
• Cornea: **abrasion**, **acute corneal oedema**
• AC: **hyphaema**, **raised IOP** (angle recession later)
• Iris: **traumatic mydriasis** (sphincter damage), iridodialysis
• Lens: **cataract**, **subluxation/dislocation**
• Posterior: **vitreous haemorrhage**, **retinal detachment**, commotio retinae, choroidal rupture, optic neuropathy
• Severe: **globe rupture**
• Orbit: blow-out fracture
cards.m: Work through the eye like a slit-lamp exam: Cornea, Chamber, Iris, Lens, Vitreous, Retina, Nerve, Orbit.

cards.q: What is a hyphaema, how is it graded, and what is the initial management?
cards.a:
• **Blood in the anterior chamber** from torn iris/ciliary body vessels
• Grade by height: microhyphaema (suspended cells), **<1/3**, **1/3-1/2**, **>1/2**, **total ('eight-ball')**
• Mx: rest, **head up 30-45°** (blood settles inferiorly, clears the visual axis), **rigid shield**
• Topical **steroid** (prednisolone acetate 1%) + **cycloplegic** (atropine 1%)
• **Check IOP daily**; treat raised IOP with topical timolol
• Admit if large, child, high IOP or sickle cell
cards.m: Hyphaema care: Head up, Hands off (shield), Hold the pressure down.

cards.q: In traumatic hyphaema, what must you avoid, when is re-bleeding most likely, and when is surgical washout needed?
cards.a:
• Avoid **aspirin and NSAIDs** (raise re-bleed risk); avoid miotics
• **Re-bleed** risk peaks around **day 2-5** (clot retraction) — often larger and worse
• **Sickle cell disease/trait** (screen at-risk patients): sickled cells block the meshwork; **avoid acetazolamide** and osmotic agents (acidosis/dehydration worsen sickling)
• Washout if **corneal blood staining**, uncontrolled IOP, or non-clearing total hyphaema
cards.m: No Aspirin, Days 2-5 watch, Sickle -> no Diamox.

cards.q: Why can IOP rise after blunt trauma, and what is angle-recession glaucoma?
cards.a:
• Early rise: **red cells blocking the trabecular meshwork** (hyphaema), trabeculitis, lens displacement
• **Angle recession**: a tear between the longitudinal and circular fibres of the **ciliary muscle**; gonioscopy shows a **widened ciliary body band**
• Damaged meshwork scars -> **glaucoma months to years later** (risk higher if >180° recessed)
• Counsel: **lifelong (at least yearly) IOP checks** in the injured eye
cards.m: A torn angle today, a silent glaucoma tomorrow.

cards.q: How do you diagnose and manage a traumatic corneal abrasion?
cards.a:
• Pain, watering, photophobia, foreign-body sensation
• **Fluorescein** stains the defect **bright green under cobalt-blue light**
• Mx: **topical antibiotic** (chloramphenicol ointment), **cycloplegic** for pain, oral analgesia
• Usually heals in **24-72 h**; no take-home anaesthetic drops
• CL wearer: **do not patch**; anti-Pseudomonal cover
• Late: **recurrent corneal erosion** (pain on waking) -> lubricant ointment at night
cards.m: Green under Blue = epithelium gone.

cards.q: What iris and lens injuries follow blunt trauma?
cards.a:
• **Traumatic mydriasis**: **sphincter tears** -> notched, dilated, poorly reactive pupil (no ptosis or motility defect, unlike CN3 palsy)
• **Iridodialysis**: iris torn from its root -> D-shaped pupil, monocular diplopia
• **Vossius ring**: ring of iris pigment imprinted on the anterior lens capsule
• **Traumatic cataract**: classically **rosette (flower-shaped)**
• **Lens subluxation/dislocation** (zonule rupture): **phacodonesis**, iridodonesis, uneven AC depth; dislocation into AC can cause pupil-block glaucoma
cards.m: Vossius = the iris 'kisses' the lens and leaves a pigment lipstick ring.

cards.q: What posterior-segment injuries follow blunt trauma?
cards.a:
• **Commotio retinae** (Berlin oedema at the macula): **grey-white retinal whitening**, usually resolves in weeks
• **Choroidal rupture**: **crescent-shaped** yellow-white streak **concentric to the disc**; risk of late CNV
• **Vitreous haemorrhage**
• **Retinal dialysis** (often inferotemporal) -> **retinal detachment**; macular hole
• **Traumatic optic neuropathy**: VA loss + **RAPD** with an initially normal disc
• Globe rupture: at the limbus or behind the rectus insertions (thinnest sclera)
cards.m: Commotio = Concussion of the retina (white); Choroidal rupture = Crescent.

cards.q: What are the clinical features of an orbital floor blow-out fracture?
cards.a:
• Object larger than the orbital rim (fist, ball) suddenly raises orbital pressure -> thin **orbital floor** (maxillary bone) breaks
• **Vertical diplopia**, worse on **upgaze**: **inferior rectus**/orbital fat **entrapment** restricts elevation
• **Infraorbital nerve** numbness: cheek, upper lip, upper teeth
• **Enophthalmos** (may be masked by early swelling)
• Periorbital bruising, **surgical emphysema** after nose blowing
• Always examine the globe (associated eye injury)
cards.m: Blow-out = Bruise, Bump-in (enophthalmos), Blunted upgaze, Benumbed cheek.

cards.q: How is an orbital floor blow-out fracture investigated and managed?
cards.a:
• **CT orbit (coronal)**: floor defect, **'teardrop sign'** (orbital tissue herniating into the maxillary sinus), sinus blood
• Forced duction test / Hess chart for restriction
• Conservative: **avoid nose blowing**, ice packs, oral antibiotics (sinus breach) ± oral steroid; review when swelling settles
• **Surgical repair** (within ~2 weeks) if persistent diplopia in primary/reading gaze with entrapment, **enophthalmos >2 mm**, or a large floor defect
• Co-manage with maxillofacial/oculoplastic surgeons
cards.m: Teardrop on CT = orbit dripping into the sinus.

cards.q: Why is the 'white-eyed' blow-out fracture in a child a surgical emergency?
cards.a:
• Elastic paediatric bone cracks like a **trapdoor** and snaps shut on the **inferior rectus**
• Eye looks **white and quiet** (little bruising) but **marked restriction** of vertical gaze with pain
• **Oculocardiac reflex** (trigeminal afferent, vagal efferent): **nausea, vomiting, bradycardia**, syncope — may be mistaken for head injury
• Needs **urgent surgical release** (within 24-48 h) to prevent muscle **ischaemia and fibrosis**
cards.m: White eye + vomiting child + stuck upgaze = trapped muscle, theatre today.

cards.q: What is a cataract?
cards.a:
• Any **opacity or discolouration of the crystalline lens**, from a small local opacity to complete loss of transparency
• Clinically matters when it **reduces visual acuity** or visual function
• Commonest cause of **reversible** blindness worldwide and in Malaysia
cards.m: Cataract = Greek ‘waterfall’ – looking through falling water.

cards.q: Why does the lens become opaque in cataract?
cards.a:
• Loss of the regular **organisation of lens proteins (crystallins)** → aggregation → progressive opacity
• Opacity causes **blockage, aberrant refraction (scatter) or forward reflection** of light
• Lens fibres are never shed, so damage accumulates with **age**, UV and oxidative stress
cards.m: Like egg white turning opaque when its proteins denature.

cards.q: List the main causes / risk factors for cataract.
cards.a:
• **Age-related** – by far the commonest
• Environmental: **UV light**, radiation, **smoking**
• **Diabetes mellitus**
• **Steroids** (systemic, topical, inhaled)
• **Uveitis**, **trauma** (blunt or penetrating)
• Congenital / syndromic (e.g. rubella, Down syndrome, galactosaemia)
cards.m: ‘ADUST’ – Age, Diabetes, UV/smoking, Steroids, Trauma (+ uveitis).

cards.q: Name the three morphological types of age-related cataract and their classic associations.
cards.a:
• **Nuclear sclerosis** – central yellow-brown nucleus; ageing; myopic shift
• **Cortical** – spoke-like wedges from the periphery; associated with **diabetes**
• **Posterior subcapsular (PSC)** – granular plaque at the back of the lens; associated with **steroids**, DM, uveitis, radiation
cards.m: Nucleus = old age, Cortex = sugar (diabetes), PSC = Prednisolone.

cards.q: Why do some elderly patients with nuclear cataract say they can read again without glasses (‘second sight’)?
cards.a:
• Nuclear sclerosis **increases the refractive index** of the lens nucleus
• The eye becomes more **myopic** (index myopia)
• A presbyopic hyperope or emmetrope now sees **near** clearly without reading glasses
• Clue: **frequent change of spectacle prescription** towards minus
cards.m: Second sight is a warning sign, not a gift – the nucleus is hardening.

cards.q: What are the typical symptoms of a posterior subcapsular cataract, and why?
cards.a:
• **Glare** and dazzle in bright light / oncoming headlights
• **Near vision worse** than distance
• Bright light constricts the pupil, so vision through the **central axial plaque** is blocked
• Often a **younger** patient on **steroids** or with diabetes; progresses relatively fast
cards.m: PSC = Pupil Small, Can’t see (worse in sunlight).

cards.q: Summarise the symptoms of cataract a patient may describe.
cards.a:
• **Gradual, painless** blurring of vision (one or both eyes)
• **Reduced contrast sensitivity**, especially in low light
• **Glare** in bright light, haloes around lights
• **Myopic shift** / frequent change of glasses
• Monocular diplopia (cortical spokes), faded colours
• Pain or red eye is **NOT** typical – look for another cause

cards.q: How do you examine a patient for cataract in clinic?
cards.a:
• **VA** with pinhole and refraction
• **Distant direct ophthalmoscopy**: opacities appear as **dark shadows against the red reflex** (reduced red reflex)
• **Dilated slit lamp**: grade nuclear, cortical, PSC
• Check **pupils (RAPD)** and **fundus** – a dense RAPD is NOT explained by cataract alone
• Measure IOP; note cornea and AC depth
cards.m: Cataract never causes an RAPD – if present, look behind the lens.

cards.q: What is the typical diabetic cataract seen in a young person with poorly controlled type 1 DM?
cards.a:
• **‘Snowflake’ cataract** – bilateral white, flake-like subcapsular / cortical opacities
• Due to **sorbitol accumulation** (osmotic swelling of lens fibres)
• Can develop rapidly, even over weeks
• Fluctuating blood glucose also causes **fluctuating refraction**
• Older diabetics get ordinary age-related cataract **earlier**
cards.m: Snow in a sugar-coated lens.

cards.q: Why is a dense congenital cataract an ophthalmic urgency?
cards.a:
• It causes **deprivational amblyopia** – the most severe and most amblyogenic type
• Presents as **leukocoria** / absent red reflex, nystagmus, squint
• Dense unilateral: surgery ideally by **~6 weeks**; bilateral by **~8-10 weeks** of life
• Then **aphakic/IOL correction + patching** – surgery alone is not enough
• Red reflex check at newborn and 6-week review (cross-ref AMB)
cards.m: White pupil in a baby = refer urgently (cataract or retinoblastoma).

cards.q: When is cataract surgery indicated?
cards.a:
• **Visual disability** that affects the patient’s lifestyle, work or **driving** – not a fixed VA number
• **Medical** indications: lens-induced glaucoma (phacomorphic, phacolytic), need to **view/treat the fundus** (e.g. diabetic retinopathy laser)
• Anisometropia after surgery on one eye
• Patient must understand **benefits vs risks** (informed consent)
cards.m: Operate on the patient, not on the lens.

cards.q: What does a pre-operative assessment for cataract surgery include?
cards.a:
• **Systemic**: BP, glucose control, cardiorespiratory fitness, ability to lie flat, drug history
• **Ophthalmic**: VA, **cover test**, pupils, cornea (endothelium), AC depth, lens grade, **fundus**, current refraction
• **Biometry** for IOL power
• **Informed consent** – expected outcome, risks (endophthalmitis, PCR, RD, need for glasses)

cards.q: What is biometry and why does an error matter?
cards.a:
• Measurement to calculate **IOL power**: **keratometry** (corneal curvature, K) + **axial length** (optical coherence biometry or A-scan)
• Values go into an IOL formula (e.g. SRK/T) with a target refraction
• An error gives a **refractive surprise** (unexpected myopia/hyperopia) post-op
• Wrong-lens / wrong-eye prevention: check both eyes, compare with fellow eye
cards.m: K + AL = IOL (curvature + length).

cards.q: Which drug history matters before cataract surgery?
cards.a:
• **Tamsulosin** (and other α1-blockers) → **intraoperative floppy iris syndrome** (poor dilation, iris billowing/prolapse); stopping it does not remove the risk – **warn the surgeon**
• **Anticoagulants**: warfarin usually continued if INR in range; DOAC/aspirin usually **continued** for topical/sub-Tenon anaesthesia
• Steroids, diabetes drugs (fasting), allergy to **povidone-iodine**
cards.m: Ask every elderly man: ‘Any prostate tablets?’

cards.q: Outline the key steps of phacoemulsification.
cards.a:
• Clean and drape; **povidone-iodine 5%** to skin and conjunctival sac
• Topical / intracameral or local block anaesthesia
• **~2.2-3 mm corneal incision**
• **Capsulorhexis** (circular opening in anterior capsule) → **hydrodissection**
• Nucleus **emulsified and aspirated** by ultrasound probe; cortex aspirated
• **Foldable IOL injected into the capsular bag**; wound **self-sealing**, no sutures
cards.m: Open (incision) – Peel (rhexis) – Spin (hydro) – Crush (phaco) – Fold (IOL) – Seal.

cards.q: Compare phacoemulsification, ECCE and ICCE.
cards.a:
• **Phaco**: commonest; ~3 mm self-sealing; posterior capsule kept; IOL in bag; **fast recovery**
• **ECCE**: nucleus expressed whole – **hard/brunescent lens**; 8-10 mm wound with **sutures**; capsule kept; slower recovery, more astigmatism
• **ICCE**: **whole lens + capsule** removed – **unstable/subluxated lens**; >10 mm; zonules dissolved by **alpha-chymotrypsin**, lens lifted with a **cryoprobe**; IOL in **front of the iris** (AC IOL)
• Note: the notes say ‘liquid nitrogen probe’; correct is a **cryoprobe** (cryoextraction)
• MSICS (manual small-incision, sutureless tunnel) is widely used in Malaysia for dense cataract
cards.m: Bigger wound, bigger lens out, slower recovery: Phaco < ECCE < ICCE.

cards.q: What are the main intra-operative complications of cataract surgery?
cards.a:
• **Posterior capsule rupture (PCR)** – the commonest serious one
• **Vitreous loss** – follows PCR (needs anterior vitrectomy)
• **Dropped nucleus** / posterior loss of lens fragments into vitreous → vitrectomy
• **IOL dislocation** posteriorly
• **Suprachoroidal haemorrhage** – rare, devastating (hypertension, anticoagulants, high myopia)
• Note: the notes list vitreous loss as post-op; it is an **intra-operative** complication. Iris prolapse can be intra-op or early post-op (wound leak)
cards.m: PCR is the domino: capsule breaks → vitreous out → nucleus drops.

cards.q: A patient has a painful red eye with falling vision 3 days after cataract surgery. What must you suspect and do?
cards.a:
• **Acute post-operative endophthalmitis** until proven otherwise
• Clues: **pain + drop in VA**, lid swelling, hypopyon, vitritis, poor red reflex
• **Same-day** ophthalmology: vitreous ± AC tap and **intravitreal vancomycin + ceftazidime within 1 hour** (MOH CPG)
• Most present within the first week; MOH CPG: usually within **2 weeks**
• Normal post-op: mild discomfort, VA improving day by day
cards.m: Post-op eye: better each day = normal; worse each day = endophthalmitis.

cards.q: What is Irvine-Gass syndrome?
cards.a:
• **Cystoid macular oedema (CMO)** after cataract surgery
• Blurred central vision after initially good outcome; peaks **~4-6 weeks** post-op
• Higher risk: **diabetes**, uveitis, PCR / vitreous loss, prostaglandin drops
• Diagnose with **OCT** (cystic spaces); FFA shows ‘petaloid’ leakage
• Treat with topical **NSAID** (e.g. ketorolac) ± topical steroid
• Note: notes spell ‘cystoid mascular edema’ – correct is cystoid **macular** oedema
cards.m: Good at week 1, blurred at week 6 = CMO.

cards.q: What is the commonest late complication of cataract surgery, and how is it treated?
cards.a:
• **Posterior capsule opacification (PCO)** – lens epithelial cells proliferate on the retained capsule
• Months to years later: gradual blur and glare, like the cataract ‘coming back’
• Treat with **Nd:YAG laser posterior capsulotomy** (outpatient, quick)
• Small risks of YAG: IOP spike, CMO, **retinal detachment**
• Also warn of **RD** after surgery (esp. high myopes): flashes, floaters, curtain → urgent review
cards.m: ‘My cataract has grown back’ = PCO – YAG it.

cards.q: What is a vitreous haemorrhage and how does it typically present?
cards.a:
• Blood in the **vitreous cavity** (intragel) or between the posterior hyaloid and retina (**subhyaloid**)
• One of the commonest causes of **sudden, painless, unilateral** loss of vision
• Symptoms: new **floaters**, cobwebs, haze, shadows, **red hue**, ± scotoma or severe visual loss
• Severity depends on the amount of blood and whether it covers the **macula**
cards.m: Painless sudden loss: VH, CRAO, CRVO, RD, AION – the ‘painless five’.

cards.q: Why is vision in vitreous haemorrhage often worse on waking?
cards.a:
• Lying flat overnight lets the blood **disperse and settle over the posterior pole / macula**
• When upright during the day, blood **settles inferiorly** by gravity, clearing the visual axis
• This is why patients are told to **sleep head-up**
cards.m: Blood obeys gravity: flat at night = blood on the macula.

cards.q: Distinguish subhyaloid (preretinal) from intragel vitreous haemorrhage.
cards.a:
• **Subhyaloid**: trapped between posterior hyaloid face and retina; **boat-shaped** with a flat upper fluid level; affects acuity when it covers the **fovea**; field loss
• **Intragel**: blood within the vitreous gel itself; causes **floaters** and diffuse haze; clears slowly
• Large subhyaloid bleeds over the macula may need laser hyaloidotomy or early vitrectomy
cards.m: Subhyaloid = boat (keel down, flat deck up).

cards.q: Classify the causes of vitreous haemorrhage by the vessels that bleed.
cards.a:
• **Normal vessels**: trauma (blunt, **shaken baby**), **PVD tearing a vessel**, retinal tear/**retinal detachment**
• **Abnormal (new) vessels**: **NVD/NVE** in proliferative diabetic retinopathy, ischaemic **CRVO/BRVO**, sickle cell retinopathy
• **Breakthrough**: subretinal neovascular membrane (wet AMD) bleeding into the vitreous
• Others: **Terson syndrome** (subarachnoid haemorrhage), bleeding disorders
cards.m: Tear, Trauma, New vessels, Neighbour (AMD), Terson.

cards.q: What is the commonest cause of vitreous haemorrhage in adults, and the most important cause in a non-diabetic?
cards.a:
• Overall commonest in adults: **proliferative diabetic retinopathy** (new vessels pulled by vitreous)
• In a **non-diabetic**: acute **posterior vitreous detachment with a retinal tear** – must be excluded urgently
• Other causes to consider: retinal vein occlusion, trauma; in a **child** without clear trauma think **non-accidental injury**
cards.m: Diabetic? Think new vessels. Non-diabetic? Think tear until proven otherwise.

cards.q: What are the examination findings in vitreous haemorrhage?
cards.a:
• **Reduced or absent red reflex**; fundus details hazy or not visible
• Slit lamp: red cells behind the lens; **‘tobacco dust’** pigment in anterior vitreous (Shafer sign) suggests a **retinal tear**
• Pupils: **no RAPD** from blood alone – an RAPD suggests RD or optic nerve/retinal ischaemia
• Check **iris for rubeosis**, IOP, and the **fellow eye fundus** (often shows the cause, e.g. PDR)
• Note: the notes say ‘detected with slit lamp’; correct is diagnosis by **red reflex and fundoscopy**, confirmed with **B-scan** if no view
cards.m: Blood blocks light but not the nerve – no RAPD unless something else is wrong.

cards.q: The fundus cannot be seen because of dense vitreous haemorrhage. What investigation is mandatory, and why?
cards.a:
• **B-scan ultrasonography** – same day/urgently
• To exclude **retinal detachment** or **retinal tear** (and IOFB/tumour) hidden behind the blood
• VH: low-reflective mobile echoes; RD: bright membrane tethered to the **optic disc**
• Repeat B-scan every **1-2 weeks** until the retina can be seen
• Also: glucose/HbA1c, BP, FBC/clotting if no obvious cause
cards.m: No view? Always B-scan.

cards.q: How do you manage vitreous haemorrhage when B-scan shows the retina is attached?
cards.a:
• **Observe** – most intragel blood clears over weeks to months
• **Elevate the head** during sleep (blood settles inferiorly, clears the macula and lets the superior retina be seen)
• Avoid strenuous activity
• Essential **antiplatelets/anticoagulants are usually continued** – discuss with the physician
• Regular review with repeat B-scan; treat the cause (e.g. **PRP** when view permits)
cards.m: Attached retina = Wait, Elevate, Re-scan.

cards.q: How is vitreous haemorrhage managed according to its cause?
cards.a:
• **Retinal detachment** → **urgent vitrectomy** + retinal repair
• **Retinal break** (no RD) → seal with **laser photocoagulation or cryotherapy**
• **Neovascularisation** (PDR, ischaemic CRVO) → **panretinal photocoagulation** ± **intravitreal anti-VEGF**
• **Non-clearing VH** or **iris neovascularisation** → **vitrectomy** (with endolaser)
• Note: notes spell ‘virectomy’ – correct is **vitrectomy**
cards.m: Treat the source, not just the blood.

cards.q: When is vitrectomy indicated for vitreous haemorrhage?
cards.a:
• **RD** (especially macula-threatening) or **retinal tear** on B-scan – urgent
• **Non-clearing VH** – usually after **~1-3 months**; earlier in **type 1 DM**, bilateral VH or an only eye
• **Rubeosis** (iris neovascularisation) with no fundus view for PRP
• **Tractional RD** involving the macula in PDR
• Large **subhyaloid haemorrhage over the macula**
cards.m: Vitrectomy when the blood won’t go, the retina is off, or the iris turns red.

cards.q: A diabetic with dense vitreous haemorrhage now has new vessels on the iris. Why is this urgent?
cards.a:
• Iris neovascularisation (**rubeosis iridis**) means severe retinal **ischaemia** with high VEGF
• Risk of **neovascular glaucoma** (angle closed by fibrovascular membrane) – painful, often blinding
• Retina needs **PRP**, but the blood blocks the laser
• Give **intravitreal anti-VEGF** and arrange **early vitrectomy with endolaser PRP**
• Refer within **1 week** at the latest (MOH CPG: rubeosis, preretinal/vitreous haemorrhage)
cards.m: Red iris + blood in vitreous = race against neovascular glaucoma.

cards.q: What are the complications of a long-standing vitreous haemorrhage?
cards.a:
• **Ghost cell glaucoma** – degenerated khaki red cells block the trabecular meshwork
• **Haemolytic glaucoma**, **haemosiderosis bulbi** (iron toxicity to retina)
• **Proliferative vitreoretinopathy** and tractional RD
• **Amblyopia** in children (deprivation) – clear early
• Missed underlying **retinal tear/RD** – the most important avoidable complication
cards.m: Old blood becomes ghosts that block the drain.

cards.q: How is glaucoma defined?
cards.a:
• A progressive **optic neuropathy** with characteristic **optic disc changes** (cupping) and matching **visual field defects**
• **Raised IOP** is the main modifiable risk factor but is **not** required (±)
• Causes **irreversible** blindness – damage cannot be undone, only progression slowed
• Treatment is **lifelong**; compliance is critical
cards.m: Glaucoma = Disc + Field (± Pressure).

cards.q: Explain ‘the trick of IOP’: ocular hypertension vs normal-tension glaucoma.
cards.a:
• Normal IOP ≈ **10-21 mmHg**
• **Ocular hypertension**: IOP >21 but **normal disc and field** – only ~10% of people with IOP >21 have glaucoma
• **Normal-tension glaucoma**: glaucomatous disc + field with IOP **≤21** – about half of glaucoma patients have IOP ≤21 at screening
• So IOP alone **cannot diagnose or exclude** glaucoma – always look at the **disc**
cards.m: High pressure without damage = OHT; damage without high pressure = NTG.

cards.q: Trace the production and drainage of aqueous humour.
cards.a:
• Produced by the **non-pigmented ciliary epithelium** (ciliary processes) into the **posterior chamber**
• Flows **through the pupil** into the **anterior chamber**
• Conventional route (~80-90%): **trabecular meshwork → Schlemm’s canal → collector channels → episcleral veins**
• Uveoscleral route: through ciliary muscle face into suprachoroidal space
• IOP rises from **increased production** or (almost always) **decreased outflow**
cards.m: Ciliary body → pupil → angle → Schlemm → veins: ‘tap, sink, drain’.

cards.q: How does raised IOP cause glaucomatous damage?
cards.a:
• **Increased resistance** to outflow in the trabecular meshwork raises IOP (open angle)
• Damage = **retinal ganglion cell death (apoptosis)** at the optic nerve head by two mechanisms:
• **Mechanical**: pressure deforms the **lamina cribrosa**, compressing axons
• **Vascular**: compromised optic nerve head perfusion → **ischaemia** (explains NTG, vasospasm, low BP links)
cards.m: Two hits on the nerve: squeeze (mechanical) and starve (vascular).

cards.q: How is glaucoma classified?
cards.a:
• **Primary**: **open-angle** (POAG, NTG) and **angle-closure** (acute, chronic)
• **Secondary**: inflammatory (**uveitic**), **traumatic** (angle recession), **neovascular**, **steroid-induced**, **lens-induced** (phacomorphic, phacolytic), pseudoexfoliation, pigment dispersion
• **Congenital / developmental** (primary congenital glaucoma, syndromic)

cards.q: What are the risk factors for primary open-angle glaucoma?
cards.a:
• **Raised IOP** (main modifiable factor) and **increasing age**
• **Family history** in a first-degree relative
• **African ancestry**; **myopia**; **thin central cornea**
• Diabetes, vascular factors (low/fluctuating BP, vasospasm – migraine, Raynaud’s, sleep apnoea) – especially NTG
• Note: notes p30 list anterior iris shift, large lens, short axial length/nanophthalmos and an ‘acute attack’ under open-angle – these belong to **angle-closure**, not POAG
cards.m: Open angle = long myopic eye; closed angle = short hyperopic eye.

cards.q: Why is POAG called the ‘silent thief of sight’?
cards.a:
• **Painless, white eye**, slow rise in IOP – no symptoms early
• Field loss starts in the **mid-periphery** and the other eye fills in the gap
• **Central VA stays good until late** → patient notices only when **tunnel vision** or loss of fixation occurs
• Hence detection depends on **opportunistic screening** (disc check, IOP) by optometrists/doctors
cards.m: POAG steals from the edges inward; the patient only notices when the centre goes.

cards.q: What optic disc signs suggest glaucoma?
cards.a:
• **Increased cup:disc ratio** (vertical enlargement of the cup)
• **Notching** / focal thinning of the neuroretinal rim (often inferior or superior pole)
• **Disc (splinter) haemorrhage** at the rim – sign of progression
• **Bayoneting** of vessels at the cup edge; **nasalisation** of vessels
• **Laminar dot sign** – exposed pores of the lamina cribrosa
• Peripapillary atrophy, RNFL defects

cards.q: What is the ISNT rule and which cup:disc findings are suspicious?
cards.a:
• Normal neuroretinal rim thickness: **Inferior ≥ Superior ≥ Nasal ≥ Temporal**
• Glaucoma thins the **inferior and superior** rims first → rule broken
• Suspicious: **vertical CDR >0.6**, or **CDR asymmetry >0.2** between eyes
• Always interpret with **disc size** – a large disc has a large physiological cup
cards.m: ISNT – ‘I Sleep Not Tonight’ (the rim is thickest Inferiorly).

cards.q: Describe the typical visual field defects of glaucoma and how they are tested.
cards.a:
• Test: **Humphrey automated perimetry** (e.g. 24-2 SITA threshold) – repeat to confirm and monitor progression
• Early: **paracentral scotoma**, **nasal step** (respects horizontal midline)
• Then: **arcuate (Bjerrum) scotoma** following the arcuate nerve fibre bundles
• Late: **tunnel vision** with a central island ± temporal island, then loss of fixation
cards.m: Nasal step → arcuate → tunnel: the field shrinks like a closing curtain.

cards.q: Which instrument is the gold standard for IOP, and how does corneal thickness affect it?
cards.a:
• **Goldmann applanation tonometry** (slit lamp, fluorescein, topical anaesthetic) = gold standard; **Tonopen** is portable (ward, children)
• Goldmann assumes a standard **central corneal thickness (~520-550 µm)**
• **Thin cornea → underestimates IOP** (true IOP higher – risk missed); thick cornea → overestimates
• Measure **CCT by pachymetry** in glaucoma suspects; thin CCT is itself a POAG risk factor
cards.m: Thin cornea is a liar: it hides a high pressure.

cards.q: Why must every glaucoma suspect have gonioscopy?
cards.a:
• A **gonioscopy lens** on the cornea lets you see the **iridocorneal angle** at the slit lamp (it is hidden by total internal reflection otherwise)
• Distinguishes **open-angle** from **angle-closure** – the treatment differs (laser PI for closure)
• Detects secondary causes: **angle recession**, neovascularisation of the angle, pigment, PAS
• Normal open angle: trabecular meshwork and scleral spur visible
cards.m: Never label ‘open-angle’ without looking at the angle.

cards.q: Classify anti-glaucoma drugs by mechanism of action.
cards.a:
• **Reduce aqueous production**: **β-blockers** (timolol), **α2-agonists** (brimonidine), **carbonic anhydrase inhibitors** (topical dorzolamide/brinzolamide; oral/IV **acetazolamide** = Diamox)
• **Increase outflow**: **prostaglandin analogues** (latanoprost – uveoscleral), **miotics** (pilocarpine – trabecular)
• Brimonidine also has a minor outflow effect
• Note: notes list **epinephrine** – obsolete; no longer used
cards.m: ‘Turn off the tap’ (BB, α2, CAI) or ‘open the drain’ (PGA, pilocarpine).

cards.q: What is the usual first-line drug for POAG, and what are its side effects?
cards.a:
• **Prostaglandin analogue**, e.g. **latanoprost 0.005% once daily at night**
• Increases **uveoscleral outflow**; lowers IOP ~25-30%; few systemic effects
• Side effects: **iris darkening** (permanent, warn if one eye only), **eyelash growth**, periocular skin pigmentation, **periorbital fat atrophy**, conjunctival hyperaemia
• Caution: may worsen **CMO** and **uveitis**, reactivate **HSV** keratitis
cards.m: Latanoprost gives you longer lashes and browner eyes.

cards.q: What are the contraindications and precautions with topical timolol?
cards.a:
• Non-selective **β-blocker** – reduces aqueous production
• Contraindicated in **asthma / COPD** (bronchospasm), **bradycardia**, **heart block**, uncontrolled heart failure
• Can mask hypoglycaemia; may cause fatigue, depression
• Reduce systemic absorption by **punctal occlusion** / closing the eyes for 2 minutes after instillation
• Always ask about **asthma** before prescribing
cards.m: Timolol: check the Chest and the Pulse before the Pressure.

cards.q: What are the key cautions with brimonidine and with acetazolamide?
cards.a:
• **Brimonidine** (α2-agonist): **contraindicated in infants/children <2 years** (CNS depression, apnoea); common **allergic follicular conjunctivitis**; drowsiness; avoid with MAOIs
• **Acetazolamide** (oral/IV CAI): **paraesthesia** of fingers, **hypokalaemia**, metabolic acidosis, **renal stones**, nausea, fatigue; avoid in **sulfonamide allergy**, renal/hepatic failure, sickle cell
• Acetazolamide is for **short-term** IOP control, not long-term POAG
cards.m: Brimonidine: not for babies. Diamox: tingling, low K, stones.

cards.q: What is the role of laser trabeculoplasty in POAG?
cards.a:
• **SLT** (selective) or **ALT** (argon) laser to the **trabecular meshwork** → improves outflow – for **open-angle** glaucoma
• Traditionally used when drops fail or are not tolerated
• **SLT is now an accepted first-line option** (LiGHT trial: as effective as drops, many patients drop-free at 3 years)
• Repeatable; effect may wane over years
• Peripheral **iridotomy** is the laser for **angle-closure**, not POAG
cards.m: SLT for Open angles; PI for closed angles.

cards.q: What are the surgical options for glaucoma and when are they used?
cards.a:
• Used when **medical and laser treatment fail** or disease progresses despite target IOP
• **Trabeculectomy**: guarded fistula draining aqueous to a **subconjunctival bleb**, with antifibrotic **mitomycin C / 5-FU**
• **Glaucoma drainage devices** (tubes/valves, e.g. Ahmed, Baerveldt) – complex/failed cases
