• **Cyclodestruction** (cyclodiode laser) – **last resort**, destroys the ciliary body to reduce production
• Risks: hypotony, bleb leak, **blebitis/endophthalmitis** (cross-ref BLEB), cataract
cards.m: Drain it (trab/tube) before you destroy the tap (cyclodestruction).

cards.q: How is POAG monitored and who should be screened?
cards.a:
• Set a **target IOP** (e.g. 20-30% below baseline, lower if advanced)
• Lifelong review: **IOP, disc** (photo/OCT RNFL), **Humphrey fields**; escalate if progression
• Check **adherence and drop technique** first if IOP not controlled
• Screen **first-degree relatives from age ~40** (risk several times higher)
• Remind patients: damage is **irreversible** – stopping drops because they feel well is the commonest cause of progression
cards.m: No symptoms ≠ no disease: keep putting the drops in.

cards.q: How does primary congenital glaucoma present and how is it treated?
cards.a:
• Triad: **epiphora, photophobia, blepharospasm** in an infant
• **Buphthalmos** (‘ox eye’ – enlarged globe; corneal diameter >12 mm in infancy), **cloudy cornea**, **Haab striae** (breaks in Descemet’s membrane), myopia
• Cause: maldeveloped trabecular meshwork (goniodysgenesis)
• Treatment is **surgical** – **goniotomy or trabeculotomy**; drops only temporise
• **Urgent** referral – risk of blindness and amblyopia
cards.m: Watery, light-shy baby with big cloudy eyes = congenital glaucoma, not blocked tear duct.

cards.q: Who is at risk of primary acute angle-closure glaucoma?
cards.a:
• Age **>40** (≈1 in 1000 people over 40 in the notes) – rising with age as the lens thickens
• **Female** sex
• **Hyperopia** (long-sighted, small eye)
• **East Asian (Chinese) ethnicity** – highly relevant in Malaysia
• Family history of angle closure; **shallow anterior chamber**
cards.m: The 4 Fs: Forty-plus, Female, Farsighted, Far East (Asian).

cards.q: Why are hyperopic eyes prone to angle closure?
cards.a:
• A hyperopic eye has a **short axial length** – everything in front is **crowded**
• **Shallow anterior chamber** and **narrow iridocorneal angle**
• The **lens keeps growing** with age, pushing the iris forward and increasing iris-lens contact
• Result: a narrow angle that can close suddenly
cards.m: Small house, growing furniture – the doorway (angle) gets blocked.

cards.q: Explain the mechanism of primary acute angle closure (pupillary block).
cards.a:
• Iris in close contact with the lens in a **mid-dilated** pupil → aqueous cannot pass from posterior to anterior chamber (**pupillary block**)
• Pressure builds **behind the iris** → peripheral iris **bows forward** (**iris bombé**)
• Peripheral iris covers the **trabecular meshwork** → angle closed
• Aqueous still produced but cannot drain → **IOP rises abruptly** (often >50-60 mmHg)
cards.m: Door (pupil) jammed → curtain (iris) balloons forward → drain (angle) blocked.

cards.q: What can precipitate an attack of acute angle closure?
cards.a:
• **Mid-dilation of the pupil**: **dim light** (cinema, evening), stress/emotion
• **Mydriatic drops** (tropicamide, phenylephrine) – check AC depth before dilating
• **Anticholinergics** (ipratropium nebuliser, hyoscine, antihistamines), **tricyclic antidepressants**, SSRIs
• **Sympathomimetics** (salbutamol, adrenaline, nasal decongestants)
• **Topiramate** – causes a different, **bilateral** secondary angle closure
cards.m: Anything that makes the pupil half-open (dark, drugs, drama) can shut the angle.

cards.q: What are the symptoms of acute angle-closure glaucoma, and why do patients see haloes?
cards.a:
• Sudden **severe eye pain**, red, **watering** eye, **photophobia**
• **Blurred vision**, often onset in the **evening**
• **Coloured haloes** around lights – IOP pushes fluid into the cornea; **epithelial oedema** separates the basal epithelial cells so they act as a **diffraction grating**
• Headache, **nausea, vomiting**, referred **abdominal pain**
• History of previous self-limiting episodes (intermittent closure)
cards.m: Haloes = rainbow through a foggy (oedematous) window.

cards.q: Why is acute angle-closure glaucoma frequently misdiagnosed, and how do you avoid it?
cards.a:
• **Nausea, vomiting, headache and abdominal pain** dominate → mislabelled **migraine**, **acute abdomen** or gastroenteritis
• Elderly patient may not localise pain to the eye
• Rule: **look at the eyes** in any older patient with headache and vomiting – red eye, hazy cornea, fixed mid-dilated pupil
• A **rock-hard globe** on gentle palpation is a useful bedside clue
cards.m: Vomiting + headache + red eye in a 60-year-old = check the IOP before the CT.

cards.q: What signs do you find in an eye with acute angle closure?
cards.a:
• **Reduced VA**; **ciliary/conjunctival injection**
• **Hazy, ‘steamy’ oedematous cornea**
• Pupil **fixed, mid-dilated and vertically oval**, unreactive (iris sphincter ischaemia)
• **Shallow AC**; **very high IOP** (often >50-60 mmHg), stony-hard globe
• **Closed angle on gonioscopy**; fellow eye has a **narrow angle**
• Note: notes list ‘increased cup:disc ratio’ – not an acute sign; in the attack the disc is often **swollen/hyperaemic** and the view is hazy
cards.m: Red eye with a hazy cornea and a big, oval, fixed pupil = angle closure.

cards.q: How can you assess anterior chamber depth at the bedside or slit lamp?
cards.a:
• **Oblique flashlight test**: shine a pen torch from the temporal side – in a shallow AC the bowed iris casts a **shadow on the nasal iris** (**‘shadow sign’**)
• **Van Herick test** (slit lamp): compare peripheral AC depth with corneal thickness – **<¼ corneal thickness** suggests an occludable angle
• Confirm with **gonioscopy**
• Shallow AC → **avoid dilating drops** until assessed
cards.m: Shadow on the nasal iris = shallow chamber – don’t dilate.

cards.q: What investigations confirm acute angle-closure glaucoma?
cards.a:
• **Goldmann applanation tonometry** – IOP markedly raised (notes: often >60 mmHg)
• **Gonioscopy** – closed iridocorneal angle (indentation gonioscopy distinguishes appositional from synechial closure); examine the **fellow eye** angle
• VA and, once settled, **visual field** and disc assessment
• Anterior segment **OCT/UBM** if available
cards.m: Pressure (tonometer) + Picture of the angle (gonioscope) = diagnosis.

cards.q: How do you distinguish acute angle closure from acute anterior uveitis in a red, painful eye?
cards.a:
• **Pupil**: AACG **mid-dilated, oval, fixed**; uveitis **small, irregular** (posterior synechiae)
• **Cornea**: AACG **hazy/oedematous**; uveitis clear with **keratic precipitates**
• **IOP**: AACG **very high**; uveitis usually normal or low (can be raised)
• **AC**: AACG **shallow**; uveitis normal depth with **cells and flare**
• **Systemic**: AACG nausea/vomiting, haloes; uveitis photophobia, HLA-B27 history
cards.m: Big pupil + high pressure = glaucoma; small pupil + cells = uveitis.

cards.q: What are the immediate steps in managing acute angle closure in ED or Klinik Kesihatan before the ophthalmologist arrives?
cards.a:
• **Lie supine** (lens falls back)
• **Acetazolamide 500 mg IV** (or oral if IV unavailable), then 250 mg QDS
• Topical **timolol 0.5%**, **apraclonidine/brimonidine**, **prednisolone acetate 1%** (reduces inflammation)
• **Pilocarpine 2%** once IOP starts to fall
• **Analgesia and antiemetic**
• **Urgent same-day** referral to ophthalmology
cards.m: ‘Lie, Diamox, Drops, Dope (analgesia), Dial ophthalmology.’

cards.q: How does pilocarpine help in acute angle closure, and why is it often ineffective at first?
cards.a:
• **Miotic** – constricts the pupil, pulling the **peripheral iris away from the angle** (and tightening it) → opens the drainage pathway
• At very high IOP (**>50 mmHg**) the iris sphincter is **ischaemic** and does not respond
• So first **lower IOP** with acetazolamide and aqueous suppressants, then give **pilocarpine 2%**
• Do not use pilocarpine in lens-induced or topiramate-induced closure
cards.m: Pilocarpine works on a living sphincter – lower the pressure first.

cards.q: What do you use when IOP stays very high despite acetazolamide and topical drops?
cards.a:
• **Hyperosmotic agents**: **IV mannitol 20% 1-2 g/kg** over 30-60 min, or **oral glycerol 1 g/kg** (avoid glycerol in diabetics)
• They dehydrate the **vitreous**, letting the lens-iris diaphragm move back
• Caution: **heart failure**, renal failure (fluid overload), dehydration
• If still refractory: **laser iridotomy** (once cornea clears) or **laser iridoplasty**, surgical iridectomy or lens extraction
cards.m: Mannitol shrinks the vitreous to make room at the front.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment of primary acute angle closure, and why treat the other eye?
cards.a:
• **Nd:YAG laser peripheral iridotomy (PI)** – a hole in the peripheral iris gives aqueous an **alternative route** from posterior to anterior chamber, bypassing the pupil → iris flattens, angle opens
• Surgical **iridectomy** if laser is not possible
• **Prophylactic PI in the fellow eye** – same anatomy; **40-80%** risk of an attack within 5-10 years untreated
• **Lens extraction** (phaco) is an option in selected eyes / when the lens is a major factor
cards.m: One attack, two holes – always laser both eyes.

cards.q: How does topiramate-induced angle closure differ from primary pupillary-block angle closure?
cards.a:
• Occurs within **days to 2 weeks** of starting topiramate (also sulfonamides, e.g. acetazolamide, co-trimoxazole)
• **Bilateral**; often acute **myopic shift**
• Mechanism: **ciliochoroidal effusion** rotates the ciliary body and pushes the lens-iris diaphragm **forward** – **no pupillary block**
• **PI and pilocarpine do not help** (pilocarpine may worsen it)
• Treat: **stop the drug**, **cycloplegics** (atropine), aqueous suppressants, topical steroids
cards.m: Bilateral + new myopia + new drug = effusion, not block.

cards.q: What are the complications and sequelae of an acute angle-closure attack?
cards.a:
• **Glaucomatous optic neuropathy** / optic atrophy and field loss – irreversible
• **Peripheral anterior synechiae** → **chronic angle-closure glaucoma**
• **Sectoral iris atrophy**, permanently **dilated pupil**
• **Glaukomflecken** – grey-white anterior subcapsular lens flecks (lens epithelial necrosis), cataract
• Corneal endothelial cell loss, **CRVO**
• Prognosis depends on **duration of the attack** – treat within hours
cards.m: The footprints of an attack: atrophic iris, flecks on the lens, PAS in the angle.

cards.q: What is hypertensive retinopathy, and which three ocular tissues can raised blood pressure damage?
cards.a:
• Retinal vascular damage from **elevated systemic blood pressure**, seen on fundoscopy
• Three types of damage:
• **Retinopathy** – arterioles, haemorrhages, exudates, cotton-wool spots
• **Choroidopathy** – choroidal infarcts (Elschnig spots, Siegrist streaks), serous RD
• **Optic neuropathy** – disc swelling in severe (malignant) hypertension
• Present in a large majority of hypertensives with chronic kidney disease
cards.m: Think 'R-C-O': Retina, Choroid, Optic nerve – the three victims of high BP.

cards.q: Why do retinal arterioles react to hypertension differently from most systemic arterioles?
cards.a:
• **No sympathetic nerve supply** – tone is set locally
• **Autoregulation** – arterioles constrict as BP rises to protect capillaries
• **Blood-retinal barrier** (tight junctions of endothelium and RPE)
• When BP overwhelms autoregulation, muscle and endothelium are damaged and the barrier breaks down -> leakage
• Note: the notes say 'blood-brain barrier'; correct term is **blood-RETINAL barrier**
cards.m: Autoregulation is the first line of defence; once it fails, the retina starts to leak.

cards.q: What are the three pathological phases of hypertensive retinopathy and the fundus sign of each?
cards.a:
• **Vasoconstrictive** – vasospasm, generalised/focal **arteriolar narrowing**
• **Sclerotic** – intimal thickening, medial hyperplasia, hyaline degeneration -> **AV nicking**, copper/silver wiring
• **Exudative** – barrier breakdown -> **flame and dot-blot haemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton-wool spots**
• Malignant hypertension adds disc swelling and choroidopathy
cards.m: Squeeze -> Stiffen -> Spill.

cards.q: What symptoms does hypertensive retinopathy cause, and how does it usually come to attention?
cards.a:
• Usually **asymptomatic** – found on fundoscopy (medical clinic, KK, eye screening)
• Blurred vision only with macular involvement (exudates, oedema, serous RD) or disc swelling
• Severe/malignant HTN may present with headache, visual blurring and other target-organ symptoms
• Findings are usually **bilateral** and roughly symmetrical
cards.m: Fundoscopy is the only window where you can see arterioles directly – look in every hypertensive.

cards.q: What is meant by copper wiring and silver wiring, and what happens to the A:V ratio in hypertension?
cards.a:
• Normal arteriole:venule calibre ratio is **2:3**; in hypertension it falls towards **1:3**
• Arteriolar wall thickening widens and brightens the **central light reflex**
• **Copper wiring** – broad, reddish-brown reflex (moderate sclerosis)
• **Silver wiring** – wall so opaque the vessel looks white/silver (severe sclerosis)
• These are sclerotic signs and do **not** reverse with BP control
cards.m: Copper comes before silver – the older the wire, the paler it gets.

cards.q: Name the three arteriovenous crossing signs and describe each.
cards.a:
• Why: thickened arteriole and venule share a **common adventitial sheath**, so the arteriole compresses the vein
• **Salus sign** – **deflection** of the vein as it crosses the arteriole
• **Gunn sign** – **tapering** of the vein on either side of the crossing (AV nicking)
• **Bonnet sign** – **banking** (dilatation) of the vein distal to the crossing
• Severe crossing changes predispose to **branch retinal vein occlusion**
cards.m: S-G-B in order of the vein's journey: it Swerves (Salus), Gets pinched (Gunn), then Backs up (Bonnet).

cards.q: Flame-shaped vs dot-blot haemorrhages: which retinal layer is each in, and why do they look different?
cards.a:
• **Flame** – superficial **nerve fibre layer**; blood spreads along axons -> feathery, splinter shape
• **Dot-blot** – deeper **inner nuclear / outer plexiform** layers (deep capillary plexus); cells run vertically, so blood forms round dots/blots
• Flame haemorrhages dominate in hypertension; dot-blot dominate in diabetes
• Note: the notes say dot-blot are in the 'inner retinal layer'; they are in the **deeper (middle) retina**
cards.m: Flames burn on the surface; dots sink deep.

cards.q: Hard exudates vs cotton-wool spots: what is each, and why is 'soft exudate' a misleading name?
cards.a:
• **Hard exudates** – yellow, well-defined **lipid/lipoprotein** deposits from leaky vessels, in the outer plexiform layer
• **Cotton-wool spots** – fluffy white patches = **infarcts of the nerve fibre layer** with axoplasmic debris (ischaemia)
• 'Soft exudate' is a misnomer: a cotton-wool spot is **not** an exudate but a micro-infarct
• Many cotton-wool spots signal accelerated hypertension
cards.m: Hard = fat that leaked out; Cotton-wool = nerve fibres that died of thirst.

cards.q: What is a macular star, and which conditions produce one?
cards.a:
• Hard exudates arranged **radially around the fovea** in Henle's fibre layer
• Seen in **severe/malignant hypertension** (exudative phase, with disc swelling)
• Main differential: **neuroretinitis** (disc swelling + star, often Bartonella – cat scratch), papilloedema
• Clears slowly over months once the cause is controlled
cards.m: A star at the macula = leakage from a swollen disc or leaky vessels – check the BP first.

cards.q: What is hypertensive choroidopathy? Describe Elschnig spots and Siegrist streaks.
cards.a:
• Seen in **acute severe/malignant hypertension**, often in young patients
• Mechanism: **fibrinoid necrosis** of choroidal arterioles -> segmental infarction of the choriocapillaris
• **Elschnig spots** – focal choroidal infarcts: yellow patches acutely, later a **black (pigmented) centre with a yellow halo**
• **Siegrist streaks** – **linear pigment flecks along choroidal vessels** (fibrinoid necrosis)
• **Serous (exudative) retinal detachment** may occur
cards.m: Elschnig = spots (dots), Siegrist = streaks (lines) – both mean the choroid has infarcted.

cards.q: What causes hypertensive optic neuropathy, and how does it look?
cards.a:
• Caused by **severe SYSTEMIC (malignant/accelerated) hypertension** -> optic nerve head ischaemia and axoplasmic stasis
• Bilateral **disc swelling** with flame haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, often a macular star
• Note: the notes say 'severe intracranial hypertension'; correct is **severe systemic hypertension**
• It marks **grade 4** (KWB) – a hypertensive emergency
cards.m: Swollen disc + very high BP = malignant hypertension until proven otherwise.

cards.q: Outline the Keith-Wagener-Barker (KWB) classification of hypertensive retinopathy.
cards.a:
• **Group 1** – slight generalised arteriolar constriction
• **Group 2** – group 1 + **focal narrowing** + **AV nicking**
• **Group 3** – group 2 + **flame haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, hard exudates**
• **Group 4** – group 3 + **optic disc swelling** (malignant hypertension)
• Originally a **prognostic** grading – group 4 carried very high mortality untreated
cards.m: 1 narrow, 2 nick, 3 bleed/spill, 4 swell.

cards.q: How does the Scheie classification differ from KWB?
cards.a:
• Scheie grades **two things separately**:
• **Hypertension**: 0 normal; 1 diffuse arteriolar narrowing; 2 + focal constriction; 3 + retinal haemorrhages (± exudates); 4 + **disc swelling** (with oedema/exudates)
• **Arteriosclerosis**: 1 broadened light reflex; 2 + AV crossing changes; 3 **copper wiring**; 4 **silver wiring**
• KWB combines everything in one scale
cards.m: Scheie splits 'acute leak' from 'chronic stiffening' – two report cards for one eye.

cards.q: What is the differential diagnosis of a swollen optic disc in a hypertensive patient, and when should you doubt the diagnosis?
cards.a:
• **Diabetic papillopathy**
• **Central retinal vein occlusion** – unilateral, haemorrhages in all four quadrants
• **AION** – sudden painless loss, altitudinal field defect, usually unilateral
• **Neuroretinitis** – unilateral, macular star, young
• **Papilloedema** (raised ICP) – check for headache, vomiting; needs neuroimaging
• Hypertensive changes are **bilateral** – strongly unilateral findings suggest **CRVO or carotid/ocular ischaemic disease**
cards.m: Hypertension hits both eyes; one-eyed changes need a different explanation.

cards.q: How is hypertensive retinopathy managed according to severity?
cards.a:
• **Mild** (narrowing, AV nicking) – BP control with regular monitoring
• **Moderate** (haemorrhages, exudates, CWS) – **refer to physician**; exclude **diabetes**, check cardiovascular status, control BP
• **Severe** (disc swelling ± choroidopathy) – **urgent** treatment; screen for **target-organ damage** (renal, cardiac, brain)
• Haemorrhages, CWS, exudates and disc swelling resolve over weeks-months; **sclerotic changes persist**
cards.m: The eye is the messenger – the treatment is the blood pressure.

cards.q: A patient has bilateral disc swelling, flame haemorrhages and BP 220/130 mmHg. What is the immediate plan and the main danger in treatment?
cards.a:
• This is **hypertensive emergency (KWB grade 4)** – **admit** under medicine (HDU), same-day ophthalmology review
• **Controlled** BP reduction: lower mean arterial pressure by about **25% in the first hours**, then gradually towards 160/100 over the next 2-6 h
• **Avoid a precipitous drop** – autoregulation is reset high, so rapid lowering causes **optic nerve (and brain) infarction** and permanent visual loss
• Look for target-organ damage: renal function, urine, ECG, troponin, neurology, CT brain if indicated
cards.m: Bring the BP down by the stairs, not the lift.

cards.q: A 28-year-old has hypertensive retinopathy. What must you think about beyond essential hypertension?
cards.a:
• **Secondary hypertension** is likely in the young:
• **Renal** – glomerulonephritis, renal artery stenosis
• **Endocrine** – phaeochromocytoma, Conn, Cushing
• **Coarctation of the aorta** (radio-femoral delay)
• **Pre-eclampsia/eclampsia** in pregnancy – choroidopathy and serous RD
• Also recreational drugs (cocaine, amphetamines)
cards.m: Young + retinopathy = look for a cause, not just a tablet.

cards.q: What are the complications of hypertensive retinopathy and why can vision be lost?
cards.a:
• Vascular: **retinal vein occlusion** (at AV crossings), **retinal artery occlusion**, **retinal arteriolar macroaneurysm**, emboli
• Optic nerve: **AION**; **secondary optic atrophy** after prolonged disc swelling
• Macula: retinal pigment changes after **exudative RD**, cystoid macular oedema, epiretinal membrane
• **Hypertension accelerates diabetic retinopathy** (mixed retinopathy) – control BP in every diabetic
cards.m: High BP blocks the veins, bursts the arterioles and starves the nerve.

cards.q: How common is diabetic retinopathy, and how does its prevalence change with duration of diabetes?
cards.a:
• **Commonest cause of visual loss in working-age adults**
• **~5%** already have DR at diagnosis (mainly T2DM – onset precedes diagnosis)
• **40-50%** after 10 years
• After 20 years: **almost all T1DM** and **>60% of T2DM**
• ~90% after 30 years
cards.m: 5 at the start, half at 10, nearly all at 20.

cards.q: What is the basic pathogenesis of diabetic retinopathy?
cards.a:
• A **microangiopathy** of retinal capillaries causing two end results: **leakage** and **occlusion**
• Capillaropathy: **pericyte loss**, **basement membrane thickening**, endothelial proliferation/dysfunction
• Haematological: RBC deformation and rouleaux, stiff activated leucocytes, **sticky platelets**, raised plasma viscosity
• Occlusion -> **ischaemia -> VEGF release -> neovascularisation**
• Leakage -> oedema and hard exudates (maculopathy)
cards.m: Leak or block: leaking gives oedema and exudates; blocking gives ischaemia and new vessels.

cards.q: What are the risk factors for diabetic retinopathy and its progression? Which is strongest?
cards.a:
• **Duration of diabetes** – strongest predictor
• **Poor glycaemic control**
• **Hypertension**, **nephropathy**, **pregnancy**
• Others: hyperlipidaemia, smoking, obesity, anaemia, **cataract surgery** (can worsen DR/DME)
• Pearl: a **rapid fall in HbA1c** can transiently worsen DR ('early worsening') – review the eyes when control is tightened quickly
cards.m: Duration you cannot change; Sugar, Pressure, Lipids you can.

cards.q: What is the earliest clinical sign of diabetic retinopathy, and what is it?
cards.a:
• **Microaneurysm**
• Saccular outpouching of a capillary wall (after pericyte loss), **10-100 µm**
• Tiny **red dots with sharp margins**, often next to areas of capillary non-perfusion
• Thin-walled with proliferated endothelium – leak fluid and lipid
• Microaneurysms alone = **mild NPDR**
cards.m: First sign = smallest red dot; pericytes go, the wall balloons.

cards.q: Describe the four haemorrhage shapes seen in DR and the retinal level of each.
cards.a:
• **Flame** – superficial **nerve fibre layer** (follow axons)
• **Dot** – small, round; **inner nuclear / outer plexiform** layers
• **Blot** – larger, from the **deep capillary plexus** in the middle retina; many blots signal ischaemia
• **Boat-shaped** – **preretinal (subhyaloid)**, flat top fluid level; a sign of **PDR**
• Blood in the gel = **vitreous haemorrhage** (also PDR)
cards.m: The deeper the blood, the rounder it looks; in front of the retina it floats like a boat.

cards.q: What are hard exudates made of, where do they lie, and what pattern is most worrying?
cards.a:
• **Lipid, lipoprotein and lipid-laden macrophages** leaked from microaneurysms/capillaries
• Lie in the **outer plexiform layer**
• Shiny yellow-white spots with distinct irregular borders
• Form **clusters, circinate rings** (around a leaking microaneurysm) or star figures
• Exudates **near the fovea** = maculopathy -> refer
cards.m: A circinate ring is a fence of fat around the leaking point – laser or inject at its centre.

cards.q: Which fundus signs indicate retinal ischaemia in DR, and why do they matter?
cards.a:
• **Cotton-wool spots** – nerve fibre layer infarcts (capillary non-perfusion)
• **Venous changes** – dilatation, tortuosity, **venous beading** ('sausage-string')
• **IRMA** – intraretinal microvascular abnormalities: dilated shunt vessels within the retina
• **Blot haemorrhages**
• They warn that **neovascularisation is coming** (pre-proliferative) – they define severe NPDR
cards.m: Ischaemic signs are the smoke; new vessels are the fire.

cards.q: List the 10 retinal layers from inner to outer, with a memory aid.
cards.a:
• **I**nner limiting membrane
• **N**erve fibre layer, **G**anglion cell layer
• **I**nner **p**lexiform, **I**nner **n**uclear
• **O**uter **p**lexiform, **O**uter **n**uclear
• **E**xternal limiting membrane, **P**hotoreceptors, **R**PE
cards.m: ING IpIn OpOn EPR – read it inner to outer.

cards.q: Outline the International Clinical Diabetic Retinopathy Severity Scale.
cards.a:
• **No apparent DR** – no abnormalities
• **Mild NPDR** – **microaneurysms only**
• **Moderate NPDR** – more than microaneurysms but less than severe
• **Severe NPDR** – any one of the **4-2-1** rule, no PDR
• **PDR** – neovascularisation and/or vitreous/preretinal haemorrhage
• **Advanced diabetic eye disease** – TRD, persistent VH, neovascular glaucoma
• **Maculopathy** graded separately – can occur at any stage
cards.m: None -> Mild -> Moderate -> Severe -> Proliferative -> Advanced; macula is a separate box.

cards.q: State the 4-2-1 rule for severe NPDR correctly.
cards.a:
• Any ONE of (and no PDR):
• **>20 intraretinal haemorrhages in each of 4 quadrants**
• **Definite venous beading in ≥2 quadrants**
• **Prominent IRMA in ≥1 quadrant**
• ~50% risk of progression to PDR within a year -> refer
• Note: the notes write 'Microaneurysm (>20 intraretinal haemorrhage)'; the criterion is **intraretinal HAEMORRHAGES**, not microaneurysms
cards.m: 4 quadrants of Haemorrhages, 2 of Beading, 1 of IRMA – H-B-I, 4-2-1.

cards.q: What defines proliferative DR and advanced diabetic eye disease?
cards.a:
• **PDR**: **NVD** (new vessels on/within 1 disc diameter of the disc) or **NVE**, and/or **preretinal or vitreous haemorrhage**
• New vessels are VEGF-driven, fragile, grow along the posterior hyaloid
• Fibrous proliferation follows -> contracts with the vitreous
• **Advanced diabetic eye disease**: **tractional RD**, significant persistent **vitreous haemorrhage**, **neovascular (rubeotic) glaucoma**
cards.m: New vessels bleed, scar, then pull – haemorrhage, fibrosis, traction.

cards.q: What is diabetic maculopathy, how is it classified, and why does it matter most for vision?
cards.a:
• Oedema, exudates or ischaemia at the macula – can occur at **any** DR stage, T1 or T2
• Types: **focal**, **diffuse**, **ischaemic**, **mixed**
• **Diabetic macular oedema** is the **commonest cause of visual loss in DR** (PDR causes the most severe loss)
• **Centre-involving DME** with reduced VA is sight-threatening
• Diagnosed clinically and confirmed/quantified with **OCT** (central subfield thickness)
cards.m: PDR blinds dramatically; maculopathy blinds commonly.

cards.q: Why screen for diabetic retinopathy, and how is screening done in Malaysian primary care?
cards.a:
• DR is often **asymptomatic** until sight-threatening (VH, maculopathy); treatment prevents loss – it does not restore it
• Methods: **non-mydriatic or mydriatic fundus camera** (KK screening), direct/indirect ophthalmoscopy, slit lamp
• Include **visual acuity** (Snellen) at every screen
• Dilate with **tropicamide 1%** in selected cases (small pupil, ungradable photo) – raises sensitivity
• Caution: dilation can precipitate angle closure in high-risk eyes; tropicamide 1% alone has not been reported to
• Ungradable photo = **refer**
cards.m: No symptoms does not mean no retinopathy – the camera sees it first.

cards.q: When should the FIRST diabetic retinopathy screening be done (MOH CPG)?
cards.a:
• **Adult T2DM** – **at diagnosis**
• **Adult T1DM** – **within 3 years** of diagnosis (CPG text 3-5 years; recommendation up to 3)
• **Pre-existing DM planning pregnancy** – **before conception**
• **GDM** – not required, unless diagnosed in the **first trimester** (then as pre-existing DM)
• **Children T1DM** – at **age 9 with 5 years'** duration or **age 11 with 2 years'**; T2DM children at diagnosis
cards.m: Type 2 = today (it has been brewing for years); Type 1 = give it up to 3 years.

cards.q: What is the MOH follow-up/referral schedule by DR grade (non-pregnant)?
cards.a:
• **No DR** – rescreen **12-24 months** (annually if high-risk: long duration, poor sugar/BP/lipid control)
• **Mild NPDR, no maculopathy** – **9-12 months**
• **Moderate NPDR, no maculopathy** – **6 months**
• **Severe NPDR** or **any maculopathy** – **refer to ophthalmologist**
• **PDR / advanced diabetic eye disease** – **refer urgently**
• Note: the notes give 'yearly' for no DR and 3-monthly review for severe NPDR; follow the **Malaysian CPG** above
cards.m: 12-24, 9-12, 6, then hand over: Severe or Macula -> eye clinic; Proliferative -> urgently.

cards.q: How often should a pregnant woman with pre-existing diabetes have her retina examined?
cards.a:
• Pregnancy **accelerates DR** (metabolic and haemodynamic changes, rapid tightening of control)
• **Before conception** – baseline exam and counselling
• **No DR to mild NPDR** – every **3 months** during pregnancy
• **Moderate NPDR or worse** – **refer to ophthalmologist**
• GDM diagnosed after the first trimester – no DR screening needed
cards.m: Pregnant diabetic: eyes every trimester.

cards.q: How urgently should a diabetic be referred to the eye clinic (MOH CPG Table 4)?
cards.a:
• **Same day (emergency)** – **sudden severe visual loss**; symptoms/signs of **acute retinal detachment**
• **Within 1 week** – **new vessels**, **preretinal or vitreous haemorrhage**, **rubeosis iridis**
• **Within 4 weeks** – unexplained VA drop, **any maculopathy**, **severe NPDR**, worsening retinopathy
cards.m: Day – Week – Month: Detachment/sudden loss, new vessels/blood, macula/severe NPDR.

cards.q: What is panretinal photocoagulation (PRP): indication, mechanism and side effects?
cards.a:
• Indication: **PDR** (and selected severe NPDR, e.g. poor follow-up, pregnancy)
• Mechanism: laser destroys ischaemic peripheral retina -> **less VEGF** -> new vessels **regress**
• Given as ~1200-2000 burns over several sessions, sparing the macula
• Side effects: **constricted visual field** (driving), **reduced night vision**, reduced VA/worsened macular oedema, haemorrhage, accidental foveal burn
• Focal/grid laser is a different treatment – applied to leaking areas in maculopathy
cards.m: PRP sacrifices the periphery to save the centre.

cards.q: What is first-line treatment for centre-involving diabetic macular oedema with reduced vision, and what is the role of laser and steroid?
cards.a:
• **Intravitreal anti-VEGF** (ranibizumab licensed; aflibercept; bevacizumab off-label) – improves VA more often than laser
• Monitor with **OCT** and VA; re-inject while improving
• **Focal/grid laser**: if anti-VEGF unavailable, persistent DME after **≥6 months** of anti-VEGF, or non-centre DME in selected cases
• **Intravitreal steroid**: persistent DME, especially **pseudophakic** eyes (watch IOP, cataract)
• Always optimise **glucose, BP and lipids**
cards.m: Centre-involving + blurred = inject; laser and steroid are the back-up team.

cards.q: When is vitrectomy indicated in DR, and what complication follows iris neovascularisation?
cards.a:
• **Vitrectomy** (pars plana):
• **Non-clearing vitreous haemorrhage** (earlier if T1DM, no prior PRP, or rubeosis)
• **Tractional RD involving or threatening the macula**
• Anti-VEGF pre-op reduces intra-operative bleeding
• **Rubeosis iridis** blocks the angle -> **neovascular glaucoma**: painful, very high IOP – PRP, anti-VEGF, IOP control
cards.m: Blood that will not clear or retina being pulled = time for the vitrectomy surgeon.

cards.q: List the main causes of optic neuropathy.
cards.a:
• **Inflammatory** – optic neuritis
• **Ischaemic** – NAION, arteritic AION, posterior ION, diabetic papillopathy
• **Hereditary** – Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON)
• **Glaucomatous**; **nutritional/toxic**; **traumatic**
• **Compressive** (orbital/pituitary mass); **infiltrative** (sarcoid, tumour, infection)
• **Papilloedema** – disc swelling from raised **INTRACRANIAL** pressure
• Note: the notes say papilloedema is 'secondary to increased IOP'; correct is **raised intracranial pressure**
cards.m: I-I-H-G-N-T-C-I-P: Inflamed, Ischaemic, Hereditary, Glaucoma, Nutrition/toxic, Trauma, Compression, Infiltration, Pressure (ICP).

cards.q: What are the clinical signs of optic nerve dysfunction, and how do you test for them?
cards.a:
• **Reduced visual acuity** (Snellen)
• **RAPD** – swinging flashlight test: affected pupil dilates when light swings to it (Marcus Gunn pupil)
• **Dyschromatopsia**, especially **red desaturation** – Ishihara plates, red-target comparison
• **Reduced contrast sensitivity** and brightness
• **Visual field defect** – central/caecocentral scotoma typical of optic neuritis
• Disc may be normal, swollen or pale depending on site and stage
cards.m: Optic nerve = ARCC: Acuity, RAPD, Colour, Contrast.

cards.q: What is optic neuritis, and how is it classified by clinical appearance?
cards.a:
• **Inflammation/demyelination of the optic nerve**
• **Retrobulbar neuritis** – nerve behind the globe; **disc normal**; commonest in **adults**, linked to **MS**
• **Papillitis** – optic nerve head; **hyperaemic swollen disc** ± peripapillary flame haemorrhages; commonest in **children**
• **Neuroretinitis** – papillitis + **macular star**; least common, rarely demyelinating
• Aetiological groups: demyelinating, infectious, parainfectious, non-infectious
cards.m: Behind the eye, on the disc, or disc + macula – Retro, Papill, Neuroretin.

cards.q: Describe the typical patient and presentation of demyelinating optic neuritis.
cards.a:
• Young adult **20-50 y**, **women** more than men
• **Subacute** unilateral visual loss over hours-days, worst at about 1-2 weeks
• **Pain on eye movement** in ~90%, periocular ache, globe tenderness
• Colours look **'washed out'**; central blur
• Signs: reduced VA, **RAPD**, **red desaturation**, central scotoma; disc **normal** (retrobulbar) or swollen
• Note: the notes list 'painless' on p44 but 'pain' on p45 – typical demyelinating optic neuritis is **PAINFUL**
cards.m: Young woman, painful eye movements, washed-out colours.

cards.q: In retrobulbar neuritis the disc looks normal. How can you still confirm an optic nerve problem at the bedside?
cards.a:
• **RAPD** in the affected eye (unless bilateral and symmetrical)
• **Red desaturation** / reduced Ishihara score – often worse than the acuity would predict
• **Central scotoma** on confrontation or perimetry
• Normal anterior segment and macula exclude other causes of visual loss
• Optic atrophy (temporal pallor) appears weeks later
cards.m: Retrobulbar neuritis: the patient sees nothing, and the doctor sees nothing.

cards.q: How do you distinguish papillitis from papilloedema?
cards.a:
• **Papilloedema** = disc swelling from **raised intracranial pressure** – by definition
• Papilloedema: **bilateral**, **VA and colour normal early**, no RAPD, **enlarged blind spot**; headache worse lying/morning, vomiting, transient obscurations
• Papillitis: usually **unilateral**, **VA and colour reduced early**, **RAPD**, central scotoma, pain on eye movement
• Papilloedema -> **urgent CT/MRI (with venography) before lumbar puncture**
cards.m: Papilloedema: big disc, good vision. Papillitis: big disc, bad vision.

cards.q: What is Uhthoff phenomenon?
cards.a:
• Transient **worsening of vision with heat or exercise** (hot shower, fever, sport) in a patient with previous optic neuritis/MS
• Raised temperature slows or blocks conduction in **demyelinated** fibres
• Recovers when the body cools
• Not a new relapse – reassure
cards.m: Heat melts the signal through damaged myelin.

cards.q: What investigations are used in suspected demyelinating optic neuritis?
cards.a:
• **MRI brain and orbits with gadolinium** – optic nerve enhancement; periventricular **white matter lesions** (best predictor of MS)
• **CSF** – **oligoclonal bands** on protein electrophoresis
• **Visual evoked potentials** – **delayed P100 latency** (conduction delay)
• Atypical cases: **AQP4 and MOG antibodies**, ESR/CRP, syphilis serology, ACE, CXR
• Perimetry and colour vision to document and follow
cards.m: MRI predicts, CSF supports, VEP times the delay.

cards.q: How does the baseline MRI change the risk of multiple sclerosis after a first optic neuritis?
cards.a:
• **≥1 typical white matter lesion** -> high risk of MS: about **50-70% over 15 years**
• **Normal MRI** -> about **25%** over 15 years
• Those with lesions are referred to neurology for **disease-modifying (immunomodulatory) therapy**, which delays progression to MS
• Optic neuritis is the presenting event in about a quarter of MS cases
cards.m: Lesions on the scan = lit fuse for MS.

cards.q: What did the Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial show about steroids?
cards.a:
• **IV methylprednisolone 1 g/day for 3 days**, then oral prednisolone ~1 mg/kg/day for 11 days
• **Speeds recovery** but **does not change final visual acuity**
• Short-term reduction in conversion to MS
• **Oral prednisolone ALONE at standard dose increased recurrence** -> avoid
• Used for severe loss, bilateral disease, poor fellow eye, or occupational need
• Note: the notes write 'steriod regimen / immunodulatory'; the agents are **steroids** and **immunomodulatory** therapy
cards.m: IV first then oral – never oral alone.

cards.q: What is the visual prognosis of typical demyelinating optic neuritis?
cards.a:
• Spontaneous recovery begins within **2-3 weeks**
• About **90% recover to 6/12 or better** by a few months to a year
• Residual **colour, contrast and brightness** deficits common; Uhthoff phenomenon
• **Temporal disc pallor** may develop
• Recurrence in either eye possible, especially with MS
cards.m: Good acuity comes back; the colours may never be quite as bright.

cards.q: Which features of optic neuritis are atypical and suggest NMOSD or MOG disease?
cards.a:
• **Bilateral** or rapidly sequential, **severe** loss (often to CF or worse)
• **Poor or no recovery** by 3 weeks; very marked disc swelling, haemorrhages
• Associated **longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis**, intractable vomiting/hiccups (NMOSD)
• **NMOSD** = **AQP4 antibody**; relatively more common in **Asian** patients; **MOG** antibody disease – bilateral, very swollen discs, steroid-dependent relapses
• Mx: high-dose IV steroids early, **plasma exchange** if poor response; long-term immunosuppression (MS drugs can worsen NMOSD)
cards.m: Both eyes, very bad, no recovery – it is not MS until NMO is excluded.

cards.q: What is neuroretinitis, and what is its classic cause?
cards.a:
• **Papillitis + macular star** (hard exudates around the fovea from disc leakage)
• Classic cause: **cat-scratch disease** – **Bartonella henselae** from a cat scratch/bite
• Also syphilis, Lyme, toxoplasmosis, viral
• **Rarely demyelinating** – low MS risk
• Star may appear 1-2 weeks after the disc swelling; usually good recovery
cards.m: Disc + star = cat scratch – ask about the kitten.

cards.q: Name the infectious and non-infectious (non-demyelinating) causes of optic neuritis.
cards.a:
• **Sinus-related** – sphenoethmoidal sinusitis: recurrent unilateral loss + severe headache; antibiotics ± drainage
• **Syphilis** – papillitis or neuroretinitis in primary/secondary stage
• **Lyme** (Borrelia, tick) – can mimic MS; **Bartonella** – neuroretinitis
• **Cryptococcal meningitis** in AIDS – bilateral acute optic neuritis
• **VZV** – spread from retinitis, immunocompromised
• **Non-infectious**: **sarcoidosis**, **SLE**, polyarteritis nodosa
cards.m: Check syphilis serology in any atypical optic neuritis – it is treatable.

cards.q: What is parainfectious optic neuritis, and how does it differ from demyelinating optic neuritis?
cards.a:
• Follows **viral infection** (measles, mumps, chickenpox, rubella) or **immunisation**
• **Children** more than adults
• Typically **bilateral papillitis**, occasionally neuroretinitis
• **Good prognosis**; most need no treatment
• Severe cases: **IV steroids** ± antiviral
• Contrast: adult demyelinating optic neuritis is usually unilateral, retrobulbar and MS-linked
cards.m: Child + both eyes + recent virus/vaccine = parainfectious; good outlook.

cards.q: Two causes of painless optic neuropathy: LHON and ethambutol toxicity – how do you recognise each?
cards.a:
• **LHON**: young **male**, painless subacute central loss in one eye then the **other within weeks-months**; **mitochondrial DNA** (maternal inheritance, e.g. 11778); disc hyperaemia with telangiectatic vessels, no leakage on FFA; idebenone, genetic counselling
• **Ethambutol** (TB treatment, common in Malaysia): dose-related, usually after **≥2 months**; bilateral central/caecocentral scotomas, **red-green dyschromatopsia**
• Ethambutol: baseline and regular **VA and colour vision** checks; **stop drug** at first symptoms (with the TB physician) – recovery possible if stopped early
• Others: methanol, B12/folate deficiency, alcohol-tobacco amblyopia
cards.m: LHON = Lads, Heredity Of mitochondria (mother), Next eye follows.

cards.q: What is anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy, and which artery is responsible?
cards.a:
• Infarction of the **optic nerve head** (partial or total)
• Due to occlusion/hypoperfusion of the **short posterior ciliary arteries** (from the ophthalmic artery)
• Two types: **non-arteritic (NAION)** – common, atherosclerotic/vascular; **arteritic (AAION)** – giant cell arteritis
• Anterior = **disc swelling** visible acutely
• Posterior ION (retrobulbar, **no disc swelling**) is much rarer – after spinal/cardiac surgery with hypotension or massive blood loss, or GCA
cards.m: Short posterior ciliaries feed the disc: block them and the disc swells and dies.

cards.q: Who gets NAION – what are the risk factors?
cards.a:
• Usually **>50 years**
• **Hypertension** (very common), **diabetes**, **hyperlipidaemia**
• **Nocturnal hypotension** / sudden hypotensive events
• **Obstructive sleep apnoea** (prolonged nocturnal hypoxia)
• Collagen vascular disease, **antiphospholipid syndrome**, hyperhomocysteinaemia
• **Cataract surgery**; drugs – **PDE5 inhibitors** (sildenafil), **amiodarone**
• Structural: a small crowded **'disc at risk'**
cards.m: A vasculopath with a small crowded disc and low BP at night.

cards.q: What is a 'disc at risk', and why is it relevant to NAION?
cards.a:
• A **small, crowded optic disc** with a **small or absent cup** (low cup:disc ratio)
• Axons are packed tightly through a narrow scleral canal
• Mild ischaemic swelling -> **compartment-syndrome** effect -> further ischaemia
• Look at the **fellow eye**: a disc at risk supports NAION
• Arteritic AION does **not** need a crowded disc – a normal or large cup in the fellow eye should raise suspicion of GCA
cards.m: No room in the canal: swelling squeezes its own blood supply.

cards.q: How does NAION typically present?
cards.a:
• **Sudden, painless, monocular** visual loss
• Frequently **noticed on waking** – supports a role for **nocturnal hypotension**
• Often described as a shadow over the lower (or upper) half of vision
• No jaw claudication, scalp tenderness or systemic symptoms (if present, think GCA)
• Fellow eye usually unaffected at presentation
cards.m: Wakes up with half the view gone, no pain.

cards.q: What are the visual function findings in NAION?
cards.a:
• **VA**: normal or only slightly reduced in ~**30%**; moderate-severe loss in ~70%
• **Visual field**: typically **inferior altitudinal** defect (respects the horizontal midline)
• **RAPD** in the affected eye
• **Dyschromatopsia proportional to the VA loss** – unlike optic neuritis, where colour is badly affected even when VA is good
cards.m: NAION halves the field horizontally; colour falls in step with acuity.

cards.q: Describe the optic disc in NAION and how it evolves.
cards.a:
• **Diffuse or sectoral hyperaemic disc swelling**
• A few **peripapillary splinter (flame) haemorrhages**
• Fellow eye: small crowded disc (disc at risk)
• Swelling resolves and **pallor** ensues at **3-6 weeks** (sectoral or diffuse optic atrophy)
• Swelling persisting >6-8 weeks is atypical – reconsider (compression, infiltration)
cards.m: NAION disc = hyperaemic and swollen; AAION disc = pale and swollen.

cards.q: What is arteritic AION, and why is it an emergency?
cards.a:
• AION caused by **giant cell arteritis** (vasculitis of the posterior ciliary arteries)
• Occurs in **30-50% of untreated GCA**, usually within weeks of GCA onset
• **Fellow eye** involved in about a third, often **within days to a week** if untreated
• Patient typically ~70 y, women more than men
• Usually preceded by **amaurosis fugax**, sometimes diplopia; GCA symptoms (headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, PMR)
cards.m: The first eye is usually lost; the emergency is the second eye.

cards.q: What does the fundus look like in arteritic AION, and what else may be seen?
cards.a:
• **Severe loss** is the rule – often **PL or worse**
• **Pale, 'chalky white' oedematous disc** – strongly suggests GCA
• May be accompanied by **cilioretinal artery occlusion** or CRAO (same ophthalmic artery territory)
• Fluorescein angiography: **delayed choroidal filling** (posterior ciliary artery occlusion)
• Severe **optic atrophy** follows over 1-2 months
cards.m: Chalky white disc + elderly + very poor vision = GCA until proven otherwise.

cards.q: Compare NAION and arteritic AION side by side.
cards.a:
• **Age**: NAION >50 (often 60s) vs AAION ~70+
• **Systemic symptoms**: none vs headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, PMR
• **Prodrome**: none vs **amaurosis fugax**
• **VA**: variable, often moderate vs **severe (CF to NPL)**
• **Disc**: **hyperaemic** swelling, crowded fellow disc vs **chalky white** swelling
• **ESR/CRP**: normal vs **markedly raised**
• **Treatment/fellow eye**: no proven treatment vs **urgent high-dose steroids** to protect the fellow eye
cards.m: Red, crowded and quiet = NAION; White, inflamed and blind = arteritic.

cards.q: How do you distinguish NAION from optic neuritis?
cards.a:
• **Age**: >50 vs 20-50
• **Pain**: painless vs **pain on eye movement**
• **Onset**: sudden (on waking) vs subacute over days
• **Colour vision**: in proportion to VA vs **disproportionately poor**
• **Field**: **altitudinal** vs central scotoma
• **Disc**: always swollen (sectoral, haemorrhages) vs normal in retrobulbar neuritis
• **Course**: little recovery vs good spontaneous recovery
cards.m: Old, painless, altitudinal = ischaemic; young, painful, central = inflamed.

cards.q: A 72-year-old has sudden visual loss with a swollen optic disc. What investigations are needed, and what is the immediate step if GCA is possible?
cards.a:
• **Urgent ESR and CRP** (and FBC – platelets often raised) in **every** AION patient over 50
• If GCA is suspected clinically or bloods are raised: **start high-dose steroids the same day** – do not wait for biopsy (IV methylprednisolone if visual loss)
• **Temporal artery biopsy** within ~2 weeks of starting steroids
• NAION work-up: **BP**, **fasting glucose/HbA1c**, **fasting lipids**, ask about **sleep apnoea** symptoms
• Cross-ref: GCA topic for steroid dosing and biopsy details
cards.m: Swollen disc over 50: bloods today, steroids today if in doubt.

cards.q: Which drug associations with NAION should you ask about in clinic?
cards.a:
• **PDE5 inhibitors** – sildenafil, tadalafil (erectile dysfunction): counsel to stop after NAION, especially if the fellow disc is at risk
• **Amiodarone** – optic neuropathy that is often **bilateral, insidious**, with prolonged disc swelling; review with cardiologist
• **Antihypertensives at night** – nocturnal hypotension
• Interferon-alpha and some anorectic drugs have also been implicated
cards.m: Ask the 3 'night' questions: the little blue pill, the heart pill, the BP pill at bedtime.

cards.q: How is NAION managed?
cards.a:
• **No proven definitive treatment** for the affected eye
• **Treat vascular risk factors**: BP, diabetes, lipids, smoking; investigate/treat **sleep apnoea**
• **Aspirin** is often given – reduces **systemic vascular events** but does **not** reduce fellow-eye involvement
• Avoid **nocturnal hypotension** – e.g. avoid taking antihypertensives at bedtime where possible
• **No role** for optic nerve sheath decompression (no benefit, possible harm in IONDT); steroids not routinely used
cards.m: Treat the patient's vessels, not the dead disc.

cards.q: What is the visual prognosis in NAION and in arteritic AION?
cards.a:
• **NAION**: some improvement is common; ~**50% reach 6/9 or better**, ~25% only 6/60 or worse
• NAION recurrence in the same eye is uncommon (~**6%**); fellow eye at risk over years (~15% in 5 years)
• **AAION**: **very poor** – visual loss is usually **permanent** (rare partial recovery with prompt steroids)
• Aim in AAION is to **save the fellow eye**: steroids ± aspirin; methotrexate or tocilizumab as steroid-sparing/adjunct
cards.m: NAION: half see 6/9. AAION: the lost eye stays lost – protect the other.

cards.q: What is the difference between age-related maculopathy (ARM) and age-related macular degeneration (AMD)?
cards.a:
• **ARM** – exaggeration of normal ageing at the macula: **drusen** and **RPE hyper-/hypopigmentation**, vision usually good
• **AMD** – the more advanced, **sight-threatening** stage: **geographic atrophy** (dry) or **choroidal neovascularisation** (wet)
• Affects people usually **>50-55 years**
• **Leading cause of legal blindness in the developed world**; rising in ageing Malaysia
cards.m: ARM = the warning signs; AMD = the damage.

cards.q: What are drusen, and exactly where do they lie?
cards.a:
• Discrete deposits of abnormal extracellular material **derived from the RPE** (failure to clear photoreceptor debris)
• Located **between the basal lamina of the RPE and the inner collagenous layer of Bruch membrane**
• Seen as **yellow excrescences** beneath the RPE
• Small hard drusen are common with age; **large soft confluent drusen** (≥125 µm) carry a high risk of progression
cards.m: Drusen are rubbish bags left under the RPE's front door.

cards.q: Why does AMD destroy reading and face recognition but spare the ability to walk around?
cards.a:
• AMD damages the **macula** (cone-rich, central ~5 mm) -> **central vision** lost
• **Peripheral (navigational) retina is preserved** -> patients rarely become totally blind
• Central scotoma means difficulty **reading, recognising faces, driving, seeing fine detail**
• Hence **low vision aids** and magnifiers are useful
cards.m: AMD takes away the bull's-eye but leaves the target.

cards.q: What are the risk factors for AMD, and which modifiable one matters most?
cards.a:
• **Non-modifiable**: **age** (strongest), **genetics**/family history (e.g. complement factor H), ethnicity
• **Modifiable**: **smoking** (about **2x** risk – most important modifiable factor), hypertension, poor diet low in antioxidants, obesity, hypercholesterolaemia
• **Stopping smoking** is the single most useful preventive advice
cards.m: Age you cannot stop – smoking you can.

cards.q: What is the key symptom of macular disease like AMD, and what other symptoms occur?
cards.a:
• **Metamorphopsia** – straight lines look **wavy/distorted** (door frames, tiles)
• **Central scotoma** / blurred central vision
• **Micropsia** (objects look smaller – photoreceptors spread apart by fluid) is more typical than macropsia
• Difficulty reading, needing more light
• Note: the notes list 'macropsia'; **micropsia** is the classic size distortion and **metamorphopsia** the key symptom
cards.m: Wavy lines in an elderly patient = macula until proven otherwise.

cards.q: How is the Amsler grid used in AMD?
cards.a:
• A **10 x 10 cm grid** with a central fixation dot, held at reading distance, **one eye at a time**, with reading glasses
• Detects **distortion** (wavy lines) or **missing areas** (scotoma) in the central 10-20°
• Used for **home self-monitoring** of dry AMD and the fellow eye
• **New distortion = attend promptly** (possible conversion to wet AMD)
cards.m: Look at the dot, not the lines – if the lines bend, see the eye doctor.

cards.q: Compare dry (atrophic) and wet (exudative) AMD.
cards.a:
• **Dry ~90%** of AMD: drusen, RPE changes, **geographic atrophy**, photoreceptor loss; **gradual over years**, often asymptomatic early
• **Wet ~10%**: **choroidal neovascularisation** -> subretinal fluid, haemorrhage, fibrosis; **rapid over weeks**, metamorphopsia
• Yet wet AMD causes about **90% of severe visual loss** from AMD
• Dry can convert to wet at any time
cards.m: Dry is common and slow; wet is rare, fast and blinding.

cards.q: What is geographic atrophy?
cards.a:
• The advanced form of **dry AMD**
• **Sharply demarcated** area(s) of **RPE and photoreceptor atrophy**; underlying **choroidal vessels become visible**
• Expands slowly over years; vision lost when the fovea is involved
• Scotoma more obvious in dim light/when light-adapting
• No restorative treatment; complement inhibitors (e.g. pegcetacoplan) slow growth in some countries but do not improve vision
cards.m: Like a map of bare land where the RPE has been eroded away.

cards.q: What are the fundus features of wet AMD, and where does the blood lie?
cards.a:
• **Choroidal neovascular membrane** grows through Bruch membrane into the **sub-RPE / subretinal** space
• Grey-green membrane, **subretinal fluid** (retinal elevation), **subretinal or sub-RPE haemorrhage**, hard exudates, pigment epithelial detachment
• End stage: **subretinal fibrosis – disciform scar**
• Large bleeds may break through into the vitreous (vitreous haemorrhage)
• Note: the notes say 'pre-retinal haemorrhage'; wet AMD bleeding is typically **SUBRETINAL/sub-RPE**
cards.m: Wet AMD bleeds UNDER the retina – a blister of blood, not a puddle on top.

cards.q: An elderly patient reports new distortion in one eye. How urgently should they be referred, and what is the key investigation?
cards.a:
• Suspect **wet AMD** – refer **urgently (seen within about 1-2 weeks)**; treatment delay = permanent loss
• **OCT** (optical coherence tomography) – **key investigation**: shows intra-/subretinal fluid, PED, CNV; also used to monitor every injection
• **Fluorescein angiography** – shows CNV leakage and type
• **ICG angiography** if **polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy** suspected (common in Asian patients)
cards.m: Sudden wavy lines = fast-track referral; OCT shows the fluid.

cards.q: How is dry AMD managed?
cards.a:
• **Stop smoking**; healthy diet rich in green leafy vegetables and fish
• **UV protection** (sunglasses)
• **Zinc and antioxidant supplements** (AREDS2) for intermediate/advanced disease
• **Low vision aids**: magnifiers, good lighting, large print; low-vision clinic
• **Amsler grid** self-monitoring for conversion to wet AMD
• Control BP, lipids, weight
cards.m: Dry AMD: Stop smoking, Supplement, Shade, Support (low vision), Self-monitor.

cards.q: What is in the AREDS2 supplement, who benefits, and why was beta-carotene removed?
cards.a:
• Contains **vitamin C, vitamin E, zinc, copper** (prevents zinc-induced copper deficiency), **lutein and zeaxanthin**
• Benefit: **intermediate AMD** (large drusen) or **advanced AMD in one eye** – reduces progression to advanced AMD by about 25% over 5 years
• **No benefit** in no or early AMD
• **Beta-carotene removed** – increases **lung cancer** risk in (ex-)smokers; lutein/zeaxanthin replaced it
cards.m: AREDS2 = 'C-E-Zinc-Copper-Lutein' – no carrots for smokers.

cards.q: How does anti-VEGF therapy work in wet AMD, and which drugs are used?
cards.a:
• **VEGF stimulates** angiogenesis and vascular permeability
• **Anti-VEGF BLOCKS** new vessel growth and leakage -> fluid resolves, vision stabilises/improves
• Given by **intravitreal injection**: **ranibizumab**, **aflibercept**, **bevacizumab** (off-label, low cost), **faricimab** (anti-VEGF + anti-angiopoietin-2)
• **First-line** for wet AMD
• Note: the notes say anti-VEGF 'stimulates angiogenesis and vascular permeability'; it is **VEGF** that stimulates them – anti-VEGF **blocks** them
cards.m: VEGF = Very Eager Growth Factor; anti-VEGF puts on the brakes.

cards.q: How are anti-VEGF injections scheduled, and what is the most serious risk to warn about?
cards.a:
• **Loading**: monthly injections **x3**
• Then **treat-and-extend** (or PRN): interval lengthened while OCT is dry, shortened if fluid returns
• Long-term, often lifelong treatment – adherence is key
• Most serious risk: **endophthalmitis** (about 1 in 1000-3000 injections); also raised IOP, RD, lens touch
• Advise: **pain, increasing redness or worsening vision after injection -> attend the same day**
cards.m: Three to load, then extend while dry.

cards.q: What are the roles of thermal laser and verteporfin photodynamic therapy in wet AMD today?
cards.a:
• **Thermal laser photocoagulation**: only for well-demarcated **extrafoveal** CNV (MPS study); burns retina -> scotoma, high recurrence – now rarely used
• **Verteporfin PDT**: IV photosensitiser activated by a **non-thermal 689 nm laser** -> closes abnormal vessels; retreatment ~3-monthly
• Today PDT is mainly used (with anti-VEGF) for **polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy**, common in Asian patients
• Note: the notes call laser and injections 'prevention' – they are **treatments**; PDT uses a specific 689 nm laser, not 'low light'
cards.m: Laser burns, PDT targets, anti-VEGF blocks – only the last is first-line.

cards.q: An 82-year-old with bilateral advanced AMD sees people and flowers that are not there but knows they are not real. What is this, and how do you manage it?
cards.a:
• **Charles Bonnet syndrome** – complex **visual hallucinations** in people with significant visual loss
• **Insight preserved**; no other psychiatric or neurological features
• Mechanism: deafferented visual cortex 'fills in' (release hallucinations)
• Mx: **explain and reassure** (patients fear dementia), maximise vision/lighting, blinking or eye movements may stop episodes
• Exclude delirium/dementia if insight is lost or other senses are involved
cards.m: Seeing things but knowing they are not real = Charles Bonnet, not madness.

mcq.stem:
A 4-year-old girl is brought to the eye clinic because her mother has noticed her left eye turning inwards for 6 months, now for most of the day. Her father had a squint treated with patching as a child. VA (picture test) is right 6/6 and left 6/12. The corneal light reflex is centred on the right cornea and displaced temporally on the left. On covering the right eye, the left eye moves outwards to take up fixation. The deviation measures about 30 prism dioptres in the primary position and is the same in right, left, up and down gaze; both eyes abduct fully. Pupils, fundi and neurological examination are normal.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Left sixth nerve palsy
Decompensated left esophoria
Left concomitant esotropia
Pseudo-esotropia from epicanthic folds
Left Duane retraction syndrome
mcq.e: An angle that is the **same in all directions of gaze**, with full eye movements and no neurological signs, defines a **concomitant (non-paralytic)** squint — typical of childhood onset, often with a family history. Movement of the left eye when the right is covered proves a **manifest** deviation (tropia), and the temporally displaced light reflex shows the eye is turned in. A sixth nerve palsy would instead limit abduction, with an angle that increases on gaze to the affected side. The lower VA in the deviating eye warns of early strabismic amblyopia.
w: Wrong - a sixth nerve palsy is inconcomitant: limited abduction and an angle that increases on gaze to the affected side.
Wrong - a phoria is latent; the eyes would look straight and the fellow eye would not move on the cover test.
Correct - constant inward deviation, equal angle in all gazes, full motility, childhood onset and family history = concomitant esotropia.
Wrong - a pseudosquint has centred symmetrical light reflexes and no movement on the cover test.
Wrong - Duane syndrome shows limited abduction (or adduction) with globe retraction and narrowing of the lid fissure on adduction.

mcq.stem:
A 10-month-old boy is referred from a Klinik Kesihatan because his parents think his eyes 'cross', especially when he looks to the side. He has a broad, flat nasal bridge with prominent epicanthic folds. He fixes and follows a small toy with each eye. Corneal light reflexes are centred and symmetrical, there is no movement on cover testing of either eye, eye movements are full and red reflexes are bright and equal. Cycloplegic refraction is +1.50 D in each eye.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Reassure; review if the concern persists
Prescribe +1.50 D glasses to be worn full time
Patch the right eye for 2 hours a day
List for bilateral medial rectus recession
Request urgent MRI brain for sixth nerve palsy
mcq.e: Broad epicanthic folds hide the nasal sclera, so the eyes **look** turned in (**pseudo-esotropia**), especially on side gaze. A true squint is excluded objectively: centred symmetrical **Hirschberg** reflexes and no refixation movement on the **cover test**, with normal red reflexes. +1.50 D is physiological hyperopia at this age and needs no glasses. The appearance improves as the nasal bridge develops; parents are asked to return if they see a definite deviation.
w: Correct - normal Hirschberg, cover test, motility and red reflexes = pseudosquint; reassure with a safety-net review.
Wrong - +1.50 D is normal infant hyperopia and does not cause esotropia; glasses are not indicated.
Wrong - there is no deviation or amblyopia; occlusion could itself make the good eye amblyopic.
Wrong - operating on a squint that does not exist would create a consecutive exotropia.
Wrong - full abduction and straight eyes exclude a sixth nerve palsy; imaging is not indicated.

mcq.stem:
A 21-year-old engineering student at a university health clinic complains of tired eyes and occasional blurring after long study sessions. Her eyes look straight and VA is 6/6 in each eye with her current glasses. On the cover test, when either eye is covered the fellow eye does not move. When the cover is removed from the right eye, that eye is seen to move inwards to regain fixation; the same happens with the left eye. Ocular movements are full.
What do these findings show?
o: Intermittent right exotropia
Constant alternating exotropia
Latent esodeviation (esophoria)
Right sixth nerve palsy
Latent exodeviation (exophoria)
mcq.e: The **cover test** (watch the uncovered eye) detects a **manifest** squint (tropia); here the uncovered eye never moved, so there is no tropia. The **uncover / alternate cover test** breaks fusion and reveals a **latent** deviation (phoria): under the cover the eye drifted outwards and, on uncovering, moved **inwards** to refixate — exophoria. Small phorias are normal; larger ones decompensate with fatigue and cause eye strain, as here.
w: Wrong - an intermittent exotropia is manifest at times, and when it breaks down the fellow eye moves on the cover test.
Wrong - a manifest alternating exotropia would show refixation of the uncovered eye on the cover test.
Wrong - in esophoria the covered eye drifts IN, so on uncovering it moves OUT to refixate.
Wrong - full movements and no manifest deviation exclude a sixth nerve palsy.
Correct - no movement on the cover test (no tropia) with inward recovery on uncovering = exophoria.

mcq.stem:
A 22-month-old girl is brought to a Klinik Kesihatan because her right eye has started drifting outwards over the past month. Her mother shows a flash photograph in which the right pupil looks white while the left looks red. The child is well and developing normally. The medical officer finds a dull, whitish right red reflex and a bright left red reflex; the right eye is exotropic on the cover test.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Patch the left eye 2 hours daily and review in 6 weeks
Urgent referral to the eye clinic for dilated fundus examination
Cycloplegic refraction and glasses at the next KK optometry clinic
Routine squint clinic referral for alignment surgery assessment
Reassure and review in 3 months as intermittent squint is common
mcq.e: A new squint with **leukocoria** in a toddler is **retinoblastoma until proven otherwise** (others: congenital cataract, Coats disease, persistent fetal vasculature). Every child with a new squint needs a red reflex check and **dilated fundus examination**, because a lesion that blocks macular vision causes a sensory squint. Patching, glasses or surgery before the fundus is seen delays potentially life-saving treatment; the referral must be urgent (seen within days).
w: Wrong - occlusion without a diagnosis delays detection of retinoblastoma or cataract.
Correct - leukocoria plus a new squint needs urgent ophthalmic assessment with dilated fundoscopy to exclude retinoblastoma.
Wrong - refraction is part of the work-up, but a routine optometry slot is far too slow for possible retinoblastoma.
Wrong - a sensory squint from an intraocular lesion is not treated by alignment surgery first, and routine priority is unsafe.
Wrong - an abnormal red reflex is never reassuring; a 3-month delay could allow extraocular spread of a tumour.

mcq.stem:
A 48-year-old woman with hypertension presents to the emergency department with a severe headache that began suddenly yesterday and double vision since this morning. The right upper lid covers most of the pupil. When the lid is lifted, the right eye is deviated down and out, cannot adduct, elevate or depress fully, and the right pupil is 7 mm and poorly reactive to light. GCS is 15 and there is no neck stiffness.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Check HbA1c and lipids and review in 3 months
Start oral prednisolone after urgent ESR and CRP
Ice-pack test and AChR antibody assay
Emergency CT brain with CT angiography
Occlude the right eye and arrange orthoptic review
mcq.e: A **third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil** is compressive — classically a **posterior communicating artery aneurysm** — until proven otherwise: the pupillomotor parasympathetic fibres run superficially on the nerve and are compressed early. With a sudden headache this may be a sentinel bleed, so **emergency CT / CT angiography** and neurosurgical referral are needed. Pupil-sparing palsies in diabetic or hypertensive patients are often microvascular, but that is a diagnosis of exclusion.
w: Wrong - managing it as a microvascular palsy is only reasonable when the pupil is spared; this pupil is involved.
Wrong - GCA rarely causes a third nerve palsy, and a dilated pupil points to compression, not vasculitis.
Wrong - myasthenia can mimic ptosis and ophthalmoplegia but never affects the pupil.
Correct - a pupil-involving third nerve palsy with headache = PCOM aneurysm until proven otherwise; image the vessels now.
Wrong - occlusion relieves diplopia, but delaying imaging risks fatal aneurysm rupture.

mcq.stem:
An 8-year-old boy is seen in the paediatric ward with 3 weeks of early-morning headaches and vomiting. Since yesterday he sees two images side by side, worse when looking at the television across the room. His eyes are straight on looking to the right, but on looking left the left eye fails to move beyond the midline and the convergent deviation increases. Both optic discs are swollen with blurred margins; VA is 6/9 in each eye.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Urgent same-day CT or MRI scan of the brain
Lumbar puncture to measure opening pressure
Fresnel prism on his glasses and review in 6 weeks
Patch the right eye to prevent amblyopia
Botulinum toxin to the left medial rectus
mcq.e: Horizontal diplopia worse for distance, with an esotropia that increases on gaze towards a side with an abduction deficit, is a **sixth nerve palsy**. With morning headache, vomiting and bilateral disc swelling it is a **false-localising sign of raised intracranial pressure** (the long intracranial course of CN6 is stretched), so a space-occupying lesion or hydrocephalus must be excluded by **urgent imaging**. Lumbar puncture before imaging risks coning.
w: Correct - raised ICP signs plus a sixth nerve palsy need same-day brain imaging to find the cause.
Wrong - LP before imaging in suspected raised ICP risks tonsillar herniation; image first.
Wrong - prisms are symptomatic and only appropriate once a serious cause has been excluded.
Wrong - amblyopia prevention is secondary; the priority is the potentially life-threatening cause.
Wrong - botulinum toxin is used for persistent palsies after the cause is dealt with, never as the first step.

mcq.stem:
A 3-year-old boy has had an inward-turning eye noticed by his grandmother for 4 months, at first only when he looked at picture books or was tired, now more often. The cover test shows a right esotropia of 25 prism dioptres at near and 15 at distance. Eye movements are full. After cyclopentolate 1%, retinoscopy shows +4.50 D in each eye; fundi and red reflexes are normal.
What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
o: Bilateral medial rectus recession under general anaesthesia
Glasses under-correcting the hyperopia by 2.00 D
Glasses with the full cycloplegic hyperopic correction
Patching of the left eye for 6 hours a day
Orthoptic convergence exercises at home
mcq.e: Onset at 2-4 years, a deviation brought on by near work and significant hyperopia point to **refractive accommodative esotropia**: the child accommodates to clear the hyperopic blur, and the linked **accommodative convergence** drives the eye in. **Full cycloplegic correction worn full time** removes the stimulus and often straightens the eyes completely; surgery is only for a residual non-accommodative angle. Amblyopia is checked and treated once glasses are worn.
w: Wrong - surgery is not first-line; much of the angle is accommodative and will resolve with glasses.
Wrong - under-correcting leaves the child accommodating, so the esotropia persists.
Correct - the full cycloplegic hyperopic prescription relaxes accommodation and with it accommodative convergence.
Wrong - patching treats amblyopia, not the deviation, and the refractive error must be corrected first.
Wrong - convergence exercises are for convergence insufficiency (exodeviation at near) and do not help an esotropia.

mcq.stem:
A 44-year-old woman attends the eye clinic with 2 months of vertical double vision, worse on looking up and in the mornings. She has lost 5 kg and feels anxious and tremulous. Both upper lids are retracted with visible sclera above the limbus, and there is mild bilateral proptosis. The left eye is lower than the right in the primary position; it cannot elevate above the midline and the vertical separation increases on up-gaze. Pupils are normal and there is no ptosis.
What is the most likely cause of her diplopia?
o: Left oculomotor nerve palsy
Ocular myasthenia gravis
Left superior oblique palsy
Decompensated childhood squint
Thyroid restrictive myopathy
mcq.e: An **inconcomitant** (gaze-dependent) vertical deviation in an adult with lid retraction, proptosis and hyperthyroid symptoms is **restrictive thyroid eye disease**. The **inferior rectus** is most often enlarged and fibrosed, tethering the eye so it cannot elevate — the left eye sits low (hypotropia) and diplopia worsens on up-gaze. The forced duction test is positive and CT/MRI shows fusiform muscle-belly enlargement sparing the tendons. Management is prisms and disease control, with surgery once the disease is inactive.
w: Wrong - a third nerve palsy causes ptosis and a down-and-out eye; here the lids are retracted.
Wrong - myasthenia causes variable ptosis and fatigable diplopia, not lid retraction and proptosis.
Wrong - a superior oblique palsy gives a HYPERtropia of the affected eye, worse on down-gaze to the opposite side.
Wrong - a long-standing concomitant squint has the same angle in all gazes and no orbital signs.
Correct - lid retraction, proptosis and limited elevation from a tight inferior rectus = thyroid restrictive myopathy.

mcq.stem:
A 6-year-old girl has worn her full hyperopic glasses for 2 years and her amblyopia has been treated, so VA is now 6/6 in each eye. With her glasses on she still has an alternating esotropia of 30 prism dioptres for both near and distance, unchanged over 12 months. Her parents agree to surgery.
Which procedure is most appropriate to reduce her esotropia?
o: Bilateral medial rectus resection
Bilateral lateral rectus recession
Bilateral superior oblique tenotomy
Bilateral medial rectus recession
Add +3.00 D over the full correction
mcq.e: Squint surgery either **weakens** a muscle by **recession** (moving its insertion back, reducing its effective pull) or **strengthens** it by **resection** (shortening it). An esotropia reflects relatively excessive medial rectus action, so the **medial recti are recessed** (or one medial rectus recession with a lateral rectus resection in the same eye). Surgery is for the residual non-accommodative angle once refraction and amblyopia are optimised; adding plus beyond the cycloplegic refraction blurs distance vision.
w: Wrong - resecting the medial recti strengthens adduction and would increase the esotropia.
Wrong - recessing the lateral recti weakens abduction and is used for EXOtropia.
Wrong - superior oblique weakening is used for A-pattern deviations, not a horizontal esotropia.
Correct - recession weakens both medial recti and reduces the convergent angle.
Wrong - over-plussing beyond the full cycloplegic correction blurs distance vision and will not fix a non-accommodative angle.

mcq.stem:
A 5-year-old boy has had a constant left esotropia since the age of 2, first noticed in family photographs. He has never complained of double vision and plays football normally. With full glasses, VA is right 6/6 and left 6/24, and neither eye has any structural abnormality. His father, who developed a squint at 40 after a head injury, asks why his son does not see double as he did.
What best explains the child's lack of diplopia?
o: Foveal immaturity of the deviating eye prevents image formation
Cortical suppression of the image from the deviating eye
Fusion overcomes the misalignment in the immature brain
Hyperopic glasses blur the second image below threshold
Large-angle squints place the second image outside the field
mcq.e: In the plastic visual system of a young child, the confusing second image from the squinting eye is **actively suppressed by the visual cortex**, so diplopia and confusion do not occur. The price is **strabismic amblyopia** (chronic suppression of the deviating eye) and loss of binocular single vision and stereopsis. Adults with an acquired squint cannot suppress and complain of **diplopia** — so new diplopia in an adult points to a paralytic or restrictive cause.
w: Wrong - the fovea forms images normally; the problem is cortical processing of them.
Correct - cortical suppression abolishes diplopia but causes amblyopia and loss of stereopsis.
Wrong - a constant manifest squint cannot be fused; that is why the eye stays deviated.
Wrong - glasses correct refractive blur in both eyes; they do not remove the second image.
Wrong - even large-angle squints place the image within the binocular field; it is suppressed, not missed.

mcq.stem:
A 7-year-old girl fails the vision test at her Year 1 school health screening. Her parents have never noticed a squint. Unaided VA is right 6/6 and left 6/24, with little improvement on pinhole. The cover test shows straight eyes. Cycloplegic refraction is right +0.50 DS and left +4.50 DS. Anterior segments, media and dilated fundi are normal in both eyes.
What is the most likely type of amblyopia in the left eye?
o: Strabismic amblyopia from a microtropia
Anisometropic (refractive) amblyopia
Stimulus-deprivation amblyopia
Bilateral isoametropic amblyopia
Meridional (astigmatic) amblyopia
mcq.e: Reduced VA in one eye with a large **difference in refractive error** (here 4 D of hyperopic anisometropia), straight eyes and normal ocular structures is **anisometropic amblyopia** — the second commonest type (~20%). Because there is no visible squint it is typically picked up **late**, at school screening. The brain receives a chronically blurred, differently sized image (aniseikonia) from the more hyperopic eye and stops developing it.
w: Wrong - a microtropia can coexist with anisometropia, but the cover test shows no manifest deviation.
Correct - a 4 D hyperopic difference with straight eyes and normal fundi = anisometropic amblyopia.
Wrong - deprivation needs an obstruction of the visual axis (cataract, ptosis, corneal opacity); the media are clear.
Wrong - isoametropic amblyopia is bilateral, from high similar errors in both eyes; the right eye is normal.
Wrong - meridional amblyopia results from uncorrected astigmatism; this refraction is purely spherical.

mcq.stem:
A 4-year-old boy is referred after a pre-school vision screen. He has a small right esotropia. VA (crowded Kay pictures) is right 6/36 and left 6/9. Cycloplegic refraction is right +3.50 DS and left +1.50 DS; fundi are normal. His mother has read about patching online and asks to start it today.
What is the most appropriate first step in his amblyopia treatment?
o: Patch the left eye for 6 hours a day starting today
Atropine 1% to the left eye daily starting today
Patch the right eye for 2 hours a day starting today
Full-time glasses first, recheck VA in 12-16 weeks
Defer treatment until he can read letter charts at 5
mcq.e: The first step in every type of amblyopia is **full correction of the refractive error, worn full time**. Glasses alone (**refractive adaptation**) improve VA by several lines in many children, and some never need occlusion; patching is added only if VA plateaus with a persisting interocular difference. Patching or atropine is applied to the **good** (left) eye, never the amblyopic one, and treatment is not delayed because younger children respond best.
w: Wrong - occlusion before optical correction is premature; the amblyopic eye would still see a blurred image.
Wrong - atropine penalisation is an alternative to patching, but only after glasses have been worn.
Wrong - patching the amblyopic right eye would deepen its amblyopia.
Correct - full-time glasses first; many children improve with refractive adaptation before occlusion is needed.
Wrong - picture tests are reliable at 4 years, and delay loses valuable time in the critical period.

mcq.stem:
A 5-year-old girl with left anisometropic amblyopia has worn full glasses for 4 months; left VA improved from 6/36 to 6/18 and has now plateaued, while the right eye sees 6/6. Her right eye is hyperopic (+2.00 D). She tears off every patch at kindergarten, and her parents ask for an alternative to patching.
Which regimen is most appropriate?
o: Atropine 1% to the right eye, daily/weekends
Atropine 1% to the left eye, daily or weekends
Cyclopentolate 1% to the left eye each morning
Pilocarpine 2% to the right eye each morning
Tropicamide 1% to both eyes each morning
