mcq.e: **Atropine penalisation** blurs the **good** eye (cycloplegia stops it focusing, especially for near), forcing use of the amblyopic eye; for moderate amblyopia it works about as well as patching and adherence is often better. It works best when the good eye is **hyperopic**, because the atropinised eye then cannot accommodate to overcome its hyperopia. Like patching it can rarely cause reverse amblyopia, so the good eye's VA is monitored.
w: Correct - atropine 1% to the good (right) eye penalises it and forces use of the amblyopic left eye.
Wrong - atropinising the amblyopic eye blurs it further and worsens the amblyopia.
Wrong - cyclopentolate is a short-acting diagnostic cycloplegic, and it is given to the wrong eye here.
Wrong - pilocarpine constricts the pupil and does not blur the good eye enough to penalise it.
Wrong - short-acting dilation of both eyes gives no differential penalty, so the brain still prefers the right eye.

mcq.stem:
A 3-week-old boy is referred from the postnatal ward after the neonatal examination found an absent red reflex in the left eye. Examination shows a dense, central 4 mm white lens opacity in the left eye; the right eye is normal. The left fundus cannot be seen, and B-scan ultrasound shows a flat retina. He is otherwise well.
What is the most appropriate management plan?
o: Observe and plan surgery at 1 year when anaesthesia is safer
Dilate the left pupil with atropine and review in 6 months
Patch the right eye now and defer surgery to age 2
Glasses for the left eye now and operate at school age
Cataract surgery within weeks, then aphakic contact lens
mcq.e: A dense central cataract in the first weeks of life is the **most amblyogenic** situation of all (**stimulus deprivation** — the least common but most severe type). A unilateral case should be operated on within about **6 weeks of age** (bilateral by about 8-10 weeks), otherwise dense irreversible amblyopia and nystagmus develop. After surgery the eye is optically corrected (aphakic contact lens, or IOL in older infants) and the good eye is patched. Waiting for a 'safer' age sacrifices the critical period.
w: Wrong - surgery at 1 year is far too late; the deprivation amblyopia would be dense and irreversible.
Wrong - pupil dilation is a temporary measure for small partial opacities, not a dense central cataract.
Wrong - patching cannot work while the visual axis of the left eye is blocked.
Wrong - glasses cannot focus light through an opaque lens; the obstruction must be removed.
Correct - urgent early surgery within the first 6 weeks, then aphakic correction and occlusion of the good eye.

mcq.stem:
A 4-year-old girl with left strabismic amblyopia has been patching her right eye for 6 hours a day for 3 months while wearing full glasses. Today left VA has improved from 6/36 to 6/12, but right VA has fallen from 6/6 to 6/12. The right fundus, pupils and refraction are unchanged, and she now prefers to fix with the left eye.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Increase right-eye patching to all waking hours
Change to patching the left eye full time
Stop patching briefly; recheck VA in 2 weeks
Arrange an urgent MRI of the right optic nerve
Add atropine 1% to the right eye with the patch
mcq.e: A fall in VA of the patched (good) eye with a normal examination is **occlusion (reverse) amblyopia** — the risk is highest in young children on intensive patching. Occlusion is **stopped or reduced for a short period**; the good eye usually recovers quickly, and treatment is then resumed at a lower dose with closer review. This is why VA in **both** eyes is checked at every amblyopia visit.
w: Wrong - more occlusion would deepen the reverse amblyopia in the right eye.
Wrong - full-time patching of the improving left eye risks losing its gains; a short break is enough.
Correct - a brief pause in occlusion lets the good eye recover, then treatment resumes at a gentler dose.
Wrong - a normal examination with an obvious cause (intensive patching) does not need urgent neuroimaging.
Wrong - adding atropine to the patched eye doubles the penalty and worsens the problem.

mcq.stem:
A 9-year-old boy is found at school screening to have right VA 6/18 and left 6/6. He has never worn glasses. His eyes are straight, cycloplegic refraction is right +5.00 DS and left +0.75 DS, and both fundi are normal. His father asks whether it is too late for treatment, as a relative told him a lazy eye can only be fixed before the age of 7.
What is the most accurate advice?
o: Too late: the critical period ended at about 7 years
Too late: only cosmetic glasses can help him now
Worth treating: anisometropia can respond to ~11-12 y
Refer for LASIK to equalise the two refractive errors
Treatment works equally well at any age into adulthood
mcq.e: The notes give amblyopia as reversible up to about **7-8 years for strabismic** and **11-12 years for anisometropic** amblyopia. A previously untreated anisometrope of 9 therefore deserves a trial of **full glasses ± occlusion**, and many gain useful acuity. The earlier treatment starts the better, and gains in adulthood are limited — so age 9 is not a reason to refuse treatment but a reason not to delay.
w: Wrong - age 7-8 is the guide for strabismic amblyopia; anisometropic amblyopia stays responsive longer.
Wrong - glasses are therapeutic here, not cosmetic; full correction often improves the amblyopic eye.
Correct - anisometropic amblyopia may still respond up to about 11-12 years, so treat now.
Wrong - refractive surgery is not the standard treatment for childhood anisometropic amblyopia.
Wrong - plasticity declines with age; adult treatment gives much smaller gains.

mcq.stem:
A 6-year-old girl with left anisometropic amblyopia was prescribed full glasses and right-eye patching for 2 hours a day 3 months ago. Left VA is unchanged at 6/24. The refraction is correct, the glasses fit well, and the left media and fundus are normal. Her mother works night shifts and her grandmother looks after her on weekdays.
What is the most likely reason for the lack of improvement?
o: Poor adherence to the patching regimen
Undetected left optic nerve hypoplasia
Patching dose too low for her amblyopia
She is beyond the age at which patching works
Occlusion amblyopia developing in the right eye
mcq.e: **Non-adherence** is the commonest cause of amblyopia treatment failure: patches are uncomfortable and socially awkward, and success depends on every carer. Before searching for hidden pathology, ask who applies the patch, use a **patching diary**, explain the aim to all carers and consider switching to atropine. Six years with anisometropia is well within the responsive age, and 2 hours a day is an effective dose for moderate amblyopia.
w: Correct - non-compliance is the main cause of failure, especially with several carers involved.
Wrong - a normal dilated fundus examination makes significant optic nerve hypoplasia unlikely.
Wrong - 2 hours a day is an effective starting dose for moderate amblyopia; no gain suggests it is not being done.
Wrong - anisometropic amblyopia remains responsive well beyond 6 years.
Wrong - reverse amblyopia would lower the right eye's VA; it does not explain an unchanged left eye.

mcq.stem:
A 6-year-old boy has right VA 6/18 and left 6/6 on a crowded logMAR chart, with no improvement on pinhole in the right eye. There is no squint and no family history. The medical officer at the Klinik Kesihatan wants to label it amblyopia and start patching.
Before amblyopia can be diagnosed, which assessment is essential?
o: Visual evoked potential testing of both eyes
Electroretinography of the right eye
MRI of the brain and orbits with contrast
Cycloplegic refraction and dilated fundoscopy
Humphrey automated visual field testing of both eyes
mcq.e: Amblyopia is a **diagnosis of exclusion**: reduced **best-corrected** VA (usually a difference of **2 or more lines**) with **no structural pathology** of the eye or visual pathway. **Cycloplegic refraction** finds the amblyogenic error and gives the true best-corrected acuity; **dilated fundoscopy** excludes macular, optic nerve or media disease (e.g. toxoplasma scar, optic nerve hypoplasia, retinoblastoma). Electrophysiology and MRI are reserved for unexplained or atypical cases.
w: Wrong - VEP is a second-line test for unexplained visual loss, not the essential first assessment.
Wrong - ERG is used when a retinal dystrophy is suspected despite a normal-looking fundus.
Wrong - MRI is not needed unless the examination is abnormal or VA fails to respond as expected.
Correct - cycloplegic refraction and dilated fundoscopy establish the refractive cause and exclude organic disease.
Wrong - formal automated fields are unreliable at 6 years and do not exclude ocular pathology.

mcq.stem:
A 5-year-old girl with right strabismic amblyopia is tested in the orthoptic clinic. With single isolated Kay pictures, right VA is 6/9. With a crowded test (a row of pictures surrounded by a box), right VA is only 6/24. Left VA is 6/6 with both methods. She is cooperative and fixing centrally.
What best explains the difference between the two right-eye results?
o: Malingering by an inattentive child
Crowding phenomenon of amblyopic vision
Eccentric fixation in the amblyopic eye
Fatigue during the longer chart test
Uncorrected astigmatism blurring rows
mcq.e: Amblyopic eyes are especially sensitive to **contour interaction**: optotypes crowded together are much harder to resolve than single ones (**crowding phenomenon**). Single-optotype tests therefore **overestimate** acuity in amblyopia, which is why crowded or logMAR-based tests are preferred for diagnosis and monitoring, and why treatment aims to improve the crowded acuity.
w: Wrong - the left eye performs identically on both tests, and a cooperative child would not selectively fail one eye.
Correct - amblyopic vision is degraded by neighbouring contours, so crowded acuity is worse than single-optotype acuity.
Wrong - she is fixing centrally; eccentric fixation would reduce acuity on both tests.
Wrong - fatigue would affect both eyes and does not explain a fourfold difference.
Wrong - an uncorrected refractive error blurs single and crowded targets alike.

mcq.stem:
A 6-year-old boy is referred because he holds books very close and his Primary 1 teacher says he cannot see the board. His eyes are straight. Unaided VA is 6/24 in each eye. Cycloplegic refraction is +6.50 DS in each eye; anterior segments and fundi are normal. After 6 weeks in glasses, VA is 6/18 in each eye.
What is the most appropriate ongoing management?
o: Alternate daily patching of each eye
Atropine 1% to both eyes at weekends
Reduce the glasses to +3.00 D for comfort
Stop glasses until his eyes mature
Keep wearing full glasses and review
mcq.e: High, **symmetrical** refractive error in both eyes from early childhood causes **bilateral isoametropic amblyopia** — neither eye has ever had a clear image. Because there is no better eye, occlusion is not needed: **full-time full correction alone** typically improves VA gradually over many months to 1-2 years. Patching is only added if an interocular difference emerges. Note: the notes list the three main types; isoametropic and meridional amblyopia are additional refractive forms.
w: Wrong - with equal VA there is no dominant eye to penalise; alternate patching adds nothing.
Wrong - atropine to both eyes blurs both and gives no differential benefit.
Wrong - under-correcting leaves both retinal images blurred and slows visual development.
Wrong - stopping glasses removes the only treatment and wastes the critical period.
Correct - continue full-time full correction; bilateral isoametropic amblyopia improves gradually with glasses alone.

mcq.stem:
A 74-year-old man with hypertension and atrial fibrillation (not anticoagulated) presents to the emergency department 2 hours after sudden painless loss of vision in his right eye during breakfast. Last month he had two brief episodes of a 'curtain' over the same eye. Right VA is counting fingers at 1 m with a marked right RAPD; left VA is 6/9. The right red reflex is normal. Fundoscopy shows a pale, opaque posterior pole with an orange-red fovea, thread-like arterioles and no haemorrhages; the disc is not swollen.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Central retinal vein occlusion
Vitreous haemorrhage
Non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy
Central retinal artery occlusion
Ophthalmic artery occlusion
mcq.e: Sudden, painless, profound monocular loss with a **marked RAPD**, a pale oedematous inner retina around a red fovea (**cherry-red spot**) and attenuated arterioles is **CRAO** — here embolic from AF, with preceding **amaurosis fugax**. The media are clear, so the **red reflex is preserved**, which separates it from vitreous haemorrhage. It is both an ophthalmic emergency and a stroke equivalent.
w: Wrong - CRVO gives a 'blood and thunder' fundus with widespread haemorrhages and dilated tortuous veins.
Wrong - vitreous haemorrhage dims or abolishes the red reflex and obscures the fundus; here both are clear.
Wrong - NAION causes a swollen disc with an altitudinal field defect; the retina is not opaque.
Correct - sudden painless profound loss, marked RAPD, pale opaque retina with a red fovea and thin arterioles = CRAO.
Wrong - ophthalmic artery occlusion also starves the choroid, so there is no red fovea and vision is usually NPL.

mcq.stem:
A 63-year-old smoker with hyperlipidaemia noticed an hour ago that the lower half of his left visual field had suddenly gone dark. Left VA is 6/9 with a mild left RAPD. Fundoscopy shows a wedge of white, oedematous retina along the superotemporal arcade, sharply demarcated from the normal retina, with a bright yellow refractile plaque lodged at an arteriolar bifurcation near the disc. There are no haemorrhages and the disc looks normal.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Superotemporal branch retinal vein occlusion
Superotemporal branch retinal artery occlusion
Superior segmental non-arteritic AION
Superior bullous retinal detachment, macula on
Multiple hypertensive cotton-wool spots
mcq.e: Embolic occlusion of a branch arteriole whitens only the retina it supplies, giving **sharply demarcated sectoral opacification** with a corresponding (here inferior) field defect; VA is spared if the fovea is not involved. The yellow refractile plaque at a bifurcation is a **Hollenhorst (cholesterol) embolus** from carotid atheroma, so the vascular work-up is the same as for CRAO.
w: Wrong - a branch vein occlusion gives a sector of flame haemorrhages and dilated veins, not pale retina.
Correct - sectoral retinal whitening with an embolus at a bifurcation and a matching field defect = BRAO.
Wrong - segmental NAION swells part of the disc; the retina itself is not white.
Wrong - a detachment is elevated and grey with undulating folds, usually after flashes and floaters, and has no embolus.
Wrong - cotton-wool spots are small fluffy patches, usually bilateral with other hypertensive signs, not a wedge.

mcq.stem:
On a teaching ward round, a 70-year-old woman admitted yesterday with sudden painless loss of vision in her left eye is examined. Left VA is perception of light with a dense RAPD. The house officer notes that the centre of the macula looks bright red while the surrounding posterior pole is milky white, and asks why.
What is the best explanation for this appearance?
o: A small haemorrhage has collected under the fovea
The fovea is supplied by a patent cilioretinal artery
Reperfusion has caused hyperaemia of foveal capillaries
Pigment in the foveal RPE has increased after ischaemia
The thin fovea lets the normal choroid show through
mcq.e: The fovea has **no inner retinal layers** (no ganglion cells or nerve fibre layer) and depends on the **choroid**, not the central retinal artery. When the inner retina elsewhere infarcts and becomes opaque and oedematous, the intact choroidal circulation remains visible through the thin foveola as the **cherry-red spot**. It fades over weeks as the oedema clears, leaving optic atrophy and attenuated arterioles.
w: Wrong - there is no haemorrhage; the red colour is normal choroid, and CRAO is typically haemorrhage-free.
Wrong - a cilioretinal artery perfuses a tongue of retina between disc and fovea and would preserve central vision.
Wrong - the foveola has no retinal capillaries (foveal avascular zone), so it cannot become hyperaemic.
Wrong - RPE pigment changes take weeks and appear dark, not as a bright red spot.
Correct - the foveola lacks the opaque inner retina, so the healthy choroid shows through as a cherry-red spot.

mcq.stem:
A 66-year-old woman with diabetes presents 3 hours after sudden painless loss of vision in her left eye. Surprisingly, left VA is 6/12, but she describes seeing only a small central island; there is a marked left RAPD. Fundoscopy shows diffuse whitening of the posterior pole except for a tongue-shaped area of normal-coloured retina extending from the temporal disc margin to the fovea.
What explains her relatively preserved central acuity?
o: A cilioretinal artery perfusing the papillomacular retina
Retrograde perfusion through the central retinal vein
A persistent hyaloid artery remnant supplying the macula
Anterior ciliary arteries supplying the macula directly
Recanalisation of the central artery within the first hour
mcq.e: In about **15-30% of eyes** a **cilioretinal artery** arises from the posterior ciliary (choroidal) circulation at the temporal disc margin and supplies the **papillomacular bundle**. It is unaffected by occlusion of the central retinal artery, so the retina it supplies stays normal-coloured and central VA can be preserved despite severe field loss. The same artery can be occluded in GCA, because it shares the posterior ciliary supply.
w: Correct - a cilioretinal artery from the ciliary circulation keeps the papillomacular retina perfused.
Wrong - veins do not perfuse the retina retrogradely; blood cannot reach the inner retina this way.
Wrong - the hyaloid artery regresses before birth and does not supply the adult macula.
Wrong - anterior ciliary arteries supply the anterior segment and ciliary body, not the macula.
Wrong - recanalisation would reperfuse the whole retina, not a sharply defined tongue next to the disc.

mcq.stem:
A 79-year-old woman presents to the eye clinic 6 hours after sudden painless loss of vision in her right eye. Right VA is perception of light with a dense RAPD, and the fundus shows a pale retina with a red fovea. For 3 weeks she has had a new right-sided headache, pain in her jaw when chewing and morning stiffness of both shoulders. Her temporal arteries are tender and pulseless.
What is the most important immediate step?
o: Ocular massage and anterior chamber paracentesis
Carotid duplex scan and start aspirin 300 mg
Urgent ESR and CRP, and high-dose steroids today
Temporal artery biopsy, then steroids if positive
Intravenous thrombolysis within the stroke window
mcq.e: In any patient over 50 with a retinal artery occlusion, ask about GCA symptoms and check **ESR/CRP urgently** — arteritic CRAO is a small but critical minority. Headache, jaw claudication, PMR symptoms and abnormal temporal arteries make it likely, and **high-dose steroids** (IV methylprednisolone when vision is affected) must start the **same day** to protect the fellow eye, which can be lost within days. Biopsy follows within 2 weeks; steroids do not wait for it. Note: the notes list temporal arteritis as a cause but omit the urgent ESR/CRP step — it is essential.
w: Wrong - IOP-lowering manoeuvres cannot reverse a vasculitic occlusion and do nothing for the fellow eye.
Wrong - carotid imaging suits embolic CRAO; missing GCA here risks bilateral blindness.
Correct - suspected arteritic CRAO: urgent ESR/CRP and immediate high-dose steroids to protect the fellow eye.
Wrong - waiting for biopsy delays treatment; histology stays positive for about 2 weeks after steroids start.
Wrong - thrombolysis has no role in a vasculitic occlusion and adds bleeding risk without benefit.

mcq.stem:
A 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and a 40-pack-year smoking history has sudden painless loss of vision in his left eye. Fundoscopy shows a whitened retina with a cherry-red spot and a bright, yellow, refractile plaque at a bifurcation of the inferotemporal arteriole. He is in sinus rhythm on ECG, and a left carotid bruit is heard.
Which investigation most directly identifies the likely source of the embolus?
o: Transthoracic echocardiography
24-hour Holter ECG monitoring
Fundus fluorescein angiography
Thrombophilia and autoimmune screen
Carotid duplex Doppler ultrasound
mcq.e: A **Hollenhorst plaque** is a **cholesterol** embolus, typically from an ulcerated atheromatous plaque at the **carotid bifurcation**, so **carotid duplex ultrasound** is the key test; significant ipsilateral stenosis may need endarterectomy to prevent stroke. Calcific emboli point to heart valves and platelet-fibrin emboli to carotid or cardiac thrombus, which is where echocardiography and Holter monitoring fit. Note: the notes say 'Doppler echocardiogram' — carotid duplex and echocardiography are two different tests, and both are usually requested in CRAO work-up.
w: Wrong - echocardiography looks for cardiac sources (valves, thrombus, myxoma); cholesterol emboli are carotid in origin.
Wrong - Holter looks for paroxysmal AF; useful in the work-up but not the source of a cholesterol plaque.
Wrong - FFA confirms delayed arterial filling but does not identify where the embolus came from.
Wrong - thrombophilia and vasculitis screens are for young patients without atherosclerotic risk factors.
Correct - a cholesterol (Hollenhorst) embolus plus a carotid bruit points to carotid atheroma; duplex ultrasound images it.

mcq.stem:
A 29-year-old man is admitted with 2 weeks of fever and night sweats and sudden painless loss of vision in his right eye this morning. He injects heroin. Right VA is hand movements with a marked RAPD, and the right retina is pale with a red fovea. He has splinter haemorrhages under his fingernails and a new pansystolic murmur at the apex.
Which investigations are most important to identify the cause?
o: Serial blood cultures and echocardiography
Carotid duplex ultrasound and fasting lipids
Haemoglobin electrophoresis for sickle cell
ESR, CRP and temporal artery biopsy
Antiphospholipid antibodies and lupus screen
mcq.e: In a **young** patient, CRAO is usually embolic from the **heart** or due to a haematological or inflammatory disorder rather than atherosclerosis. Fever, IV drug use, a new murmur and splinter haemorrhages indicate **infective endocarditis** with septic emboli (valve vegetations are listed among embolic sources in the notes): take **at least 3 sets of blood cultures** before antibiotics and arrange **echocardiography** (transoesophageal if transthoracic is negative). Thrombophilia and vasculitis screens are for young patients without a cardiac source.
w: Correct - suspected infective endocarditis: blood cultures and echocardiography identify the embolic source.
Wrong - carotid atheroma is unlikely at 29; this suits older patients with vascular risk factors.
Wrong - sickle cell can cause CRAO but does not explain fever, a new murmur and splinter haemorrhages.
Wrong - GCA does not occur under 50; biopsy is irrelevant here.
Wrong - antiphospholipid syndrome is a cause of young CRAO, but the clinical picture points to endocarditis first.

mcq.stem:
A 71-year-old woman walks into a Klinik Kesihatan 40 minutes after sudden painless loss of vision in her left eye. Left VA is perception of light with a dense RAPD, and on direct ophthalmoscopy the medical officer sees a pale retina with a red fovea. The nearest eye clinic is 1 hour away and transport is being arranged.
Which measure is most appropriate while awaiting transfer?
o: Pad the eye firmly and keep her lying flat
Instil tropicamide; refer to next eye clinic
Give oral prednisolone 60 mg; review in a week
Intermittent digital massage of the closed eye
Instil pilocarpine 2% every 5 minutes for an hour
mcq.e: **'Time is retina'**: complete CRAO causes irreversible inner retinal damage after about **90-100 minutes**, so any measure must be immediate and must accompany, not replace, urgent transfer. **Digital massage** (firm pressure through the closed lid for ~10 s, release ~10 s, for ~5 min) creates pressure swings that may dislodge the embolus; lowering IOP (e.g. acetazolamide) has the same aim. The evidence of benefit is weak, but these simple measures are reasonable in very early presenters, and transfer also starts the same-day stroke work-up.
w: Wrong - a firm pad raises IOP continuously and reduces perfusion; it does not dislodge the embolus.
Wrong - dilating the pupil is fine for examination, but a non-urgent referral wastes the only window for reperfusion.
Wrong - steroids are for suspected GCA after ESR/CRP, and a week's delay is never appropriate in CRAO.
Correct - intermittent globe massage while arranging immediate transfer is a reasonable early measure.
Wrong - pilocarpine constricts the pupil but does not meaningfully lower IOP or restore retinal flow.

mcq.stem:
A 76-year-old man attends the eye clinic complaining that his right eye went dark 4 days ago; he waited, hoping it would improve. Right VA is perception of light with a dense RAPD, and the retina is pale and oedematous with a cherry-red spot. ESR is 12 mm/h and CRP is normal; he has no headache or jaw claudication. BP is 168/96 mmHg.
What is the most appropriate management now?
o: Anterior chamber paracentesis and IV acetazolamide
Same-day stroke work-up and vascular risk control
Nd:YAG laser embolysis of the occluding plaque
Intra-arterial thrombolysis via the ophthalmic artery
Oral prednisolone 60 mg daily pending a biopsy
mcq.e: After several days the inner retina is irreversibly infarcted: massage, paracentesis, embolysis and thrombolysis offer nothing and carry risks (infection or lens injury with paracentesis; haemorrhage with thrombolysis). With GCA excluded clinically and by a normal ESR/CRP, the priority is to treat CRAO as a **stroke equivalent**: urgent work-up (BP, glucose, lipids, ECG/Holter for AF, carotid duplex, echocardiography) and **secondary prevention**, because these patients have a high early risk of stroke and myocardial infarction. The notes put the reversible window at under 6 hours and attempts at under 24 hours; beyond that, prevention is the goal.
w: Wrong - lowering IOP cannot rescue retina that has been infarcted for 4 days and adds procedural risk.
Correct - late presenters need urgent TIA/stroke-pathway work-up and secondary prevention.
Wrong - YAG embolysis is an early, unproven measure with a risk of vitreous haemorrhage; useless at 4 days.
Wrong - thrombolysis is not beneficial this late and carries a risk of intracranial bleeding.
Wrong - a normal ESR/CRP and no GCA symptoms make arteritis very unlikely; steroids are not indicated.

mcq.stem:
A 72-year-old man had a right retinal arterial event 7 weeks ago, after which his vision remained at hand movements. He now presents with 3 days of aching pain and redness in the right eye. IOP is 46 mmHg right and 15 mmHg left. The cornea is mildly hazy and the anterior chamber is deep and quiet; fine, irregular vessels are seen at the pupil margin and, on gonioscopy, crossing the open angle.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Primary acute angle-closure glaucoma
Hypertensive anterior uveitis
Neovascular glaucoma from ischaemia
Steroid-induced ocular hypertension
Phacolytic glaucoma from a mature lens
mcq.e: Ischaemic retina releases **VEGF**, which drives new vessels on the iris (**rubeosis**) and in the angle; a fibrovascular membrane then obstructs the trabecular meshwork and later zips the angle closed — **neovascular glaucoma**. It develops in a minority of eyes after CRAO (less often than after ischaemic CRVO), typically weeks to months later, so these patients need follow-up with iris and gonioscopy checks. Treatment is **PRP ± anti-VEGF** plus IOP control.
w: Wrong - primary angle closure has a shallow AC and closed angle; here the AC is deep and the angle open.
Wrong - hypertensive uveitis shows AC cells, flare and keratic precipitates; the AC here is quiet.
Correct - new vessels on the iris and open angle weeks after an ischaemic retinal event = neovascular glaucoma.
Wrong - steroid response needs steroid exposure and does not produce iris new vessels.
Wrong - phacolytic glaucoma has a mature cataract with AC cells and protein; no new vessels.

mcq.stem:
A 74-year-old retired teacher attends the Klinik Kesihatan with 3 weeks of a new, constant headache over both temples. Combing her hair is painful, and her jaw aches after a few minutes of chewing, easing when she stops. Both shoulders are stiff every morning and she has lost 3 kg. Yesterday the vision in her right eye 'went black like a curtain' for 5 minutes, then fully recovered. VA 6/9 both eyes, no RAPD, fundi unremarkable.
Which diagnosis best explains the whole picture?
o: Polymyalgia rheumatica without any vascular involvement
Giant cell arteritis with impending ocular ischaemia
Carotid atheroembolism causing amaurosis fugax
Temporomandibular joint dysfunction with tension headache
Late-onset migraine with a monocular visual aura
mcq.e: New headache after 50, scalp tenderness and **jaw claudication** are the classic triad of GCA, and polymyalgia rheumatica coexists in about 30%. A transient monocular blackout in this setting is a warning of ophthalmic/posterior ciliary artery ischaemia and precedes permanent loss. The trap is to choose a diagnosis that explains only one part — PMR (shoulders only) or carotid emboli (eye only).
w: Wrong - PMR explains the girdle stiffness but not jaw claudication, scalp tenderness or the visual blackout; PMR with these features is GCA until proven otherwise.
Correct - the combination of systemic, cranial and transient visual symptoms in a patient over 50 is GCA; same-day ESR/CRP and steroids are needed.
Wrong - carotid emboli cause amaurosis fugax but not jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, weight loss or morning girdle stiffness.
Wrong - TMJ pain is present at the start of chewing and is joint-related; claudication (pain that builds with use and settles with rest) is ischaemic.
Wrong - migraine rarely starts after 70, aura is usually binocular and homonymous, and it does not cause scalp tenderness or weight loss.

mcq.stem:
A 72-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a 10-day new right temporal headache and jaw pain on chewing. The right temporal artery is tender, thickened and pulseless. VA 6/6 both eyes, no RAPD, optic discs normal. ESR 88 mm/h, CRP 64 mg/L. The surgical team can perform a temporal artery biopsy next week.
What is the most appropriate management today?
o: Withhold steroids until the biopsy so histology is not falsely negative
Start oral prednisolone 15 mg daily, as used for polymyalgia rheumatica
Give IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days before any biopsy
Start oral prednisolone 60 mg daily today; biopsy within 2 weeks
Start aspirin 300 mg daily and refer to the rheumatology clinic
mcq.e: In suspected GCA **treat first, biopsy later**: oral prednisolone 60 mg daily is started the same day, and the biopsy remains diagnostic for about 2 weeks after steroids begin. Without visual symptoms oral steroid is adequate; IV pulses are reserved for visual loss or amaurosis. Waiting for histology risks blindness, which is the trap.
w: Wrong - histology stays positive for around 2 weeks on steroids; delaying treatment risks sudden irreversible visual loss.
Wrong - 15 mg is a PMR dose; cranial GCA needs about 40-60 mg (notes: 60 mg) to protect the eyes.
Wrong - IV methylprednisolone is for evolving visual loss or amaurosis fugax; this patient has no visual symptoms.
Correct - high-dose oral prednisolone today with biopsy arranged within 2 weeks of starting treatment.
Wrong - aspirin may be considered as an adjunct, but alone it does not suppress the arteritis and routine referral is far too slow.

mcq.stem:
A 78-year-old woman woke with almost no vision in her left eye. For 2 weeks she has had headache and a 'tired jaw' when eating. VA right 6/9, left hand movements, left RAPD. The left optic disc is swollen and chalky white; the right disc is normal. ESR 104 mm/h, CRP 120 mg/L.
What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
o: IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days, then oral prednisolone
Oral prednisolone 20 mg daily, tapered over the following month
IV alteplase within 4.5 hours of onset via the acute stroke team
Ocular massage, IV acetazolamide and anterior chamber paracentesis
Aspirin 300 mg with clopidogrel, then statin and BP optimisation
mcq.e: With established visual loss (or amaurosis fugax) from GCA, most units give **IV methylprednisolone 500 mg-1 g daily for 3 days** followed by high-dose oral prednisolone (notes p8: IV if visual loss is evolving). The aim is mainly to protect the fellow eye, as the affected eye rarely recovers. Thrombolysis and CRAO manoeuvres do not treat an inflammatory arteritis.
w: Correct - pulsed IV methylprednisolone then oral prednisolone is the standard response to visual loss in GCA.
Wrong - 20 mg is far too low for GCA with visual loss, and a 1-month course invites relapse; treatment usually lasts 1-2 years.
Wrong - thrombolysis is for embolic/thrombotic stroke; arteritic occlusion is inflammatory and steroids are the treatment.
Wrong - these are conservative CRAO measures for an embolus; they do nothing for arteritic optic nerve head infarction.
Wrong - antiplatelets may be added, but without high-dose steroid the fellow eye remains at high risk.

mcq.stem:
A 70-year-old woman with a new occipital headache, scalp tenderness and jaw claudication was started on prednisolone 60 mg daily by the medical team. Her ESR fell from 96 to 28 mm/h and her symptoms settled within 72 hours. A 1.5 cm temporal artery biopsy taken on day 6 is reported as normal artery with no inflammation. VA 6/6 both eyes. She asks whether she can stop her tablets.
What is the best advice?
o: Stop prednisolone now, because a normal biopsy excludes the diagnosis
Taper prednisolone off over 1 week, as the biopsy was taken too late
Switch to methotrexate alone, as biopsy-negative disease is milder
Stop prednisolone and repeat the biopsy only if the headache comes back
Continue the full steroid course, as skip lesions give false negatives
mcq.e: GCA involves the artery **patchily (skip lesions)**, so even an adequate biopsy (>1 cm, within 2 weeks of steroids) can be negative in up to about 10% (notes p8). The diagnosis is clinical: she already meets 3 of 5 ACR criteria (age ≥50, new headache, ESR ≥50) and responded promptly to steroids. Stopping treatment because of a negative biopsy is the trap.
w: Wrong - a negative biopsy does not exclude GCA; the clinical picture and steroid response outweigh it.
Wrong - a biopsy on day 6 is within the 2-week window when histology is still reliable; lateness does not explain this result.
Wrong - methotrexate is only a steroid-sparing adjunct; it is not used alone, and a negative biopsy does not mean milder disease.
Wrong - stopping risks blindness before a relapse is recognised; vision can be lost without warning.
Correct - treat as GCA and continue the full taper, monitoring symptoms and ESR/CRP.

mcq.stem:
A 76-year-old man in the medical ward has 4 weeks of fatigue, night sweats, a new left-sided headache and aching thighs on rising from a chair. The physicians ask the eye team to review him before his blood results return. VA 6/9 both eyes, pupils normal, optic discs healthy.
Which set of blood results is most consistent with the suspected diagnosis?
o: ESR 18 mm/h, normal CRP, Hb 15 g/dL, platelets 250 x10^9/L
ESR 95 mm/h, microcytic anaemia, low ferritin and raised CK
ESR 95 mm/h, high CRP, normocytic anaemia, raised platelets and ALP
ESR 95 mm/h, high CRP, neutropenia, raised serum amylase and bilirubin
ESR 40 mm/h, normal CRP, eosinophilia and positive ANCA
mcq.e: GCA with PMR gives an acute-phase picture: **ESR usually 50-120 mm/h with a very high CRP**, normochromic normocytic anaemia of chronic disease, reactive thrombocytosis and raised ALP/GGT from hepatic acute-phase response (notes p8). Creatine kinase is normal — PMR is not a myositis. A normal ESR and CRP makes GCA very unlikely, though not impossible.
w: Wrong - normal inflammatory markers make GCA very unlikely and would not fit this systemic illness.
Wrong - the anaemia is normocytic (chronic disease), not iron-deficient, and CK is normal in PMR/GCA.
Correct - high ESR and CRP with normocytic anaemia, thrombocytosis and raised ALP is the typical GCA profile.
Wrong - neutropenia, high amylase and bilirubin suggest pancreatobiliary or marrow disease, not GCA.
Wrong - eosinophilia with ANCA suggests eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis; GCA is ANCA-negative with a high CRP.

mcq.stem:
An 81-year-old woman has sudden painless loss of vision in the right eye to perception of light. She has had headaches and jaw pain for a month; ESR is 110 mm/h. The right optic disc is swollen and strikingly pale; the retinal arterioles look normal and there is no cherry-red spot. The left eye is normal.
Occlusion of which vessel best explains the visual loss?
o: Short posterior ciliary arteries supplying the optic nerve head
Superficial temporal artery, the vessel sampled at biopsy
Central retinal vein at the level of the lamina cribrosa
Anterior ciliary arteries supplying the iris and the ciliary body
Middle cerebral artery branches supplying the optic radiation
mcq.e: GCA is a granulomatous vasculitis of **large and medium-sized arteries, especially extracranial branches of the carotid** (ophthalmic, posterior ciliary, superficial temporal). Visual loss is usually from **posterior ciliary artery** occlusion causing arteritic AION (pale swollen disc); central retinal artery occlusion (cherry-red spot) is less common. Note: the notes call it an arteritis of 'large cerebral arteries' — intracranial involvement is in fact rare.
w: Correct - posterior ciliary artery occlusion infarcts the optic nerve head, giving a chalky white swollen disc (arteritic AION).
Wrong - the superficial temporal artery causes headache and scalp tenderness and is biopsied, but it does not supply the eye.
Wrong - CRVO causes widespread haemorrhages and dilated veins ('blood and thunder'), not a pale disc with normal vessels.
Wrong - anterior ciliary arteries supply the anterior segment; their occlusion causes anterior segment ischaemia, not optic disc infarction.
Wrong - optic radiation lesions cause binocular homonymous field loss with normal discs, not monocular loss with a swollen disc.

mcq.stem:
A 68-year-old post-menopausal woman with biopsy-proven giant cell arteritis is starting prednisolone 60 mg daily, with a taper expected over 1-2 years. She has a history of dyspepsia; her DEXA scan is pending. Renal function is normal. VA 6/6 both eyes, discs normal.
Which additional prescription is most appropriate to start now?
o: Oral fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily to prevent adrenal crisis
Hydroxychloroquine 200 mg daily as the first steroid-sparing drug
Prednisolone acetate 1% drops to both eyes to protect the optic discs
Weekly alendronate with calcium, colecalciferol and a daily PPI
Enoxaparin 40 mg daily for 6 weeks to prevent arterial occlusion
mcq.e: Long-term steroid toxicity is the main cause of morbidity and death in treated GCA (notes p8), so **bone protection (bisphosphonate + calcium + vitamin D) and gastroprotection (PPI)** start with the steroid, without waiting for DEXA in an older patient on high-dose prednisolone. Low-dose aspirin may be considered. Topical steroids do not reach the posterior ciliary circulation.
w: Wrong - fludrocortisone is not needed during high-dose glucocorticoid therapy; adrenal suppression matters when tapering or stopping.
Wrong - hydroxychloroquine has no proven role in GCA; tocilizumab (and sometimes methotrexate) are the steroid-sparing options.
Wrong - eye drops treat anterior segment inflammation; the disc is protected only by systemic steroid.
Correct - bisphosphonate, calcium with colecalciferol and a PPI are the standard adjuncts to long-term high-dose prednisolone.
Wrong - anticoagulation is not standard in GCA; ischaemia is due to inflammatory narrowing, not thrombus.

mcq.stem:
A 74-year-old woman was treated for biopsy-proven giant cell arteritis 3 years ago. She is now off steroids and well. At her final eye clinic visit, VA is 6/9 right and 6/60 left (old left optic atrophy). She asks what long-term check-ups she still needs.
Which surveillance is recommended?
o: Annual MRI brain to detect intracranial aneurysm formation
Annual renal artery Doppler to detect renovascular hypertension
Six-monthly ESR, restarting prednisolone whenever it exceeds 30
Annual spirometry to detect steroid-related pulmonary fibrosis
Yearly chest X-ray ± abdominal ultrasound for aortic aneurysm
mcq.e: GCA carries a long-term **increased risk of thoracic aortic aneurysm and aortic dissection**, often years after diagnosis, so the notes advise yearly CXR ± abdominal ultrasound (many centres now use CT or MR aortography). Large-vessel involvement can also cause aortic arch syndrome with absent arm pulses. Treat symptoms and clinical relapse, not an isolated ESR number.
w: Wrong - intracranial involvement in GCA is rare and berry aneurysm is not a recognised association.
Wrong - renal arteries are rarely affected in GCA; that pattern suggests polyarteritis nodosa or Takayasu arteritis.
Wrong - ESR rises for many reasons in the elderly; relapse is a clinical diagnosis supported by markers, not a number alone.
Wrong - prednisolone does not cause pulmonary fibrosis; its long-term risks are osteoporosis, diabetes, cataract and glaucoma.
Correct - aortic aneurysm and dissection are late complications of GCA and need imaging surveillance.

mcq.stem:
An 80-year-old man has had hand-movements vision in the left eye since yesterday, with a chalky white swollen left disc, jaw claudication and ESR 92 mm/h. The right eye sees 6/9 and its disc is normal. He refuses steroids, saying: 'My left eye is already gone, so what is the point?'
What is the most important counselling point?
o: Prompt steroids will usually restore useful vision in the left eye
Steroids are needed only if the headache and jaw pain persist
Without steroids the right eye is at high risk within days
Daily aspirin alone gives the right eye equivalent protection
The right eye is safe unless its own disc looks small and crowded
mcq.e: In arteritic AION the affected eye rarely recovers, so steroids are given to **protect the fellow eye**, which is involved in up to a third of untreated patients, usually within days to a week (notes p47). This is why steroids are an emergency even when one eye is already lost. A crowded 'disc at risk' is a NAION concept and gives no reassurance in GCA.
w: Wrong - visual loss from arteritic AION is usually permanent; promising recovery is dishonest counselling.
Wrong - symptom relief is not the goal; the arteritis can blind the other eye even when the headache settles.
Correct - untreated GCA often involves the fellow eye within days, and steroids are given mainly to prevent bilateral blindness.
Wrong - aspirin may be added as an adjunct but does not replace high-dose steroid.
Wrong - the small crowded 'disc at risk' applies to non-arteritic AION; GCA can infarct any disc.

mcq.stem:
A 73-year-old man with giant cell arteritis has been well on a slow prednisolone taper. At 10 mg daily his temporal headache and jaw ache return over a week, and ESR rises from 20 to 58 mm/h. He has no visual symptoms; VA 6/6 both eyes and discs normal.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Stop prednisolone and start indomethacin for the headache
Increase prednisolone back to the last dose that controlled it
Admit for IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days
Keep prednisolone at 10 mg and repeat the ESR in 3 months
Repeat the temporal artery biopsy before changing any treatment
mcq.e: Relapse during tapering is common; the notes' rule is **raise the dose if symptoms recur**, usually back to the last dose that controlled the disease, then taper more slowly. Without visual symptoms there is no need for IV pulses. Repeated relapses or steroid toxicity are the indication for a steroid-sparing agent such as tocilizumab (lecturer pearl).
w: Wrong - stopping steroid during active relapse risks blindness, and NSAIDs do not control vasculitis.
Correct - return to the last effective dose, then taper more slowly; consider steroid-sparing therapy for repeated relapse.
Wrong - IV pulses are reserved for visual loss or amaurosis; this is a cranial relapse with normal vision.
Wrong - symptoms with a rising ESR mean active disease; waiting 3 months risks visual loss.
Wrong - the diagnosis is already established; a relapse is managed clinically, not by re-biopsy.

mcq.stem:
A 22-year-old university student attends the Klinik Kesihatan with 3 days of a red, watery right eye; the left eye became red yesterday. She had fever and a sore throat last week, as did two housemates. The lids are puffy, there is a tender pre-auricular node, and the lower tarsal conjunctiva shows multiple pale, dome-shaped elevations with vessels around their base. VA 6/6 both eyes, corneas clear with fluorescein, no lid vesicles.
Which organism is most likely?
o: Staphylococcus aureus from the lid margin
Haemophilus influenzae (non-typeable)
Chlamydia trachomatis serotypes D-K
Herpes simplex virus type 1 (primary)
Adenovirus serotypes 3 and 7
mcq.e: Watery discharge, lid oedema, **lower tarsal follicles** (pale domes with vessels at the base) and a **tender pre-auricular node** point to viral conjunctivitis; with fever, pharyngitis and household spread this is adenoviral pharyngoconjunctival fever. Follicles also occur in chlamydia, but that is sexually acquired and runs a chronic course over weeks. Note: the notes place 'pre-auricular LN enlarged' between the two columns — it is a VIRAL (and chlamydial) sign, not bacterial.
w: Wrong - staphylococcal conjunctivitis gives mucopurulent discharge and papillae, without follicles or a tender pre-auricular node.
Wrong - Haemophilus gives purulent discharge with papillae; it does not explain the follicles, node and sore-throat outbreak.
Wrong - chlamydial inclusion conjunctivitis also gives follicles and a node, but it is chronic (weeks to months) and sexually transmitted, not an acute household outbreak after a sore throat.
Wrong - primary HSV is usually unilateral with lid or skin vesicles and may show dendrites; neither is present.
Correct - adenovirus (types 3 and 7) causes pharyngoconjunctival fever: fever, pharyngitis, follicular conjunctivitis and pre-auricular lymphadenopathy.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old office worker has 2 days of bilateral red eyes with yellow discharge that glues the lashes together each morning. There is no pain, photophobia or contact lens wear. VA 6/6 both eyes. The injection is diffuse, involving the tarsal conjunctiva, with a fine velvety papillary reaction; corneas clear with fluorescein, pupils normal, no pre-auricular node.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Topical dexamethasone-neomycin drops four times daily for a week
Conjunctival swab, withholding treatment until culture is reported
Chloramphenicol 0.5% drops 2-hourly, lid cleaning and hand hygiene
Fortified ceftazidime 5% drops hourly with same-day eye referral
Oral amoxicillin 500 mg 8-hourly with a double eye pad overnight
mcq.e: Acute bacterial conjunctivitis is usually self-limiting, but a **broad-spectrum topical antibiotic** (chloramphenicol, fusidic acid or a fluoroquinolone) shortens it; a swab is reserved for cases that fail to resolve, are hyperacute or occur in neonates. Note: the notes list 'Ceftazidine' among first-line drugs — ceftazidime is not a routine topical for simple conjunctivitis; fortified preparations are hospital treatment for keratitis.
w: Wrong - steroid combinations are not used for undiagnosed red eye; they risk worsening HSV or fungal infection and raising IOP.
Wrong - a swab is indicated only if the condition fails to resolve or is severe; withholding treatment adds nothing here.
Correct - topical chloramphenicol with lid hygiene and hand washing is appropriate for uncomplicated bacterial conjunctivitis.
Wrong - fortified ceftazidime is for microbial keratitis in hospital; this eye has a clear cornea and normal vision.
Wrong - systemic antibiotics are not needed for simple bacterial conjunctivitis, and padding a discharging eye encourages bacterial growth.

mcq.stem:
A 38-year-old man attends the Klinik Kesihatan with 2 days of a red, watery, gritty right eye. VA is 6/6 in each eye and he does not wear contact lenses. The medical officer plans to treat it as conjunctivitis with review in a week, but first examines further.
Which additional finding should prompt same-day referral to the eye clinic?
o: Ciliary flush with redness concentrated around the limbus
Mucoid discharge that crusts on the lashes on waking
Redness most marked in the fornices, fading towards the cornea
A tender pre-auricular lymph node on the affected side
Redness and watering spreading to the fellow eye after 2 days
mcq.e: Conjunctival injection is maximal in the fornices and fades towards the limbus; **ciliary (circumcorneal) flush** means inflammation of the cornea, iris or ciliary body (keratitis, anterior uveitis, acute angle closure, scleritis). Other red flags are reduced VA, photophobia, severe pain, an abnormal pupil, corneal staining or opacity and raised IOP. Discharge, a tender node and spread to the other eye are features of ordinary infective conjunctivitis.
w: Correct - circumcorneal flush signals deeper ocular inflammation and is a red flag for same-day ophthalmic review.
Wrong - crusting discharge on waking is typical of bacterial conjunctivitis and is not a red flag by itself.
Wrong - fornix-predominant redness fading towards the cornea is the pattern of conjunctivitis, which is reassuring.
Wrong - a tender pre-auricular node is a feature of viral conjunctivitis and does not by itself need same-day referral.
Wrong - spread to the fellow eye within days is typical of contagious viral conjunctivitis.

mcq.stem:
A 20-year-old engineering student who sleeps in his monthly soft contact lenses has had a painful red left eye for 1 day with watering and marked photophobia. A private clinic diagnosed 'conjunctivitis' this morning. VA left 6/12 (6/6 last month). The lens is still in place and the conjunctiva is diffusely injected.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Chloramphenicol 0.5% drops 2-hourly, with review in 1 week if not better
Steroid-antibiotic combination drops to settle the inflammation quickly
Continue the lenses but switch to daily disposables with lubricant drops
Remove the lens, keep the case, same-day slit-lamp fluorescein review
Cold compresses, artificial tears and no lens wear for the next 48 hours
mcq.e: Any contact lens wearer with a red, painful, photophobic eye and reduced vision has **microbial keratitis until proven otherwise** — classically Pseudomonas, or Acanthamoeba if lenses meet tap water. The lens must come out, the case and lenses are kept for culture, and the cornea is examined with fluorescein the same day so that a corneal scrape can be taken before intensive antibiotics. Labelling it conjunctivitis is the trap (cross-ref keratitis).
w: Wrong - weak antibiotic drops and a week's delay can allow Pseudomonas to perforate the cornea.
Wrong - steroids before diagnosis can make bacterial, fungal or Acanthamoeba keratitis much worse.
Wrong - lenses must stop completely; continuing wear in an inflamed eye fuels infection.
Correct - remove the lens, keep the case for culture and arrange same-day slit-lamp examination of the cornea.
Wrong - pain, photophobia and a fall in VA are red flags; conservative care without corneal examination is unsafe.

mcq.stem:
A 24-year-old man presents to the emergency department 12 hours after his right eye became red. Thick creamy-yellow pus reappears within a minute of being wiped away. The lids are tense and swollen, there is marked chemosis and a tender pre-auricular node, and he admits dysuria with urethral discharge. VA right 6/12; fluorescein shows a small peripheral epithelial defect.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Chloramphenicol 0.5% drops 2-hourly and GP review in 5 days
Gram stain and culture, IM ceftriaxone, saline lavage, eye team today
Oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days and partner notification
Topical aciclovir 3% ointment five times daily and cool compresses
Topical dexamethasone 0.1% hourly to reduce the lid swelling
mcq.e: **Hyperacute** copious purulent conjunctivitis in a sexually active adult is gonococcal until proven otherwise; Neisseria can penetrate intact corneal epithelium and perforate within 24-48 hours. Management is urgent Gram stain (Gram-negative intracellular diplococci) and culture, **systemic ceftriaxone** (e.g. 1 g IM single dose), frequent saline irrigation, same-day ophthalmology review and GUM referral, with treatment for possible chlamydial co-infection. Topical therapy alone is inadequate.
w: Wrong - topical chloramphenicol alone does not control gonococcal infection, and a 5-day delay risks corneal perforation.
Correct - urgent microbiology, systemic ceftriaxone, saline lavage and same-day ophthalmic review protect the cornea.
Wrong - doxycycline covers chlamydia (often co-existent) but not Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
Wrong - HSV gives a watery discharge with vesicles or dendrites, not torrential pus.
Wrong - steroids are contraindicated in active bacterial infection and could speed corneal melting.

mcq.stem:
A 28-year-old primary school teacher has had red, watery eyes for 3 days with lid swelling and a tender pre-auricular node. The lower tarsal conjunctiva shows follicles and the corneas are clear; VA 6/6 both eyes. She asks when she can return to her classroom and how to protect her husband and baby.
What is the best advice?
o: She can return tomorrow if she starts antibiotic drops tonight
Wash hands, use her own towel, stay off work while eyes red and watery
She is infectious only while the discharge is purulent, so can return now
Spread is by droplets, so a face mask at work is sufficient protection
She may return after 48 hours, once the node is no longer tender
mcq.e: Adenoviral conjunctivitis is **highly contagious for about 2 weeks** from onset and spreads by hands, towels, pillowcases and contaminated surfaces (including clinic tonometers). Advice is frequent hand washing, separate towels, avoiding eye rubbing, and staying off work or school while the eyes are red and discharging. Antibiotic drops do not shorten viral shedding.
w: Wrong - antibiotics do not treat adenovirus or reduce infectivity.
Correct - hygiene measures and time off work during the red, watery phase are the key to limiting spread.
Wrong - adenoviral discharge is watery; she is infectious throughout the red, watery phase.
Wrong - spread is mainly by direct contact via hands and fomites, so a mask alone does not prevent it.
Wrong - shedding continues for up to about 2 weeks, whatever happens to the node.

mcq.stem:
A 33-year-old factory supervisor had red, watery, swollen eyes with a tender lump in front of the ear 3 weeks ago; it settled without treatment. He now has glare and blurred vision in the left eye when driving at night. VA left 6/12. The conjunctiva is white; the central cornea shows multiple small, round, whitish opacities just beneath the epithelium that do not stain with fluorescein. IOP 14 mmHg.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Recurrent herpes simplex epithelial keratitis
Acanthamoeba keratitis with early perineural infiltrates
Marginal keratitis from staphylococcal hypersensitivity
Fungal keratitis with feathery satellite lesions
Post-adenoviral subepithelial immune infiltrates
mcq.e: Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis is followed 1-2 weeks later by **subepithelial infiltrates** — an immune response to viral antigen, not active infection. They are non-staining, central and cause glare and reduced acuity that can last months. Most fade with lubricants alone; topical steroid is reserved for disabling cases under an ophthalmologist because infiltrates often recur when it is stopped.
w: Wrong - HSV epithelial keratitis is a branching dendritic ulcer that stains with fluorescein, usually in a red eye.
Wrong - Acanthamoeba occurs in contact lens wearers, causes severe pain out of proportion and progresses to a ring infiltrate.
Wrong - marginal keratitis lies at the peripheral cornea with a clear zone from the limbus, linked with blepharitis.
Wrong - fungal keratitis follows vegetative trauma and causes a painful, red eye with a stromal infiltrate.
Correct - multiple central non-staining subepithelial opacities weeks after viral conjunctivitis are adenoviral immune infiltrates.

mcq.stem:
A 40-year-old lorry driver has had a red, watery right eye for 4 days with mild photophobia and a foreign-body sensation. The Klinik Kesihatan has no slit lamp and has run out of fluorescein strips. VA right 6/9, left 6/6; the redness is diffuse. The medical officer refers him to the eye clinic tomorrow and wants to give something today.
Which treatment must be avoided before he is examined by the eye team?
o: Dexamethasone-chloramphenicol combination drops four times daily
Chloramphenicol 0.5% drops four times daily as a temporary measure
Preservative-free artificial tears every 2-4 hours while awake
Oral paracetamol 1 g up to four times daily for the discomfort
Fusidic acid 1% viscous drops twice daily for up to 1 week
mcq.e: Topical steroids in an **undiagnosed red eye** can turn an HSV dendrite into a large geographic ulcer, accelerate fungal, Acanthamoeba or bacterial keratitis, mask signs, and raise IOP with prolonged use. Steroid drops should be started only by an ophthalmologist after slit-lamp examination. Topical antibiotics, lubricants and analgesia are safe holding measures.
w: Correct - steroid-containing drops must not be started before slit-lamp examination; the antibiotic component does not make them safe.
Wrong - chloramphenicol is a safe temporary measure while awaiting review.
Wrong - lubricants are harmless and soothe the surface.
Wrong - oral analgesia is safe and appropriate.
Wrong - fusidic acid is a safe topical antibiotic for presumed bacterial conjunctivitis.

mcq.stem:
A 58-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has a 2-week history of a sticky red left eye. She has used chloramphenicol 0.5% drops four times daily for 10 days without improvement. There is mucopurulent discharge and diffuse injection with a papillary tarsal reaction, no follicles and no pre-auricular node. VA 6/9, cornea clear with fluorescein, lid margins normal, lacrimal sac non-tender with no reflux on pressure.
What is the most appropriate investigation?
o: Adenovirus PCR on a dry swab taken from the lower fornix
Conjunctival scraping for Giemsa-stained inclusion bodies
Conjunctival swab for Gram stain, culture and sensitivity
Tear break-up time and Schirmer test for dry eye disease
CT of the orbits and sinuses to exclude a deep infection
mcq.e: Simple bacterial conjunctivitis should settle within about a week; **failure to resolve** is the notes' indication for a conjunctival swab for culture and sensitivity, to identify a resistant organism and guide the change of antibiotic. Papillae with mucopurulent discharge and no follicles or node favour bacteria over virus or chlamydia. Normal lids and lacrimal sac exclude blepharitis and dacryocystitis as sources.
w: Wrong - adenovirus gives watery discharge with follicles and a tender node, none of which is present.
Wrong - chlamydial infection gives a follicular reaction and node; scraping is not the first test for a papillary picture.
Correct - a swab for Gram stain, culture and sensitivity is indicated when bacterial conjunctivitis fails to resolve.
Wrong - dry eye causes grittiness and redness but not persistent mucopurulent discharge.
Wrong - there is no proptosis, pain or motility problem to suggest orbital disease.

mcq.stem:
During one week in August, 40 workers at an electronics factory in Penang develop sudden red eyes. A 26-year-old worker's eyes became red and watery within a day of her roommate's, with a foreign-body sensation and lid swelling. Both eyes show bright red subconjunctival haemorrhages over the bulbar conjunctiva, a few follicles and a tender pre-auricular node. VA 6/6 both eyes; corneas clear. Most colleagues recover within a week.
Which organism is most likely responsible?
o: Neisseria gonorrhoeae (hyperacute purulent infection)
Adenovirus serotype 8 (keratoconjunctivitis)
Haemophilus influenzae (biotype aegyptius)
Enterovirus 70 or coxsackievirus A24 variant
Chlamydia trachomatis (serotypes D-K)
mcq.e: Explosive outbreaks in crowded tropical settings, a **1-2 day incubation**, watery follicular conjunctivitis with prominent **subconjunctival haemorrhages** and recovery within about a week is acute haemorrhagic conjunctivitis caused by picornaviruses (enterovirus 70, coxsackievirus A24) — the notes list coxsackie and picornavirus as viral causes. Adenovirus 8 has a longer incubation (about a week), a 2-3 week course and corneal infiltrates.
w: Wrong - gonococcal conjunctivitis produces torrential pus in a sexually active patient, not watery factory outbreaks.
Wrong - adenoviral EKC can cause haemorrhages, but it has a longer incubation and course and typically involves the cornea.
Wrong - Haemophilus aegyptius can give petechiae but produces a mucopurulent discharge with papillae rather than follicles.
Correct - enterovirus 70 and coxsackievirus A24 cause rapidly spreading acute haemorrhagic conjunctivitis that resolves within a week.
Wrong - chlamydial conjunctivitis is sexually transmitted and chronic, not an explosive workplace outbreak.

mcq.stem:
A 3-day-old boy on a district hospital postnatal ward develops red, swollen eyes. He was born by vaginal delivery to a mother who had an untreated vaginal discharge in late pregnancy; no ocular prophylaxis was given. Both lids are tense and swollen, copious creamy pus re-accumulates within minutes of cleaning, there is marked chemosis, and fluorescein shows a small peripheral corneal epithelial defect on the right.
Which organism is most likely?
o: Staphylococcus aureus from maternal skin
Chlamydia trachomatis serotypes D-K
Neisseria gonorrhoeae from the mother
Herpes simplex virus type 2 (genital)
Pseudomonas aeruginosa from the ward
mcq.e: Timing and discharge point to the organism: chemical irritation day 1, **gonococcus day 1-5 (hyperacute, copious pus, tense lid swelling, chemosis)**, chlamydia day 5-14 (moderate discharge), HSV 1-2 weeks (watery, vesicles). Neisseria can penetrate intact epithelium, so an early corneal defect is a warning of ulceration and perforation (notes p12). This is a same-day emergency.
w: Wrong - Staph aureus gives a milder purulent conjunctivitis, usually later, without such rapid re-accumulating pus and corneal threat.
Wrong - chlamydia typically starts at day 5-14 with a moderate mucopurulent discharge, not hyperacute pus on day 3.
Correct - hyperacute bilateral purulent conjunctivitis in the first days of life with early corneal involvement is gonococcal.
Wrong - neonatal HSV presents at 1-2 weeks with watery discharge, lid vesicles and dendritic keratitis.
Wrong - Pseudomonas affects sick, ventilated preterm babies in NICU; this is a well term baby exposed in the birth canal.

mcq.stem:
A 2-day-old girl weighing 3.0 kg is born to a mother found at delivery to have untreated gonorrhoea. The baby now has bilateral lid swelling with copious purulent discharge; a conjunctival smear shows Gram-negative intracellular diplococci. Corneas are clear with fluorescein. She is afebrile and feeding well; serum bilirubin is normal.
What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Topical penicillin drops hourly plus IV benzylpenicillin for 7 days
Topical chloramphenicol 0.5% 2-hourly alone, as the corneas are clear
Oral erythromycin 50 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses for 14 days
Topical gentamicin drops four times daily, reviewing in clinic at 1 week
Single dose of ceftriaxone 25-50 mg/kg IV/IM and frequent saline lavage
mcq.e: Gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum needs **systemic ceftriaxone, a single IV/IM dose of 25-50 mg/kg (max 125 mg)**, frequent saline irrigation to clear pus, evaluation for disseminated infection (sepsis, arthritis, meningitis), and treatment of both parents. Note: the notes advise topical and systemic penicillin — this is outdated because of widespread penicillinase-producing resistance. Topical antibiotics alone are inadequate.
w: Wrong - penicillin is no longer reliable against N. gonorrhoeae because of resistance; the notes' regimen is outdated.
Wrong - topical therapy alone does not eradicate gonococcus or treat systemic spread, and the cornea can perforate within days.
Wrong - oral erythromycin is the treatment for neonatal chlamydia, not gonococcus.
Wrong - topical gentamicin with delayed review is unsafe for a sight-threatening hyperacute infection.
Correct - single-dose systemic ceftriaxone with saline lavage, plus a disseminated-infection screen and treatment of the parents.

mcq.stem:
A 10-day-old boy is brought to the Klinik Kesihatan with 4 days of sticky, swollen eyelids on both sides. Chloramphenicol drops from a private GP for 5 days have not helped. The discharge is moderate and mucopurulent, the tarsal conjunctiva is red and thickened, and the corneas are clear. He is afebrile and feeding well. The mother was not screened antenatally, and the father has had dysuria for a month.
Which organism is most likely?
o: Staphylococcus aureus
Chlamydia trachomatis
Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Herpes simplex virus type 2
Streptococcus pneumoniae
mcq.e: Onset at **day 5-14** with moderate mucopurulent discharge, failure of topical chloramphenicol and an untreated parental genital infection suggest **chlamydial** ophthalmia neonatorum. Neonates cannot form follicles until about 6-8 weeks (immature conjunctival lymphoid tissue), so the conjunctiva looks papillary or even pseudomembranous. The infection also colonises the nasopharynx and can cause pneumonitis at 4-12 weeks, which is why systemic treatment is needed.
w: Wrong - Staph aureus usually responds to chloramphenicol and is not linked with a parental sexually transmitted infection.
Correct - day 5-14 onset, poor response to topical antibiotics and parental urethritis point to Chlamydia trachomatis.
Wrong - gonococcus is hyperacute with copious pus, usually within the first 1-5 days.
Wrong - neonatal HSV gives watery discharge with lid vesicles or dendrites, often with systemic illness.
Wrong - pneumococcus causes acute purulent conjunctivitis that usually responds to chloramphenicol, without the parental STI history.

mcq.stem:
A 2-week-old girl has had bilateral mucopurulent conjunctivitis since day 8. A conjunctival swab is positive for Chlamydia trachomatis on nucleic acid amplification testing. She fixes and follows, the corneas are clear and her chest is clear. Her 19-year-old mother and the father live together.
What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Oral erythromycin 12.5 mg/kg 6-hourly for 14 days; treat both parents
Topical tetracycline 1% ointment four times daily for 3 weeks, baby alone
Single-dose IM ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg with hourly saline irrigation
Oral doxycycline 2 mg/kg daily for 7 days for the baby only
Topical chloramphenicol with lacrimal sac massage for 1 month
mcq.e: Neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis needs **oral erythromycin 50 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses for 14 days**, which clears nasopharyngeal carriage and prevents chlamydial pneumonitis; topical therapy alone is inadequate. **Both parents** must be treated (e.g. azithromycin or doxycycline) via the STD/GUM clinic, otherwise reinfection follows. Note: the notes give topical tetracycline plus systemic erythromycin — the systemic course is the essential part; watch for infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis with macrolides in the first weeks.
w: Correct - a 14-day course of oral erythromycin for the baby with treatment of both parents.
Wrong - topical tetracycline alone leaves nasopharyngeal infection untreated and does not prevent pneumonitis.
Wrong - ceftriaxone with saline lavage is the regimen for gonococcal ophthalmia, not chlamydia.
Wrong - tetracyclines such as doxycycline are avoided in young children (tooth staining, bone effects), and the parents also need treatment.
Wrong - chloramphenicol does not treat chlamydia, and this is not a lacrimal drainage problem.

mcq.stem:
A 7-week-old girl is brought to the eye clinic because her left eye has watered since she was 2 weeks old, with yellowish crusting on the lashes each morning. She is feeding and thriving. The conjunctiva is white, the cornea is clear and of normal diameter, there is no photophobia, and gentle pressure over the medial canthus produces reflux of mucoid material from the lower punctum.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Late chlamydial ophthalmia neonatorum
Primary congenital glaucoma presenting with epiphora
Partially treated gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum
Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction
Neonatal herpes simplex blepharoconjunctivitis
mcq.e: A **white, quiet eye** with watering, sticky lashes and **mucoid reflux on pressure over the lacrimal sac** is congenital NLDO from an imperforate membrane at the valve of Hasner — the main differential of a 'sticky eye' in infancy. About 90% resolve spontaneously within the first year with lacrimal sac massage and lid cleaning; probing is considered if it persists around 12 months. Always exclude congenital glaucoma (photophobia, enlarged or cloudy cornea).
w: Wrong - chlamydial conjunctivitis gives a red, swollen, inflamed conjunctiva, not a white eye with sac reflux.
Wrong - congenital glaucoma causes watering with photophobia and an enlarged or hazy cornea, but no mucoid reflux from the sac.
Wrong - gonococcal infection is hyperacute with red chemosed conjunctiva and copious pus, not 5 weeks of quiet watering.
Correct - epiphora with reflux of mucus on sac pressure and a white eye is congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction.
Wrong - HSV gives lid vesicles, a red eye and sometimes dendritic keratitis, often with systemic illness.

mcq.stem:
A 12-day-old boy on the neonatal ward develops a watery red right eye. There is a cluster of small vesicles on the upper lid margin, the conjunctiva is injected, and fluorescein shows a branching epithelial lesion on the cornea. His mother had painful genital ulcers in the week before delivery. The baby is mildly lethargic and feeding less.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Topical aciclovir 3% ointment alone, with outpatient review in 1 week
Topical dexamethasone with chloramphenicol to limit corneal scarring
Oral erythromycin 50 mg/kg/day for 14 days and treat both parents
IV aciclovir plus topical antiviral, with LP and a full sepsis screen
Single-dose IV ceftriaxone with hourly saline lavage of both eyes
mcq.e: Neonatal HSV (usually HSV-2 from the birth canal) appears at 1-2 weeks with vesicles, watery discharge and dendritic keratitis, and can be part of **disseminated or CNS disease**. A lethargic neonate needs **IV aciclovir** with a lumbar puncture and sepsis work-up under the paediatric team, plus topical antiviral to protect the cornea. Note: the notes mention topical antiviral only — in a neonate systemic aciclovir is required.
w: Wrong - topical therapy alone ignores the risk of disseminated or CNS infection in a lethargic neonate.
Wrong - steroids are contraindicated with a dendritic ulcer; they extend the epithelial infection.
Wrong - erythromycin treats chlamydia; it has no activity against herpes simplex.
Correct - systemic aciclovir with full neonatal work-up plus topical antiviral cover for the cornea.
Wrong - ceftriaxone and lavage are for gonococcal ophthalmia; this picture is viral.

mcq.stem:
A 4-day-old girl on the postnatal ward of a district hospital has had a red, sticky left eye since yesterday. The lids are mildly swollen with mucopurulent discharge. She is feeding well and afebrile. The house officer plans to start chloramphenicol drops and discharge mother and baby home today.
Which step is mandatory before treatment begins?
o: Lacrimal sac massage and discharge home, as most such cases are duct-related
Conjunctival swabs for Gram stain, bacterial culture and chlamydial testing
CT of the orbits to exclude orbital cellulitis before giving antibiotics
Blood culture and lumbar puncture, since sepsis must always be excluded
Oral erythromycin first, taking swabs only if there is no response
mcq.e: Any conjunctivitis in the **first 28 days of life** is ophthalmia neonatorum: it is a **notifiable disease, swabs are mandatory** and the cornea must be examined to exclude ulceration (notes p12). Swabs go for Gram stain, culture (including gonococcus) and chlamydial testing, plus HSV PCR if suspected, before antibiotics alter the result. Blood culture and LP are reserved for gonococcal or HSV disease or an unwell baby.
w: Wrong - duct obstruction gives a white watery eye, not an inflamed sticky eye at day 4; this must be investigated as ophthalmia neonatorum.
Correct - swabs for Gram stain, culture and chlamydia (and HSV if suspected) are mandatory, with corneal examination and notification.
Wrong - nothing suggests orbital disease; CT exposes a neonate to radiation without benefit.
Wrong - a well, afebrile baby does not need an LP routinely; invasive tests are for suspected disseminated disease.
Wrong - empirical treatment before swabbing loses the microbiological diagnosis that guides therapy and parental treatment.

mcq.stem:
A 23-year-old woman has had a red, sticky right eye for 6 weeks despite two courses of chloramphenicol drops. She has a tender pre-auricular node, prominent follicles on the upper and lower tarsal conjunctiva, and fine new vessels growing a short way into the upper cornea. VA right 6/9. She has a new sexual partner and a vaginal discharge.
What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Topical tetracycline ointment alone until the follicles have disappeared
Topical prednisolone acetate 1% to settle the follicular reaction
A further 2 weeks of chloramphenicol drops, then swab if no better
Topical aciclovir 3% ointment five times daily for 2 weeks
Oral azithromycin 1 g once, GUM clinic referral and partner tracing
mcq.e: Chronic (weeks to months) unilateral **follicular** conjunctivitis with a node and **superior micropannus** in a sexually active adult is adult inclusion keratoconjunctivitis (C. trachomatis D-K). It is a genital infection with eye involvement, so treatment is **systemic: azithromycin 1 g single dose or doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days**, with STD/GUM referral, screening for other STIs and partner treatment. Note: the notes list topical and systemic tetracycline — the systemic drug is what matters.
w: Wrong - topical treatment alone leaves the genital infection, and therefore reinfection, untreated.
Wrong - steroids do not treat chlamydia and may prolong infection.
Wrong - chloramphenicol has already failed twice; chlamydia needs a macrolide or tetracycline given systemically.
Wrong - HSV conjunctivitis is usually acute with lid vesicles and dendrites, not 6 weeks of follicles with micropannus.
Correct - single-dose oral azithromycin with sexual health referral and partner tracing.

mcq.stem:
A 52-year-old woman, recently resettled in Malaysia from a rural village in Ethiopia, attends the eye clinic with a painful, watering left eye. VA left 3/60. Several upper lashes turn inwards and rub the cornea, which has a dense vascularised central opacity. Everting the upper lid shows a white linear scar parallel to the lid margin, and small depressions are seen at the upper limbus. Two of her grandchildren have chronic sticky eyes.
What is the main mechanism of her visual loss?
o: Reinfection causing tarsal scarring, entropion, trichiasis and corneal scarring
Chlamydial spread to the retina causing chorioretinal scarring at the macula
Chronic inflammation causing secondary angle closure and glaucomatous optic atrophy
Posterior subcapsular cataract induced by many years of chronic inflammation
Primary chlamydial stromal keratitis arising without any eyelid involvement
mcq.e: Trachoma (C. trachomatis A-C) blinds through **repeated reinfection** in childhood (poor hygiene, crowding, flies) causing subconjunctival fibrosis of the upper tarsus (Arlt line), lid entropion and **trichiasis**; lashes abrade the cornea, causing recurrent keratitis and **corneal scarring** (notes p12). Herbert pits are healed limbal follicles. It remains the commonest infective cause of blindness worldwide.
w: Correct - cicatricial lid changes from reinfection cause trichiasis, and the corneal scarring is what blinds.
Wrong - trachoma is an ocular surface disease; it does not involve the retina.
Wrong - trachoma does not cause angle closure or glaucomatous optic neuropathy.
Wrong - cataract is not the mechanism of trachomatous blindness; the dense corneal scar explains her vision.
Wrong - the corneal damage is secondary to lid scarring and lash trauma, which are clearly present.

mcq.stem:
A 6-year-old girl in a refugee settlement health programme has had chronic sticky eyes for months. The upper tarsal conjunctiva of each eye shows more than five follicles, flies are seen on her face, and her siblings are similarly affected. The corneas are clear, the lashes and lid margins are normal, and VA is 6/9 in both eyes.
Which management is most appropriate?
o: Topical chloramphenicol drops four times daily for the child alone for 1 week
Bilateral tarsal rotation surgery now to prevent future trichiasis
Oral azithromycin 20 mg/kg once, face washing and treating the household
Topical prednisolone drops to suppress the follicles and prevent scarring
Oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 3 weeks for the child only
mcq.e: Active follicular trachoma is managed with the **WHO SAFE strategy**: Surgery for trichiasis, **Antibiotics (single-dose oral azithromycin 20 mg/kg, 1 g in adults, often mass-treating the community)**, Facial cleanliness and Environmental improvement (water, latrines, fly control). Treating contacts prevents the reinfection that drives scarring. Note: the notes give oral/topical tetracycline — single-dose azithromycin is the current standard (topical tetracycline 1% is an alternative for infants).
w: Wrong - chloramphenicol does not treat chlamydia, and treating one child alone allows reinfection from the household.
Wrong - lid surgery is for established trichiasis; her lashes and lids are normal.
Correct - single-dose azithromycin plus facial cleanliness and household treatment follow the SAFE strategy.
Wrong - steroids do not treat infection and would not prevent scarring.
Wrong - doxycycline is avoided under 8 years and needs weeks of compliance; single-dose azithromycin is preferred.

mcq.stem:
An 11-year-old boy with asthma and eczema is brought to the eye clinic with 2 years of intensely itchy eyes and photophobia that worsen in the hot months but never fully settle. He rubs his eyes constantly and his mother removes thick, stringy white mucus each morning. VA 6/9 in both eyes.
