Upper lid eversion shows large flat-topped polygonal papillae; there are gelatinous nodules at the superior limbus studded with discrete chalk-white dots, and fine punctate epithelial erosions superiorly. No preauricular lymphadenopathy.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Atopic keratoconjunctivitis
Adenoviral epidemic keratoconjunctivitis
Vernal keratoconjunctivitis
Giant papillary conjunctivitis
Chlamydial inclusion conjunctivitis
mcq.e: Atopic boy, perennial itch with seasonal worsening, ropy mucus, giant cobblestone papillae on the UPPER tarsus and limbal gelatinous nodules = **vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC)**. The white dots are **Horner-Trantas dots**, aggregates of eosinophils and degenerate epithelium (the notes call them 'limbal follicles and white spots'). AKC is the adult counterpart in people with eczema and favours the lower tarsus; GPC needs a contact lens, exposed suture or prosthesis.
w: Wrong - AKC affects adults (30s-50s) with atopic dermatitis, involves the lower tarsus more and causes conjunctival scarring.
Wrong - adenovirus causes acute watery follicular conjunctivitis with a tender preauricular node, not years of itch with giant papillae.
Correct - atopic boy, perennial itch, ropy mucus, giant upper tarsal papillae and limbal Horner-Trantas dots are classic VKC.
Wrong - GPC gives giant upper tarsal papillae but requires a contact lens, suture or ocular prosthesis; there are no limbal Trantas dots.
Wrong - chlamydial disease gives a chronic mucopurulent FOLLICULAR conjunctivitis with micropannus in sexually active adults, not itch-dominant papillae.

mcq.stem:
A 23-year-old university student attends Klinik Kesihatan with 2 days of red, watery eyes in both eyes that started an hour after she spring-cleaned a dusty hostel store room. VA 6/6 in both eyes. Both bulbar conjunctivae look glassy and puffed up like jelly, with only mild injection; the corneas are clear and pupils react normally. A friend in the same hostel recently had 'sore eyes'.
Which additional finding would most strongly favour an allergic rather than an adenoviral cause?
o: Intense itch as the dominant symptom, with no tender preauricular node
Watery discharge from both eyes, with lids that feel puffy each morning
Onset in one eye followed by involvement of the other eye 2 days later
Follicles on the lower tarsal conjunctiva with a tender preauricular node
A gritty foreign-body sensation with mild crusting of the lashes on waking
mcq.e: **Itch is the cardinal symptom of allergic conjunctivitis**; a tender preauricular node and lower tarsal follicles point to adenovirus (a node also occurs in chlamydia). Watery discharge, lid puffiness, bilaterality and grittiness occur in both, so they do not discriminate. The glassy swelling is **chemosis = conjunctival OEDEMA** (the notes describe it as 'injection and swelling'; injection is a separate sign).
w: Correct - itch dominates allergic disease, and the absence of a tender preauricular node argues against adenovirus.
Wrong - watery discharge and lid puffiness occur in both allergic and viral conjunctivitis, so they do not discriminate.
Wrong - sequential second-eye involvement over a few days is typical of adenoviral spread, not a pointer to allergy.
Wrong - lower tarsal follicles plus a tender preauricular node are the signature of adenoviral (or chlamydial) conjunctivitis.
Wrong - grittiness and mild lash crusting are non-specific and are, if anything, more typical of viral or bacterial disease.

mcq.stem:
A 19-year-old Malaysian student studying in the United Kingdom has had itchy, watery, chemotic eyes every May and June for the past 2 years during the grass-pollen season. He is reviewed in the eye clinic in March while home on holiday and wants to prevent this year's attacks. Examination today is entirely normal and he has no other medical problems.
Which advice about sodium cromoglycate 2% eye drops is most appropriate?
o: Use them only on days when the itch starts, as they relieve itch within minutes
Use them for 3 days at the onset of symptoms, then stop to avoid rebound redness
Combine them with a topical steroid for the whole season to speed up their onset
Start once symptoms are severe, because they act by blocking histamine receptors
Start about 2 weeks before the season and use them regularly four times a day
mcq.e: Mast-cell stabilisers (sodium cromoglycate, nedocromil, lodoxamide) PREVENT degranulation; they do not block histamine already released, so they take **about 2 weeks** of regular use to work. Start them before the pollen season and continue throughout. For immediate itch relief use a topical antihistamine or a dual-action drop (olopatadine, ketotifen). Steroids are reserved for severe disease, short-term only.
w: Wrong - cromoglycate has no rapid antihistamine effect; on-demand use gives little benefit.
Wrong - cromoglycate causes no rebound redness and needs continuous regular use; 3 days is far too short to work.
Wrong - routine season-long steroid exposes the eye to steroid glaucoma and cataract; it does not speed cromoglycate's onset.
Wrong - cromoglycate stabilises mast cells rather than blocking H1 receptors, so starting late when severe is ineffective.
Correct - mast-cell stabilisers need about 2 weeks of regular use, so start before allergen exposure and continue through the season.

mcq.stem:
A 14-year-old boy with long-standing itchy eyes and giant upper tarsal papillae has been buying dexamethasone 0.1% eye drops over the counter and using them four times a day for 8 months because they 'stop the itch'. He has no pain or haloes. VA 6/9 in both eyes. IOP 34 mmHg right and 32 mmHg left (Goldmann). Gonioscopy shows wide open angles, the anterior chambers are quiet, and cup-disc ratios are 0.7 with inferior rim thinning.
What is the most likely mechanism of the raised IOP?
o: Pupillary block from posterior synechiae causing secondary angle closure
Reduced aqueous outflow through the trabecular meshwork induced by steroid
Trabeculitis from active anterior uveitis obstructing the drainage angle
Increased aqueous production by the ciliary body driven by histamine release
Pigment granules shed by eye rubbing clogging the trabecular meshwork
mcq.e: Chronic topical steroid in a 'steroid responder' increases extracellular matrix in the **trabecular meshwork**, reducing outflow: an open-angle, painless rise in IOP that can cause **steroid-induced glaucoma** (here already with disc damage). Children are frequent high responders. This is why the notes allow steroids only for severe disease, short-term, with IOP monitoring; steroids also cause posterior subcapsular cataract. Manage by stopping the steroid, lowering IOP and switching to steroid-sparing therapy.
w: Wrong - angles are wide open and there is no inflammation to form synechiae, so pupillary block is excluded.
Correct - steroid-induced reduction of trabecular outflow gives open-angle, quiet-eye IOP elevation in a steroid responder.
Wrong - the anterior chamber is quiet; uveitic trabeculitis needs active cells and flare.
Wrong - histamine does not increase aqueous secretion; steroid glaucoma is an outflow problem.
Wrong - pigment dispersion occurs in young myopes with iris transillumination and Krukenberg spindle, not from rubbing.

mcq.stem:
A 10-year-old boy with known vernal disease, using olopatadine drops, presents to the eye clinic with 5 days of severe photophobia, pain on blinking and blurred vision in the right eye. VA right 6/24, left 6/9. The right upper tarsus is covered in giant papillae. Fluorescein shows a shallow, oval, well-demarcated epithelial defect in the upper half of the cornea with a grey-white opaque plaque at its base. There is no hypopyon.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Add oral cetirizine, continue olopatadine and review in the clinic in 2 weeks
Firm double pad with chloramphenicol ointment for 48 hours until it heals
Topical aciclovir 3% ointment five times a day for a herpetic dendritic ulcer
Urgent ophthalmic treatment: topical steroid, antibiotic cover, plaque removal
Reassure that this is self-limiting punctate keratitis and give lubricants only
mcq.e: An oval superior epithelial defect with a plaque of mucus and eosinophil products in VKC is a **shield ulcer**: sight-threatening (risk of infection, scarring and, in a child, amblyopia) and needs **same-day ophthalmology**. The plaque prevents re-epithelialisation, so treatment is intensive topical steroid, antibiotic prophylaxis and **debridement or superficial keratectomy** of the plaque (amniotic membrane if non-healing). Antihistamines alone are inadequate and patching is avoided.
w: Wrong - this undertreats a sight-threatening corneal complication; a 2-week delay risks infection and scarring.
Wrong - pressure patching does not remove the plaque, which is what blocks healing, and raises infection risk.
Wrong - a herpetic dendrite is branching with terminal bulbs and no plaque; this is a VKC shield ulcer.
Correct - shield ulcer needs urgent ophthalmic care with steroid, antibiotic cover and debridement of the plaque.
Wrong - a well-demarcated ulcer with a plaque and VA 6/24 is not simple punctate keratitis.

mcq.stem:
A 21-year-old engineering student has worn the same pair of monthly soft contact lenses for about 3 months. She complains of 6 weeks of itch, stringy mucus coating the lenses and increasing lens intolerance; the lenses ride up when she blinks. VA 6/6 with spectacles. Upper lid eversion shows papillae larger than 1 mm across the superior tarsal plate. The cornea is clear with no infiltrate or staining, and the limbus looks normal.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Vernal keratoconjunctivitis
Acanthamoeba keratitis
Superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis
Giant papillary conjunctivitis
Bacterial conjunctivitis
mcq.e: **Giant papillary conjunctivitis (GPC)** is a mechanical and immune reaction of the upper tarsus to a foreign surface (contact lens deposits, exposed suture, prosthesis): itch, mucus on lenses, lens decentration and papillae >1 mm. Management is to stop lens wear until settled, then switch to daily disposables with better hygiene, plus a mast-cell stabiliser. The cornea is clear, so keratitis is not present.
w: Wrong - VKC affects atopic boys before puberty and often shows limbal Horner-Trantas dots; it is not tied to lens wear.
Wrong - Acanthamoeba causes severe pain out of proportion with a corneal infiltrate or ring, and this cornea is clear.
Wrong - SLK causes superior bulbar injection and limbal staining, often with thyroid disease, not giant tarsal papillae.
Correct - overworn soft lenses, mucus, lens riding up and giant upper tarsal papillae with a clear cornea is GPC.
Wrong - bacterial conjunctivitis is acute with mucopurulent discharge and is not itch-dominant with giant papillae.

mcq.stem:
A 16-year-old boy has had vernal disease since the age of 6. He has never used steroid drops but admits to rubbing his eyes 'all the time'. Over 2 years his spectacles have needed frequent changes and VA is now 6/18 right and 6/12 left, improving only partly with pinhole. Retinoscopy shows a scissoring reflex, the right cornea is thinned centrally, and on downgaze the lower lid shows a V-shaped indentation. Lenses are clear and fundi normal.
What is the most likely cause of his progressive visual decline?
o: Posterior subcapsular cataract related to atopy
Keratoconus (progressive corneal ectasia)
Central corneal scar from a healed shield ulcer
Progressive axial myopia of adolescence
Bilateral ametropic (refractive) amblyopia
mcq.e: Chronic eye rubbing in VKC and atopy is a major risk factor for **keratoconus**: progressive irregular myopic astigmatism, scissoring retinoscopy reflex, central thinning and **Munson sign** (V-shaped lower lid indentation on downgaze). This is why patients with VKC are told to avoid rubbing and use cold compresses. Refer for corneal topography and consider corneal cross-linking to halt progression.
w: Wrong - the lenses are clear; steroid-related PSC is also unlikely without steroid exposure.
Correct - rubbing in VKC causes keratoconus: irregular astigmatism, scissoring reflex, central thinning and Munson sign.
Wrong - there is no history of a shield ulcer, and a scar would not give a scissoring reflex and Munson sign.
Wrong - simple axial myopia corrects fully with spectacles and causes neither corneal thinning nor scissoring.
Wrong - amblyopia does not progress at 16 and does not cause corneal thinning; vision was previously normal.

mcq.stem:
A 40-year-old man with lifelong atopic eczema attends the eye clinic with years of itchy, burning eyes in every season. His lower lids are thickened, scaly and fissured with cracking at the lateral canthi. Papillae are most marked on the LOWER tarsal conjunctiva, the inferior fornix is shortened by fine subconjunctival scarring, there is punctate keratopathy with superficial corneal vessels, and both lenses show anterior subcapsular plaques.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Ocular mucous membrane pemphigoid
Cicatricial trachoma
Seasonal allergic conjunctivitis
Chronic staphylococcal blepharitis
Atopic keratoconjunctivitis
mcq.e: **Atopic keratoconjunctivitis (AKC)** is the chronic, scarring allergic disease of ADULTS with atopic dermatitis: eczematous lids, lower tarsal papillae, forniceal shortening, keratopathy with vascularisation and an atopic (anterior subcapsular, shield-like) cataract. VKC is the childhood disease of the upper tarsus; seasonal allergy never scars. Pemphigoid also shortens the fornix but is not itch-dominant and lacks eczema.
w: Wrong - pemphigoid causes progressive symblepharon in older adults, but without lifelong eczema and itch-dominant disease.
Wrong - trachoma scars the UPPER tarsus (Arlt line) with trichiasis and follows repeated childhood chlamydial infection.
Wrong - seasonal allergy is intermittent, itchy and chemotic but never causes conjunctival scarring or keratopathy.
Wrong - staphylococcal blepharitis gives lash-base crusts and marginal keratitis, not forniceal scarring and atopic cataract.
Correct - adult eczema, lower tarsal papillae, forniceal scarring, keratopathy and atopic cataract define AKC.

mcq.stem:
A 12-year-old boy with vernal disease has needed four courses of topical prednisolone in the past year. During the last course his IOP rose to 30 mmHg and settled only after the drops were stopped. He is now on olopatadine twice daily but still has frequent flare-ups with limbal gelatinous nodules and giant upper tarsal papillae. VA 6/9 in both eyes.
What is the most appropriate long-term treatment to add?
o: Topical ciclosporin as a steroid-sparing immunomodulator
Continuous low-dose topical dexamethasone with IOP checks
Oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg/day tapered over three months
Topical chloramphenicol four times a day to prevent infection
Topical tetracaine drops at night to stop him rubbing his eyes
mcq.e: In steroid-dependent VKC, especially in a proven **steroid responder**, the steroid-sparing option is topical **ciclosporin** (or tacrolimus), which inhibits T-cell activation. Continuous steroid risks glaucoma and cataract; systemic steroid is unjustified for a local disease. Topical anaesthetics must never be prescribed for home use (toxic keratopathy). Antibiotics do not treat allergy.
w: Correct - topical ciclosporin controls VKC and allows steroid courses to be avoided in a steroid responder.
Wrong - he has already shown a steroid IOP response; continuous steroid risks glaucoma and cataract.
Wrong - systemic steroid exposes a child to growth, bone and metabolic toxicity for a local disease.
Wrong - antibiotics have no role in allergic inflammation in the absence of infection.
Wrong - home topical anaesthetic causes toxic, non-healing keratopathy and is never prescribed.

mcq.stem:
An 8-year-old boy is referred from Klinik Kesihatan with 1 year of itchy eyes, photophobia and frequent blinking. The referral letter says 'mild injection only, lower lid conjunctiva normal'. In the eye clinic VA is 6/9 in both eyes, the bulbar conjunctiva is mildly injected and the cornea shows faint superior punctate fluorescein staining.
Which examination step is most likely to reveal the key diagnostic sign?
o: Pull down the lower lids and inspect the inferior fornix for follicles
Palpate in front of the tragus for a tender preauricular node
Evert the upper lids to inspect the superior tarsal conjunctiva
Dilate the pupils and examine the fundi with indirect ophthalmoscopy
Perform a Schirmer test to measure aqueous tear production over 5 min
mcq.e: Itch, photophobia and superior punctate keratopathy in a boy suggest **vernal disease**, whose giant cobblestone papillae sit on the **UPPER tarsal plate** and are missed unless the upper lid is everted. Lower fornix follicles and a preauricular node are viral or chlamydial signs; Schirmer and fundoscopy do not help. Always evert the upper lid in a chronically itchy, photophobic child.
w: Wrong - the lower lid has already been examined and is normal; follicles there point to viral or chlamydial disease.
Wrong - a tender preauricular node supports adenoviral or chlamydial infection, which this chronic itchy picture is not.
Correct - upper lid eversion shows the giant cobblestone papillae of VKC on the superior tarsus.
Wrong - the posterior segment is not involved in allergic eye disease.
Wrong - Schirmer assesses dry eye; it would not explain itch with superior keratopathy in a child.

mcq.stem:
A 72-year-old man with type 2 diabetes had uneventful phacoemulsification of the left eye 3 days ago. On day 1 his VA was 6/12 and the eye was comfortable. He returns to the eye clinic with aching pain that worsened overnight and blurred vision. VA left hand movements. The lids are swollen, the conjunctiva is chemosed and injected, there is a 2 mm hypopyon with fibrin over the IOL, and the red reflex is poor with no fundal view. IOP 18 mmHg.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Toxic anterior segment syndrome
Expected post-operative inflammation
Retained lens fragment with lens-induced uveitis
Acute post-operative endophthalmitis
Acute angle closure from retained viscoelastic
mcq.e: An eye that was quiet on day 1 and then becomes **painful with falling VA, hypopyon and vitreous involvement (poor red reflex)** is acute post-operative endophthalmitis until proven otherwise. Most cases present in the first week; the **MOH CPG defines acute cases as presenting within 2 weeks** (the notes say 'within 7 days'). TASS appears within 12-24 h with limbus-to-limbus corneal oedema, little pain and no vitritis. Diabetes is a recognised risk factor.
w: Wrong - TASS starts 12-24 h after surgery with diffuse corneal oedema, mild pain and no vitreous involvement.
Wrong - normal post-op inflammation improves daily; pain, a VA drop and hypopyon are never expected.
Wrong - retained fragments give corneal oedema and raised IOP, usually without a hypopyon and loss of red reflex.
Correct - pain, VA drop to HM, hypopyon and vitritis after a quiet day 1 is acute post-operative endophthalmitis.
Wrong - retained viscoelastic raises IOP in the first 24 h; this IOP is normal and the picture is infective.

mcq.stem:
A 66-year-old woman presents to the eye clinic at 4 pm, 5 days after phacoemulsification of the right eye, with 1 day of pain and blurred vision. VA right hand movements, left 6/9. There is a 1.5 mm hypopyon, fibrin in the anterior chamber and a hazy red reflex. B-scan ultrasound shows diffuse vitreous opacities with a flat retina.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Start hourly fortified topical antibiotics and review her first thing tomorrow
Vitreous tap and intravitreal vancomycin plus ceftazidime within the hour
Immediate pars plana vitrectomy in theatre with intravitreal antibiotics
Take a conjunctival swab and start antibiotics once the culture returns
Intensive topical prednisolone acetate 1% hourly and review in 24 hours
mcq.e: The MOH CPG requires a **vitreous tap (± AC tap) and intravitreal antibiotics within ONE hour** of clinical diagnosis: **vancomycin 2 mg/0.1 mL + ceftazidime 2 mg/0.1 mL** (amikacin 0.4 mg is the alternative but is more retinotoxic). In the EVS, immediate vitrectomy helped only eyes with **light perception** vision; with HM or better, tap-and-inject is enough. Topical drops do not reach therapeutic vitreous levels, and conjunctival swabs do not reflect the intraocular organism.
w: Wrong - topical antibiotics do not reach the vitreous; delaying intravitreal treatment overnight loses vision.
Correct - tap-and-inject with vancomycin plus ceftazidime within 1 hour is the CPG standard for VA of HM or better.
Wrong - EVS showed immediate vitrectomy benefits only eyes presenting with light perception vision.
Wrong - waiting for culture wastes critical hours, and surface flora do not identify the intraocular organism.
Wrong - steroid alone without intravitreal antibiotic lets the infection progress; steroids are an adjunct only.

mcq.stem:
A 79-year-old man returns 6 days after extracapsular cataract extraction of the left eye with severe pain since the previous evening. VA left is perception of light only, with accurate projection. There is lid oedema, marked chemosis, a 3 mm hypopyon and no red reflex. B-scan ultrasound shows dense vitreous opacities with an attached retina.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Immediate vitrectomy plus intravitreal vancomycin and ceftazidime
Vitreous tap with intravitreal antibiotics, then review in 48-72 hours
IV ceftazidime and amikacin for 10 days, then reassess the vision
Hourly fortified topical antibiotics plus subconjunctival cefuroxime
Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg first to settle inflammation, then a tap
mcq.e: The **Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study** decision rule: presenting VA of **light perception only -> immediate pars plana vitrectomy** (with intravitreal antibiotics); hand movements or better -> tap-and-inject. Vitrectomy debulks organisms and toxins and gives a large sample for culture. EVS also showed no benefit from systemic IV ceftazidime/amikacin, and steroids must never precede antibiotics.
w: Correct - with only light perception, EVS showed immediate vitrectomy with intravitreal antibiotics improves outcome.
Wrong - tap-and-inject is the EVS choice for HM or better; at light perception immediate vitrectomy is better.
Wrong - systemic IV antibiotics had no effect on outcome in EVS and delaying intravitreal therapy loses the eye.
Wrong - topical and subconjunctival routes do not achieve vitreous levels sufficient for endophthalmitis.
Wrong - steroid before antibiotic can worsen infection; oral prednisolone is considered only 24 h after antibiotics.

mcq.stem:
A 32-year-old grass-cutter in Johor is struck in the right eye by a fragment thrown up by his brush-cutter while trimming a muddy roadside verge. A small self-sealing corneal laceration is noted in the ED. Eighteen hours later he has severe pain, fever of 38.4 °C and swollen lids; VA right is perception of light. There is a ring-shaped corneal infiltrate, a hypopyon and no fundal view. Total white cell count is raised.
Which organism is most likely responsible?
o: Staphylococcus epidermidis
Propionibacterium acnes
Candida albicans
Toxocara canis
Bacillus cereus
mcq.e: Post-traumatic endophthalmitis after a **soil- or vegetation-contaminated injury** is classically caused by **Bacillus cereus**: fulminant onset within 24-48 h, **corneal ring abscess**, fever and leucocytosis, with very poor prognosis. Its toxins destroy the retina rapidly, so intravitreal **vancomycin** (Bacillus is usually vancomycin-sensitive) and early vitrectomy plus search for a retained IOFB are needed. S. epidermidis is the commonest post-cataract organism and is far less aggressive.
w: Wrong - CoNS dominates post-cataract endophthalmitis and gives a milder course, not a febrile ring abscess within 18 h.
Wrong - P. acnes causes indolent delayed-onset endophthalmitis months after cataract surgery.
Wrong - Candida causes slowly evolving endogenous or post-traumatic infection over weeks, not fulminant 18-hour disease.
Wrong - Toxocara causes a chronic granuloma or endophthalmitis in children exposed to puppies, not acute trauma sepsis.
Correct - soil-contaminated trauma with fever, ring infiltrate and fulminant 24-hour onset is classic Bacillus cereus.

mcq.stem:
A 52-year-old woman has been in the ICU for 3 weeks after bowel surgery, receiving total parenteral nutrition through a central line and broad-spectrum antibiotics. Blood cultures grew yeast last week. She now reports floaters and blurring in the left eye. VA left 6/24. There are mild anterior chamber cells, vitreous haze with fluffy white balls strung together like beads, and several small creamy-white chorioretinal lesions.
What is the most appropriate treatment for the eye?
o: Intravitreal vancomycin and ceftazidime plus oral moxifloxacin
Hourly topical natamycin 5% drops with a topical cycloplegic
Systemic plus intravitreal antifungal therapy, e.g. voriconazole
Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day to control the vitritis first
Intravitreal ganciclovir injections with oral valganciclovir
mcq.e: Line sepsis, TPN, broad-spectrum antibiotics and candidaemia with **'string of pearls' cotton-ball vitritis** and creamy chorioretinitis = **endogenous Candida endophthalmitis**. Treat with **systemic antifungal (voriconazole or fluconazole; amphotericin B) plus intravitreal antifungal (amphotericin B or voriconazole)**, ± vitrectomy. The notes list 'intravitreal and oral fluoroquinolone' under this heading: a fluoroquinolone has no antifungal activity. The CPG warns that **fungal endophthalmitis must not receive oral prednisolone**.
w: Wrong - antibacterials have no activity against Candida; this regimen is for bacterial post-operative infection.
Wrong - topical natamycin is for fungal KERATITIS and does not penetrate to the vitreous or retina.
Correct - endogenous Candida needs systemic plus intravitreal antifungal such as voriconazole or amphotericin B.
Wrong - systemic steroid worsens fungal infection; the CPG says fungal endophthalmitis should not receive prednisolone.
Wrong - ganciclovir treats CMV retinitis, which gives haemorrhagic retinal necrosis, not beaded fluffy vitreous balls.

mcq.stem:
A 61-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes presents to the ED with 3 days of fever and right upper quadrant pain and, since this morning, a painful red left eye with blurred vision. He has never had eye surgery or trauma. Temperature 38.9 °C. VA left 6/60. There is lid swelling, ciliary injection, a 1 mm hypopyon and dense vitritis; the right eye is normal. A vitreous tap and intravitreal antibiotics are given.
Which further investigation is now most important?
o: HLA-B27 typing with sacroiliac joint radiographs
Serum ACE level and chest radiograph for sarcoidosis
Blood cultures and abdominal imaging for the source
Conjunctival swab for culture and antibiotic sensitivity
Temporal artery biopsy and ESR to exclude arteritis
mcq.e: Endophthalmitis without surgery or trauma is **endogenous**: the eye is seeded from bacteraemia or fungaemia, and the systemic source can kill the patient. Work-up = **blood cultures (± urine, line tips), echocardiogram and imaging for the focus**. In diabetic patients in Southeast Asia, **Klebsiella pneumoniae liver abscess** is a classic source (fever + RUQ pain), so abdominal ultrasound/CT is essential, with systemic IV antibiotics and physician co-management.
w: Wrong - HLA-B27 relates to acute anterior uveitis, which does not cause febrile sepsis with dense vitritis.
Wrong - sarcoid uveitis is granulomatous and chronic, not an acute febrile hypopyon with dense vitritis.
Correct - endogenous endophthalmitis needs blood cultures and a hunt for the source, here a likely liver abscess.
Wrong - conjunctival flora do not reflect a haematogenous intraocular infection.
Wrong - GCA causes ischaemic visual loss with a white eye, not hypopyon and vitritis with fever.

mcq.stem:
A 70-year-old woman had uneventful phacoemulsification with an in-the-bag IOL 5 months ago. Since then she has had three episodes of mild painless blurring and floaters, each settling on topical steroid and recurring within weeks of stopping. Today VA is 6/18, with large mutton-fat keratic precipitates on the IOL, a small hypopyon and a white plaque on the posterior capsule inside the bag. A vitreous tap grew a slow anaerobic Gram-positive bacillus, and inflammation recurred despite intravitreal vancomycin 6 weeks ago.
What is the most appropriate definitive management?
o: Long-term topical prednisolone acetate 1% at the lowest effective dose
Nd:YAG posterior capsulotomy to clear the plaque from the visual axis
Oral moxifloxacin 400 mg daily continued indefinitely as suppression
Oral clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily as the sole long-term treatment
Vitrectomy, capsular bag and IOL removal, and intravitreal vancomycin
mcq.e: Delayed-onset (chronic) endophthalmitis from **Propionibacterium (Cutibacterium) acnes** begins weeks to years after surgery, is steroid-responsive but relapses on taper, and sequesters in a **capsular plaque**. Antibiotics alone fail because organisms hide in the bag, so recurrent cases need **vitrectomy with removal of the capsular bag ± IOL** and intravitreal vancomycin (MOH CPG). The notes' initial empirical oral fluoroquinolone is 'moxifloxacin' (spelt 'moxifloxacilin' in the notes).
w: Wrong - steroids only mask the infection; it relapses each time they are tapered.
Wrong - YAG capsulotomy can release sequestered organisms into the vitreous and worsen the infection.
Wrong - oral antibiotics cannot eradicate organisms sheltered in the capsular plaque; this has already recurred.
Wrong - clarithromycin is an adjunct in culture-negative acute cases, not sole therapy for sequestered P. acnes.
Correct - recurrent P. acnes needs vitrectomy with removal of the capsular bag (± IOL) and intravitreal vancomycin.

mcq.stem:
A 74-year-old man is being prepared for phacoemulsification of the left eye in an MOH hospital. He has mild anterior blepharitis controlled with lid hygiene and no drug allergies. The theatre team is auditing its endophthalmitis prophylaxis protocol after two cases last year.
Which measure has the strongest evidence for reducing post-operative endophthalmitis?
o: Povidone-iodine 5% into the conjunctival sac just before surgery
Trimming the eyelashes of the operated eye on the day before surgery
Irrigating the lacrimal passages with saline before the operation
Intravenous cefuroxime given at the start of the operation
Topical antibiotic drops four times a day for 3 days before surgery
mcq.e: The MOH CPG gives a **Grade A** recommendation to **povidone-iodine 5%** for the skin and **conjunctival sac** before surgery (chlorhexidine 0.05% if allergic) and to **intracameral cefuroxime 1 mg/0.1 mL** at the end of surgery. Lash trimming, lacrimal irrigation, preoperative topical antibiotics and IV prophylaxis have no proven benefit. Never use povidone-iodine containing detergent (it damages the cornea).
w: Correct - 5% povidone-iodine in the conjunctival sac is the Grade A, best-evidence antiseptic measure.
Wrong - lash trimming has not been shown to reduce endophthalmitis; proper draping of the lashes matters instead.
Wrong - preoperative lacrimal irrigation has no significant prophylactic effect.
Wrong - IV antibiotic prophylaxis is not proven to prevent post-operative endophthalmitis.
Wrong - there is insufficient evidence that preoperative topical antibiotics reduce endophthalmitis.

mcq.stem:
A 68-year-old woman is reviewed by a house officer on day 4 after phacoemulsification of the right eye because her daughter says the eye is 'still red'. The house officer is unsure whether this is normal and calls the eye registrar for advice before examining her further.
Which finding would most strongly indicate infection rather than expected post-operative inflammation?
o: Grade 1+ anterior chamber cells and flare on the first day
Mild stromal oedema around the main corneal incision site
IOP of 26 mmHg on day 1 that settles promptly with timolol
Worsening pain on day 4 with VA dropping from 6/12 to 6/60
Subconjunctival haemorrhage at the anaesthetic injection site
mcq.e: After uneventful cataract surgery the eye should get **more comfortable and see better each day**. **Pain (74-85%) and reduced vision (>90%)** are the commonest features of acute endophthalmitis in the CPG, with hypopyon/fibrin and vitritis. Mild cells, wound-edge oedema, a transient IOP spike and subconjunctival haemorrhage are all expected. Any post-op patient with increasing pain and falling VA needs same-day assessment.
w: Wrong - mild AC cells and flare are expected after any intraocular surgery.
Wrong - localised oedema at the incision is common and resolves within days.
Wrong - an early IOP spike from retained viscoelastic is common and settles with treatment.
Correct - new or worsening pain with a falling VA is the hallmark of post-operative endophthalmitis.
Wrong - a subconjunctival haemorrhage from local anaesthetic is harmless and painless.

mcq.stem:
A 66-year-old woman without diabetes or peptic ulcer disease presents 6 days after phacoemulsification with pain, VA hand movements and a 2 mm hypopyon. A vitreous tap is done and intravitreal vancomycin 2 mg plus ceftazidime 2 mg are injected within the hour. The house officer drafts the ward treatment plan.
Which proposed treatment is NOT supported by evidence as a routine measure?
o: Fortified topical antibiotic drops hourly round the clock at first
Routine IV ceftazidime and amikacin for 10 days, as used in the EVS
Intensive topical prednisolone acetate 1% soon after the injection
Repeat intravitreal antibiotics at 48-72 h if the eye is worsening
Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day starting 24 h after the injection
mcq.e: The **EVS showed systemic IV ceftazidime and amikacin had no effect** on outcome after cataract surgery; the CPG reserves IV antibiotics for severe virulent cases, with oral moxifloxacin 400 mg daily for 10 days as an alternative. Hourly topical antibiotics, intensive topical steroid soon after the injection, repeat injection at 48-72 h if needed, and **oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day from 24 h after intravitreal antibiotics** (not in fungal cases) are all in the CPG. The notes' 'oral steroids (topical dexa)' means topical steroid ± oral steroid AFTER antibiotics.
w: Wrong - the CPG recommends hourly round-the-clock topical antibiotics to treat surface and anterior segment infection.
Correct - EVS found routine systemic IV ceftazidime and amikacin gave no benefit; it is reserved for severe cases.
Wrong - intensive topical steroid soon after intravitreal antibiotics is recommended to control AC inflammation.
Wrong - repeating intravitreal antibiotics at 48-72 h is advised if the eye fails to improve.
Wrong - oral prednisolone 24 h after intravitreal antibiotics did no harm in EVS and may be given if not fungal.

mcq.stem:
A 64-year-old man had a left trabeculectomy with mitomycin C 4 years ago for advanced primary open-angle glaucoma. He presents to the eye clinic with 1 day of a sore, red, watering left eye, photophobia and a little sticky discharge. VA left 6/12 (6/9 at his last visit). The bleb is opaque and milky white, surrounded by intensely injected conjunctiva. There are 2+ anterior chamber cells without hypopyon. The red reflex is bright and B-scan shows a clear vitreous.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Bacterial conjunctivitis around a healthy bleb
Blebitis with anterior chamber involvement
Bleb-related endophthalmitis
Encapsulated bleb (Tenon cyst)
Nodular episcleritis overlying the bleb
mcq.e: A **milky-white bleb ringed by injected conjunctiva ('white on red')** with pain, photophobia and discharge years after trabeculectomy is **blebitis**: infection in or around the bleb WITHOUT vitreous involvement. Bleb-related infection is staged: **stage 1 bleb only, stage 2 + AC reaction (as here), stage 3 vitreous = bleb-related endophthalmitis**. A clear vitreous and bright red reflex exclude stage 3. Conjunctivitis does not opacify the bleb.
w: Wrong - conjunctivitis does not turn the bleb itself milky white or cause an AC reaction.
Correct - white-on-red bleb with AC cells but a clear vitreous is blebitis (stage 2 bleb-related infection).
Wrong - bleb-related endophthalmitis requires vitreous involvement; here the red reflex is bright and the vitreous clear.
Wrong - a Tenon cyst is a tense, thick-walled, vascularised dome in the early weeks after surgery, not an infected bleb.
Wrong - episcleritis causes mild discomfort and sectoral redness, without discharge, an opaque bleb or AC cells.

mcq.stem:
A 70-year-old woman who had a trabeculectomy in the right eye 7 years ago presents with 2 days of severe pain and blurring. VA right hand movements. The bleb is milky white with surrounding intense injection and a positive Seidel test. There is a 2 mm hypopyon, dense vitreous cells on slit lamp and a dull red reflex. B-scan shows diffuse vitreous opacities with an attached retina.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Hourly fortified topical vancomycin and cefazolin, reviewing in 24 hours
Intensive topical antibiotics with topical steroid started at the same time
Oral ciprofloxacin 750 mg twice daily and review in clinic within 48 hours
Bleb needling with 5-fluorouracil to restore filtration through the bleb
Vitreous tap and intravitreal vancomycin plus ceftazidime within one hour
mcq.e: Vitreous involvement turns blebitis into **bleb-related endophthalmitis (stage 3)**, which is treated as endophthalmitis: **vitreous tap and intravitreal vancomycin + ceftazidime within 1 hour**, plus intensive topical antibiotics (vitrectomy if light perception only). The organisms (streptococci, H. influenzae) are more virulent than post-cataract CoNS, so outcomes are often poor and delay is disastrous. Topical drops alone are adequate only when the vitreous is clear.
w: Wrong - topical treatment alone is for blebitis without vitreous involvement; here the vitreous is infected.
Wrong - steroid from the outset without intravitreal antibiotic risks rapid progression of a virulent infection.
Wrong - oral antibiotics alone do not achieve sterilising vitreous levels for established endophthalmitis.
Wrong - needling with an antimetabolite in an infected eye spreads infection and is contraindicated.
Correct - vitritis means bleb-related endophthalmitis: tap and inject intravitreal antibiotics within 1 hour.

mcq.stem:
A 55-year-old man with advanced primary open-angle glaucoma and progressive field loss on maximal medical therapy is listed for trabeculectomy. The glaucoma surgeon discusses with the trainee how surgical choices affect his lifetime risk of bleb-related infection, which can appear many years after surgery.
Which surgical choice would most increase his long-term risk of bleb-related infection?
o: Fornix-based conjunctival flap giving a diffuse superior bleb
Guarded partial-thickness scleral flap with releasable sutures
Siting the bleb inferiorly, close to the 6 o'clock limbus
Placing the bleb superiorly, under cover of the upper lid
Post-operative topical steroid tapered over 6-8 weeks
mcq.e: Bleb location is a major risk factor: per the notes, **inferior blebs have ~7.8% vs superior blebs ~1.3% infection risk per patient-year**, because an inferior bleb is exposed to the tear lake and debris and is not covered by the upper lid. Other risk factors are **bleb leak, intraoperative mitomycin C, thin/elevated blebs, full-thickness (unguarded) procedures, chronic post-op antibiotic use, high axial length, conjunctivitis and URTI**. Trabeculectomy is therefore sited superiorly.
w: Wrong - a fornix-based flap tends to give a diffuse, posteriorly draining superior bleb, which carries a lower risk.
Wrong - a guarded partial-thickness flap is SAFER than a full-thickness procedure, which carries a higher risk.
Correct - an inferior bleb, exposed to the tear lake and not covered by the lid, has a much higher infection risk.
Wrong - superior placement under the upper lid protects the bleb and is standard to reduce infection.
Wrong - standard post-op topical steroid controls scarring and is not a recognised risk factor for bleb infection.

mcq.stem:
A 62-year-old woman had a right trabeculectomy with mitomycin C 6 years ago. She complains of intermittent watering of the right eye without pain. VA 6/9. The bleb is thin-walled, avascular and cystic. IOP 5 mmHg. The anterior chamber is deep and quiet, with no discharge or conjunctival injection.
Which test is most useful to confirm the suspected cause of her symptoms?
o: Seidel test with concentrated fluorescein over the bleb
Schirmer test with filter paper strips in the lower fornix
Gonioscopy to inspect the internal ostium of the fistula
B-scan ultrasonography to look for choroidal detachment
Jones dye test of the nasolacrimal drainage system
mcq.e: A thin, avascular cystic bleb after mitomycin C with **low IOP and watering** suggests a **bleb leak**. The **Seidel test** (concentrated fluorescein over the bleb, viewed with cobalt blue light) shows dilute green aqueous streaming from the leak. A leak is a major risk factor for blebitis and endophthalmitis, so it needs repair (bandage CL, autologous blood, compression suture or bleb revision) and patient education.
w: Correct - Seidel testing with concentrated fluorescein shows aqueous streaming from a leaking bleb.
Wrong - Schirmer measures tear production for dry eye and cannot detect aqueous leaking from the bleb.
Wrong - gonioscopy shows whether the internal ostium is open but does not detect an external leak.
Wrong - B-scan can show hypotony-related choroidal effusion but does not identify the leak.
Wrong - the Jones test assesses tear drainage obstruction, which does not lower IOP.

mcq.stem:
A 59-year-old man presents with a painful, photophobic left eye with discharge 3 years after trabeculectomy. VA 6/12. The bleb is milky white with surrounding injection and 1+ anterior chamber cells; the vitreous is clear. Discharge is sent for culture, and hourly fortified topical vancomycin and cefazolin are started. At review 24 hours later, pain and injection are clearly improving and the culture is still pending.
What is the most appropriate change to treatment now?
o: Avoid steroid entirely until the culture result is available
Should have started topical steroid with the first antibiotic dose
Give a subconjunctival steroid injection directly into the bleb
Add topical steroid now, since it has improved after 24 hours
Start oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg and stop the topical antibiotics
mcq.e: The notes' rule: **add topical steroid about 24 h after clinical improvement** on intensive antibiotics. Steroid then limits fibrosis and scarring that would close the filtering bleb, so it helps to **salvage bleb function**; starting it before the antibiotics have taken effect risks worsening infection. Antibiotics continue alongside, tapering with response.
w: Wrong - waiting for culture is unnecessary once there is clear clinical improvement; delay favours bleb scarring.
Wrong - starting steroid before antibiotics have taken effect may worsen infection; the timing is 24 h after improvement.
Wrong - injecting into or near an infected thin bleb risks perforation and spread of infection.
Correct - once clearly improving at 24 h, add topical steroid to limit scarring and preserve bleb filtration.
Wrong - stopping antibiotics at 24 h risks relapse, and oral steroid is not needed for a bleb-limited infection.

mcq.stem:
A 66-year-old woman had a trabeculectomy with mitomycin C 9 years ago and has had well-controlled IOP without drops since. She now presents with a painful red eye, a milky-white bleb and anterior chamber cells. She asks why an infection should appear so many years after a successful operation. Her bleb is known to be thin, avascular and cystic.
Which explanation best accounts for her late infection?
o: A thin, avascular, leaky bleb wall lets surface bacteria enter the bleb
Organisms implanted at surgery lay dormant in the scleral flap for years
Mitomycin C suppresses systemic immunity for years after it is applied
Rising IOP closed the fistula so that stagnant aqueous became infected
Ageing removes all tear lysozyme, so every elderly eye is infection-prone
mcq.e: Antifibrotics (**mitomycin C, 5-FU**) improve filtration but leave a **thin, avascular, cystic bleb** whose wall may **leak** or transmit organisms, giving a lifelong risk of blebitis, often years later. Surface organisms, especially after conjunctivitis or URTI, then reach the bleb and the eye. Avoiding contact lenses, treating conjunctivitis promptly and repairing leaks reduce risk.
w: Correct - antimetabolite blebs are thin, avascular and may leak, allowing surface organisms to invade years later.
Wrong - late bleb infections come from new surface organisms, not organisms dormant since surgery.
Wrong - MMC acts locally on fibroblasts during surgery; it has no long-term systemic immune effect.
Wrong - her IOP is controlled, so the bleb is functioning; a failed fistula lowers, not raises, infection risk.
Wrong - ageing does not abolish tear defences; the specific risk is the thin, leaky bleb.

mcq.stem:
A 59-year-old man had a superior trabeculectomy 5 years ago. He had a cough and sore throat last week. Over 12 hours he has developed pain, photophobia and discharge in the operated eye; VA has dropped from 6/9 to 6/18. The bleb is milky white with intense surrounding injection and there is a small hypopyon. His surgeon warns that bleb infections behave differently from those after cataract surgery.
Which organisms are most likely?
o: Coagulase-negative staphylococci from the lid margin
Propionibacterium acnes sequestered in the bleb
Candida albicans from haematogenous spread
Streptococci and Haemophilus influenzae
Acanthamoeba from exposure to tap water
mcq.e: Late (chronic) bleb-related infections are typically caused by **streptococci and Gram-negative organisms, especially Haemophilus influenzae** (MOH CPG table), often after URTI or conjunctivitis. They are **more virulent** than the coagulase-negative staphylococci that dominate acute post-cataract endophthalmitis, so bleb infections progress fast and need intensive, early treatment. P. acnes is the delayed post-cataract organism.
w: Wrong - CoNS cause acute post-operative infection after cataract or early glaucoma surgery, not most late bleb infections.
Wrong - P. acnes causes indolent delayed endophthalmitis in the capsular bag after cataract surgery.
Wrong - Candida endophthalmitis is endogenous in line-dependent or immunosuppressed patients, with fluffy vitritis.
Correct - late bleb infections are mainly streptococci and H. influenzae, often after URTI, and are virulent.
Wrong - Acanthamoeba causes contact-lens keratitis with a ring infiltrate, not blebitis after a sore throat.

mcq.stem:
A 48-year-old taxi driver is discharged after an uneventful right trabeculectomy with mitomycin C. He lives 40 km from the hospital, and his wife asks what they should do if problems arise in the years ahead. He is due for routine glaucoma clinic review every 4 months.
Which advice is most appropriate?
o: Wait for the next routine visit if the eye turns red, as most redness is allergic
Use leftover chloramphenicol at home first and attend if not better in a week
Attend the same day for any redness, light sensitivity, blurred vision or pain
Wear soft contact lenses to shield the thin bleb from rubbing by the eyelid
Expect occasional painful red eyes and treat them with cold compresses at home
mcq.e: Bleb-related infection is a **lifelong risk**, and outcome depends on how fast it is treated. Teach **'RSVP': Redness, Sensitivity to light, Vision decrease, Pain -> attend the eye clinic the SAME DAY**. Self-treatment with old drops delays care and masks cultures; contact lenses raise infection risk; red eyes after trabeculectomy are never assumed to be trivial.
w: Wrong - waiting up to 4 months risks progression to endophthalmitis; a red eye after trabeculectomy needs same-day review.
Wrong - a week of self-treatment with old drops delays definitive care and can blunt cultures.
Correct - RSVP symptoms (redness, photophobia, blurring, pain) mean same-day attendance for possible blebitis.
Wrong - contact lenses abrade the bleb and increase infection risk; they should be avoided.
Wrong - painful red eyes after trabeculectomy must be assessed urgently, not managed at home.

mcq.stem:
A 67-year-old woman who had a left trabeculectomy 6 years ago saw her general practitioner yesterday with a red, sticky left eye and was given chloramphenicol drops. Today the eye is more painful and photophobic and she attends the eye clinic. VA left 6/12. There is mucopurulent discharge, 1+ anterior chamber cells and a clear vitreous.
Which slit-lamp finding most specifically indicates that the bleb itself is infected?
o: Diffuse injection of the bulbar and tarsal conjunctiva with discharge
A diffuse, elevated bleb containing many fine clear microcysts
Corkscrew vessels running across the surface of the bleb
A tense, dome-shaped bleb with thick, vascularised walls
Opaque milky bleb contents ringed by intensely red conjunctiva
mcq.e: The pathognomonic sign of blebitis is the **'white on red' appearance: an opaque, milky-white (infiltrated) bleb surrounded by intensely hyperaemic conjunctiva**. Diffuse conjunctival injection and discharge occur in simple conjunctivitis; microcysts are a feature of a healthy functioning bleb; corkscrew vessels and a thick-walled dome suggest a failing or encapsulated bleb. A post-trabeculectomy red eye must never be treated as simple conjunctivitis without slit-lamp examination of the bleb.
w: Wrong - diffuse injection with discharge is seen in simple conjunctivitis and does not localise infection to the bleb.
Wrong - a diffuse, microcystic bleb is the appearance of a healthy, well-functioning bleb.
Wrong - corkscrew vessels indicate a vascularised, scarring or failing bleb rather than infection.
Wrong - a tense, thick-walled dome is an encapsulated bleb (Tenon cyst), usually weeks after surgery.
Correct - a milky-white infiltrated bleb within intensely red conjunctiva ('white on red') is the sign of blebitis.

mcq.stem:
A 72-year-old man presents 2 years after a superior trabeculectomy with 1 day of pain, photophobia and discharge in the operated eye. VA 6/9 (unchanged). The bleb is opaque white with surrounding injection; the anterior chamber is quiet, the red reflex is bright, and there are no vitreous cells on dilated examination.
What is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Vitreous tap and intravitreal vancomycin plus ceftazidime within 1 hour
Culture any discharge, then intensive fortified topical antibiotics
Oral co-amoxiclav for 1 week with review in the clinic afterwards
Topical prednisolone acetate 1% hourly alone to protect bleb function
Immediate surgical excision of the bleb and closure of the fistula
mcq.e: Infection confined to the bleb (**stage 1 blebitis**, vitreous clear) is treated with **culture of any purulent material and intensive topical antibiotics** (e.g. fortified vancomycin/cefazolin, or a fluoroquinolone, hourly) with close daily review, adding topical steroid 24 h after improvement. Intravitreal antibiotics are reserved for vitreous involvement. Re-examine the vitreous at every visit, because progression to endophthalmitis can be rapid.
w: Wrong - tap-and-inject is for vitreous involvement (bleb-related endophthalmitis); here the vitreous is clear.
Correct - stage 1 blebitis is treated with culture then intensive topical antibiotics and close review.
Wrong - oral antibiotics alone and a week's delay are inadequate for a virulent bleb infection.
Wrong - steroid without antibiotic cover risks rapid spread; steroid is added only after 24 h of improvement.
Wrong - excising the bleb sacrifices IOP control and is not first-line for uncomplicated blebitis.

mcq.stem:
A 6-year-old boy is brought to the paediatric ED of a district hospital with 3 days of fever and a progressively swollen, tender left upper and lower lid after a week of rhinorrhoea. VA is 6/9 left and 6/6 right. The left globe is proptosed and pushed slightly laterally, with pain and limitation on both adduction and abduction. There is no RAPD.
From which structure has the infection most likely spread?
o: Maxillary sinus through the orbital floor
Frontal sinus through the orbital roof
Sphenoid sinus through the orbital apex
Ethmoid sinus via the lamina papyracea
Upper molar abscess via the maxillary sinus
mcq.e: **Ethmoid sinusitis** is the source in about 90% of childhood orbital cellulitis (notes p17). The **lamina papyracea** is paper-thin, perforated by neurovascular foramina and drained by valveless veins, so infection crosses easily into the medial orbit — often forming a medial subperiosteal collection that pushes the globe laterally. Frontal sinus spread is more typical of adolescents and displaces the globe downwards.
w: Wrong - maxillary sinusitis can spread through the floor, but it is a much less common source and tends to push the globe upwards.
Wrong - frontal sinus disease is a source mainly in teenagers and adults (frontal sinuses are poorly developed at 6) and displaces the globe down and out.
Wrong - sphenoid sinusitis is rare and presents with an orbital apex picture (early visual loss, ophthalmoplegia) rather than lateral displacement.
Correct - the thin, porous lamina papyracea makes the ethmoid air cells the commonest route, especially in children; lateral displacement fits a medial process.
Wrong - odontogenic spread via the maxillary sinus is recognised (notes p17) but uncommon, and there is no dental history here.

mcq.stem:
A 9-year-old girl is seen in the eye clinic with 2 days of a red, swollen right upper lid that began after a mosquito bite on the brow. Temperature is 38.2 °C. The lids are tense and erythematous but can be parted; VA is 6/6 in both eyes, pupils are equal with no RAPD, and Ishihara colour vision is normal. The conjunctiva is mildly injected.
Which additional finding would most clearly indicate that the infection has spread behind the orbital septum?
o: Pain and diplopia on attempted upgaze
Swelling spreading across the nasal bridge
Tender pre-auricular lymph node enlargement
A white cell count of 16 x 10^9/L
Fever rising to 39.5 °C overnight
mcq.e: The **orbital septum** is the barrier: once infection is post-septal it involves the extraocular muscles and orbital fat, producing **painful, restricted eye movements**, diplopia, proptosis and, later, reduced VA, colour loss and RAPD. Fever, leucocytosis and the extent of lid swelling occur in both preseptal and orbital cellulitis, so they do not localise the infection. Remember the post-septal 4 Ps: Proptosis, Pain on movement, Poor vision, Paralysis of gaze.
w: Correct - painful ophthalmoplegia means the muscles and orbital fat are inflamed, i.e. orbital (post-septal) cellulitis; admit, IV antibiotics and CT.
Wrong - lid oedema readily tracks across the loose subcutaneous tissue of the nasal bridge in preseptal cellulitis; extent of swelling does not localise.
Wrong - pre-auricular lymphadenopathy points to viral or chlamydial conjunctivitis, not to the depth of a lid infection.
Wrong - leucocytosis occurs in both preseptal and orbital cellulitis (notes p17 table) and cannot tell them apart.
Wrong - fever may be present in preseptal cellulitis too; height of fever is not a reliable marker of post-septal spread.

mcq.stem:
A 52-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes has been on IV antibiotics in the ward for 2 days for right orbital cellulitis from pansinusitis. Overnight he becomes drowsy with a temperature of 39.8 °C. The right eye is now immobile with a fixed dilated pupil, and the left eye has newly developed chemosis, proptosis and limited abduction. Forehead sensation is reduced on both sides. Fundoscopy shows dilated, tortuous retinal veins in both eyes.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Right orbital abscess with apex compression
Right medial subperiosteal abscess
Bacterial meningitis with raised ICP
Direct carotid-cavernous fistula
Septic cavernous sinus thrombosis
mcq.e: **Bilateral involvement**, rapidly progressive proptosis, multiple cranial nerve palsies (III, IV, VI and V1) and congestion of conjunctival and retinal veins in a toxic patient signal **cavernous sinus thrombosis** (notes p18). The two cavernous sinuses communicate through the intercavernous sinuses, so the fellow eye becomes involved — an orbital or subperiosteal abscess stays on one side. Arrange urgent contrast CT/MR venography, high-dose IV antibiotics and neurology/ID input.
w: Wrong - an orbital abscess can cause an apex syndrome on the right, but it cannot explain new signs in the left eye.
Wrong - a subperiosteal abscess is a unilateral complication (Chandler III) that displaces the globe; it does not cause bilateral cranial nerve palsies.
Wrong - meningitis causes drowsiness and fever but not bilateral proptosis, chemosis and ophthalmoplegia with venous congestion.
Wrong - a direct carotid-cavernous fistula gives pulsatile proptosis, an orbital bruit and arterialised corkscrew vessels, usually after trauma, without sepsis.
Correct - spread of orbital signs to the opposite eye with III/IV/VI/V1 palsies and venous congestion is the hallmark of cavernous sinus thrombosis.

mcq.stem:
A 14-year-old boy admitted with left orbital cellulitis has marked, tense proptosis on day 2. At the 4-hourly check he can only count fingers with the left eye (6/12 earlier that morning). There is a dense left RAPD and the left IOP is 38 mmHg. Fundoscopy shows a whitened, opaque posterior pole with a red spot at the fovea and thread-like arterioles; the disc is not swollen.
Which complication best explains the visual loss?
o: Compressive optic neuropathy at the orbital apex
Central retinal artery occlusion
Central retinal vein occlusion with venous stasis
Exposure keratopathy with corneal ulceration
Septic endophthalmitis spreading from the orbit
mcq.e: Retinal whitening with a **cherry-red spot** and attenuated arterioles is **central retinal artery occlusion** — a listed ocular complication of orbital cellulitis (notes p18), caused by raised orbital pressure, raised IOP and septic vasculitis. Compressive optic neuropathy also gives a RAPD but leaves the retina normal in colour. Either way this is a sight-threatening emergency: urgent CT and surgical decompression/drainage with the orbital team.
w: Wrong - compressive optic neuropathy reduces VA and gives a RAPD, but the retina would not be white with a cherry-red spot.
Correct - opaque white retina, cherry-red fovea and thread-like arterioles in a tense orbit indicate central retinal artery occlusion.
Wrong - CRVO gives dilated tortuous veins, widespread haemorrhages and disc swelling ('blood and thunder'), not a pale retina.
Wrong - exposure keratopathy occurs with marked proptosis but causes corneal staining, not retinal whitening or a RAPD.
Wrong - endophthalmitis would cause vitritis, hypopyon and loss of the fundal view rather than a clear view of a white retina.

mcq.stem:
A 60-year-old woman is brought to the ED in diabetic ketoacidosis (glucose 32 mmol/L, pH 7.1). She has right facial pain, periorbital swelling, proptosis, ptosis, total ophthalmoplegia and VA of hand movements with a RAPD. ENT nasal endoscopy shows a black, necrotic middle turbinate, and a black eschar is visible on the hard palate.
Apart from correcting the ketoacidosis, which is the most appropriate management?
o: IV ceftazidime plus metronidazole, reviewing response at 48 hours
IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for the orbital apex inflammation
IV liposomal amphotericin B with urgent surgical debridement
Oral voriconazole with outpatient ENT review in one week
IV vancomycin plus meropenem with repeat CT in 24 hours
mcq.e: A diabetic in **ketoacidosis** with orbital apex signs and **black necrotic eschar** has **rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis** until proven otherwise. The fungus invades vessels and causes infarction, so antibiotics fail; treatment is IV **liposomal amphotericin B**, urgent radical **surgical debridement** (sometimes exenteration) and reversal of the acidosis. Delay of even days increases mortality sharply.
w: Wrong - this is the standard bacterial orbital cellulitis regimen, but antibiotics have no activity against Mucorales and waiting 48 hours costs the eye and the patient.
Wrong - high-dose steroids worsen hyperglycaemia and fungal invasion; they are contraindicated here.
Correct - angio-invasive mucormycosis needs IV liposomal amphotericin B plus urgent debridement of necrotic tissue and correction of DKA.
Wrong - voriconazole does not cover Mucorales (it can even select for them), and outpatient care is unsafe in DKA with orbital apex involvement.
Wrong - broad-spectrum antibacterials do not treat a fungal infarctive infection; debridement and antifungals are needed.

mcq.stem:
A 7-year-old girl was admitted 36 hours ago with right periorbital swelling, fever and pain on eye movement, and was started on IV antibiotics without imaging. Today she is still febrile at 38.9 °C, the proptosis has increased, VA has fallen from 6/9 to 6/18 and she has new red desaturation in the right eye.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Contrast CT of orbits, sinuses and brain
Bedside B-scan ultrasound of the globe
Lumbar puncture for CSF microscopy and culture
Continue antibiotics and repeat FBC in 24 hours
MRI of brain and orbits on the next routine list
mcq.e: Worsening proptosis, falling VA/colour vision and no improvement after 24-48 hours of IV antibiotics are classic indications for **urgent high-resolution contrast CT of the orbits, sinuses and brain** (notes p18) — mainly to find a **subperiosteal or orbital abscess** needing drainage and to look for intracranial spread. CT is quick and shows bone and sinuses well; routine MRI wastes time when the optic nerve is threatened.
w: Correct - non-response plus optic nerve compromise demands urgent contrast CT to look for an abscess that needs surgical drainage.
Wrong - B-scan images the globe and can hint at orbital fluid, but it cannot assess the sinuses, the orbital apex or the brain.
Wrong - LP is reserved for meningeal signs and only after imaging has excluded a mass; it does not explain worsening orbital signs.
Wrong - the eye is getting worse despite IV treatment; simply continuing and repeating bloods risks permanent visual loss.
Wrong - MRI is useful for cavernous sinus/intracranial detail, but delaying to a routine list is unacceptable when vision is falling.

mcq.stem:
A 12-year-old boy on day 2 of IV antibiotics for left orbital cellulitis has a CT showing a rim-enhancing, lens-shaped collection beneath the periosteum of the medial orbital wall, displacing the medial rectus, with opacified ethmoid air cells. Over the past 6 hours his VA has dropped from 6/9 to 6/36 and a new left RAPD has appeared.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Continue the same IV antibiotics and repeat the CT in 48 hours
Add IV dexamethasone to reduce orbital oedema and observe
Switch to IV vancomycin and meropenem and observe closely
Urgent surgical drainage of the abscess with ethmoidectomy
Ultrasound-guided needle aspiration in the eye clinic
mcq.e: This is a **subperiosteal abscess** (Chandler III) with **optic nerve compromise** (VA drop + RAPD). Small medial abscesses in young children with normal vision may settle on IV antibiotics, but visual compromise, large abscess, age over about 9 or no response in 48 hours are indications for **urgent drainage** (often endoscopic ethmoidectomy with ENT) while IV antibiotics continue (notes p18: drainage of orbital abscess/infected sinuses).
w: Wrong - watchful waiting is reasonable only for a small abscess with normal optic nerve function; a new RAPD needs decompression now.
Wrong - steroids are only an adjunct to antibiotics (notes p18) and do not drain pus that is compressing the optic nerve.
Wrong - escalating antibiotics does not relieve a closed collection that is already threatening vision.
Correct - abscess plus falling VA and RAPD = urgent surgical drainage (with the sinus source) under continued IV antibiotics.
Wrong - blind needle aspiration in clinic is unsafe and incomplete; drainage is done in theatre with the sinus treated.

mcq.stem:
A 5-year-old boy is admitted to the paediatric ward with right orbital cellulitis and started on IV antibiotics. On admission VA is 6/9 right and 6/6 left, there is 3 mm of right proptosis with painful restricted upgaze, and no RAPD. The house officer is asked to write the nursing chart for 4-hourly eye observations.
Which pair of observations gives the earliest warning that the optic nerve is being compromised?
o: Degree of proptosis and lid swelling
Temperature curve and pulse rate
Range of eye movement and diplopia
Chemosis and conjunctival injection
Pupil reactions and colour vision
mcq.e: Optic nerve function — **VA, pupil reactions (swinging-light test for a new RAPD) and colour vision (red desaturation)** — must be charted every 4 hours (notes p18). Red desaturation and a RAPD often appear before a big drop in Snellen acuity, giving time for urgent CT and drainage. Proptosis, motility and systemic observations matter but do not directly measure the nerve.
w: Wrong - proptosis and lid swelling track the inflammation but can look static while the nerve is being compressed at the apex.
Wrong - fever and pulse monitor sepsis, not optic nerve function.
Wrong - motility worsens with myositis and orbital oedema, but it does not tell you the nerve is failing.
Wrong - chemosis reflects orbital venous congestion; it is not a measure of optic nerve function.
Correct - a new RAPD and red desaturation are early, sensitive signs of optic neuropathy and should trigger urgent review and CT.

mcq.stem:
A 16-year-old boy is on day 3 of IV ceftriaxone and metronidazole for left orbital cellulitis secondary to frontal and ethmoid sinusitis. His eye is improving (VA 6/6, less proptosis), but he now has a severe frontal headache, repeated vomiting, a GCS of 13/15 and a right-sided pronator drift. Neck stiffness is equivocal.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Immediate lumbar puncture before any change in antibiotics
Urgent contrast CT brain, then neurosurgical referral
Add oral prednisolone for the residual orbital inflammation
Switch to oral antibiotics as the eye is clearly improving
EEG and review by the paediatric neurologist next week
mcq.e: Headache, vomiting, falling GCS and a focal deficit in a teenage boy with **frontal sinusitis** suggest an **intracranial complication** — brain abscess or subdural/epidural empyema — which can progress even while the orbit improves (notes p18). **Image first**: LP with a possible mass lesion risks coning. Note: the notes list LP (under 'biochemistry') if meningeal signs — correct practice is CT before LP whenever GCS is reduced or there are focal signs.
w: Wrong - LP with a reduced GCS and focal signs risks tonsillar herniation; imaging must come first.
Correct - contrast CT brain (or MRI) to look for abscess/empyema, then neurosurgical drainage with continued IV antibiotics.
Wrong - steroids are an orbital adjunct only and would mask a deteriorating intracranial infection.
Wrong - an improving eye does not mean the infection is controlled; new neurological signs need escalation, not step-down.
Wrong - this is not a seizure work-up; delaying imaging could be fatal.

mcq.stem:
A 35-year-old construction worker presents to the ED with 2 days of fever, right upper molar toothache and a painful, proptosed right eye with restricted movements; VA is 6/12 with no RAPD. CT confirms post-septal inflammation with maxillary and ethmoid sinusitis but no abscess. He has no drug allergies.
Which initial antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?
o: Oral co-amoxiclav 625 mg 8-hourly with clinic review in 48 hours
IV cloxacillin alone until afebrile, then oral cloxacillin
IV ceftazidime with oral metronidazole for anaerobic cover
Topical chloramphenicol drops with oral doxycycline 100 mg BD
IV acyclovir with oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg for orbital oedema
mcq.e: Orbital cellulitis needs **admission and IV broad-spectrum antibiotics** covering streptococci, staphylococci, H. influenzae and — with a sinus or **dental** source — **anaerobes**. The notes give IV ceftazidime + oral metronidazole (vancomycin if penicillin-allergic), continued until afebrile for about 4 days; IV ceftriaxone or co-amoxiclav plus metronidazole per local protocol is equally acceptable. Oral therapy is for preseptal disease only.
w: Wrong - oral co-amoxiclav is the preseptal regimen (notes p18); post-septal infection needs admission and IV therapy.
Wrong - cloxacillin alone covers staphylococci but misses H. influenzae, Gram-negatives and the anaerobes of a dental/sinus source.
Correct - broad IV cover plus metronidazole for anaerobes, with ENT/dental input for the source.
Wrong - topical drops do not penetrate the orbit, and doxycycline alone is inadequate for a sight- and life-threatening infection.
Wrong - this is bacterial sinogenic infection; antivirals have no role, and steroids are never used without antibiotic cover.

mcq.stem:
A 7-year-old boy is brought to a Klinik Kesihatan at 8 am because both upper lids were puffy and pale pink on waking, the right more than the left, after an afternoon playing in long grass. He keeps rubbing his eyes. Temperature is 36.8 °C. The lids are soft and non-tender, the conjunctiva shows marked watery chemosis, VA is 6/6 in each eye and eye movements are full and painless.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Bilateral preseptal cellulitis
Early orbital cellulitis
Acute allergic lid oedema
Adenoviral keratoconjunctivitis
Nephrotic syndrome periorbital oedema
mcq.e: **Itch**, rubbing, soft **non-tender** pale lid swelling, watery chemosis and no fever after allergen exposure point to **acute allergic (histamine-mediated) lid oedema**. Infection hurts: preseptal cellulitis is tender, warm, red and usually unilateral, often with fever. Treat with cold compresses and an oral/topical antihistamine — antibiotics are not needed.
w: Wrong - preseptal cellulitis is tender, warm and erythematous and is rarely bilateral; this lid is soft, pale and itchy.
Wrong - there is no proptosis, pain on movement or visual change, and the child is afebrile.
Correct - itch, chemosis and soft, painless, pale swelling after grass exposure are typical of allergic oedema.
Wrong - adenovirus gives a red eye with watery discharge, follicles and a tender pre-auricular node, not pale itchy lid swelling.
Wrong - nephrotic oedema is morning periorbital puffiness but without itch or chemosis; check urine protein only if oedema elsewhere or recurrent.

mcq.stem:
A 62-year-old woman presents to the eye clinic with 3 days of a painful, hot, red swelling at the inner corner of the left eye. She has had a watery left eye for a year. The swelling lies just below the medial canthal tendon, and pressure over it produces pus from the lower punctum. VA 6/9, eye movements full, no proptosis; temperature 37.9 °C.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Preseptal cellulitis from an infected stye
Infected chalazion of the lower lid
Frontoethmoidal mucocoele with infection
Medial orbital subperiosteal abscess
Acute dacryocystitis on a blocked duct
mcq.e: Chronic epiphora (nasolacrimal duct obstruction) followed by a tender swelling **below the medial canthal tendon** with **pus regurgitating from the punctum** is **acute dacryocystitis** — a recognised source of preseptal cellulitis (notes p17). A swelling above the tendon suggests a mucocoele. Treat with systemic antibiotics and warm compresses; avoid probing while acute; definitive cure is a dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) once it settles.
w: Wrong - a stye is a tender pustule at the lid margin; it does not produce pus from the punctum or follow chronic watering.
Wrong - a chalazion is a firm, usually painless lump within the tarsal plate, away from the medial canthus.
Wrong - frontoethmoidal mucocoeles present above the medial canthal tendon and displace the globe; reflux from the punctum is not a feature.
Wrong - a subperiosteal abscess is post-septal and causes proptosis, restricted motility and often reduced vision.
Correct - lacrimal sac infection behind a blocked nasolacrimal duct: medial swelling below the tendon with punctal pus.

mcq.stem:
A 74-year-old man attends the ED with 2 days of a swollen, red, tender right upper lid that is almost closed. He had burning pain over the right forehead for 3 days before any rash appeared. There are crusted vesicles in a band over the right forehead and scalp ending sharply at the midline, and a few vesicles on the tip of the nose. VA is 6/12 right; eye movements are full.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus, nasociliary branch
Preseptal cellulitis following an insect bite
Impetigo with secondary preseptal cellulitis
Primary herpes simplex blepharoconjunctivitis
Contact dermatitis from topical eye medication
mcq.e: A painful prodrome then a **dermatomal vesicular rash** respecting the midline is **herpes zoster ophthalmicus**; vesicles on the nasal tip (**Hutchinson sign**, nasociliary nerve) predict ocular involvement — keratitis, uveitis, raised IOP. The swollen lid can mimic preseptal cellulitis. Start oral acyclovir 800 mg five times daily for 7 days (ideally within 72 h of rash) and arrange ophthalmic review for slit-lamp examination.
w: Correct - dermatomal V1 vesicles with Hutchinson sign; give oral antivirals and examine the eye for keratitis and uveitis.
Wrong - an insect bite causes a localised swollen lid but not a prodrome and a band of vesicles stopping at the midline.
Wrong - impetigo gives honey-coloured crusts around the nose and mouth in children, not a dermatomal vesicular band.
Wrong - primary HSV occurs mainly in young children with scattered lid vesicles and follicular conjunctivitis, not a dermatomal rash.
Wrong - contact dermatitis is itchy, eczematous and confined to where drops run, without vesicles over the scalp.

mcq.stem:
A 24-year-old university student is seen in the eye clinic 2 days after a small cut to his left upper lid during futsal. The lid is red, warm, swollen and tender around a crusted wound; he can open the eye. VA is 6/6 in each eye, there is no RAPD, colour vision is normal, eye movements are full and painless, there is no proptosis and the conjunctiva is white. Temperature is 37.6 °C and he feels well.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Admit for IV ceftazidime and metronidazole with 4-hourly obs
Topical chloramphenicol ointment only, review in one week
Urgent contrast CT of the orbits before deciding on antibiotics
Oral co-amoxiclav 625 mg 8-hourly, review within 48 hours
Oral acyclovir 400 mg five times daily and cool compresses
mcq.e: A well adult with **preseptal cellulitis** — normal VA, pupils, colour vision and painless full motility — can be treated as an **outpatient with oral co-amoxiclav** (notes p18: 500 mg amoxicillin component, i.e. 625 mg tablet, 8-hourly) and reviewed within 24-48 hours with clear safety-net advice. Check tetanus status after a wound. IV therapy and CT are for post-septal signs, systemic illness, inability to assess or failure to improve.
w: Wrong - this is the orbital cellulitis regimen; a well adult with no post-septal signs does not need admission.
Wrong - topical antibiotics do not reach the infected soft tissue, and a week is too long without review.
Wrong - CT is indicated for post-septal signs, failure to improve or inability to examine; none apply here.
Correct - oral co-amoxiclav with early review is the first-line outpatient treatment for uncomplicated preseptal cellulitis.
Wrong - there are no vesicles or dermatomal pain; this is a bacterial wound infection, not herpes.

mcq.stem:
A 10-month-old girl is brought to the paediatric ED with 1 day of a red, swollen right upper and lower lid after a cold. She is febrile at 39.2 °C, irritable and feeding poorly. The lids are so swollen that the globe cannot be seen without forcing them apart, and she will not fix and follow with either eye.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Oral co-amoxiclav syrup with review in the eye clinic in 48 hours
Admit for IV antibiotics with paediatric and ophthalmic review
Topical fusidic acid gel and warm compresses at home
Oral antihistamine and cold compresses, return if feverish
Discharge with paracetamol and review by the GP tomorrow
mcq.e: Even if the infection looks preseptal, **infants under 1 year, systemically unwell children and any patient whose vision and motility cannot be assessed** should be **admitted for IV antibiotics** with joint paediatric and ophthalmology care (CT if post-septal disease cannot be excluded). Infants deteriorate quickly and may be bacteraemic; outpatient oral therapy is only for well, fully examinable patients.
w: Wrong - oral outpatient therapy is unsafe in a febrile, irritable infant whose eye cannot be examined.
Correct - age under 1, systemic illness and an unassessable eye are all reasons to admit for IV antibiotics and close review.
Wrong - topical treatment does not treat soft-tissue infection and leaves a septic infant at home.
Wrong - fever, redness and irritability indicate infection, not allergy; delay risks orbital spread or sepsis.
Wrong - symptomatic treatment alone ignores a possibly bacteraemic infant with an unassessable eye.

mcq.stem:
A 32-year-old woman presents to a Klinik Kesihatan with a red, tender, swollen left upper lid around an infected insect bite. VA is 6/6, eye movements are full and painless and there is no proptosis; she is afebrile and well. Two years ago she had anaphylaxis (wheeze and hypotension) after amoxicillin.
Which oral antibiotic is most appropriate?
o: Clindamycin 300 mg 6-hourly
Co-amoxiclav 625 mg 8-hourly
Cefalexin 500 mg 6-hourly
Flucloxacillin 500 mg 6-hourly
Ciprofloxacin 500 mg 12-hourly
mcq.e: Skin-entry preseptal cellulitis is caused mainly by **S. aureus and S. pyogenes**. With true **penicillin anaphylaxis**, all penicillins are contraindicated and cephalosporins sharing a similar side chain (cefalexin with amoxicillin) are best avoided, so **clindamycin** (or a macrolide per local guideline) is used. Ciprofloxacin has weak streptococcal cover.
w: Correct - clindamycin covers staphylococci and streptococci and is safe in penicillin anaphylaxis.
Wrong - co-amoxiclav contains amoxicillin, the drug that caused her anaphylaxis.
Wrong - cefalexin shares a near-identical side chain with amoxicillin; avoid after anaphylaxis.
Wrong - flucloxacillin is a penicillin and is contraindicated after penicillin anaphylaxis.
Wrong - ciprofloxacin is mainly Gram-negative and covers streptococci poorly, the commonest skin-entry organism.

mcq.stem:
A 4-year-old boy was started on oral co-amoxiclav by the Klinik Kesihatan doctor 48 hours ago for a swollen, red left upper lid after a scratch. He is brought back because the swelling has increased and now involves both lids, and he has a fever of 38.8 °C. The lids are too swollen, and he is too distressed, for VA, pupils or eye movements to be assessed.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Change to oral cefuroxime and review again in 48 hours
Incise and drain the upper lid in the treatment room
Add topical chloramphenicol and a warm compress
Lumbar puncture to exclude early meningitis
Admit for IV antibiotics and CT orbits and sinuses
