mcq.e: Preseptal cellulitis may progress to orbital cellulitis (notes p18). **Failure to improve after 24-48 hours of oral antibiotics** and **inability to assess vision, pupils and motility** are both indications to **admit for IV antibiotics and contrast CT of the orbits and sinuses** to exclude post-septal spread or abscess. Never assume a swollen-shut eye is 'only preseptal'.
w: Wrong - switching oral agents and waiting another 48 hours ignores clinical failure and an unexaminable eye.
Wrong - there is no localised lid abscess; blind incision does not address possible orbital spread.
Wrong - topical drops do not treat soft-tissue infection and add nothing here.
Wrong - there are no meningeal signs; the priority is IV treatment and orbital imaging.
Correct - worsening on oral therapy plus an unassessable eye = admit, IV antibiotics and CT orbits/sinuses.

mcq.stem:
A 6-year-old girl with right lid cellulitis after a mosquito bite is fit for discharge on oral co-amoxiclav: VA 6/6, full painless eye movements, no proptosis and afebrile after paracetamol. Her mother asks what should make her bring the child back immediately rather than waiting for the 48-hour review.
Which advice is most important?
o: Return if the redness has not faded completely by tomorrow
Return if there is yellow crusting at the lashes each morning
Return if the eye bulges, vision blurs or eye movement hurts
Return if loose stools develop on the antibiotic syrup
Return if the swelling is still present after 3 days of improvement
mcq.e: The key **safety-net** is to return at once with features of **post-septal spread** — proptosis, blurred or double vision, pain on eye movement — or with drowsiness, headache or vomiting, because preseptal cellulitis can progress to orbital cellulitis (notes p18). Slow fading of redness and mild crusting are expected; antibiotic diarrhoea is managed at routine review.
w: Wrong - redness normally takes several days to settle; slow resolution alone is not an emergency.
Wrong - mild crusting from the inflamed lid is expected and is not a red flag.
Correct - proptosis, visual change or painful eye movement mean possible orbital cellulitis and need same-day review.
Wrong - mild diarrhoea on co-amoxiclav is common and can wait for the scheduled review unless the child is dehydrated.
Wrong - some residual swelling after improvement is expected and does not need emergency return.

mcq.stem:
A 2-year-old boy is brought to the ED with a temperature of 39.8 °C and rapidly developing purplish-red swelling of the right upper and lower lids. He had a right ear infection 3 days ago. There is no skin wound or bite. His parents declined all childhood vaccinations. He is lethargic. When the lids are parted the eye is white, he fixes on a toy and eye movements appear full.
Which organism is most likely responsible?
o: Staphylococcus aureus from a skin breach
Streptococcus pyogenes from the throat
Pseudomonas aeruginosa from the ear canal
Haemophilus influenzae type b via the blood
Methicillin-resistant S. aureus from the nose
mcq.e: Preseptal cellulitis without a skin wound in a young child after **otitis media or URTI** arises by **haematogenous spread** (notes p17); in an **unvaccinated** toddler the classic organism is **H. influenzae type b**, which gives violaceous lid swelling and carries a risk of **bacteraemia and meningitis**. Admit, take blood cultures and give IV antibiotics. Hib vaccination has made this rare in vaccinated children.
w: Wrong - S. aureus is the usual organism when there is a skin breach (laceration, bite), which this child does not have.
Wrong - S. pyogenes also follows skin trauma; a bacteraemic picture after otitis in an unvaccinated child points elsewhere.
Wrong - Pseudomonas causes otitis externa and contact lens keratitis, not paediatric periorbital cellulitis.
Correct - unvaccinated toddler, preceding otitis, no wound, high fever and violaceous swelling = Hib bacteraemic preseptal cellulitis.
Wrong - MRSA is possible in skin-entry infection but is not the classic organism after otitis in an unvaccinated child.

mcq.stem:
A 48-year-old man with type 2 diabetes was started on oral co-amoxiclav yesterday for a red, swollen left upper lid after a minor scratch. Today the lid skin has become dusky purple-grey with blisters; he describes severe pain although the central skin is now numb, and the redness is spreading quickly onto the forehead. Temperature is 39.5 °C and BP 88/50 mmHg. VA is 6/9 and eye movements are full.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Switch to IV co-amoxiclav and mark the margins for review in 24 hours
Resuscitate, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics and urgent debridement
Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily to settle the inflammatory lid oedema
Warm compresses with bedside incision of the lid to release pus
Contrast MRI of the orbit and face on the next elective imaging list
mcq.e: Dusky violaceous skin, **bullae**, pain out of proportion with later **anaesthesia**, rapid spread and **septic shock** indicate **periorbital necrotising fasciitis** (usually group A streptococcus), a rare must-not-miss mimic of preseptal cellulitis. It needs resuscitation, high-dose IV antibiotics (including clindamycin to suppress toxin) and **urgent surgical debridement** — antibiotics alone fail because of tissue necrosis.
w: Wrong - marking margins and waiting 24 hours is fine for simple cellulitis but lethal in necrotising fasciitis with shock.
Correct - necrotising fasciitis with shock: resuscitate, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics with clindamycin, and urgent debridement.
Wrong - steroids impair the immune response to a rapidly spreading necrotising infection.
Wrong - there is no pus collection; a bedside incision does not remove necrotic tissue and delays theatre.
Wrong - imaging must not delay surgery in a shocked patient; an elective list is far too late.

mcq.stem:
A 34-year-old woman attends the eye clinic with 6 months of burning, itchy, gritty eyes, worse in the morning, and recurrent styes. The anterior lid margins are red, with hard, brittle yellow crusts encircling the bases of the lashes; lifting a crust leaves a small bleeding ulcer. Several lashes are broken, misdirected or missing. The meibomian orifices look normal and she has no scalp dandruff.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Seborrhoeic anterior blepharitis
Staphylococcal anterior blepharitis
Demodex folliculorum blepharitis
Meibomian gland dysfunction
Phthiriasis palpebrarum (lash lice)
mcq.e: **Hard yellow crusts** (collarettes) at the lash bases that leave **small bleeding ulcers** when removed, with lash damage (trichiasis, madarosis) and recurrent styes, are the signature of **staphylococcal (ulcerative) anterior blepharitis** (notes p19). Seborrhoeic blepharitis gives soft greasy scales with scalp dandruff and no ulcers; posterior blepharitis affects the meibomian orifices, which are normal here.
w: Wrong - seborrhoeic blepharitis gives soft, greasy white scales without ulceration and is usually accompanied by scalp dandruff.
Correct - brittle crusts, bleeding ulcers on removal and lash loss/misdirection are classic staphylococcal anterior blepharitis.
Wrong - Demodex produces clear waxy cylindrical sleeves around the lash shafts, not hard crusts with bleeding ulcers.
Wrong - MGD is posterior blepharitis with capped, blocked orifices and toothpaste-like secretion; her orifices are normal.
Wrong - lice show nits cemented to the lashes and visible adult lice, usually with pubic infestation.

mcq.stem:
A 52-year-old man has persistent facial flushing, telangiectasia and papules over the nose and cheeks. He complains of burning, gritty eyes that are worst on waking. At the slit lamp the posterior lid margins are thickened and vascularised, the meibomian orifices are capped with oil globules, the tear film is frothy with a break-up time of 4 seconds, and firm pressure on the lid expresses thick, cloudy secretion.
What is the main mechanism of his ocular surface irritation?
o: Staphylococcal exotoxins causing lid-margin hypersensitivity
IgE-mediated mast-cell degranulation in the conjunctiva
Demodex mites blocking the lash follicles and glands
Bacterial lipases splitting meibum into free fatty acids
Lymphocytic infiltration of the lacrimal gland reducing aqueous
mcq.e: This is **meibomian gland dysfunction (posterior blepharitis) with acne rosacea**. Lid commensals — **Propionibacterium (Cutibacterium) acnes** and staphylococci — release **lipases** that break abnormal meibum into **irritant free fatty acids**, destabilising the tear film (rapid break-up, froth) and inflaming the ocular surface. Note: the notes say 'Corynebacterium acne' and place this under seborrhoeic blepharitis; the correct organism is P. acnes and the process is chiefly MGD/rosacea-related.
w: Wrong - staphylococcal toxins and hypersensitivity drive anterior blepharitis and marginal keratitis, not the meibomian picture described.
Wrong - IgE-mediated allergy causes itch, chemosis and papillae, not capped orifices and turbid meibum.
Wrong - Demodex can contribute to blepharitis but is identified by cylindrical lash sleeves, which are not described.
Correct - lipase breakdown of meibum into free fatty acids explains the unstable, frothy tear film and burning in MGD with rosacea.
Wrong - aqueous deficiency (e.g. Sjögren) reduces tear volume; here the problem is the lipid layer from the meibomian glands.

mcq.stem:
A 70-year-old woman has chronic itchy lids, worst in the morning, that have not improved after 3 months of warm compresses and baby-shampoo lid scrubs. At the slit lamp there are clear, waxy cylindrical sleeves wrapped around the bases of many lashes and extending a short way up the shafts; the lid margins are mildly red and the cornea is clear. An epilated lash viewed under the microscope shows tiny elongated organisms with legs clustered at one end.
Which treatment is most appropriate?
o: Tea tree oil lid scrubs daily for 6 weeks
Topical chloramphenicol ointment 4x daily
Topical dexamethasone 0.1% four times daily
Sodium cromoglycate 2% drops 4x daily
Oral doxycycline 100 mg daily for 3 months
mcq.e: **Cylindrical sleeves** (cuffs) around the lash bases and mites on lash microscopy indicate **Demodex blepharitis**. Ordinary lid hygiene does not kill the mites; **tea tree oil** (terpinen-4-ol) lid scrubs or wipes for about 6 weeks (to cover the mite life cycle) are the standard treatment (notes p19 list tea tree oil). Note: staphylococcal crusts are collarettes at the lash base; cylindrical sleeves are the Demodex sign.
w: Correct - tea tree oil is acaricidal; a course of several weeks covers the mite life cycle.
Wrong - chloramphenicol treats bacterial folliculitis but has no effect on Demodex mites.
Wrong - steroids may reduce redness but do not kill mites and risk raised IOP and cataract with prolonged use.
Wrong - cromoglycate is a mast-cell stabiliser for allergic conjunctivitis and does nothing for mite infestation.
Wrong - doxycycline helps meibomian gland dysfunction through anti-inflammatory effects but does not eradicate Demodex.

mcq.stem:
A 40-year-old man with dandruff and seborrhoeic dermatitis of the eyebrows and nasolabial folds presents to a Klinik Kesihatan with years of red, irritable lid margins. There are greasy, waxy scales among the lashes, VA is 6/6 in each eye, the cornea is clear and the conjunctiva is only mildly injected. He asks whether there is a medicine that will cure it.
What is the most appropriate first-line management and advice?
o: Topical dexamethasone for 6 weeks, which usually cures it
Oral doxycycline for 3 months, which will eradicate it
Topical chloramphenicol long term to sterilise the lids
Refer for meibomian gland probing as a definitive cure
Daily warm compresses and lid scrubs; control, not cure
mcq.e: Blepharitis has **no permanent cure** but symptoms can be controlled (notes p19). First-line for every type is **lid hygiene** — warm compresses to soften scales, then mechanical lid cleaning (diluted baby shampoo or commercial lid wipes) daily, continued long term — plus treating the scalp with anti-dandruff shampoo in seborrhoeic disease. Antibiotics, oral tetracyclines and short steroid courses are add-ons for active folliculitis, MGD or inflammatory flares.
w: Wrong - steroids are only for short flares; long courses risk glaucoma and cataract, and they do not cure blepharitis.
Wrong - oral tetracyclines are used for posterior blepharitis/rosacea and control, rather than eradicate, the disease.
Wrong - long-term topical antibiotics promote resistance and are reserved for active staphylococcal folliculitis.
Wrong - probing is a specialist option for refractory MGD, not first-line, and still does not cure the condition.
Correct - daily lid hygiene is the cornerstone; explaining that it is chronic and needs ongoing care improves compliance.

mcq.stem:
A 29-year-old woman who is 14 weeks pregnant has severe posterior blepharitis with recurrent chalazia and an unstable tear film despite 2 months of regular warm compresses, lid massage and lubricants. She is otherwise well and on folic acid only.
Which oral treatment is most appropriate?
o: Doxycycline 100 mg daily for 6-12 weeks
Minocycline 100 mg daily for 6-12 weeks
Azithromycin 500 mg daily, 3-day pulses
Oxytetracycline 250 mg twice daily for 3 months
Isotretinoin 20 mg daily for 4 months
mcq.e: Oral tetracyclines help MGD mainly through **anti-inflammatory and anti-lipase** effects at low dose, but they are **contraindicated in pregnancy, breastfeeding and children under about 8-12 years** (tooth discolouration, bone deposition). The notes list oral azithromycin as an alternative; pulsed **azithromycin** (e.g. 500 mg daily for 3 days, repeated weekly for 3 cycles) or erythromycin is used instead. Isotretinoin is teratogenic and itself worsens MGD.
w: Wrong - doxycycline is the usual first choice in adults, but tetracyclines are contraindicated in pregnancy (fetal teeth and bone).
Wrong - minocycline is a tetracycline with the same pregnancy contraindication, plus pigmentation and autoimmune side effects.
Correct - a macrolide such as azithromycin is the safe oral alternative for MGD when tetracyclines are contraindicated.
Wrong - oxytetracycline is still a tetracycline and must be avoided in pregnancy.
Wrong - isotretinoin is highly teratogenic and causes meibomian gland atrophy and dry eye.

mcq.stem:
A 38-year-old man with long-standing lid-margin crusting and recurrent styes presents with 3 days of a painful, photophobic, watering left eye. He does not wear contact lenses. VA is 6/9. There is localised injection at 4 o'clock, where a white, oval subepithelial infiltrate lies parallel to the limbus, separated from it by a clear zone of cornea. There is only a tiny overlying epithelial defect, no discharge and no AC cells.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Early bacterial keratitis
Peripheral ulcerative keratitis
Staphylococcal marginal keratitis
Acanthamoeba keratitis
Herpes simplex dendritic keratitis
mcq.e: **Marginal keratitis** is a **hypersensitivity reaction to staphylococcal antigens** in patients with chronic blepharitis: peripheral infiltrates at 2, 4, 8 or 10 o'clock (where the lid margin rests on the cornea), with a **clear zone** next to the limbus and little epithelial loss. Once infection is excluded it settles with a short course of weak topical steroid plus treatment of the blepharitis. Infective ulcers are larger, have a big epithelial defect and purulent discharge.
w: Wrong - bacterial keratitis shows a dense infiltrate with a larger epithelial defect, discharge and AC reaction; scrape if in doubt.
Wrong - PUK (e.g. rheumatoid) causes crescentic limbal thinning with no clear zone, often in systemic vasculitis.
Correct - peripheral sterile infiltrate with a clear zone in a blepharitis patient is staphylococcal marginal keratitis.
Wrong - Acanthamoeba typically follows contact lens wear and causes severe pain with a central/paracentral ring infiltrate.
Wrong - HSV epithelial keratitis shows a branching dendritic ulcer staining with fluorescein, not a peripheral infiltrate.

mcq.stem:
A 74-year-old woman is referred with 'blepharitis' of the right upper lid for 14 months that has not responded to lid hygiene, topical antibiotics or a course of doxycycline. The left lids are normal. The right upper lid is diffusely thickened and yellowish with loss of lashes along its middle third, and a 'chalazion' at the same site has been incised twice in the past year.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Lid-margin swab for bacterial culture and sensitivity
Lash epilation and microscopy for Demodex mites
Switch to oral azithromycin pulses and review in 3 months
Repeat incision and curettage of the presumed chalazion
Full-thickness lid biopsy with conjunctival map biopsies
mcq.e: **Unilateral, treatment-resistant blepharitis with madarosis** or a **recurrent chalazion** in an elderly patient is **sebaceous gland carcinoma** until proven otherwise — the great masquerader of the lid. It spreads pagetoid through the conjunctiva and metastasises to pre-auricular and submandibular nodes. Arrange a **full-thickness lid biopsy** (with conjunctival map biopsies and histology of any recurrent 'chalazion'); delay worsens survival.
w: Wrong - culture would grow lid commensals and delay the diagnosis of a malignancy.
Wrong - Demodex causes bilateral lash sleeves; it does not explain a unilateral thickened lid with lash loss.
Wrong - another course of antibiotics postpones the biopsy that this masquerade syndrome needs.
Wrong - a recurrent chalazion at the same site in an elderly patient must be biopsied, not simply curetted again.
Correct - full-thickness biopsy (plus conjunctival maps) confirms or excludes sebaceous gland carcinoma.

mcq.stem:
A 46-year-old office worker attends the eye clinic with burning, tired eyes that are worse after long hours at the computer. VA is 6/6 in each eye. The lashes are clean with no crusts or sleeves, but the posterior lid margins are rounded and vascularised and the tear film breaks up after 5 seconds.
Which simple bedside manoeuvre best confirms the suspected diagnosis?
o: Pressing the lid margin to express the glands
Schirmer strip in the lower fornix for 5 minutes
Eversion of the upper lid to look for papillae
Epilating lashes for microscopy of the roots
Swabbing the lid margin for bacterial culture
mcq.e: Rounded, vascularised posterior lid margins with a short tear break-up time suggest **posterior blepharitis (meibomian gland dysfunction)**. The notes call **pressure on the lid margin** the 'simple and excellent diagnostic test': healthy glands express clear oil, while MGD yields **cloudy, toothpaste-like** secretion or nothing from capped orifices. Schirmer measures aqueous production and is often normal in MGD (evaporative dry eye).
w: Correct - expressing turbid, toothpaste-like meibum confirms meibomian gland dysfunction at the slit lamp.
Wrong - Schirmer tests aqueous tear volume; MGD causes evaporative dry eye, so it may be normal.
Wrong - upper tarsal papillae suggest allergic or contact-lens-related disease, not MGD.
Wrong - lash microscopy looks for Demodex, which is unlikely with clean lashes and no sleeves.
Wrong - culture grows normal commensals and does not establish the diagnosis, which is clinical.

mcq.stem:
A 31-year-old woman with long-standing meibomian gland dysfunction notices a lump in her left upper lid that has grown slowly over 6 weeks. It is painless and non-tender, about 5 mm, lies within the tarsal plate away from the lid margin, and on lid eversion there is a localised grey-red area on the conjunctival surface. The lashes and lid margin over it are normal.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: External hordeolum of a lash follicle
Chalazion from a blocked meibomian gland
Internal hordeolum with abscess formation
Sebaceous gland carcinoma of the tarsus
Molluscum contagiosum of the lid skin
mcq.e: A slowly enlarging, **painless, non-tender lump within the tarsus** is a **chalazion** — a chronic lipogranuloma from retained meibomian secretion, a common complication of posterior blepharitis. Hordeola are acute and painful (external at the lash follicle/gland of Zeis, internal in a meibomian gland). Most chalazia settle with warm compresses and lid massage; persistent ones are incised and curetted. A recurrent chalazion in an elderly patient needs histology.
w: Wrong - an external hordeolum (stye) is an acute, tender pustule at the lash base, not a painless lump within the tarsus.
Correct - painless, slowly growing tarsal lump in a patient with MGD is a chalazion (meibomian lipogranuloma).
Wrong - an internal hordeolum is an acutely painful, inflamed meibomian gland infection.
Wrong - malignancy is suspected with recurrence at the same site, lash loss or lid distortion in older patients — none are present.
Wrong - molluscum gives pearly umbilicated papules on the skin, often with a follicular conjunctivitis.

mcq.stem:
A 57-year-old man with chronic blepharitis has been using dexamethasone 0.1% eye drops four times daily for 5 months on a repeat prescription because they make his lids feel better. He has no other symptoms. VA is 6/9 in each eye. IOP is 33 mmHg right and 31 mmHg left; the optic discs have a cup:disc ratio of 0.4 with healthy rims, and early posterior subcapsular lens opacities are present.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Continue the steroid and add timolol to control the pressure
Switch to a stronger steroid used only twice daily
List him for trabeculectomy in both eyes
Taper off the steroid and recheck IOP within weeks
Reassure him, as IOP below 35 mmHg is safe
mcq.e: Topical steroids are for **short courses only** in blepharitis (notes p19) because long-term use causes **steroid-induced ocular hypertension/glaucoma** and **posterior subcapsular cataract** (notes p13). The first step is to **taper and stop** the steroid and recheck IOP — it usually falls within weeks in a steroid responder; temporary IOP-lowering drops may be added, and lid hygiene remains the long-term treatment. Surgery is only for uncontrolled pressure with progressive damage.
w: Wrong - adding drops while continuing the cause treats the number but not the problem, and cataract will progress.
Wrong - a stronger steroid raises IOP further; if one is truly needed, a weak, short, pulsed course is used.
Wrong - the discs are healthy and the cause is reversible; trabeculectomy is not indicated at this stage.
Correct - withdraw the steroid and monitor IOP (with temporary drops if needed); continue lid hygiene.
Wrong - an IOP above 30 mmHg is not safe and needs action, especially with a removable cause.

mcq.stem:
A 52-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis attends the eye clinic with 2 weeks of a red right eye and a severe, boring ache that wakes her at night and radiates to the temple and jaw. VA 6/9. The redness has a deep bluish-violet hue over the nasal and inferior sclera (two quadrants) and the globe is tender to touch. Ten minutes after a drop of phenylephrine 10%, the deep vessels remain engorged. There is no avascular area or scleral thinning, and the anterior chamber is quiet.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Simple sectoral episcleritis
Nodular episcleritis
Diffuse anterior non-necrotising scleritis
Necrotising anterior scleritis with inflammation
Scleromalacia perforans
mcq.e: Deep boring pain that wakes the patient, a violaceous hue, a tender globe and deep vessels that do not blanch with phenylephrine 10% point to **scleritis** rather than episcleritis. Involvement of more than one quadrant without an avascular patch or thinning makes it **diffuse non-necrotising** scleritis, the commonest type. The trap is calling every red eye in an RA patient episcleritis because the vision is good.
w: Wrong - episcleritis gives mild discomfort, superficial mobile vessels and blanches with phenylephrine 10%.
Wrong - an episcleral nodule is mobile over the sclera, only mildly tender and blanches; pain is not severe.
Correct - severe deep pain, violaceous non-blanching vessels in more than one quadrant, no necrosis.
Wrong - necrotising disease shows white avascular areas and scleral thinning; none are present.
Wrong - scleromalacia perforans is typically painless and white with thinning, not a painful red eye.

mcq.stem:
A 38-year-old man is referred from a Klinik Kesihatan with a painful red left eye for 10 days. VA 6/6. There is a deep, dusky red, tender, immobile nodule at the temporal limbus that does not blanch with phenylephrine 10%. There are no avascular patches, no scleral thinning and the cornea is clear. He has no asthma, renal disease or peptic ulcer history.
What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
o: Oral NSAID, e.g. flurbiprofen or indomethacin, with PPI cover
Topical prednisolone acetate 1% two-hourly as the sole therapy
Subconjunctival triamcinolone injected beside the nodule
IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for three days
Topical ketorolac with preservative-free lubricant drops
mcq.e: Non-necrotising (diffuse or nodular) anterior scleritis is treated first with a **systemic NSAID**; topical steroids alone rarely control deep scleral inflammation and topical NSAIDs are too weak. Oral steroids are added if NSAIDs fail, and immunosuppressants are used for refractory or necrotising disease. Note: the notes list topical steroid first for non-necrotising scleritis; topical drops are only adjunctive and the first-line drug is an oral NSAID.
w: Correct - a systemic NSAID is first-line for non-necrotising scleritis; protect the stomach.
Wrong - topical steroid alone is usually inadequate for deep scleral inflammation.
Wrong - periocular steroid is never first-line and carries a risk of scleral melt.
Wrong - pulsed IV steroid is for severe necrotising or sight-threatening posterior disease.
Wrong - topical NSAIDs and lubricants suit episcleritis, not scleritis.

mcq.stem:
A 64-year-old woman with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis has had a red, intensely painful right eye for 3 weeks. VA 6/18. Slit lamp shows inflamed sclera with a central white avascular patch surrounded by engorged vessels, and the underlying sclera looks thin with a bluish tinge. ESR is 88 mm/h. The rheumatologist asks which treatment should NOT be used.
Which of the following is contraindicated?
o: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day with gastric protection
IV cyclophosphamide pulses arranged with rheumatology
Rituximab as a steroid-sparing biological agent
Weekly methotrexate with folic acid supplementation
Subconjunctival triamcinolone injection near the lesion
mcq.e: A white avascular area with thinning in a painful inflamed eye is **necrotising scleritis with inflammation**. It needs systemic steroid plus immunosuppression (cyclophosphamide, rituximab, methotrexate, ciclosporin) with rheumatology. **Periocular or subconjunctival steroid is contraindicated** because it can precipitate scleral melting and perforation. Note: the notes list subconjunctival steroid under necrotising scleritis; this is wrong.
w: Wrong - high-dose systemic steroid is a cornerstone of treating necrotising scleritis.
Wrong - cyclophosphamide is the classic agent when necrotising scleritis accompanies systemic vasculitis.
Wrong - rituximab is an accepted option for refractory RA- or ANCA-related necrotising disease.
Wrong - methotrexate is a reasonable steroid-sparing immunosuppressant here.
Correct - subconjunctival or periocular steroid risks scleral melt and perforation in necrotising scleritis.

mcq.stem:
A 74-year-old woman with 30 years of deforming rheumatoid arthritis is seen for a cataract assessment. She has no eye pain or redness. Both eyes are white and quiet. On the upper sclera of both eyes there are several yellow-white patches; within one, the sclera is so thin that the dark blue choroid shows through. There is no surrounding injection and the globe is not tender.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Senile hyaline scleral plaques
Scleromalacia perforans
Necrotising scleritis with inflammation
Bilateral pingueculae
Healed nodular episcleritis
mcq.e: Painless, white, bilateral scleral thinning in an elderly woman with long-standing RA is **scleromalacia perforans**, necrotising scleritis WITHOUT inflammation. Note: the notes describe 'yellow nodules'; the correct picture is yellow-white necrotic patches that slough, leaving thin sclera through which the **blue uvea** shows. Spontaneous perforation is rare, but trauma (including surgery) is risky, so tell the cataract surgeon.
w: Wrong - senile hyaline plaques are small grey translucent areas near the horizontal rectus insertions, without necrosis.
Correct - painless, quiet, bilateral necrotic thinning in long-standing RA.
Wrong - necrotising scleritis with inflammation is intensely painful and red.
Wrong - pingueculae are yellowish interpalpebral conjunctival lesions with no scleral thinning.
Wrong - healed episcleritis leaves no scleral necrosis or thinning.

mcq.stem:
A 46-year-old woman presents to the eye clinic with 1 week of severe pain around the left eye, worse on eye movement, and blurred vision. VA 6/24. The eye is only mildly injected anteriorly. There is mild proptosis and restricted abduction. Fundus shows choroidal folds, a swollen optic disc and an inferior shallow exudative retinal detachment. She is afebrile with a normal white cell count.
Which investigation is most likely to confirm the diagnosis at the first visit?
o: Fundus fluorescein angiography
Optical coherence tomography of the macula
MRI brain with gadolinium for demyelination
B-scan ultrasonography of the globe
Visual evoked potentials of both eyes
mcq.e: Pain, reduced vision, proptosis, choroidal folds, disc swelling and exudative RD in a fairly white eye are **posterior scleritis**, a commonly misdiagnosed condition. **B-scan** shows a thickened posterior sclera with fluid in sub-Tenon's space outlining the optic nerve (**T-sign**); CT also shows posterior scleral thickening. Being afebrile with a normal WCC makes orbital cellulitis less likely.
w: Wrong - FFA may show pinpoint leaks but does not demonstrate scleral thickening.
Wrong - OCT shows the subretinal fluid but not the sclera behind the globe.
Wrong - demyelinating optic neuritis does not cause proptosis, choroidal folds or exudative RD.
Correct - B-scan shows posterior scleral thickening and the sub-Tenon fluid T-sign.
Wrong - VEPs measure optic nerve conduction and cannot identify the cause.

mcq.stem:
A 41-year-old man with 3 months of blood-stained nasal crusting and recurrent sinusitis presents with a painful red right eye. VA 6/12. There is diffuse violaceous scleral injection with an early area of peripheral corneal thinning. Urine dipstick shows blood 2+ and protein 1+. Chest X-ray shows two cavitating nodules.
Which blood test is most likely to identify the underlying cause?
o: ANCA with PR3 specificity (c-ANCA)
Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies
Anti-dsDNA with complement C3 and C4
HLA-B27 tissue typing
Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme
mcq.e: Sinonasal disease, haematuria/proteinuria and cavitating lung nodules with scleritis and peripheral corneal thinning point to **granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)**, detected by **PR3-ANCA (c-ANCA)**. Note: the notes use the old name 'Wegener's granulomatosis'; the current name is GPA (and 'polyarthritis nodosa' should read polyarteritis nodosa). A scleritis work-up usually includes FBC, ESR/CRP, RF/anti-CCP, ANCA, ANA, syphilis serology, TB screen and CXR.
w: Correct - PR3-ANCA is the marker for GPA (sinus, lung and kidney disease with necrotising scleritis).
Wrong - RA is the commonest association overall but does not explain sinus disease, lung cavities and nephritis.
Wrong - SLE can cause scleritis but not cavitating lung nodules with destructive sinus disease.
Wrong - HLA-B27 relates to acute anterior uveitis, not necrotising scleritis.
Wrong - ACE supports sarcoidosis, which rarely cavitates or destroys nasal tissue.

mcq.stem:
A 67-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate is diagnosed in the eye clinic with a painful, red left eye showing a white avascular scleral patch with surrounding thinning; ESR is 95 mm/h. Her daughter asks what this means for her mother beyond the eye.
Which statement is the most accurate counselling?
o: It is a localised eye problem and needs no change to her systemic treatment
It usually settles with lubricant drops and topical NSAIDs within two weeks
It may signal active systemic vasculitis, with raised mortality if untreated
It suggests her arthritis is in remission and methotrexate can now be stopped
It is mainly a cosmetic problem because scleral thinning rarely affects sight
mcq.e: Necrotising scleritis in RA is often the first sign of a **systemic vasculitis** and historically carried a high mortality within a few years, largely from vascular events, unless treated with **systemic immunosuppression**. It is managed jointly with rheumatology, not as a local eye problem. Vision is threatened by perforation, peripheral keratitis, uveitis and glaucoma.
w: Wrong - necrotising scleritis needs escalation of systemic immunosuppression.
Wrong - lubricants and topical NSAIDs are for episcleritis; necrotising disease is progressive.
Correct - it can herald systemic vasculitis with increased mortality, so systemic therapy is needed.
Wrong - it indicates active, not quiescent, disease.
Wrong - it is sight-threatening through perforation, keratitis, uveitis and glaucoma.

mcq.stem:
A 26-year-old female university student attends the Klinik Kesihatan with a sectoral patch of redness on the nasal side of her right eye for 3 days. She describes mild grittiness only and no photophobia. VA 6/6. The injected vessels move when the conjunctiva is pushed with a cotton bud and blanch 10 minutes after phenylephrine 10%. The globe is not tender, the cornea is clear and the anterior chamber is quiet.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Oral indomethacin 25 mg three times daily for two weeks
Same-day eye referral and oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily
Topical chloramphenicol four times daily for one week
Vasculitis screen with ANCA, RF and ANA before any treatment
Reassurance, cold compresses and lubricants, ± topical NSAID
mcq.e: Mild discomfort, superficial mobile vessels that blanch with phenylephrine and a non-tender globe make this **simple episcleritis**: benign and usually self-limiting in 1-3 weeks. **Reassurance, cold compresses and lubricants** (± a short topical NSAID or mild topical steroid) are enough. Oral NSAIDs are kept for recurrent or nodular cases, and a systemic work-up only for recurrent disease or features of scleritis.
w: Wrong - oral NSAIDs are for recurrent or troublesome episcleritis, or for scleritis.
Wrong - systemic steroids are not indicated for self-limiting episcleritis.
Wrong - there is no discharge or infection; antibiotics do not help.
Wrong - a first episode of simple episcleritis does not need a vasculitis screen.
Correct - simple episcleritis is benign and self-limiting; treat the symptoms.

mcq.stem:
A 71-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis and treated necrotising scleritis returns with a 5 x 4 mm area of severe scleral thinning superonasally. The dark uvea bulges under a thin conjunctival layer, the Seidel test is negative and IOP is 14 mmHg. Inflammation is controlled on oral prednisolone and methotrexate.
What is the most appropriate next step to protect the globe?
o: Firm pressure patch over the eye and review in one week
Scleral patch graft, continuing immunosuppression
Subconjunctival triamcinolone over the thinned area
Primary enucleation to prevent sympathetic ophthalmia
Stop methotrexate and observe for spontaneous repair
mcq.e: Extensive scleral thinning with impending perforation is the indication for surgical reinforcement with a **donor scleral patch graft**, as the notes list. Grafts melt unless the underlying inflammation is controlled, so **systemic immunosuppression continues**. Pressure on a thin globe and periocular steroid can provoke perforation.
w: Wrong - pressure on a thinned globe risks rupture and does not reinforce the sclera.
Correct - patch grafting reinforces the sclera; ongoing immunosuppression prevents graft melt.
Wrong - periocular steroid is contraindicated in necrotising scleritis because of melt and perforation.
Wrong - the eye is intact and seeing; enucleation is not indicated.
Wrong - stopping immunosuppression risks reactivation and further necrosis.

mcq.stem:
A 59-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis and active diffuse anterior scleritis of the left eye develops worsening pain and reduced VA (6/18). Slit lamp shows a crescent-shaped area of peripheral corneal stromal thinning with an overlying epithelial defect and infiltrate, directly adjacent to the inflamed sclera at the limbus. There is no clear zone between the lesion and the limbus.
What is the most likely complication?
o: Staphylococcal marginal keratitis
Terrien marginal degeneration
Dellen from local tear-film drying
Peripheral ulcerative keratitis
Mooren ulcer
mcq.e: **Peripheral ulcerative keratitis (PUK)**, a crescentic peripheral stromal melt with an epithelial defect next to active scleritis, is a sight-threatening complication of RA- or vasculitis-associated scleritis and, like necrotising scleritis, signals systemic vasculitis needing systemic immunosuppression. Staphylococcal marginal keratitis has a clear zone, Terrien degeneration is painless with intact epithelium, and Mooren ulcer is a diagnosis of exclusion in patients without systemic disease.
w: Wrong - marginal keratitis infiltrates are separated from the limbus by a clear zone, with blepharitis.
Wrong - Terrien degeneration is painless, usually superior, with intact epithelium.
Wrong - dellen are shallow saucer-shaped thinning beside an elevated lesion, without infiltrate.
Correct - crescentic peripheral melt with an epithelial defect next to RA scleritis is PUK.
Wrong - Mooren ulcer is idiopathic, a diagnosis of exclusion when there is no systemic disease.

mcq.stem:
A 21-year-old female university student who wears monthly soft contact lenses, often overnight, presents to the eye casualty with 2 days of a rapidly worsening painful red right eye. VA 6/60. There is a 4 mm central ulcer with a dense yellow-white suppurative infiltrate, surrounding ground-glass stromal oedema, adherent mucopurulent discharge and a 2 mm hypopyon. Corneal sensation is normal.
Which organism is most likely?
o: Staphylococcus aureus
Acanthamoeba castellanii
Fusarium solani
Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Herpes simplex virus type 1
mcq.e: Rapid (24-48 h) suppurative central ulceration with stromal melt, ground-glass oedema, mucopurulent discharge and hypopyon in an overnight soft lens wearer is classic **Pseudomonas aeruginosa** keratitis. Note: the notes imply Staphylococcus is the common contact-lens organism; the classic CL organism is Pseudomonas, with Acanthamoeba as the must-not-miss. It can perforate within days, so treat it as a same-day emergency.
w: Wrong - Staph aureus infects compromised corneas but progresses less explosively and is not the classic CL organism.
Wrong - Acanthamoeba is CL-related but slower, with pain out of proportion and radial keratoneuritis early.
Wrong - Fusarium follows vegetable-matter trauma and gives a dry feathery infiltrate with satellites.
Correct - overnight soft CL wear with rapid suppurative melt and hypopyon is Pseudomonas.
Wrong - HSV gives dendritic or stromal disease with reduced corneal sensation, not suppurative melt.

mcq.stem:
A 55-year-old man with type 2 diabetes who works as a grass cutter comes to the eye clinic 3 days after a stone flicked into his left eye. VA 6/36. There is a 3 mm central white stromal infiltrate with an overlying epithelial defect, a purulent discharge and cells in the anterior chamber. He has not used any eye drops yet.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Start topical dexamethasone with chloramphenicol cover today
Corneal scrape for Gram stain and culture before drops
Double pad the eye and review in the eye clinic in 24 hours
Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily and review in a week
Empirical topical natamycin hourly, then await improvement
mcq.e: A central suppurative ulcer must be **scraped (Gram ± KOH stain, blood/chocolate agar, Sabouraud) before the first antibiotic drop**, because a sterilised surface gives false-negative cultures. Then start **intensive fortified topical antibiotics** (e.g. cefuroxime or cefazolin + gentamicin, hourly day and night) and adjust to culture and response. Steroids, pads and oral antibiotics alone are the traps.
w: Wrong - steroids in an undiagnosed ulcer enhance bacterial, fungal and herpetic growth.
Correct - scrape for microscopy and culture first, then start intensive fortified antibiotics.
Wrong - padding a suppurative ulcer encourages bacterial growth and hides progression.
Wrong - oral antibiotics do not reach therapeutic corneal levels; keratitis needs intensive topical therapy.
Wrong - empirical antifungal before microbiology risks missing a bacterial ulcer; scrape first.

mcq.stem:
A 48-year-old oil palm plantation worker in Pahang was struck in the right eye by a palm frond 12 days ago. He has used topical moxifloxacin hourly for a week without improvement. VA 6/60. There is a 5 mm dry, grey-white, slightly raised stromal infiltrate with feathery margins, two small satellite lesions and a 1 mm hypopyon. A KOH mount of the corneal scrape shows septate hyphae.
What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
o: Topical natamycin 5% hourly by day and night
Fortified cefazolin 5% and gentamicin 1.4% hourly
Topical acyclovir 3% ointment five times a day
Topical PHMB 0.02% and propamidine hourly
Topical prednisolone acetate 1% with moxifloxacin
mcq.e: Vegetable-matter trauma, a dry feathery infiltrate with satellite lesions and septate hyphae mean **filamentous fungal keratitis** (Fusarium/Aspergillus). First-line is **topical natamycin 5%** (voriconazole 1% is an alternative or add-on); Sabouraud culture confirms. Note: the notes call fungal keratitis an 'unusual cause'; in tropical Malaysia it is common after agricultural trauma. Steroids worsen fungal keratitis.
w: Correct - natamycin 5% is first-line for filamentous fungal keratitis.
Wrong - antibacterials do not treat fungi, and he has already failed antibacterial therapy.
Wrong - acyclovir treats HSV epithelial keratitis, not fungi.
Wrong - PHMB and propamidine are anti-Acanthamoeba agents.
Wrong - steroids enhance fungal growth and risk perforation.

mcq.stem:
A 24-year-old female clerk who wears reusable soft contact lenses and rinses her lens case with tap water has had 3 weeks of a painful right eye that has not responded to topical antibiotics. The pain is severe and keeps her awake, yet the eye looks only moderately red. VA 6/18. Slit lamp shows patchy epithelial irregularity, a faint stromal infiltrate and thickened corneal nerves radiating from the centre.
Which investigation is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
o: Conjunctival swab for viral PCR
Corneal sensation testing with a cotton wisp
Gram stain of a corneal scrape as the only test
Fluorescein staining under cobalt blue light
In vivo confocal microscopy of the cornea
mcq.e: Pain out of proportion to signs, **radial keratoneuritis** and tap-water exposure in a soft lens wearer are early **Acanthamoeba keratitis**; the ring infiltrate is a late sign. Diagnosis is by **in vivo confocal microscopy** showing double-walled cysts, or a corneal scrape with PAS/calcofluor staining and culture on non-nutrient agar with an E. coli overlay; send the lens case too. A routine Gram stain usually misses it.
w: Wrong - viral PCR suits adenovirus or HSV, not a protozoal keratitis.
Wrong - reduced sensation suggests HSV or neurotrophic disease; it does not confirm Acanthamoeba.
Wrong - Gram stain alone usually misses cysts; PAS/calcofluor stain or special culture is needed.
Wrong - fluorescein shows the epithelial defect but does not identify the organism.
Correct - confocal microscopy shows Acanthamoeba cysts in the corneal epithelium and stroma.

mcq.stem:
A 34-year-old man who does not wear contact lenses presents to the Klinik Kesihatan with a watery, photophobic left eye for 4 days. There is no history of trauma and no skin rash. VA 6/12. Fluorescein shows a linear branching epithelial ulcer with bulb-like swellings at the end of each branch; the ulcer bed stains brightly. Corneal sensation is reduced compared with the right eye. There are no conjunctival follicles.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Acanthamoeba pseudodendritic keratitis
Herpes zoster pseudodendritic keratitis
Herpes simplex epithelial keratitis
Healing corneal abrasion with an epithelial ridge
Adenoviral epidemic keratoconjunctivitis
mcq.e: A true **dendrite with terminal end-bulbs** whose bed stains with fluorescein, plus **reduced corneal sensation**, is herpes simplex epithelial keratitis. Zoster pseudodendrites are raised, lack end-bulbs and stain poorly, with a dermatomal rash; Acanthamoeba pseudodendrites occur in lens wearers. Treat with topical acyclovir 3% ointment or ganciclovir 0.15% gel, and **never a topical steroid** for a dendritic ulcer.
w: Wrong - Acanthamoeba pseudodendrites occur in contact lens wearers and lack terminal bulbs.
Wrong - zoster pseudodendrites are raised, without end-bulbs, and come with a dermatomal rash.
Correct - a true dendrite with terminal bulbs and reduced sensation is HSV epithelial keratitis.
Wrong - a healing abrasion follows trauma and has no branching with end-bulbs.
Wrong - adenovirus gives follicles and subepithelial infiltrates, not a dendritic ulcer.

mcq.stem:
A 42-year-old woman with two previous episodes of dendritic ulcers in her right eye presents with 1 week of blurred vision and a mild ache. VA 6/24. The corneal epithelium is intact with no fluorescein staining. There is a central disc-shaped area of stromal oedema with underlying keratic precipitates and mild anterior chamber flare. Corneal sensation is reduced and IOP is 18 mmHg.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Topical acyclovir 3% ointment alone, five times daily
Epithelial debridement followed by an eye pad
Topical steroid drops under prophylactic antiviral cover
Intensive fortified cefazolin and gentamicin drops
Early penetrating keratoplasty while the eye is inflamed
mcq.e: Disc-shaped stromal oedema with KPs under intact epithelium in a patient with past dendrites is **HSV disciform keratitis**, an immune reaction rather than active epithelial viral replication. It is treated with **topical steroid, cautiously tapered, under antiviral cover** (topical or oral acyclovir). Antiviral alone does not settle the stromal inflammation, and grafting a hot eye risks rejection and recurrence.
w: Wrong - antiviral alone does not control immune-mediated stromal inflammation.
Wrong - debridement is for epithelial dendrites; the epithelium here is intact.
Correct - disciform HSV keratitis needs steroid with antiviral cover.
Wrong - there is no bacterial infection, so fortified antibiotics are not indicated.
Wrong - keratoplasty is for visually significant scarring once the eye has been quiet for months.

mcq.stem:
A 19-year-old male student who wears soft contact lenses presents to the emergency department with a painful, watery left eye after sleeping in his lenses. VA 6/9. Fluorescein shows a 2 mm central epithelial defect with no stromal infiltrate and a quiet anterior chamber. The ED doctor is planning his treatment before the ophthalmology review.
Which of the following should be AVOIDED?
o: Remove the lenses and keep the case for culture
Topical moxifloxacin or ofloxacin every two hours
Cyclopentolate 1% drop to relieve ciliary spasm
Next-day eye clinic review to look for infiltrate
Firm double eye pad overnight to aid the healing
mcq.e: A corneal abrasion in a contact lens wearer is treated as potential **Pseudomonas** keratitis: remove the lenses, keep the lens and case for culture, use an anti-pseudomonal **fluoroquinolone** and review within 24 h. **Never patch** a CL-related abrasion, because a pad creates a warm closed space in which Pseudomonas multiplies. A cycloplegic helps the pain.
w: Wrong - stopping lens wear and keeping the case for culture is correct practice.
Wrong - an anti-pseudomonal fluoroquinolone is the appropriate cover.
Wrong - a cycloplegic relieves ciliary spasm pain and is reasonable.
Wrong - early review to detect an evolving infiltrate is appropriate.
Correct - patching a CL-related abrasion promotes Pseudomonas keratitis and must be avoided.

mcq.stem:
A 70-year-old woman being treated for bacterial keratitis in her left eye reports a sudden gush of warm fluid down her cheek. VA HM. There is a 1 mm central perforation within the ulcer bed with a positive Seidel test, a shallow anterior chamber and IOP of 5 mmHg. The surrounding cornea is still infiltrated and inflamed.
What is the most appropriate immediate management?
o: Cyanoacrylate glue with a bandage contact lens
Urgent penetrating keratoplasty the same day
Firm pressure pad and stop all eye drops
Topical dexamethasone to reduce corneal melting
Primary evisceration to prevent endophthalmitis
mcq.e: A small (under about 2-3 mm) perforation in active keratitis is sealed with **tissue adhesive (cyanoacrylate glue) and a bandage contact lens** while intensive antibiotics continue. **Corneal grafting is deferred until inflammation has settled**, because a hot graft fails and reinfects, unless the perforation is too large to glue (tectonic graft). Steroids would accelerate melting in active infection.
w: Correct - glue plus a bandage lens seals small perforations; continue the antibiotics.
Wrong - grafting an actively infected cornea risks failure; reserve it for large perforations or later.
Wrong - stopping antibiotics lets infection progress, and pressure does not seal the leak.
Wrong - steroids in active infection promote further melting.
Wrong - evisceration is not indicated for a small, sealable perforation.

mcq.stem:
A 68-year-old man attends the Klinik Kesihatan with 2 days of a painful vesicular rash over the right forehead and upper eyelid, now with vesicles on the tip and side of the nose. The right eye is mildly red with VA 6/9. The doctor explains that the nasal vesicles change his risk.
Involvement of which nerve explains why the nasal lesions predict a high risk of ocular involvement?
o: Supratrochlear branch of the frontal nerve
Nasociliary branch of the ophthalmic nerve
Infraorbital branch of the maxillary nerve
Lacrimal branch of the ophthalmic nerve
Zygomaticotemporal branch of the maxillary nerve
mcq.e: Vesicles on the tip, side or root of the nose (**Hutchinson sign**) mean the **nasociliary nerve** is involved; it also supplies the cornea, iris and ciliary body through the long ciliary nerves, so keratitis and uveitis are likely. Start **oral acyclovir 800 mg five times daily for 7 days** (or valaciclovir/famciclovir), ideally within 72 h of rash onset, and refer to the eye clinic. Topical steroids are not started before ophthalmic assessment.
w: Wrong - the supratrochlear nerve supplies the medial forehead but not the globe or nasal tip.
Correct - the nasociliary nerve supplies the nasal tip and the globe (Hutchinson sign).
Wrong - the infraorbital nerve is a V2 branch, which spares the cornea.
Wrong - the lacrimal nerve supplies the lateral lid and gland, not the nasal tip.
Wrong - the zygomaticotemporal nerve is a V2 branch supplying the temple skin.

mcq.stem:
A 20-year-old female student is reviewed in the eye clinic after successful treatment of contact-lens-related Pseudomonas keratitis, which left a small paracentral scar (VA 6/9). She wants to resume wearing her monthly soft lenses.
Which advice most reduces her risk of a further episode?
o: Instil prophylactic chloramphenicol drops each morning with lenses
Rinse the lenses and case in boiled tap water to sterilise them
Wear the same monthly lenses for two months to limit handling
Never sleep or swim in lenses; keep lenses and case away from water
Wear lenses overnight only at weekends to rest the cornea midweek
mcq.e: **Overnight wear** is the single biggest risk factor for contact-lens keratitis, and **water exposure** (tap-water rinsing, swimming, showering) is the main route for Acanthamoeba. Advise daily wear only, fresh solution, rub-and-rinse, case replacement every 1-3 months, no water contact, and to remove lenses and attend the same day with any red painful eye. Prophylactic antibiotic drops breed resistance and are not recommended.
w: Wrong - prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended and encourage resistance.
Wrong - tap water, even boiled, is a source of Acanthamoeba; use fresh lens solution.
Wrong - using lenses beyond their replacement schedule increases infection risk.
Correct - avoiding overnight wear and water exposure addresses the two biggest risk factors.
Wrong - any overnight wear, even occasional, substantially raises keratitis risk.

mcq.stem:
A 28-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 2 days of a painful, red, photophobic right eye and blurred vision. He has had low back pain and stiffness every morning for a year, easing with exercise. VA 6/12. There is circumcorneal injection, a clear cornea with no fluorescein staining, fine white deposits on the inferior corneal endothelium, cells and flare in the anterior chamber, and a small, sluggish, slightly irregular pupil. IOP 12 mmHg (left 15 mmHg).
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Acute primary angle-closure glaucoma
Acute anterior uveitis
Bacterial keratitis
Diffuse anterior scleritis
Adenoviral keratoconjunctivitis
mcq.e: Ciliary flush, photophobia, AC cells and flare, endothelial **keratic precipitates** and a **small irregular pupil** (early posterior synechiae) with normal or low IOP are **acute anterior uveitis**; inflammatory back pain suggests HLA-B27 ankylosing spondylitis, the commonest association. Angle closure gives a mid-dilated fixed oval pupil, corneal oedema and IOP often above 50 mmHg; keratitis stains with fluorescein. Note: the notes group KPs and hypopyon under 'reduced red reflex'; they are anterior chamber signs seen on the slit lamp.
w: Wrong - angle closure has a mid-dilated fixed pupil, a hazy oedematous cornea and very high IOP.
Correct - ciliary flush, cells and flare, KPs, a small pupil and normal IOP with inflammatory back pain.
Wrong - keratitis shows a staining epithelial defect with a stromal infiltrate.
Wrong - scleritis causes deep boring pain and violaceous injection, without KPs or a small pupil.
Wrong - adenovirus gives watery discharge, follicles and a normal pupil without AC cells.

mcq.stem:
A 45-year-old woman is referred with bilateral blurred vision and mild photophobia for 6 weeks. Both eyes show large greasy keratic precipitates on the inferior endothelium, nodules at the pupil margin and broad posterior synechiae. She also has painful red nodules on both shins and a dry cough. VDRL is non-reactive and she has no back pain.
Which investigation is most useful next?
o: HLA-B27 typing and sacroiliac joint X-ray
Antinuclear antibody and anti-dsDNA titres
Anterior chamber tap for viral PCR
MRI brain for demyelinating white-matter lesions
Chest X-ray with serum ACE and calcium
mcq.e: **Mutton-fat KPs** and iris nodules mean **granulomatous** uveitis; with erythema nodosum and cough, **sarcoidosis** is likely, so a chest X-ray (bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy) and serum ACE/calcium come first, with TB (Mantoux/IGRA) and syphilis serology also part of the granulomatous screen. HLA-B27 is linked to acute, unilateral, non-granulomatous uveitis and is a commonly mis-ordered test here.
w: Wrong - HLA-B27 disease causes acute unilateral non-granulomatous anterior uveitis.
Wrong - SLE rarely causes granulomatous uveitis; ANA matters mainly in JIA.
Wrong - AC tap PCR is for suspected viral uveitis, usually unilateral with raised IOP.
Wrong - MS-associated uveitis is mainly intermediate and does not explain erythema nodosum and cough.
Correct - CXR for hilar lymphadenopathy with ACE and calcium supports sarcoidosis.

mcq.stem:
A 33-year-old woman with acute anterior uveitis of her left eye is prescribed prednisolone acetate 1% drops and cyclopentolate 1% three times daily. She works as an accounts clerk and asks the house officer why she needs the second drop, since it blurs her near vision.
What is the main reason for prescribing cyclopentolate?
o: It lowers intraocular pressure by increasing uveoscleral outflow
It provides antimicrobial cover against secondary bacterial infection
It relaxes ciliary spasm and dilates the pupil to prevent synechiae
It reduces aqueous production and so lowers the anterior chamber flare
It enhances corneal penetration of the steroid drop into the chamber
mcq.e: Cycloplegic-mydriatics such as cyclopentolate (or atropine/homatropine) **relieve pain from ciliary muscle spasm** and **dilate the pupil so the inflamed iris cannot stick to the lens** (posterior synechiae), or break fresh ones. The steroid treats the inflammation itself. Cyclopentolate does not lower IOP and has no antimicrobial action.
w: Wrong - prostaglandin analogues increase uveoscleral outflow; cyclopentolate has no IOP-lowering role.
Wrong - cyclopentolate has no antimicrobial action.
Correct - cycloplegia relieves ciliary spasm pain and mydriasis prevents posterior synechiae.
Wrong - it does not reduce aqueous production; flare reflects protein leaking from inflamed vessels.
Wrong - it does not alter steroid penetration.

mcq.stem:
A 50-year-old man with recurrent anterior uveitis in his right eye presents with sudden pain, haloes and vomiting. VA 6/60. The cornea is hazy, the pupil is small and fixed with 360° adhesions of the iris to the lens, and the peripheral iris bows forward so that the peripheral chamber is very shallow while the central chamber is deep. IOP 52 mmHg. He has been given IV acetazolamide and topical timolol.
What is the definitive next step?
o: Nd:YAG laser peripheral iridotomy
Pilocarpine 2% every 15 minutes
Selective laser trabeculoplasty
Stop topical steroid to avoid steroid response
Atropine 1% to break the adhesions
mcq.e: 360° posterior synechiae (**seclusio pupillae**) block aqueous flow from the posterior to the anterior chamber, so the iris balloons forward (**iris bombé**) and closes the angle: a secondary angle closure. After medical IOP lowering, **laser peripheral iridotomy** (or surgical iridectomy) re-opens a bypass, while intensive topical steroid controls the inflammation. Pilocarpine worsens inflammation and synechiae.
w: Correct - an iridotomy bypasses the pupillary block caused by seclusio pupillae.
Wrong - miotics increase inflammation and synechiae and cannot open a bound pupil.
Wrong - trabeculoplasty is for open-angle glaucoma; here the angle is closed by iris.
Wrong - steroid is needed to control the inflammation; this is not a steroid response.
Wrong - atropine cannot break established 360° synechiae and does not relieve the block.

mcq.stem:
A 4-year-old girl with oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis diagnosed 6 months ago is ANA-positive. Her mother says the child's eyes have never been red or painful and she seems to see well. Her paediatrician refers her to the eye clinic.
What is the most appropriate advice about eye follow-up?
o: Eye review only if she develops red eyes or photophobia
A single baseline eye examination is enough at this age
Annual fundus photography at the Klinik Kesihatan
Slit-lamp checks about every 3 months, even if eyes are white
HLA-B27 testing first to decide whether screening is needed
mcq.e: JIA-associated uveitis (highest risk: **oligoarticular, ANA-positive, girls, onset under 7 years, early in the disease**) is a **chronic, painless, white-eye anterior uveitis** that stays silent until band keratopathy, cataract, glaucoma or amblyopia have developed. High-risk children therefore need **slit-lamp screening about every 3 months**, spacing out as risk falls. Waiting for symptoms is the trap.
w: Wrong - JIA uveitis is typically asymptomatic and white until complications develop.
Wrong - risk persists for years, so repeated screening is needed.
Wrong - fundus photographs miss anterior chamber cells; a slit lamp is required.
Correct - high-risk JIA needs 3-monthly slit-lamp screening regardless of symptoms.
Wrong - HLA-B27 relates to acute symptomatic uveitis; ANA-positive oligoarticular JIA is the risk group.

mcq.stem:
A 24-year-old man complains of floaters and blurred vision in his left eye for 10 days. VA 6/18. The anterior chamber has mild cells. There is dense vitreous haze, through which a fluffy, creamy-white focus of retinitis is seen at the edge of an old, flat, heavily pigmented chorioretinal scar near the macula. He is HIV-negative and otherwise well.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Cytomegalovirus retinitis
Acute retinal necrosis
Endogenous Candida endophthalmitis
Toxoplasma retinochoroiditis
Tuberculous serpiginous-like choroiditis
mcq.e: A fluffy active focus of retinochoroiditis next to a pigmented scar, seen through dense vitritis (the '**headlight in the fog**'), is reactivated **toxoplasmosis**, the commonest infectious posterior uveitis in immunocompetent adults. CMV retinitis occurs in immunosuppression with little vitritis, acute retinal necrosis shows peripheral confluent necrosis, and Candida gives 'string of pearls' vitreous balls in at-risk patients.
w: Wrong - CMV retinitis occurs with CD4 below 50 and shows haemorrhagic necrosis with little vitritis.
Wrong - acute retinal necrosis shows rapidly spreading peripheral confluent necrosis with occlusive vasculitis.
Wrong - Candida affects IV-drug users or line patients and gives fluffy vitreous balls without a pigmented scar.
Correct - reactivation at the edge of a pigmented scar with dense vitritis is toxoplasmosis.
Wrong - TB choroiditis is multifocal and creeping, not a single active edge on an old scar.

mcq.stem:
A 35-year-old man with advanced HIV (CD4 count 30 cells/µL), not yet on antiretroviral therapy, attends the eye clinic with painless floaters and a shadow in his right visual field. VA 6/9. The eye is white and quiet with minimal vitreous cells. The fundus shows a wedge of yellow-white, granular retinal necrosis along the inferotemporal arcade with scattered intraretinal haemorrhages.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Cytomegalovirus retinitis
Toxoplasma retinochoroiditis
HIV microvasculopathy
Progressive outer retinal necrosis
Syphilitic posterior placoid chorioretinitis
mcq.e: Painless, white-eyed, slowly progressive **haemorrhagic granular necrosis along the vessels** ('pizza pie') with minimal vitritis in a patient with **CD4 below 50** is **CMV retinitis**, the commonest opportunistic eye infection in AIDS. Treatment is systemic (val)ganciclovir ± intravitreal ganciclovir plus starting antiretroviral therapy (watch for immune-recovery uveitis). Note: the notes write 'Acquired Immuno-Deficiency Virus'; AIDS is acquired immunodeficiency SYNDROME, caused by HIV.
w: Correct - granular haemorrhagic necrosis along vessels with minimal vitritis at CD4 below 50.
Wrong - toxoplasmosis gives dense vitritis; in AIDS lesions are often multifocal, without the haemorrhagic pattern.
Wrong - HIV microvasculopathy shows cotton-wool spots and small haemorrhages, without necrosis.
Wrong - PORN (VZV) is rapidly progressive outer retinal whitening with few haemorrhages, spreading in days.
Wrong - syphilitic placoid lesions are yellowish macular plaques, not haemorrhagic necrosis along vessels.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old woman has her first episode of unilateral acute anterior uveitis. VA 6/9. There is ciliary flush, 3+ anterior chamber cells, fine keratic precipitates and a few fresh posterior synechiae. IOP is 14 mmHg and the fundus is normal. There are no signs of infection and herpetic keratitis has been excluded.
What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
o: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily, tapered over a month
Topical fluorometholone 0.1% four times daily
Prednisolone acetate 1% hourly plus a cycloplegic drop
Topical chloramphenicol and preservative-free lubricants
Posterior sub-Tenon triamcinolone injection
mcq.e: Anterior uveitis is treated with **potent topical steroid (prednisolone acetate 1%) frequently, e.g. hourly**, tapered over weeks as cells settle, plus a **cycloplegic** to relieve pain and break or prevent synechiae. Fluorometholone is too weak for intraocular inflammation, and systemic or periocular steroids are reserved for posterior, severe bilateral or refractory disease. Always exclude infection such as HSV before starting steroids.
w: Wrong - systemic steroid is for posterior, severe bilateral or refractory disease, not first-episode AAU.
Wrong - fluorometholone penetrates poorly and is too weak for anterior chamber inflammation.
Correct - intensive potent topical steroid plus a cycloplegic is first-line for AAU.
Wrong - uveitis is not an infection; antibiotics and lubricants do not treat it.
Wrong - periocular depot steroid is for intermediate or posterior uveitis and macular oedema.

mcq.stem:
A 40-year-old construction worker had primary repair of a penetrating injury to his right eye with uveal prolapse 6 weeks ago. He now has photophobia and blurred vision in his LEFT eye. Both eyes show mutton-fat keratic precipitates, vitritis and multiple small yellow-white lesions at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium. VA right 6/60, left 6/18.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Immediate enucleation of the injured eye as sole treatment
Topical prednisolone acetate 1% to both eyes only
Intravitreal vancomycin and ceftazidime to both eyes
Observation, as the fellow-eye reaction is self-limiting
High-dose systemic steroid then steroid-sparing therapy
mcq.e: Bilateral granulomatous panuveitis with Dalen-Fuchs nodules weeks to months after a penetrating injury is **sympathetic ophthalmia**, an autoimmune reaction to uveal antigens released from the injured (exciting) eye. Treatment is **high-dose systemic corticosteroid** (often IV then oral) with **steroid-sparing immunosuppression** for long-term control. Once it is established, enucleating the exciting eye does not reliably help, and that eye may end up the better-seeing one. Note: the notes write 'sympathetic ophthalmitis'; the correct term is sympathetic ophthalmia.
w: Wrong - once sympathetic ophthalmia has started, enucleation alone does not control the fellow eye.
Wrong - topical steroid alone cannot control a bilateral panuveitis.
Wrong - this is autoimmune, not infective endophthalmitis; intravitreal antibiotics are not indicated.
Wrong - untreated sympathetic ophthalmia can blind both eyes.
Correct - systemic steroid with steroid-sparing immunosuppression controls this bilateral panuveitis.

mcq.stem:
A 38-year-old man with chronic anterior uveitis of his left eye has been using prednisolone acetate 1% four times daily for 3 months. The eye has had no anterior chamber cells for the last 2 months. IOP has risen from 15 to 34 mmHg over 6 weeks. Gonioscopy shows a wide open angle without peripheral anterior synechiae or new vessels, and the cup:disc ratio is 0.3.
What is the most likely cause of the raised IOP?
o: Uveitic trabeculitis from active inflammation
Corticosteroid-induced ocular hypertension
Secondary angle closure from iris bombé
Neovascular glaucoma from iris rubeosis
Primary angle-closure from a crowded angle
mcq.e: A quiet eye, an open angle without PAS or new vessels, and an IOP rise weeks after starting a potent topical steroid point to a **steroid response** (reduced trabecular outflow), which is commoner in uveitis patients. Manage by tapering or switching the steroid (e.g. to loteprednol or fluorometholone) or adding a steroid-sparing agent, plus IOP-lowering drops, and monitor the disc and field. Other long-term complications of chronic uveitis and its treatment include **posterior subcapsular cataract**, band keratopathy and cystoid macular oedema.
w: Wrong - trabeculitis occurs with active inflammation; this eye has had no cells for 2 months.
Correct - an open angle, a quiet eye and an IOP rise weeks into potent steroid use is a steroid response.
Wrong - iris bombé gives a shallow peripheral chamber and a closed angle.
Wrong - gonioscopy shows no new vessels.
Wrong - the angle is wide open on gonioscopy.

mcq.stem:
A 34-year-old construction worker attends the MOH hospital eye clinic 2 days after he felt something strike his right eye while hammering a steel chisel. He has only mild grittiness. VA right 6/18, left 6/6. Slit lamp: a 1.5 mm self-sealed full-thickness linear corneal scar inferotemporally (Seidel negative), a small iris transillumination defect in the same meridian and a localised feathery lens opacity behind it. AC deep with mild cells; IOP 14 mmHg. The fundus view is hazy.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Corneal abrasion with traumatic anterior uveitis
Embedded superficial corneal foreign body with rust ring
Retained intraocular metallic foreign body
Blunt-trauma rosette cataract with commotio retinae
Self-sealed corneal laceration alone
mcq.e: Hammering metal on metal throws off tiny, hot, high-velocity steel chips that can enter the eye through a self-sealing corneal wound with surprisingly few symptoms. An entry wound, an iris transillumination defect and a focal lens opacity lying on one straight line trace the track of the fragment, so an **IOFB** must be assumed until **CT** excludes it. The trap is to treat the healed wound as the whole injury.
w: Wrong - an abrasion is epithelial only; it cannot produce a full-thickness scar, an iris hole or a lens opacity.
Wrong - no foreign body is seen on the corneal surface, and a superficial FB does not breach the iris or lens.
Correct - entry wound, iris defect and lens opacity in line after hammering metal = IOFB until CT proves otherwise.
Wrong - a rosette cataract follows concussion, but blunt injury does not make a full-thickness corneal wound or an iris hole.
Wrong - the wound has sealed, but the iris and lens damage show something travelled further into the eye.

mcq.stem:
A 19-year-old grass-cutter is brought to the emergency department after a stone thrown up by his strimmer struck his left eye 1 hour ago. VA left hand movements. The upper lid is swollen; gently parting the lids shows a 6 mm corneoscleral laceration at 9 o'clock with dark tissue in the wound, a teardrop-shaped pupil pointing towards it and a very shallow anterior chamber. He ate lunch 2 hours ago.
What is the most appropriate immediate management?
o: Rigid shield, nil by mouth, IV antibiotics, CT orbits and urgent repair
Tonopen IOP and gonioscopy to look for an angle foreign body first
Firm double eye pad, oral analgesia and eye clinic review next morning
MRI orbits to localise any foreign body, then chloramphenicol drops
Saline irrigation of the wound and repositioning of the tissue with a bud
mcq.e: Peaked pupil, shallow AC and uveal tissue in the wound mean an **open globe**. Protect the eye with a **rigid shield** resting on the orbital rim, keep **nil by mouth**, give antiemetic, analgesia, tetanus cover and systemic antibiotics, image with **CT**, and refer for primary repair (ideally within 24 h). Note: the notes say 'fundoscopy and gonioscopy is a must' — in a suspected open globe NO pressure is applied (no gonioscopy, tonometry or padding) until the globe is closed.
w: Correct - shield without pressure, NBM, antibiotics, CT and same-day ophthalmic repair is the open-globe pathway.
Wrong - tonometry and gonioscopy press on the globe and can extrude intraocular contents; defer until after repair.
Wrong - a pressure pad squeezes an open globe, and overnight delay raises endophthalmitis risk.
Wrong - MRI is contraindicated until a metallic FB is excluded (strimmer injuries may carry wire), and drops alone are inadequate.
Wrong - prolapsed uvea is never manipulated in ED; repositioning or excision is done in theatre.

mcq.stem:
A 41-year-old lathe operator presents to the eye clinic after a metal fragment flew into his right eye. VA right 6/60. There is a 2 mm self-sealed corneal wound, a small hyphaema and a vitreous haemorrhage that obscures the fundus. The left eye is normal. The team needs to confirm and localise a suspected intraocular fragment before planning surgery.
Which investigation is most appropriate?
o: MRI orbits with gadolinium
Fundus fluorescein angiography of the right eye
Contact B-scan with firm probe pressure on the lid
Optical coherence tomography of the right macula
Thin-slice non-contrast CT of the orbits
mcq.e: **Thin-slice (about 1 mm) CT** is the imaging of choice: it detects and localises metallic and most non-metallic fragments without touching the eye. **MRI is contraindicated** when a ferromagnetic FB is possible because the magnet can move the fragment and cause further damage. Ultrasound can help once the wound is secure but must never be done with pressure on a possibly open globe.
w: Wrong - MRI is contraindicated with a possible metallic (ferromagnetic) IOFB; the fragment can move in the magnetic field.
Wrong - FFA shows the retinal circulation, not a foreign body, and the vitreous haemorrhage blocks the view anyway.
Wrong - pressing on a recently wounded globe risks extrusion of contents; any B-scan must be gentle and only once the wound is secure.
Wrong - OCT needs clear media and images only the macula; it cannot localise a fragment in the vitreous or eye wall.
Correct - thin-slice CT orbits detects and localises a metallic IOFB safely and is the standard first imaging.

mcq.stem:
A 46-year-old welder complains of gradually dimming vision and poor night vision in his right eye. Eight months ago something hit that eye while he was hammering, but he did not seek care. VA right 6/24, left 6/6. The right iris is a darker reddish-brown than the left, the right pupil is mid-dilated and sluggish, and there are rust-brown dots on the anterior lens capsule. Electroretinogram shows a reduced b-wave on the right.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Chalcosis from a retained copper fragment
Siderosis bulbi from a retained iron fragment
Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis of the right eye
Sympathetic ophthalmia affecting the injured eye
Traumatic angle-recession glaucoma
mcq.e: Iron from a retained steel chip dissociates and deposits in epithelial tissues — iris (**heterochromia**, darker iris), pupil muscles (**mydriasis**), lens epithelium (**rust-brown spots**) and retina (pigmentary retinopathy with a falling **ERG b-wave**). Copper causes **chalcosis** instead: greenish iris, sunflower cataract and a Descemet copper ring; pure copper causes an acute sterile endophthalmitis. Serial ERG monitors siderosis, and the fragment should be removed.
w: Wrong - chalcosis gives a greenish iris, sunflower cataract and Descemet copper ring, not rust-brown capsular spots.
Correct - hammering history, darker iris, dilated pupil, rust-brown lens deposits and reduced ERG = iron toxicity.
Wrong - Fuchs makes the affected iris LIGHTER and has stellate KPs; it is not linked to trauma or ERG loss.
Wrong - sympathetic ophthalmia is a bilateral granulomatous uveitis, recognised mainly by inflammation in the fellow eye.
Wrong - angle recession follows blunt trauma and raises IOP; it does not darken the iris or reduce the ERG.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old factory worker had primary repair of a large right scleral laceration with uveal prolapse 7 weeks ago; the right eye now sees perception of light only. He returns with 4 days of photophobia and blurred vision in his LEFT eye. VA left 6/24. Left eye: mutton-fat keratic precipitates, AC cells 2+, vitritis and multiple small yellow-white deep lesions in the mid-periphery. The right eye also shows increased inflammation. He has no hearing loss, rash or whitening of the lashes.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Endogenous bacterial endophthalmitis
Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease
Toxoplasma retinochoroiditis
Sympathetic ophthalmia
Sarcoid uveitis
mcq.e: A **bilateral granulomatous panuveitis** starting weeks to months after a penetrating injury (especially with uveal prolapse) is **sympathetic ophthalmia**: exposure of hidden uveal antigens triggers autoimmunity against both eyes; the yellow-white deep lesions are **Dalen-Fuchs nodules**. It needs high-dose systemic steroids and immunosuppression; enucleation of a blind, painful injured eye within about 2 weeks of injury may reduce the risk. Note: the notes call it 'sympathetic ophthalmitis' — the correct term is sympathetic ophthalmia.
w: Wrong - endogenous endophthalmitis needs a septic source and does not give bilateral granulomatous KPs after one-eye trauma.
Wrong - VKH gives a similar uveitis but without injury, typically with meningism, tinnitus or deafness, vitiligo or poliosis.
Wrong - toxoplasmosis is usually unilateral, with a focal 'headlight in the fog' lesion beside a pigmented scar.
Correct - bilateral granulomatous panuveitis weeks after a penetrating injury with uveal prolapse = sympathetic ophthalmia.
Wrong - sarcoid can be granulomatous and bilateral, but onset weeks after a penetrating injury points to sympathetic ophthalmia.

mcq.stem:
A 27-year-old mechanic presents to the emergency department the day after using an angle grinder without goggles. His right eye is gritty and watery. VA right 6/6. After topical anaesthetic, the slit lamp shows a tiny dark metallic speck embedded in the paracentral corneal epithelium with a surrounding orange-brown ring. Seidel test is negative, the AC is deep and quiet, the pupil is round and the lens is clear. Lid eversion shows nothing else.
What is the best management?
o: Urgent CT orbits to exclude an IOFB before attempting any removal
Double-pad the eye overnight and remove the speck once epithelium heals
Steroid-antibiotic combination drops four times daily for one week
Slit-lamp needle removal, burr the rust ring, antibiotic ointment
Leave in situ, as embedded metal extrudes by itself within a few days
mcq.e: A **superficial corneal FB** with a quiet eye, deep AC, round pupil and negative Seidel test needs no imaging. Under topical anaesthetic it is lifted off with irrigation, a moistened cotton bud or a 25G needle tip at the slit lamp, the **rust ring is burred** (now or at 24-48 h if deep), and topical antibiotic is given. Steroids are avoided on an epithelial defect, and rust left behind keeps the eye inflamed and delays healing.
w: Wrong - CT is for suspected penetration (hammering, a wound, Seidel positive, abnormal pupil or AC); none is present here.
Wrong - the speck will not dislodge by itself; leaving it with rust delays healing, and padding adds no benefit.
Wrong - topical steroid on an epithelial defect risks infection (including fungal) and does not remove the FB.
Correct - remove under topical anaesthesia, burr the rust ring and give topical antibiotic cover.
Wrong - embedded metal oxidises and spreads rust into the stroma; it must be removed rather than left to extrude.

mcq.stem:
A 52-year-old oil palm harvester undergoes primary repair of a right corneal laceration caused by a soil-covered metal sickle. CT shows no retained foreign body. VA right 6/36; the AC is formed after repair and there is no hypopyon. He has no drug allergies.
Which prophylactic systemic antibiotic is most appropriate?
o: Oral moxifloxacin 400 mg once daily
Oral amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily
Oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily
Oral metronidazole 400 mg three times daily
Oral fluconazole 200 mg once daily
