mcq.e: After an open-globe injury, systemic prophylaxis must reach therapeutic levels **inside the eye** and cover Bacillus plus common gram-positive and gram-negative organisms. Fluoroquinolones such as **oral moxifloxacin 400 mg OD** (or ciprofloxacin 750 mg BD, as in the notes) penetrate the vitreous well. Soil contamination raises the risk of fulminant **Bacillus** endophthalmitis, so agent choice matters.
w: Correct - moxifloxacin achieves good vitreous levels and covers Bacillus and common post-traumatic organisms.
Wrong - amoxicillin penetrates the vitreous poorly and Bacillus cereus produces beta-lactamase.
Wrong - doxycycline is used for blepharitis and chlamydia; it does not give reliable intraocular cover.
Wrong - metronidazole covers anaerobes only; it misses Bacillus, staphylococci and gram-negatives.
Wrong - fungal prophylaxis is not routine; fluconazole would also miss the bacteria that cause most post-traumatic infection.

mcq.stem:
A 74-year-old woman is seen in the emergency department after falling face-first onto the edge of a coffee table. VA right hand movements. There is 360° bullous subconjunctival haemorrhage with chemosis, the AC is unusually deep compared with the left eye with a 1 mm hyphaema, and the IOP recorded at triage was 5 mmHg. Eye movements are limited in all directions and there is no corneal wound.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Isolated traumatic subconjunctival haemorrhage
Retrobulbar haemorrhage with orbital compartment syndrome
Occult scleral rupture behind the rectus insertions
Orbital floor blow-out fracture with muscle entrapment
Traumatic carotid-cavernous fistula
mcq.e: Blunt force can burst the globe where the sclera is thinnest — **behind the rectus insertions** or at the limbus — and the wound hides under haemorrhage. A dense 360° bullous subconjunctival haemorrhage, **very low IOP**, an abnormally **deep AC**, hyphaema and poor vision mean an occult rupture: shield the eye, stop examining, CT and explore in theatre. Retrobulbar haemorrhage gives the opposite picture — tense proptosis with a HIGH IOP.
w: Wrong - a simple subconjunctival haemorrhage leaves VA, AC depth and IOP normal.
Wrong - retrobulbar haemorrhage causes tense proptosis and a HIGH IOP, needing lateral canthotomy.
Correct - 360° bullous haemorrhage, low IOP, deep AC and poor VA after a blow = occult scleral rupture.
Wrong - a blow-out fracture restricts mainly upgaze with infraorbital numbness; it does not drop the IOP to 5 mmHg or deepen the AC.
Wrong - a carotid-cavernous fistula gives pulsatile proptosis, arterialised vessels and raised IOP, usually days to weeks later.

mcq.stem:
A 23-year-old plantation worker had a small corneal laceration from a soil-contaminated metal wire sutured yesterday; CT showed a tiny retained intravitreal fragment awaiting removal. Twelve hours later he has severe pain. VA right has dropped from 6/24 to perception of light, with lid swelling, a corneal ring infiltrate, a 2 mm hypopyon and dense vitritis. Temperature 38.4 °C.
Which organism is most likely?
o: Staphylococcus epidermidis
Propionibacterium acnes
Aspergillus
Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Bacillus cereus
mcq.e: Fulminant endophthalmitis within 12-24 h of a **soil-contaminated** penetrating injury, often with a **corneal ring infiltrate**, fever and leucocytosis, is classic **Bacillus cereus**: its toxins destroy the retina within hours. It resists many beta-lactams, so **intravitreal vancomycin** is essential, with urgent vitrectomy and IOFB removal. P. acnes is the slow, low-grade, months-later post-cataract organism.
w: Wrong - S. epidermidis is the commonest organism after cataract surgery and causes a milder, slower picture.
Wrong - P. acnes gives delayed, indolent, low-grade inflammation weeks to years after cataract surgery.
Wrong - fungi such as Aspergillus cause slowly progressive inflammation over days to weeks, not within 12 hours.
Wrong - Pseudomonas is the classic contact-lens keratitis organism; Bacillus is the hallmark of soil-contaminated trauma.
Correct - explosive onset within a day of soil-contaminated trauma, ring infiltrate and fever = Bacillus cereus.

mcq.stem:
A 36-year-old landscaper walks into a Klinik Kesihatan with a 2 cm piece of strimmer wire protruding from the centre of his left cornea; it struck him 30 minutes ago. VA left counting fingers. He is anxious and in pain. His last tetanus booster was 15 years ago. The nearest eye unit is 40 minutes away.
What should the KK doctor do?
o: Pull the wire out along its line of entry, then apply an eye pad and refer
Leave the wire, tape a cup over it without contact, tetanus cover, transfer
Instil atropine 1% and steroid drops, then refer to the next eye clinic
Perform a Seidel test, then press on the globe to check for a wound leak
Apply a firm pressure pad to limit leakage and request an urgent MRI
mcq.e: A **protruding foreign body** may be plugging the wound; pulling it out in primary care can release vitreous or cause haemorrhage, so it is removed **only in theatre**. Stabilise it, protect the eye with a cup or rigid shield that does not touch the wire, keep nil by mouth, give analgesia, antiemetic and **tetanus prophylaxis**, and transfer urgently. Never pad with pressure, and never send a possible metallic FB for MRI.
w: Wrong - removing a protruding FB outside theatre can unplug the wound and cause expulsion of intraocular contents.
Correct - leave it in situ, shield without touching it, update tetanus and transfer urgently for surgery.
Wrong - drops add nothing now, and topical steroid on an open wound raises the infection risk.
Wrong - pressing on an open globe can extrude its contents; the diagnosis is already obvious.
Wrong - pressure pads squeeze an open globe, and MRI is contraindicated with a metallic FB.

mcq.stem:
A 14-year-old boy is hit in the right eye by a squash ball. In the eye clinic 3 hours later VA right is 6/12. There is a 2 mm layered blood level in the inferior anterior chamber, the cornea is clear, the pupil is round and IOP is 19 mmHg. Gentle dilated examination shows a normal fundus. He has no bleeding disorder and is not of African ancestry. He asks for something for the pain.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Oral aspirin for pain, normal activity and review in two weeks
Head-up rest, topical steroid and cycloplegic, daily IOP checks
Same-day anterior chamber washout in theatre to clear all of the blood
Topical pilocarpine 2% four times daily to keep the angle open
Firm double padding of both eyes and lying flat for 48 hours
mcq.e: A small traumatic **hyphaema** with normal IOP is managed conservatively: **head elevated 30-45°** so blood settles inferiorly away from the visual axis, limited activity, **topical steroid** (less inflammation and re-bleeding) and a **cycloplegic** (comfort, stabilises the iris), with daily IOP checks because **re-bleeding peaks at days 2-5**. Avoid aspirin and NSAIDs — paracetamol is used for pain. Washout is reserved for uncontrolled IOP, corneal blood staining or a non-clearing total hyphaema.
w: Wrong - aspirin and NSAIDs increase the risk of re-bleeding; paracetamol is the analgesic of choice.
Correct - head-up rest, steroid plus cycloplegic and daily IOP monitoring through the re-bleed window is standard.
Wrong - washout is for IOP not controlled medically, corneal blood staining or a persistent total hyphaema.
Wrong - miotics increase inflammation and break down the blood-aqueous barrier; a cycloplegic is used instead.
Wrong - lying flat spreads blood over the visual axis and angle; head elevation is advised and bilateral padding is unnecessary.

mcq.stem:
A 21-year-old Nigerian engineering student at a Malaysian university is struck in the left eye by a hockey ball. VA left 6/18. There is a 3 mm hyphaema and the IOP is 34 mmHg. Haemoglobin electrophoresis, sent because of his ancestry, shows sickle cell trait (HbAS). The registrar plans to lower the IOP and control his pain.
Which drug should be AVOIDED?
o: Topical timolol 0.5%
Topical prednisolone acetate 1%
Topical atropine 1%
Oral acetazolamide 500 mg
Oral paracetamol 1 g six-hourly
mcq.e: In sickle cell disease or trait, **carbonic anhydrase inhibitors** (especially systemic acetazolamide) acidify the aqueous and blood and cause haemoconcentration, increasing **sickling** of red cells in the AC; rigid sickled cells block the trabecular meshwork and IOP climbs further. The optic nerve in these patients also tolerates raised IOP poorly, so the threshold for washout is lower (e.g. IOP ≥24 mmHg for over 24 h). Use a topical beta-blocker first, avoid hyperosmotics too, and screen at-risk patients with hyphaema for sickle status.
w: Wrong - topical timolol is the first-line IOP-lowering drug in sickle hyphaema.
Wrong - topical steroid is standard in hyphaema to reduce inflammation and re-bleeding.
Wrong - a cycloplegic is standard for comfort and to stabilise the iris and ciliary body.
Correct - systemic acetazolamide causes acidosis and haemoconcentration that promote sickling and worsen IOP.
Wrong - paracetamol is the safe analgesic in hyphaema; it is aspirin and NSAIDs that are avoided.

mcq.stem:
A 25-year-old man is punched on the left eye outside a mamak stall. In the emergency department he has left periorbital bruising and complains of double vision on looking up. The left eye appears sunken; elevation is restricted and painful. VA left 6/6, pupils equal with no RAPD, globe intact. Sensation is reduced over the left cheek, side of the nose, upper lip and upper gum.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Orbital floor fracture with inferior rectus entrapment
Medial orbital wall fracture with medial rectus entrapment
Traumatic left trochlear nerve palsy from orbital contusion
Retrobulbar haemorrhage with orbital compartment syndrome
Traumatic left oculomotor palsy, superior division
mcq.e: A blow from an object larger than the orbital rim (fist, ball) raises orbital pressure and **blows out the thin orbital floor** into the maxillary sinus. **Inferior rectus or fat entrapment** limits upgaze (diplopia on looking up), orbital volume expansion gives **enophthalmos**, and injury to the **infraorbital nerve** running in the floor numbs the cheek, side of the nose, upper lip and gum. Confirm with CT (coronal 'teardrop sign'), advise no nose blowing, and consider repair at 1-2 weeks if diplopia or enophthalmos persists.
w: Correct - upgaze diplopia, enophthalmos and infraorbital numbness = orbital floor blow-out with inferior rectus trapping.
Wrong - medial wall fractures limit horizontal movement and cause orbital emphysema; they do not numb the cheek.
Wrong - a fourth nerve palsy gives vertical diplopia worse looking down and in, without enophthalmos or cheek numbness.
Wrong - retrobulbar haemorrhage gives tense proptosis, raised IOP and threatened vision, not a sunken eye.
Wrong - superior division CN3 palsy causes ptosis and weak elevation, but no enophthalmos or infraorbital numbness.

mcq.stem:
A 10-year-old boy is kneed in the right eye during a football match. Two hours later in the emergency department he has very little bruising and a white, quiet eye, but upgaze is markedly restricted and painful. He keeps vomiting and his heart rate is 48/min. VA right 6/9, no RAPD. CT orbits shows a small linear floor fracture with the inferior rectus incarcerated in it.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Observe for 10-14 days until swelling settles, then repair if diplopia persists
Oral co-amoxiclav, nasal decongestant and outpatient review in one week
Admit for IV ondansetron and head-injury observation, then reassess
IV atropine to correct the bradycardia, then discharge with eye clinic follow-up
Same-day surgical release of the trapped muscle and floor repair
mcq.e: In children the elastic orbital floor cracks and springs back like a **trapdoor**, pinching the inferior rectus, and the eye can look deceptively **white** ('white-eyed blow-out'). Traction on the muscle triggers the **oculocardiac reflex** (bradycardia, nausea, vomiting, syncope) and the trapped muscle becomes ischaemic, so **urgent release within 24-48 h** is needed. Applying the adult strategy of waiting 1-2 weeks for swelling to settle is the trap.
w: Wrong - the delayed approach suits adults; a trapped muscle in a child becomes ischaemic and fibrosed if left.
Wrong - antibiotics and decongestants are supportive only; they do not free the incarcerated muscle.
Wrong - the vomiting and bradycardia are vagal (oculocardiac reflex), not a head injury; treating symptoms misses the cause.
Wrong - atropine may help the bradycardia briefly, but the reflex persists until the muscle is released.
Correct - a trapdoor fracture with muscle entrapment and oculocardiac reflex needs urgent surgical release.

mcq.stem:
A 32-year-old man was hit in the left eye by a recoiling elastic luggage strap 4 weeks ago, causing a hyphaema that has now cleared. VA left 6/6, IOP 18 mmHg (right 15 mmHg), and the optic disc is healthy. Gonioscopy of the left eye shows an irregularly widened ciliary body band over 200° compared with the right.
What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Discharge, as no follow-up is needed now that the hyphaema has cleared
Laser peripheral iridotomy now to prevent angle closure later on
Long-term regular IOP and optic disc checks for late-onset glaucoma
Prophylactic trabeculectomy within six months to protect the nerve
Annual dilated retinal review only, to detect late commotio retinae
mcq.e: A widened, irregular **ciliary body band** on gonioscopy is **angle recession** — a tear between the longitudinal and circular ciliary muscle fibres and a marker of trabecular meshwork damage. Up to about 10% of eyes with extensive (over 180°) recession develop **glaucoma months to many years later**, so these patients need lifelong periodic IOP and disc review; the fellow eye also carries a higher POAG risk. Iridotomy treats pupil block, not this open-angle mechanism.
w: Wrong - the glaucoma risk persists for years; discharging him misses a silent, treatable disease.
Wrong - the angle is open and recessed; iridotomy treats pupil-block angle closure, which is not the mechanism.
Correct - extensive angle recession carries a lifelong risk of secondary open-angle glaucoma; monitor IOP and disc.
Wrong - surgery is not offered prophylactically with normal IOP and a healthy disc.
Wrong - commotio retinae is an acute finding that resolves; the late threat here is glaucoma.

mcq.stem:
A 17-year-old sepak takraw player is struck in the right eye by the ball. A week later he complains of blurred central vision. VA right 6/36, no RAPD. Fundus: a curved yellow-white streak lying concentric to the optic disc, passing between the disc and the fovea, with a little overlying subretinal blood. The retina is otherwise flat and no retinal whitening remains.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Choroidal rupture
Commotio retinae (Berlin oedema)
Retinal dialysis
Full-thickness traumatic macular hole
Purtscher retinopathy
mcq.e: Blunt compression of the globe tears the inelastic **Bruch membrane**-RPE-choriocapillaris complex, producing a **crescentic yellow-white streak concentric to the disc**, often temporal and through the macula. Acute subretinal blood may hide it at first. Vision is poor when the fovea is involved, and the main late risk is **choroidal neovascularisation** at the rupture site — so warn about new distortion (Amsler grid) and review.
w: Correct - a curved streak concentric with the disc after blunt trauma = choroidal rupture; watch for later CNV.
Wrong - commotio retinae is grey-white retinal whitening that fades within days to weeks, not a curved streak.
Wrong - a dialysis is a peripheral retinal break at the ora serrata, usually inferotemporal, that can cause RD.
Wrong - a macular hole is a round foveal defect, not a curved streak running around the disc.
Wrong - Purtscher retinopathy follows chest or head compression and gives bilateral cotton-wool patches.

mcq.stem:
A 40-year-old man is hit in the left eye by a champagne cork at a wedding dinner. VA left hand movements. There is no wound, the Seidel test is negative and the AC has a small hyphaema; IOP 16 mmHg. There is no red reflex and the fundus cannot be seen because of vitreous haemorrhage. He has no diabetes.
Which investigation is most important today?
o: Fundus fluorescein angiography
Optical coherence tomography of the macula
Gentle B-scan ultrasound of the eye
MRI orbits with gadolinium
Full-field electroretinogram
mcq.e: When blunt trauma causes a vitreous haemorrhage with no fundal view, **B-scan ultrasound** is mandatory to look for **retinal detachment, retinal tear or dialysis**, occult posterior rupture and a dislocated lens — findings that turn management into urgent surgery. It is done gently through closed lids once an open globe has been excluded. FFA and OCT need clear media, so they cannot help here.
w: Wrong - FFA needs a clear view of the fundus, which the vitreous haemorrhage blocks.
Wrong - OCT also needs clear media and only images the macula.
Correct - B-scan shows whether the retina is attached behind the haemorrhage and detects posterior rupture.
Wrong - MRI images the orbit but is not the first test for retinal detachment, and is risky if a metallic FB is possible.
Wrong - ERG measures retinal function but does not identify a detachment that needs urgent surgery.

mcq.stem:
A 62-year-old lorry driver is struck on the right eye by a bungee cord while loading his lorry. A week later he notices double vision when covering the left eye and fluctuating blur. VA right 6/24, improving with pinhole. The AC depth is uneven, the iris trembles with eye movement, and after dilatation a curved edge with stretched fibres is seen across the temporal pupil. IOP 17 mmHg.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Iridodialysis with a second pupil-like opening
Traumatic mydriasis from sphincter tears
Cyclodialysis cleft with hypotony
Angle recession with early glaucoma
Lens subluxation from zonular rupture
mcq.e: Blunt trauma stretches and tears the **zonules**; the lens decentres (**subluxation**) or fully dislocates. Clues are **phacodonesis and iridodonesis**, uneven AC depth, vitreous in the AC and the **lens equator** visible in the dilated pupil, causing monocular diplopia and fluctuating blur. Complications include pupil-block glaucoma (anterior dislocation) and vitreous prolapse; suspect Marfan syndrome or homocystinuria if the trauma was trivial.
w: Wrong - iridodialysis is a peripheral iris root disinsertion; it does not make the iris tremble or show a lens edge.
Wrong - traumatic mydriasis gives a dilated, poorly reactive pupil but no uneven AC depth or visible lens edge.
Wrong - a cyclodialysis cleft causes low IOP and hypotony maculopathy; IOP here is normal.
Wrong - angle recession is a gonioscopic finding linked to late glaucoma; it causes no diplopia or lens edge.
Correct - trembling iris and lens, uneven AC and a visible lens equator = traumatic lens subluxation.

mcq.stem:
A 9-year-old boy has a total hyphaema in his left eye after being hit by a shuttlecock. Despite topical timolol, oral acetazolamide and head elevation, his IOP has stayed at 38-42 mmHg for 5 days and the blood has darkened to a black clot. VA left perception of light. He has no sickle cell disease. The family ask what the main threat to the cornea is if nothing more is done.
Which complication is most likely to develop?
o: Band keratopathy from calcium deposition
Corneal blood staining
Exposure keratopathy
Recurrent corneal erosion syndrome
Acanthamoeba keratitis
mcq.e: A **total ('eight-ball') hyphaema** with **raised IOP for several days** forces haemoglobin breakdown products into the corneal stroma — **corneal blood staining**, which clears slowly from the periphery over months to years and is amblyogenic in a child. Endothelial stress and high IOP are the drivers, so IOP over 25 mmHg for 5 days with a total hyphaema (or over 60 mmHg for 2 days, which threatens the optic nerve) is an indication for **AC washout**.
w: Wrong - band keratopathy follows chronic uveitis or hypercalcaemia over months, not a high-pressure hyphaema.
Correct - a total hyphaema with days of high IOP drives blood breakdown products into the stroma.
Wrong - exposure keratopathy needs poor lid closure (proptosis, CN7 palsy), which this boy does not have.
Wrong - recurrent erosion follows a sharp abrasion (fingernail, paper) because of weak epithelial adhesion.
Wrong - Acanthamoeba keratitis is linked to contact lenses and water exposure, not hyphaema.

mcq.stem:
A 16-year-old futsal player is hit in the left eye by the ball. The next day VA left is 6/12. The anterior segment is normal, IOP 15 mmHg, and dilated fundoscopy shows a patch of grey-white, opaque retina at the posterior pole involving the macula, with no retinal breaks, no haemorrhage and a flat retina. OCT shows hyper-reflectivity of the outer retinal layers without fluid.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Urgent laser retinopexy around the whitened area within 24 hours
Intravitreal anti-VEGF injection to reduce the retinal oedema
High-dose oral prednisolone for two weeks to protect photoreceptors
Observe and review, as the whitening usually fades within weeks
Pars plana vitrectomy with internal limiting membrane peel
mcq.e: Grey-white retinal opacification after a blunt blow, without breaks or fluid, is **commotio retinae (Berlin oedema)** — disruption of photoreceptor outer segments rather than true extracellular oedema. It needs **no treatment** and usually fades within days to weeks; vision often recovers, although macular involvement can leave pigmentary change and permanently reduced acuity. Review with dilated peripheral examination is still needed to exclude retinal tears or dialysis.
w: Wrong - retinopexy treats retinal breaks; commotio is not a break and laser would scar the macula.
Wrong - there is no leakage or neovascularisation for anti-VEGF to act on.
Wrong - steroids have no proven benefit in commotio retinae and carry systemic risks.
Correct - commotio retinae is self-limiting; observe and review, warning that macular cases may not fully recover.
Wrong - vitrectomy is for RD, macular hole or non-clearing haemorrhage, not for photoreceptor concussion.

mcq.stem:
A 29-year-old woman with SLE has taken oral prednisolone for 3 years. She attends the eye clinic because oncoming headlights dazzle her when driving at night and reading has become difficult, especially in bright sunlight. Distance VA 6/12 both eyes, near N10. Pupils are normal. On retroillumination each lens shows a central, granular, plaque-like opacity in the axial posterior part of the lens; the nucleus is clear. HbA1c is 5.2%.
What type of cataract is this?
o: Nuclear sclerotic cataract
Cortical cataract with spoke opacities
Diabetic snowflake cataract
Myotonic 'Christmas tree' cataract
Posterior subcapsular cataract
mcq.e: **Posterior subcapsular cataract** is classically caused by **corticosteroids** (any route) and is also seen with diabetes, uveitis and radiation. Because the opacity sits centrally near the nodal point, symptoms are out of proportion to the Snellen acuity: **glare** from headlights and **near vision worse in bright light**, when the pupil constricts and light must pass through the plaque. Nuclear cataract instead gives slow distance blur with a myopic shift.
w: Wrong - nuclear sclerosis is central yellow-brown hardening in the elderly with a myopic shift, and the nucleus here is clear.
Wrong - cortical spokes start peripherally and cause glare, but they are not the classic steroid cataract.
Wrong - snowflake cataract occurs in poorly controlled young type 1 diabetics; her HbA1c is normal.
Wrong - polychromatic 'Christmas tree' crystals occur in myotonic dystrophy, not with steroid use.
Correct - steroid exposure, glare and worse near vision in bright light with an axial posterior plaque = PSC.

mcq.stem:
A 74-year-old retired teacher at a Klinik Kesihatan says she can now read the newspaper without her +2.50 D reading glasses, but her distance vision has become blurred over a year. VA right 6/18, pinhole 6/9. Refraction shows a shift from +1.00 D to -1.50 D in the right eye. HbA1c is 5.6%. The red reflex is dimmed centrally.
What is the mechanism of her improved near vision?
o: Elongation of the axial length of the globe with age
Steepening of the corneal curvature with age
Rising refractive index of the sclerosing nucleus
Spasm of accommodation from ciliary muscle hypertonia
Osmotic swelling of the lens cortex from hyperglycaemia
mcq.e: In **nuclear sclerosis** the lens nucleus hardens and its **refractive index increases**, making the eye more myopic (**index myopia**). A presbyopic hypermetrope therefore 'regains' near vision — **'second sight'** — while distance vision blurs. It signals progressing nuclear cataract, not improvement; the normal HbA1c excludes a hyperglycaemic refractive shift.
w: Wrong - axial elongation causes myopia in childhood and in high myopes, not new myopia at 74.
Wrong - age-related corneal change is mainly a shift in astigmatism axis, not a 2.5 D myopic change.
Correct - a sclerosing nucleus bends light more strongly (index myopia), giving 'second sight'.
Wrong - accommodative spasm occurs in young people with active accommodation; at 74 accommodation is lost.
Wrong - hyperglycaemia can cause a temporary myopic shift, but her HbA1c of 5.6% is normal.

mcq.stem:
A 58-year-old e-hailing driver in Kuala Lumpur complains that he is dazzled by headlights and street lamps when driving at night, and he has stopped taking night shifts, halving his income. VA is 6/9 in each eye with spectacles. Slit lamp shows bilateral peripheral cortical spoke opacities that encroach on the visual axis on dilatation. The fundi and IOP are normal and he is otherwise well.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Reassure; surgery is not indicated until the VA falls to 6/18 or worse
Offer cataract surgery, since symptoms are limiting his work and driving
Update his spectacles and defer surgery until the cataracts are mature
Start antioxidant N-acetylcarnosine eye drops to dissolve the opacities
Nd:YAG laser to the lens opacities to clear the visual axis
mcq.e: The indication for cataract surgery is **visual disability that affects daily life, work or driving**, not a particular Snellen number — glare from cortical or PSC opacities can be disabling with VA still 6/9. Modern phaco or MSICS is safe at any stage, so waiting for 'maturity' only makes surgery harder (hard nucleus, weaker zonules). No eye drop reverses cataract.
w: Wrong - there is no VA threshold; surgery is offered when the cataract limits lifestyle or occupation.
Correct - disabling glare affecting his livelihood and driving is the indication, even with VA 6/9.
Wrong - waiting for a mature cataract is outdated and makes surgery riskier; glasses do not remove glare.
Wrong - no topical drug has been shown to reverse or prevent lens opacity.
Wrong - Nd:YAG opens an opacified posterior capsule after surgery; it does not treat the lens itself.

mcq.stem:
A 71-year-old man is listed for right phacoemulsification. At the pre-operative assessment clinic his medication list includes metformin, amlodipine, aspirin and tamsulosin 0.4 mg for benign prostatic hyperplasia, which he stopped 2 months ago. VA right 6/36 with a dense nuclear cataract; the pupil dilates to 7 mm today.
Which intra-operative problem should the surgeon particularly prepare for?
o: Intraoperative floppy iris syndrome
Suprachoroidal haemorrhage
Toxic anterior segment syndrome
Descemet membrane detachment
Zonular dialysis with a dropped nucleus
mcq.e: **Tamsulosin** (an alpha-1A blocker) causes lasting relaxation of the iris dilator; even after stopping the drug, the iris may billow, prolapse through the wounds and constrict progressively during surgery — **intraoperative floppy iris syndrome (IFIS)**. Good pre-op dilatation does not exclude it. Always ask about **alpha-blockers** so the surgeon can plan iris hooks or rings or intracameral phenylephrine; aspirin is usually continued.
w: Correct - tamsulosin, even if stopped, predisposes to IFIS; prepare iris hooks, rings or intracameral phenylephrine.
Wrong - suprachoroidal haemorrhage is linked to age, hypertension, anticoagulation and large incisions, not tamsulosin.
Wrong - TASS is a sterile reaction to contaminated solutions or instruments, not a drug-history risk.
Wrong - Descemet detachment is a wound-construction complication unrelated to alpha-blockers.
Wrong - zonular weakness is linked to pseudoexfoliation and trauma; tamsulosin affects the iris dilator.

mcq.stem:
A 64-year-old woman is seen on day 1 after an uneventful left phacoemulsification with an in-the-bag IOL. Unaided VA left is 6/60, improving to 6/9 with a -5.00 D lens. The wound is Seidel negative, the cornea is clear, the AC is quiet and formed, the IOL is centred and IOP is 16 mmHg. The fundus is normal.
What is the most likely cause of her poor unaided vision?
o: Early pseudophakic cystoid macular oedema
Retained lens fragment in the anterior chamber
Early posterior capsule opacification
Error in biometry or IOL power calculation
Acute post-operative endophthalmitis
mcq.e: Vision that **corrects fully with a lens** after uncomplicated surgery is a **refractive surprise** — usually an error in **biometry** (axial length or keratometry measurement, data entry, IOL formula, or the wrong lens implanted). A 1 mm axial length error gives roughly 2.5-3 D of refractive error, so -5 D means the IOL is far too strong. Options are spectacles or contact lens, IOL exchange or a piggyback lens; prevention is careful pre-op biometry, checked against the fellow eye.
w: Wrong - CMO peaks around 6 weeks and reduces best-corrected VA; it is not corrected by a -5 D lens.
Wrong - a retained fragment causes corneal oedema, inflammation and raised IOP, all absent here.
Wrong - PCO develops months to years later and does not correct with spectacles.
Correct - a large myopic error fully correctable with a lens after uneventful surgery = biometry or IOL power error.
Wrong - endophthalmitis gives pain, AC cells or hypopyon and VA that does not correct with a lens.

mcq.stem:
A 67-year-old diabetic man had an uneventful right phacoemulsification 6 weeks ago. His VA was 6/6 at week 1 but is now 6/18 with central blur and mild distortion. The eye is white and painless, the AC shows trace cells, the IOL and posterior capsule are clear, and IOP is 14 mmHg. OCT shows central macular thickening with intraretinal cystic spaces arranged around the fovea; his pre-operative OCT was normal.
What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
o: Nd:YAG laser posterior capsulotomy
Topical NSAID and corticosteroid drops
Focal macular laser photocoagulation
Intravitreal vancomycin and ceftazidime
Pars plana vitrectomy with membrane peel
mcq.e: Reduced vision about **6 weeks after cataract surgery** with cystic foveal thickening on OCT is **pseudophakic cystoid macular oedema (Irvine-Gass)** — prostaglandin-mediated perifoveal capillary leakage; diabetes, uveitis, PCR and vitreous loss raise the risk. First-line is a **topical NSAID (e.g. ketorolac, nepafenac) plus topical steroid**; resistant cases get sub-Tenon or intravitreal steroid. Note: the notes spell it 'cystoid mascular oedema' — the term is cystoid macular oedema.
w: Wrong - the capsule is clear; YAG capsulotomy treats PCO, which would not show as foveal cysts on OCT.
Correct - topical NSAID plus steroid is first-line for Irvine-Gass CMO.
Wrong - focal laser is a diabetic macular oedema treatment and is not used for pseudophakic CMO.
Wrong - intravitreal antibiotics are for endophthalmitis; this eye is white and painless with trace cells only.
Wrong - vitrectomy is reserved for refractory CMO with vitreous traction or vitreous in the wound.

mcq.stem:
A 61-year-old woman had uneventful left phacoemulsification 2 years ago with excellent early vision. Over 6 months she has developed gradual blurring and glare. VA left 6/24, not improving with pinhole. The IOL is centred in the bag; behind it, retroillumination shows a wrinkled, hazy membrane with clusters of glistening clear globules. The AC is quiet, IOP 15 mmHg and the macula looks normal through the haze.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Repeat surgery with IOL exchange in theatre
Topical prednisolone acetate 1% for four weeks
Intravitreal anti-VEGF injection to the left eye
New spectacles after refraction
Nd:YAG laser posterior capsulotomy
mcq.e: **Posterior capsule opacification** is the commonest late complication of cataract surgery: residual lens epithelial cells migrate across the posterior capsule, forming **Elschnig pearls** (the glistening globules) or fibrosis. It is treated in clinic with **Nd:YAG laser capsulotomy**, which opens a clear central window; risks include an IOP spike, IOL pitting, CMO and a small risk of retinal detachment.
w: Wrong - the IOL is fine; the opacity is the capsule behind it, which YAG laser opens without surgery.
Wrong - the eye is not inflamed, and steroids do not clear an opacified capsule.
Wrong - there is no macular neovascularisation; the macula is normal.
Wrong - VA does not improve with pinhole, so spectacles will not help a capsular opacity.
Correct - Elschnig pearls on the posterior capsule after cataract surgery = PCO, treated with YAG capsulotomy.

mcq.stem:
An 82-year-old hypertensive man with high myopia is having left ECCE for a brunescent cataract under peribulbar block. After nucleus expression his blood pressure rises to 190/105 mmHg and he complains of sudden severe eye pain. The eye becomes rock hard, the red reflex is lost and a dark dome rises behind the pupil while iris and vitreous push forward through the wound.
What is the most likely complication?
o: Posterior capsule rupture with vitreous loss
Intraoperative floppy iris syndrome
Retrobulbar haemorrhage from the block
Expulsive suprachoroidal haemorrhage
Aqueous misdirection (malignant glaucoma)
mcq.e: **Suprachoroidal haemorrhage** — rupture of a posterior ciliary artery into the suprachoroidal space — is the most feared intra-operative complication. Risk factors are age, **hypertension**, high myopia, glaucoma, anticoagulation, tachycardia and **large-incision surgery (ECCE)** with sudden hypotony. Signs are pain, a hard eye, loss of red reflex, a dark choroidal mound and prolapse of iris, vitreous and even retina; the wound must be closed at once. Note: the notes list vitreous loss as post-operative — it is an intra-operative event, usually after PCR.
w: Wrong - PCR with vitreous loss deepens the AC and brings vitreous to the wound, but not pain, a hard eye and a dark dome.
Wrong - IFIS causes iris billowing and miosis with alpha-blockers, not a rock-hard painful eye.
Wrong - retrobulbar haemorrhage occurs soon after the block with proptosis and tight lids, before surgery starts.
Correct - pain, a rock-hard eye, lost red reflex and a dark choroidal dome in a hypertensive myope = suprachoroidal haemorrhage.
Wrong - aqueous misdirection gives a shallow AC with high IOP, usually after glaucoma surgery, without a dark mound or pain.

mcq.stem:
A 68-year-old woman from a rural district attends the eye clinic with a white pupil in her right eye, which she says has been blind for 3 years. VA right hand movements with accurate projection of light in all quadrants, left 6/9. The right lens is completely white and no fundal view is possible. IOP 16 mmHg; there is no RAPD.
In addition to biometry, which pre-operative investigation is most important?
o: B-scan ultrasonography of the right eye
Fundus fluorescein angiography
Optical coherence tomography of the macula
Humphrey 24-2 visual field test
Corneal topography of the right eye
mcq.e: When a dense cataract hides the fundus, **B-scan ultrasound** is needed before surgery to exclude **retinal detachment, intraocular tumour, vitreous haemorrhage or staphyloma**, which change the prognosis, consent and surgical plan. Accurate light projection and no RAPD are reassuring tests of retinal and optic nerve function but do not exclude a localised problem. OCT, FFA and perimetry all need clear media.
w: Correct - B-scan excludes RD, tumour or haemorrhage behind an opaque lens before surgery and consent.
Wrong - FFA needs a clear view of the fundus, which the white cataract blocks.
Wrong - OCT cannot penetrate a mature cataract; it helps with macular disease when the media are clearer.
Wrong - perimetry is unreliable with HM vision and gives no structural information.
Wrong - topography maps corneal shape (useful for astigmatism) but cannot look behind the lens.

mcq.stem:
A 69-year-old man with a coronary stent inserted 4 months ago takes aspirin and clopidogrel. He is listed for left phacoemulsification under topical anaesthesia for a cataract that has reduced his VA to 6/36. His cardiologist says stopping dual antiplatelet therapy now carries a high risk of stent thrombosis. His platelet count is normal.
What is the most appropriate peri-operative advice?
o: Stop both aspirin and clopidogrel 7 days before surgery
Stop clopidogrel 5 days before and continue aspirin only
Continue both drugs; topical-anaesthesia phaco is low bleeding risk
Switch both drugs to subcutaneous enoxaparin bridging for one week
Defer surgery until dual therapy ends and use low-vision aids meanwhile
mcq.e: Phacoemulsification through a small clear-corneal incision under **topical or intracameral anaesthesia** is a **very low bleeding-risk** procedure, so **antiplatelets (and warfarin with the INR in range) are continued**. Stopping clopidogrel within months of a coronary stent risks fatal stent thrombosis — far worse than a small subconjunctival haemorrhage. Needle blocks carry more bleeding risk, which is why topical or sub-Tenon anaesthesia is preferred.
w: Wrong - stopping both drugs within months of a stent risks stent thrombosis, for little benefit in phaco.
Wrong - even stopping clopidogrel alone is unnecessary for topical phaco and risks stent thrombosis.
Correct - phaco under topical anaesthesia is low risk for bleeding; continue both antiplatelets.
Wrong - heparin bridging is for anticoagulants in high thrombotic risk and does not replace antiplatelet protection.
Wrong - delaying sight-restoring surgery is unnecessary when it can be done safely on dual antiplatelet therapy.

mcq.stem:
A 61-year-old non-diabetic woman with high myopia attends the eye clinic with a sudden shower of floaters and flashing lights in her right eye two days ago, followed by hazy vision. VA is 6/24 right, 6/6 left. There is no RAPD and IOP is 15 mmHg. Pigmented cells are seen in the anterior vitreous on slit lamp, and the red reflex is dull. Dense haemorrhage obscures the fundus view except for a glimpse of the superior disc margin.
Which investigation should be done next?
o: Fundus fluorescein angiography to look for leaking vessels
Optical coherence tomography of the macula
B-scan ultrasonography of the posterior segment
CT scan of the orbits with fine cuts
Automated Humphrey visual field testing
mcq.e: When vitreous haemorrhage hides the fundus, **B-scan ultrasound** is mandatory to look for a **retinal tear or detachment** (and a PVD) behind the blood; it decides urgency. Pigment ('tobacco dust', Shafer sign) with acute floaters and flashes strongly suggests a retinal break. Note: the notes say VH is 'detected with slit lamp' — diagnosis is by red reflex and fundoscopy, and ultrasound when the fundus cannot be seen.
w: Wrong - FFA needs a clear view of the fundus, which the blood prevents; it maps leakage and ischaemia, not detachment.
Wrong - OCT is optical and cannot image through a dense haemorrhage; it is for macular disease once the media clear.
Correct - B-scan sees through blood and shows whether the retina is attached, torn or detached, which sets the urgency of surgery.
Wrong - CT is for suspected intraocular foreign body or orbital pathology, not for routine assessment of retinal attachment.
Wrong - a field test adds nothing here; the field loss is from the blood and the priority is to exclude a detachment.

mcq.stem:
A 54-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 15 years (HbA1c 10.8%, never screened) presents to the eye clinic after waking with a 'red cloud' and floaters in his right eye. There was no pain or trauma. VA is HM right, 6/12 left. The right fundus cannot be seen. The left fundus shows blot haemorrhages in four quadrants, venous beading and a frond of fine vessels on the optic disc.
What is the most likely source of the bleeding in the right eye?
o: Rupture of fragile new vessels on the disc or retina
Tearing of a retinal vessel by a posterior vitreous detachment
Breakthrough bleeding from a choroidal neovascular membrane
Leakage from a ruptured retinal arteriolar macroaneurysm
Bleeding from dilated veins after a central vein occlusion
mcq.e: **Proliferative diabetic retinopathy** is the commonest cause of VH in adults: ischaemic retina releases VEGF, and **NVD/NVE** grow along the posterior hyaloid and bleed when the vitreous pulls on them. The fellow eye with NVD and severe NPDR features tells you the diagnosis even when the affected fundus is hidden.
w: Correct - abnormal new vessels (NVD/NVE) from diabetic ischaemia bleed into the vitreous; the fellow eye shows the same process.
Wrong - PVD with a torn vessel is the leading cause in non-diabetics; here the fellow eye points to proliferative DR.
Wrong - CNV breakthrough bleeding is seen in wet AMD, usually an older patient with prior distortion and subretinal blood.
Wrong - macroaneurysms occur in elderly hypertensive women and cause multilevel haemorrhage; nothing here suggests it.
Wrong - an ischaemic CRVO can cause VH from new vessels, but the bilateral diabetic picture makes PDR far more likely.

mcq.stem:
A 58-year-old non-diabetic man presented a week ago with acute floaters in his left eye and a mild vitreous haemorrhage; B-scan then showed an attached retina. Today the blood has settled inferiorly. VA is 6/9. Indirect ophthalmoscopy shows a small horseshoe-shaped flap at the superotemporal periphery with a bridging vessel, and the retina around it is flat.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Observation with head-up posture and review in 3 months
Panretinal photocoagulation of the ischaemic periphery
Intravitreal anti-VEGF injection to stop further bleeding
Vitrectomy with silicone oil tamponade within 48 hours
Laser retinopexy or cryotherapy around the flap promptly
mcq.e: A symptomatic **retinal break** with attached retina is sealed by **laser retinopexy (or cryotherapy)** to create a chorioretinal scar and prevent detachment. Observation alone risks progression to RD, and PRP/anti-VEGF treat neovascularisation, not tears. Vitrectomy is reserved for detachment or non-clearing haemorrhage.
w: Wrong - head-up posture helps the blood settle, but leaving an untreated horseshoe tear risks a rhegmatogenous detachment.
Wrong - PRP treats ischaemic neovascularisation (diabetes, CRVO); this patient has a mechanical tear, not ischaemia.
Wrong - anti-VEGF acts on new vessels; the bleeding here came from a vessel torn by vitreous traction.
Wrong - vitrectomy is too aggressive for an attached retina with a small tear that can be sealed with laser.
Correct - sealing the break with laser or cryo creates an adhesive scar and prevents retinal detachment.

mcq.stem:
A 47-year-old non-diabetic lorry driver presents to the eye clinic with sudden loss of vision in the right eye for four days after seeing floaters and flashes. VA is CF right, 6/6 left. There is a mild RAPD on the right and the fundus view is obscured by blood. B-scan shows a thick, highly reflective membrane tethered to the optic disc, elevated and folded in the superior half, with only slight after-movement.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Observation for 3 months for spontaneous clearing
Urgent vitreoretinal referral for vitrectomy and repair
Panretinal photocoagulation once the view allows
Bed rest with head elevation and review in 2 weeks
Nd:YAG laser to drain the blood into the vitreous gel
mcq.e: A thick, highly reflective membrane tethered to the disc with folds and little after-movement on B-scan is a **retinal detachment** behind the haemorrhage; the RAPD supports a large detachment. VH with RD needs **urgent vitrectomy and retinal repair** — waiting for the blood to clear allows the macula to detach further and PVR to develop.
w: Wrong - observation is only for VH with an attached retina; delay with a detachment worsens visual prognosis.
Correct - VH with retinal detachment on ultrasound is a surgical emergency: vitrectomy, repair and tamponade.
Wrong - PRP is for neovascularisation and cannot be applied through dense blood or repair a detachment.
Wrong - head elevation is for an attached retina; two weeks of waiting with a detachment risks macula-off loss.
Wrong - YAG hyaloidotomy is used for a premacular subhyaloid bleed, not for a retinal detachment.

mcq.stem:
A 27-year-old man attends the eye casualty after noticing a dark patch in the centre of his left vision while lifting heavy weights at the gym this morning. He is healthy and not diabetic. VA is 6/60 left, 6/6 right. The left fundus shows a dark-red, dome-like collection of blood over the macula, with a flat horizontal upper border and a rounded lower edge; retinal vessels are hidden by it. The rest of the retina is normal.
What is this haemorrhage?
o: Intragel vitreous haemorrhage
Flame haemorrhage of the nerve fibre layer
Dot-blot intraretinal haemorrhage
Subhyaloid (preretinal) haemorrhage
Sub-RPE haemorrhage from a neovascular net
mcq.e: Blood trapped between the **posterior hyaloid and the retina** forms a **boat-shaped** collection with a horizontal fluid level (cells settle under gravity) and hides the retinal vessels — a **subhyaloid (preretinal)** haemorrhage, here from a Valsalva rise in venous pressure. It reduces acuity only when it covers the fovea; most clear spontaneously, and a large premacular bleed may be drained with Nd:YAG hyaloidotomy.
w: Wrong - intragel blood is diffuse within the gel, gives floaters and a hazy view, and has no sharp fluid level.
Wrong - flame haemorrhages are small and feathery in the nerve fibre layer, not a large dome with a fluid level.
Wrong - dot-blot haemorrhages are small and round in the deeper retina and do not obscure the vessels.
Correct - a preretinal bleed under the hyaloid forms a boat shape with a fluid level and hides the retinal vessels.
Wrong - sub-RPE blood is dark grey-green under the retina, seen in older patients with AMD, and has no fluid level.

mcq.stem:
A 49-year-old woman is on the neurosurgical ward five days after a sudden 'worst ever' headache and collapse; CT showed subarachnoid blood and an anterior communicating artery aneurysm was coiled. Now alert, she reports she cannot see clearly with either eye. VA is HM right and 6/36 left. Pupils react briskly, with no RAPD. Both red reflexes are dull and the fundi are hazy with blood in the vitreous.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Purtscher retinopathy
Valsalva retinopathy
Bilateral central retinal vein occlusion
Terson syndrome
Grade 4 hypertensive retinopathy
mcq.e: **Terson syndrome** is intraocular (vitreous, subhyaloid or intraretinal) haemorrhage due to the sudden rise in intracranial pressure from **subarachnoid haemorrhage**, thought to rupture peripapillary and retinal vessels. It is often bilateral and marks a more severe SAH; vitrectomy is offered if the blood does not clear, especially in children (amblyopia risk). Look for it in any SAH patient who complains of poor vision.
w: Wrong - Purtscher retinopathy follows crush injury or pancreatitis and causes white retinal patches, not vitreous blood.
Wrong - Valsalva retinopathy is a premacular bleed after straining; the link here is to the subarachnoid haemorrhage.
Wrong - bilateral simultaneous CRVO is rare; it would show dilated veins and four-quadrant haemorrhages with no SAH link.
Correct - vitreous haemorrhage after a sudden intracranial pressure rise from SAH is Terson syndrome.
Wrong - hypertensive retinopathy causes intraretinal haemorrhages, exudates and disc swelling, not vitreous blood.

mcq.stem:
A 4-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department with irritability, vomiting and poor feeding for a day. His father says the baby rolled off a sofa yesterday. There are no external injuries. The ophthalmology registrar finds bilateral vitreous haemorrhage and extensive multilayered retinal haemorrhages reaching the ora serrata in both eyes.
What is the most important next step?
o: Reassure the family and review in the eye clinic in 2 weeks
Admit under paediatrics with child-protection referral and neuroimaging
Book urgent bilateral vitrectomy under general anaesthesia within 24 hours
Check full blood count and clotting, and discharge home if they are normal
Arrange B-scan ultrasound and discharge with advice to keep the head raised
mcq.e: Extensive bilateral **multilayered retinal haemorrhages to the periphery** with VH in an infant after a minor fall is strongly suggestive of **abusive head trauma (shaken baby)** — a short fall does not cause this picture. The priority is the child's safety and brain: admit, involve paediatrics and **child protection**, and arrange CT/MRI and a skeletal survey; clotting studies exclude mimics but do not replace safeguarding. Vitrectomy may be needed later for non-clearing VH because of amblyopia.
w: Wrong - discharging the infant risks further injury or death; the findings demand safeguarding today.
Correct - this pattern suggests non-accidental injury: admit, child protection, neuroimaging and skeletal survey.
Wrong - vitrectomy may be needed later for amblyopia risk, but it is not the first priority over safety and the brain.
Wrong - a coagulopathy screen is part of the work-up, but normal results would not make discharge safe.
Wrong - imaging the eye does not address the suspected head injury or the risk of further harm at home.

mcq.stem:
A 52-year-old man with type 2 diabetes had a dense vitreous haemorrhage in the left eye six weeks ago. B-scan showed an attached retina, and he was told to wait for it to clear. Today VA is HM left. IOP has risen to 34 mmHg, and fine new vessels are seen at the pupil margin and on the iris surface. B-scan shows the retina is still attached.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Continue observation for another 6 weeks before deciding
Start topical pilocarpine 2% four times daily for the IOP
Selective laser trabeculoplasty to lower the pressure
Nd:YAG laser iridotomy to open the drainage angle
Early vitrectomy with endolaser PRP, with anti-VEGF first
mcq.e: A **non-clearing VH with rubeosis** is an indication for **early vitrectomy** so that **PRP (endolaser)** can be delivered to the ischaemic retina that drives the new vessels; intravitreal anti-VEGF beforehand regresses the iris vessels and reduces bleeding during surgery. Waiting allows neovascular glaucoma to close the angle. Note: the notes write 'virectomy' — the procedure is vitrectomy.
w: Wrong - rubeosis with rising IOP shows untreated ischaemia; further delay risks angle closure by fibrovascular tissue.
Wrong - pilocarpine is avoided in neovascular glaucoma; it worsens inflammation and does nothing for ischaemia.
Wrong - SLT does not work when new vessels and fibrovascular tissue cover the meshwork.
Wrong - neovascular glaucoma is not due to pupillary block, so an iridotomy does not help.
Correct - vitrectomy clears the blood and allows full PRP, treating the ischaemic drive behind the iris new vessels.

mcq.stem:
A 71-year-old man with atrial fibrillation on warfarin (INR 2.6, target 2-3) and treated proliferative diabetic retinopathy presents to the eye clinic with a fresh vitreous haemorrhage in his right eye. VA is 6/60 right. B-scan shows an attached retina with no tear. He had a stroke three years ago before starting warfarin. He asks whether he should stop his 'blood thinner'.
What is the best advice?
o: Continue warfarin in the target range and inform his physician
Stop warfarin permanently, as it caused the haemorrhage
Switch from warfarin to aspirin until the blood has cleared
Withhold warfarin for 2 weeks until the vitreous has fully cleared
Give oral vitamin K now to reverse the anticoagulation
mcq.e: Anticoagulants and antiplatelets do **not** cause diabetic VH — the bleeding comes from **new vessels** — and they do not meaningfully worsen visual outcome. Stopping warfarin in a patient with AF and a previous stroke exposes him to a far greater risk of another stroke. Continue therapy with the INR in range, liaise with the physician, and treat the eye cause (PRP once the view allows, or vitrectomy).
w: Correct - an essential anticoagulant is continued (INR in range, physician informed); the eye cause is treated instead.
Wrong - the new vessels caused the bleed, and stopping warfarin permanently leaves AF with a previous stroke unprotected.
Wrong - aspirin gives poor stroke protection in AF and swapping does not change the course of the haemorrhage.
Wrong - a two-week gap exposes him to stroke and does not speed up clearance of the vitreous blood.
Wrong - reversing a therapeutic INR is for life-threatening bleeding, not a vitreous haemorrhage with an attached retina.

mcq.stem:
A 63-year-old woman with a vitreous haemorrhage in her left eye from a retinal vein occlusion is being observed; B-scan confirms an attached retina. At review in the eye clinic she says her vision is always at its worst when she wakes, then gradually improves through the morning. She was told to sleep propped up on two or three pillows and asks why.
What is the explanation?
o: Intraocular pressure rises overnight and compresses the optic nerve
The cornea swells overnight under closed lids and blurs the image
Blood settles over the macula lying flat, and sitting up moves it away
Low blood pressure at night reduces blood flow to the optic disc
Surges in blood pressure during sleep trigger fresh bleeding each night
mcq.e: Vitreous blood settles by **gravity**: lying flat it sinks backwards over the **macula**, so vision is worst on waking; when upright it sinks inferiorly, out of the visual axis. **Head-up sleeping** keeps the blood inferior, clears the central view and lets the superior retina be examined or lasered sooner.
w: Wrong - a small overnight IOP rise does not explain morning blur in VH, and raising the head is not a glaucoma treatment.
Wrong - morning corneal oedema occurs in Fuchs dystrophy; it is not why patients with VH are told to sleep propped up.
Correct - gravity makes the blood settle over the macula when supine and inferiorly when upright.
Wrong - nocturnal hypotension is linked to NAION on waking, not to the position of vitreous blood.
Wrong - fresh bleeding is not timed to sleep, and posture advice is about where the existing blood settles.

mcq.stem:
A 52-year-old Malay man is referred by his optometrist to the eye clinic with 'high eye pressure'. He has no symptoms. Goldmann IOP is 26 mmHg right and 27 mmHg left on three separate visits. Central corneal thickness is 560 µm in both eyes. Gonioscopy shows open angles with visible trabecular meshwork for 360°. Both optic discs have a cup-to-disc ratio of 0.3 with healthy, even neuroretinal rims, and Humphrey 24-2 fields are full and reliable.
What is the diagnosis?
o: Primary open-angle glaucoma
Ocular hypertension
Normal-tension glaucoma
Primary angle-closure suspect
Pigmentary glaucoma
mcq.e: Glaucoma is defined by **optic neuropathy (disc + field change)**, not by the pressure. IOP above 21 mmHg with **healthy discs, full fields and open angles** is **ocular hypertension**; only about 10% of people with IOP above 21 have glaucoma (Notes p28). Treatment is considered when the risk of conversion is high (higher IOP, thin cornea, older age, family history), and all need regular monitoring.
w: Wrong - POAG needs glaucomatous disc change and/or a matching field defect; both are normal here.
Correct - raised IOP with normal discs, fields and open angles is ocular hypertension.
Wrong - NTG is glaucomatous damage with IOP that stays at or below 21 mmHg, the opposite of this picture.
Wrong - gonioscopy shows open angles with visible meshwork, which excludes an angle-closure suspect.
Wrong - pigmentary glaucoma shows Krukenberg spindle, iris transillumination and heavy angle pigment, with disc damage.

mcq.stem:
A 66-year-old Chinese woman with migraine and cold, painful fingers in winter attends the eye clinic after a diabetic screening photograph showed an abnormal left disc. Goldmann IOP on a diurnal phasing curve is 14-18 mmHg in both eyes. Central corneal thickness is 548 µm and gonioscopy shows open angles. The left disc has an inferior rim notch with a splinter haemorrhage at the disc margin, and Humphrey fields show a matching superior arcuate defect. Her neurology examination is normal.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Ocular hypertension
Previous non-arteritic ischaemic optic neuropathy
Compressive optic neuropathy from a pituitary tumour
Normal-tension glaucoma
Chronic angle-closure glaucoma
mcq.e: Glaucomatous cupping with a **disc haemorrhage** and a matching **arcuate defect** but IOP that never exceeds 21 mmHg is **normal-tension glaucoma**; about half of glaucoma patients have IOP of 21 or less at diagnosis (Notes p28). Vascular dysregulation — **migraine, Raynaud phenomenon**, nocturnal hypotension — is a recognised risk factor. Atypical features (pallor more than cupping, young age, fields that respect the vertical midline) should prompt neuroimaging.
w: Wrong - ocular hypertension is raised IOP with a healthy disc; here the IOP is normal and the disc is damaged.
Wrong - NAION leaves a pale, flat disc with an altitudinal defect after sudden loss, not a deep notch with a splinter haemorrhage.
Wrong - compression causes pallor more than cupping and fields that respect the vertical midline (bitemporal).
Correct - glaucomatous disc and field loss with IOP that stays at or below 21 mmHg is normal-tension glaucoma.
Wrong - gonioscopy shows open angles, which rules out chronic angle-closure glaucoma.

mcq.stem:
A 59-year-old man with moderate persistent asthma (salbutamol and budesonide-formoterol inhalers) is diagnosed in the eye clinic with primary open-angle glaucoma. IOP is 29 mmHg right and 27 mmHg left, with inferior rim thinning and early superior arcuate field loss on the right. Resting pulse is 76/min and ECG is normal. The doctor is choosing his first eye drop.
Which drop must be avoided in this patient?
o: Timolol 0.5% twice daily
Latanoprost 0.005% once at night
Brinzolamide 1% twice daily
Brimonidine 0.2% twice daily
Bimatoprost 0.01% once at night
mcq.e: **Timolol** is a non-selective beta-blocker; drops drain through the nasolacrimal duct to the nasal mucosa, **bypass first-pass metabolism** and can cause life-threatening **bronchospasm**. It is contraindicated in asthma and COPD, and in bradycardia or heart block. A prostaglandin analogue is the usual first choice; punctal occlusion after drops reduces systemic absorption of any drug.
w: Correct - topical non-selective beta-blockade is absorbed systemically and can precipitate severe bronchospasm.
Wrong - latanoprost has no beta-blocking effect and is a safe first-line choice in asthma.
Wrong - topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitors do not affect the airways; they sting and taste bitter.
Wrong - brimonidine causes allergy and fatigue but not bronchospasm; it is avoided in infants, not asthmatics.
Wrong - bimatoprost is a prostaglandin analogue without respiratory effects.

mcq.stem:
A 57-year-old woman with no medical problems is newly diagnosed with primary open-angle glaucoma in the eye clinic. IOP is 27 mmHg right and 25 mmHg left, with a CDR of 0.7 right and early nasal step on the right field. Target IOP is set at about 18 mmHg. She wants the simplest treatment possible.
Which first-line drop and mechanism is most appropriate?
o: Timolol at bedtime — suppresses aqueous production most strongly during sleep
Pilocarpine four times daily — opens the trabecular meshwork by miosis
Brimonidine twice daily — reduces production with no allergy risk
Acetazolamide drops twice daily — blocks carbonic anhydrase in the ciliary body
Latanoprost once at night — increases uveoscleral outflow of aqueous
mcq.e: A **prostaglandin analogue** (latanoprost once at night) is first line: it lowers IOP by about 25-30%, needs one drop a day (good adherence) and works mainly by **increasing uveoscleral outflow**. Aqueous production falls naturally at night, so timolol has little effect then and is given in the morning. Note: the notes list epinephrine as an outflow drug — it is obsolete in glaucoma care.
w: Wrong - aqueous production is lowest during sleep, so timolol at night adds little; morning dosing is used.
Wrong - pilocarpine needs four doses a day and causes brow ache and dim vision; it is no longer first line for POAG.
Wrong - brimonidine is second line and has a high allergy rate (follicular conjunctivitis), so 'no allergy risk' is false.
Wrong - acetazolamide is oral or IV; the topical CAIs are dorzolamide and brinzolamide, used as second line.
Correct - a once-nightly prostaglandin analogue increases uveoscleral outflow and is first line for POAG.

mcq.stem:
A 64-year-old woman has been using one drop in her right eye only for a year for primary open-angle glaucoma; the left eye has ocular hypertension and is being observed. At the eye clinic she complains that her right eye 'looks different'. Her right iris is now browner than the left, her right lashes are longer and thicker, and her right upper lid looks hollow. IOP is 16 mmHg right.
Which drop is she most likely using?
o: Timolol 0.5%
Brimonidine 0.2%
Latanoprost 0.005%
Dorzolamide 2%
Pilocarpine 2%
mcq.e: **Prostaglandin analogues** cause **iris darkening** (more melanin in stromal melanocytes, permanent), **eyelash growth** (hypertrichosis), periocular skin darkening and **periorbitopathy** (orbital fat atrophy, deep upper lid sulcus). Using it in one eye makes the asymmetry obvious, so warn patients before starting. Other effects are conjunctival hyperaemia and, rarely, CMO or reactivation of HSV keratitis.
w: Wrong - timolol causes systemic effects (bradycardia, bronchospasm), not iris or lash changes.
Wrong - brimonidine typically causes allergic follicular conjunctivitis and fatigue, not iris darkening.
Correct - iris pigmentation, lash growth and upper lid hollowing are classic prostaglandin analogue effects.
Wrong - dorzolamide causes stinging and a bitter taste; it does not change iris colour or lashes.
Wrong - pilocarpine gives a small pupil, brow ache and dim vision, not iris darkening or lash growth.

mcq.stem:
A 44-year-old woman who had LASIK for myopia 10 years ago attends the eye clinic because her brother has glaucoma. Goldmann IOP is 17 mmHg right and 18 mmHg left. Central corneal thickness is 468 µm in both eyes. Gonioscopy shows open angles. The right disc has a CDR of 0.7 with inferior rim thinning, and there is a matching early superior arcuate defect on Humphrey fields.
How should her Goldmann readings be interpreted?
o: They underestimate the true IOP because the cornea is thin
They overestimate the true IOP because LASIK stiffens the cornea
They are accurate, because Goldmann is not affected by corneal thickness
They show that glaucoma is excluded, as both are within the normal range
They show that a thin cornea protects the disc against the IOP
mcq.e: Goldmann applanation assumes an average cornea (about 520-550 µm); a **thin cornea** (congenital or after LASIK/PRK) is easier to flatten, so the reading **underestimates** the true IOP. Thin CCT is also an independent risk factor for progression to POAG. Here the disc and field confirm glaucoma whatever the number; the normal-looking IOP is misleading.
w: Correct - a thin (post-LASIK) cornea flattens easily, so Goldmann reads lower than the true pressure.
Wrong - LASIK thins and weakens the cornea; thick corneas cause overestimation, not thin ones.
Wrong - Goldmann readings are significantly affected by corneal thickness and rigidity.
Wrong - glaucoma is diagnosed from the disc and field; a normal-range IOP does not exclude it.
Wrong - a thin cornea is a risk factor for glaucoma, not a protective factor.

mcq.stem:
A 69-year-old man with primary open-angle glaucoma is seen in the eye clinic. Right IOP is 23 mmHg on treatment. The right disc has a vertical CDR of 0.8 with marked thinning of the neuroretinal rim at the inferotemporal pole, a bayoneted vessel at the rim and a laminar dot pattern in the cup; the superior rim is relatively preserved.
Which visual field defect would you expect in the right eye?
o: Inferior arcuate scotoma from the blind spot to the nasal midline
Bitemporal hemianopia that respects the vertical meridian
Superior arcuate scotoma from the blind spot to the nasal midline
Central scotoma with a normal peripheral field
Enlarged blind spot with otherwise full peripheral field
mcq.e: Nerve fibres from the inferior retina enter the **inferior pole** of the disc, and the inferior retina sees the **superior field** — so inferotemporal rim loss gives a **superior arcuate (Bjerrum) defect** arching from the blind spot and ending at the **horizontal nasal midline** (nasal step). Rims normally follow ISNT (Inferior ≥ Superior ≥ Nasal ≥ Temporal); the poles are lost first in glaucoma.
w: Wrong - an inferior arcuate defect matches loss of the superior rim, which is preserved here.
Wrong - bitemporal defects that respect the vertical midline point to chiasmal compression, not glaucoma.
Correct - inferior rim loss gives a superior arcuate defect ending at the horizontal nasal midline.
Wrong - a central scotoma suggests macular or optic neuritis disease; glaucoma spares central vision until late.
Wrong - an isolated enlarged blind spot suggests papilloedema or peripapillary disease, not focal rim loss.

mcq.stem:
A 71-year-old man with advanced primary open-angle glaucoma in the left eye is reviewed in the eye clinic. He uses latanoprost, timolol and brinzolamide; the pharmacy refill record and his wife confirm he uses them correctly every day. Left IOP is 24 mmHg (target 14 mmHg), and three reliable Humphrey fields over 18 months show steady progression of a double arcuate defect towards fixation. The bleb area is unscarred and he has no other eye disease.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Add pilocarpine 2% four times daily as a fourth drop
Swap latanoprost for bimatoprost and review in 6 months
Start long-term oral acetazolamide 250 mg four times daily
Trabeculectomy with mitomycin C in the left eye
Cyclodiode laser to the ciliary body
mcq.e: Proven progression on **maximal tolerated medical therapy** with good adherence means it is time for **surgery**: **trabeculectomy with an antifibrotic (MMC)** creates a guarded fistula to a subconjunctival bleb and can reach a low target IOP. Adding drops gives little further fall, and long-term acetazolamide is poorly tolerated. Cyclodestruction is a **last resort** for eyes with poor visual potential or failed surgery (Notes p32).
w: Wrong - a fourth drop adds little IOP lowering, more side effects and worse adherence.
Wrong - swapping one prostaglandin analogue for another gives only a small extra fall, far short of the target.
Wrong - long-term acetazolamide causes paraesthesia, hypokalaemia, renal stones and fatigue; it is a bridge, not a plan.
Correct - progression despite maximal adherent therapy calls for trabeculectomy with MMC to reach a low target.
Wrong - cyclodestruction is a last resort for refractory or blind painful eyes, not the first surgical step.

mcq.stem:
A 48-year-old Indian accountant has just been diagnosed with primary open-angle glaucoma in the eye clinic. He asks what this means for his family: his brother is 52, his sister is 43, his son is 20, and his mother had 'eye pressure' before she died. He wants to know who should be checked and when.
What is the most appropriate advice?
o: POAG is not hereditary, so his relatives need no special checks
Relatives need an eye check only if they develop pain or haloes
Every relative should have genetic testing for the myocilin gene now
His brother and sister should start timolol drops as a precaution
First-degree relatives over 40 should have regular full eye checks
mcq.e: **Family history in a first-degree relative** is a major POAG risk factor (siblings at highest risk), and because POAG is **painless and symptomless** until late, relatives need screening — disc, IOP and fields — from **about 40 years**, earlier if a relative was diagnosed young. Note: the notes list a large lens, short axial length and an anterior iris shift under POAG risk factors — these are **angle-closure** risk factors; POAG risk factors are age, raised IOP, family history, African ancestry, myopia, thin cornea and vascular factors.
w: Wrong - first-degree relatives of POAG patients have a several-fold higher risk.
Wrong - POAG is painless and causes no haloes; waiting for symptoms means late, irreversible field loss.
Wrong - myocilin mutations explain only a small proportion of adult POAG; genetic testing is not routine.
Wrong - drops are not started without proven ocular hypertension or glaucoma; screening comes first.
Correct - first-degree relatives over 40 need regular disc, IOP and field checks because POAG is silent.

mcq.stem:
A 19-year-old man with vernal keratoconjunctivitis since childhood has been buying dexamethasone 0.1% eye drops from a pharmacy and using them four times daily for the last 8 months. He attends the eye clinic with blurred vision. IOP is 38 mmHg right and 36 mmHg left. The anterior chambers are deep and quiet, with open angles of normal pigmentation on gonioscopy. CDR is 0.7 in both eyes with superior and inferior rim thinning.
What is the mechanism of his raised IOP?
o: Pupillary block pushing the peripheral iris into the angle
Reduced aqueous outflow through the trabecular meshwork
Fibrovascular membrane growing over the drainage angle
Pigment granules from the iris clogging the meshwork
Inflammatory cells and trabeculitis blocking drainage
mcq.e: **Steroid-induced glaucoma** is a secondary open-angle glaucoma: corticosteroids cause extracellular matrix deposition and reduced phagocytosis in the **trabecular meshwork**, increasing outflow resistance. About a third of people are steroid responders, young people with atopy and myopia especially. Stop or switch the steroid (mast-cell stabiliser, ciclosporin), treat the IOP, and monitor anyone on steroid drops beyond a few weeks.
w: Wrong - pupillary block causes angle closure; this patient has deep chambers and open angles.
Correct - steroids increase trabecular outflow resistance, giving a secondary open-angle glaucoma.
Wrong - a fibrovascular membrane means neovascular glaucoma with rubeosis, which ischaemic eyes develop.
Wrong - pigment dispersion gives heavy angle pigmentation, Krukenberg spindle and iris transillumination.
Wrong - uveitic trabeculitis needs AC inflammation; the chambers here are quiet.

mcq.stem:
A 62-year-old Chinese woman comes to the emergency department at 11 pm, two hours after watching a film in a cinema. She has a severe left brow ache, has vomited three times and sees rainbow-coloured rings around the ward lights. She wears reading glasses for long-sightedness. Left VA is 6/36 and right 6/6. The left eye shows circumcorneal injection, a hazy cornea and a mid-dilated, vertically oval pupil that does not react to light. The left globe feels stony hard on gentle palpation. The ED medical officer suspects migraine.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Acute anterior uveitis
Acute migraine with visual aura
Microbial keratitis
Diffuse anterior scleritis
Acute primary angle closure
mcq.e: Dim light (mid-dilation), a small hyperopic eye, **haloes** from corneal epithelial oedema, vomiting, a **fixed mid-dilated vertically oval pupil** and a rock-hard eye are classic **acute angle closure** — a common misdiagnosis as migraine or an acute abdomen. Note: the notes list 'increased cup:disc ratio' as a sign — in the acute attack the disc is usually swollen or hyperaemic and hard to see through the hazy cornea; cupping is a later sign of damage.
w: Wrong - uveitis gives a SMALL pupil (spasm, synechiae) with photophobia and usually normal or low IOP.
Wrong - migraine does not cause a red eye, a hazy cornea, a fixed pupil or a hard globe.
Wrong - keratitis shows a white corneal infiltrate that stains, often in a contact lens wearer, with a reactive pupil.
Wrong - scleritis gives a deep boring pain with violaceous scleral injection but a clear cornea and normal pupil.
Correct - haloes, vomiting, a hazy cornea, a fixed mid-dilated pupil and a stony-hard eye mean acute angle closure.

mcq.stem:
A 71-year-old woman is on the surgical ward with adhesive small bowel obstruction being managed conservatively. This evening she received several drugs. Four hours later she develops a severe right headache with vomiting, which the surgical team attributes to her bowel. The ophthalmology registrar finds right VA 6/60, a red eye with a cloudy cornea, a fixed mid-dilated pupil and IOP 58 mmHg; the left anterior chamber is very shallow.
Which drug most likely precipitated this?
o: IV paracetamol 1 g
IV pantoprazole 40 mg
IV hyoscine butylbromide 20 mg
SC enoxaparin 40 mg once daily
IV ceftriaxone 1 g
mcq.e: **Anticholinergics** (hyoscine, ipratropium nebulisers, atropine, tricyclics, antihistamines) and **sympathomimetics** dilate the pupil and can precipitate pupillary-block angle closure in an eye with a shallow anterior chamber. On the wards the attack is often masked by the presenting illness — always look at the eye in a patient with headache and vomiting after new drugs. The very shallow fellow eye confirms the anatomical risk.
w: Wrong - paracetamol has no effect on the pupil or anterior chamber anatomy.
Wrong - proton pump inhibitors are not linked to pupil dilation or angle closure.
Correct - hyoscine is an antimuscarinic that dilates the pupil and can trigger acute angle closure.
Wrong - enoxaparin does not affect the pupil; it is linked to bleeding, not angle closure.
Wrong - ceftriaxone does not dilate the pupil or close the angle.

mcq.stem:
A 31-year-old woman with migraine and myopia (-3.00 D) started a new oral migraine-prevention tablet 10 days ago. She presents to the eye clinic with sudden blurring of distance vision in both eyes, haloes and aching. VA is 6/36 in both eyes, improving with extra minus lenses. IOP is 44 mmHg right and 46 mmHg left. Both anterior chambers are uniformly very shallow and both angles are closed. B-scan shows bilateral ciliochoroidal effusions.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Laser peripheral iridotomy to both eyes today
Stop the tablet; give aqueous suppressants and cycloplegic
Pilocarpine 2% to both eyes every 15 minutes
Clear lens extraction in both eyes within the next 48 hours
Continue the tablet and add oral acetazolamide QID
mcq.e: Bilateral angle closure with a **myopic shift** and ciliochoroidal effusion soon after starting a migraine preventer is **topiramate-induced secondary angle closure**: the effusion rotates the ciliary body and lens-iris diaphragm forward — **no pupillary block**. Treat by **stopping the drug** (with the neurologist), lowering IOP with aqueous suppressants, and using a **cycloplegic** (atropine) plus topical steroid to rotate the ciliary body back. Iridotomy does not help and pilocarpine worsens it by pulling the lens forward.
w: Wrong - there is no pupillary block, so an iridotomy does not open the angle in drug-induced effusion.
Correct - stopping the drug, aqueous suppressants and a cycloplegic reverse the ciliary body rotation.
Wrong - miotics contract the ciliary muscle and move the lens forward, making this type worse.
Wrong - lens surgery is not needed; the effusion resolves within days once the drug is stopped.
Wrong - continuing the causative drug keeps the effusion going; acetazolamide is also a sulfonamide like topiramate.

mcq.stem:
A 63-year-old woman attends a Klinik Kesihatan two hours by road from the nearest hospital eye clinic. Since last night she has had a severe right eye ache, headache, vomiting and blurred vision with haloes. Right VA is 6/60. The right eye is red with a hazy cornea and a mid-dilated, non-reactive pupil, and it feels stony hard through the closed lid. She has no asthma, heart disease, kidney stones or sulfonamide allergy. The clinic has no tonometer.
What is the most appropriate immediate management?
o: Lie her flat; acetazolamide 500 mg, timolol 0.5%, analgesia, antiemetic; refer urgently
Instil tropicamide 1% to examine the fundus fully, then refer to the eye clinic next week
Instil pilocarpine 4% every 5 minutes for an hour, then refer to the eye clinic tomorrow
Pad the eye, give oral analgesia and an antiemetic, and book a routine eye clinic visit
Start dexamethasone and chloramphenicol drops and review her at the clinic in 24 hours
mcq.e: At primary care, start **IOP-lowering treatment before transfer**: **acetazolamide 500 mg** (IV or oral), **timolol 0.5%**, analgesia and an **antiemetic**, lie the patient supine, and refer **urgently the same day** to ophthalmology (Notes p33: acetazolamide, pilocarpine and beta-blocker). Never dilate, and do not delay — every hour of very high IOP damages the optic nerve. Intensive 4% pilocarpine can worsen the block and cause systemic toxicity.
w: Correct - aqueous suppressants, analgesia, antiemetic, supine posture and same-day urgent referral.
Wrong - dilating an eye in angle closure worsens the attack; this is the classic error to avoid.
Wrong - intensive 4% pilocarpine can worsen the block and cause toxicity, and next-day referral is too late.
Wrong - this is an emergency; padding and a routine appointment leave the optic nerve at risk.
Wrong - antibiotic and steroid drops do not lower IOP, and waiting 24 hours risks permanent loss.

mcq.stem:
A 66-year-old woman in the emergency department has a right IOP of 66 mmHg with a hazy cornea and a fixed mid-dilated pupil. The ED medical officer has instilled pilocarpine 2% twice over 30 minutes before any other treatment. The pupil remains mid-dilated and unreactive and the IOP is unchanged. The medical officer asks the on-call ophthalmologist why the drop has not worked.
What is the best explanation?
o: Pilocarpine lowers IOP only by reducing aqueous production
Pilocarpine is broken down quickly by enzymes in an inflamed eye
Pilocarpine needs a full 24 hours of regular dosing before it acts
At this IOP the iris sphincter is ischaemic and cannot constrict
A sympathetic surge holds the pupil open against any miotic
mcq.e: At very high IOP (roughly above 50 mmHg) the **iris sphincter is ischaemic** and does not respond to miotics, so pilocarpine is given **after** aqueous suppressants (acetazolamide, timolol, apraclonidine) have started to lower the pressure. Once it works, miosis pulls the peripheral iris away from the trabecular meshwork. It increases trabecular outflow; it does not reduce production.
w: Wrong - pilocarpine increases trabecular outflow by miosis; it does not reduce aqueous production.
Wrong - inflammation does not inactivate pilocarpine; the problem is an ischaemic iris muscle.
Wrong - pilocarpine acts within about an hour in a responsive eye; no 24-hour delay exists.
Correct - the ischaemic sphincter cannot respond until aqueous suppressants bring the IOP down.
