Wrong - the mid-dilated pupil is from ischaemic sphincter paralysis, not sympathetic overactivity.

mcq.stem:
A 61-year-old Chinese woman was admitted three days ago with an acute attack in her right eye; IOP fell from 62 to 14 mmHg on medical treatment and her right cornea is now clear. Gonioscopy of the right eye shows a closed angle that partly opens with indentation. Her left eye has never had symptoms: VA 6/6, IOP 15 mmHg, very shallow peripheral chamber, and gonioscopy shows iris touching the meshwork for 270°.
What is the definitive management?
o: Laser peripheral iridotomy to the right eye only
Laser peripheral iridotomy to both eyes
Trabeculectomy right eye, observation of the left
Long-term pilocarpine 2% to both eyes
Selective laser trabeculoplasty to both eyes
mcq.e: The definitive treatment of pupillary-block angle closure is a **laser peripheral iridotomy**, which lets aqueous bypass the pupil and flattens the iris. The **fellow eye** shares the same anatomy and has about a 40-80% risk of an attack within 5-10 years, so it must have a **prophylactic iridotomy** too. Lens extraction is an alternative in selected eyes; trabeculectomy is for uncontrolled IOP after the angle has been dealt with.
w: Wrong - treating only the affected eye leaves the occludable fellow eye at high risk of its own attack.
Correct - iridotomy treats the attack eye and prevents an attack in the fellow eye with the same anatomy.
Wrong - the IOP is now controlled; filtering surgery is not first line and the left eye still needs protection.
Wrong - long-term miotics do not remove the pupillary block and cause brow ache and dim vision.
Wrong - SLT works on a visible meshwork in open angles; it does not relieve pupillary block.

mcq.stem:
A 56-year-old woman is seen in the eye clinic a month after an acute attack in her left eye. She has worn +4.50 D glasses for distance since her twenties. Biometry shows an axial length of 21.3 mm in both eyes, a thick crystalline lens and a central anterior chamber depth of 2.1 mm. She asks why her eye pressure suddenly shot up that night.
What was the mechanism of her attack?
o: Forward rotation of the ciliary body caused by a ciliochoroidal effusion
Contraction of a fibrovascular membrane across the drainage angle
Peripheral iris roll from anteriorly placed ciliary processes
Pigment from the back of the iris blocking the trabecular meshwork
Iris-lens contact trapping aqueous behind the iris, bowing it forward
mcq.e: In a **small hyperopic eye with a thick lens**, the iris lies against the lens and resists aqueous flow through the pupil (**relative pupillary block**). Pressure builds in the posterior chamber, the peripheral iris **bows forward (iris bombé)** and closes the angle, so IOP rises abruptly — worst when the pupil is mid-dilated (Notes p32). This is why an iridotomy, which bypasses the pupil, works.
w: Wrong - ciliochoroidal effusion causes drug-induced (e.g. topiramate) closure, usually bilateral with a myopic shift.
Wrong - a fibrovascular membrane is neovascular glaucoma after retinal ischaemia, not an attack in a hyperope.
Wrong - plateau iris is a less common mechanism, typically in younger patients, and persists after iridotomy.
Wrong - pigment dispersion causes an open-angle glaucoma in young myopes, not acute closure in a small eye.
Correct - relative pupillary block in a small, crowded hyperopic eye bows the iris forward and closes the angle.

mcq.stem:
A 57-year-old Chinese shopkeeper attends the eye clinic with several months of evening episodes of mild brow ache and rainbow-coloured rings around lights, each settling after she sleeps. Today she is symptom-free: VA 6/6 both eyes, IOP 19 mmHg right and 18 mmHg left, clear corneas, and normal discs. A pen torch shone from the temporal side casts a shadow over the nasal iris in both eyes, and van Herick shows a peripheral chamber less than a quarter of corneal thickness.
Which investigation will confirm the diagnosis?
o: Gonioscopy with indentation in both eyes
Humphrey visual field testing
Optical coherence tomography of the macula
Diurnal IOP phasing over 24 hours
MRI of the brain and orbits with contrast
mcq.e: Recurrent self-limiting haloes and brow ache in the evening (mid-dilation in dim light) suggest **intermittent angle closure**, and the shadow sign and van Herick show a shallow chamber — but only **gonioscopy** directly shows whether the angle is **occludable** (iridotrabecular contact) and, with **indentation**, whether it is appositional or synechial. A normal IOP between episodes does not exclude it; the treatment is laser iridotomy to both eyes.
w: Correct - gonioscopy shows the angle structures directly and, with indentation, separates apposition from synechiae.
Wrong - fields show damage but cannot show whether the angle is narrow or closed.
Wrong - macular OCT images the retina, not the drainage angle; anterior segment OCT would be needed.
Wrong - IOP phasing may be normal between episodes and does not show the angle anatomy.
Wrong - neuroimaging is for headache with neurological signs; the haloes here are from corneal oedema.

mcq.stem:
A 68-year-old woman stayed at home for three days with a painful red right eye, thinking it was a migraine, before attending the hospital. She was treated medically and had a laser iridotomy. Six weeks later in the eye clinic, right VA is 6/18 and IOP 17 mmHg. There is a patent superior iridotomy, patchy sectoral iris atrophy, and a pupil that remains mid-dilated and sluggish. Small grey-white flecks lie just under the anterior lens capsule in the pupillary area.
What are these flecks?
o: Pseudoexfoliation material on the anterior lens capsule
Posterior subcapsular cataract caused by steroid drops
Glaukomflecken from focal necrosis of lens epithelium
Keratic precipitates from chronic anterior uveitis
Pigment dusting of the lens from pigment dispersion
mcq.e: **Glaukomflecken** are small grey-white **anterior subcapsular** opacities from focal ischaemic necrosis of the lens epithelium during a severe pressure spike; with **sectoral iris atrophy** and a **permanently dilated pupil** (sphincter ischaemia) they are the 'footprints' of a previous acute attack (Vogt triad). They warn that delayed treatment has already caused ischaemic damage — check the disc and field for glaucomatous optic neuropathy.
w: Wrong - pseudoexfoliation forms a white target pattern on the capsule and is not caused by an attack.
Wrong - steroid cataract lies at the back of the lens (posterior subcapsular), not just under the anterior capsule.
Correct - these ischaemic anterior subcapsular flecks with iris atrophy mark a past acute attack.
Wrong - keratic precipitates sit on the corneal endothelium, not under the lens capsule.
Wrong - pigment dispersion gives brown dusting in young myopes with open angles, not grey-white flecks.

mcq.stem:
A 69-year-old woman (not diabetic, normal renal function, no heart failure) is in the emergency department with an acute attack in her left eye. One hour after IV acetazolamide 500 mg, timolol 0.5%, apraclonidine 1% and prednisolone acetate 1%, her left IOP is still 56 mmHg. The cornea is too hazy for laser, and she is still vomiting.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Repeat pilocarpine 4% every 5 minutes for the next hour
Take her for emergency trabeculectomy tonight
Instil atropine 1% to relieve the ciliary spasm
Give IV mannitol 20% 1-2 g/kg over about 45 minutes
Wait 24 hours for acetazolamide to take full effect
mcq.e: When IOP stays high despite aqueous suppressants, a **hyperosmotic agent** is added: **IV mannitol** draws water out of the vitreous and lowers IOP within an hour (oral glycerol is an alternative but unsuitable when vomiting or diabetic). Check for heart failure and renal impairment first. Once IOP falls and the cornea clears, pilocarpine starts working and **laser iridotomy** can be done; surgery is a last resort in an inflamed eye.
w: Wrong - intensive 4% pilocarpine does not work on an ischaemic iris and can cause systemic cholinergic toxicity.
Wrong - filtering surgery in an acutely inflamed, high-pressure eye has a high complication rate and is not first.
Wrong - cycloplegics dilate the pupil and can worsen pupillary-block angle closure.
Correct - IV mannitol lowers IOP by dehydrating the vitreous when aqueous suppressants have failed.
Wrong - IOP above 50 mmHg for another day causes ischaemic optic nerve damage; treatment must be escalated.

mcq.stem:
A 54-year-old lorry driver attends a Klinik Kesihatan for a pre-licence medical check; he has never seen a doctor before. BP is 176/104 mmHg on three readings and urine dipstick shows 1+ protein. VA is 6/9 in both eyes. Dilated fundoscopy shows generalised and focal arteriolar narrowing, arteriovenous nicking, scattered flame-shaped haemorrhages, several cotton-wool spots and hard exudates in both eyes. Both optic discs have sharp margins with no swelling.
Using the Keith-Wagener-Barker classification, which grade best describes this fundus?
o: Keith-Wagener-Barker group 1
Keith-Wagener-Barker group 2
Keith-Wagener-Barker group 3
Keith-Wagener-Barker group 4
Scheie hypertensive stage 1
mcq.e: Keith-Wagener-Barker grading builds up step by step: group 1 is generalised arteriolar narrowing, group 2 adds focal narrowing and AV nicking, group 3 adds **exudative signs** (flame haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, hard exudates), and group 4 adds **optic disc swelling**. The trap is to call any haemorrhagic fundus 'malignant'. In KWB the **disc** is what separates group 3 from group 4, and his discs are sharp. He still needs prompt physician referral because of the proteinuria and the level of BP.
w: Wrong - Group 1 is mild generalised arteriolar constriction only, with no AV nicking, haemorrhages or exudates.
Wrong - Group 2 adds focal narrowing and AV nicking, but haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and exudates move the grade up.
Correct - Flame haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and hard exudates on top of group 2 changes, with normal discs, make this group 3.
Wrong - Group 4 needs optic disc swelling (hypertensive optic neuropathy). Both discs here are sharp.
Wrong - Scheie stage 1 is diffuse arteriolar narrowing only. It badly under-grades a fundus with exudative changes.

mcq.stem:
A 36-year-old man comes to the emergency department with 3 days of severe headache and blurred vision in both eyes. BP is 236/142 mmHg in both arms. Serum creatinine is 210 µmol/L, with no previous result. VA is 6/24 right and 6/18 left; pupils react normally. Fundoscopy shows bilateral swollen hyperaemic optic discs, flame-shaped haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and a partial star of exudates at each macula. He is alert with no focal neurological deficit.
What is the most appropriate immediate management?
o: Sublingual nifedipine in the department, aiming for a BP of 140/90 mmHg within the hour
Admit for titrated IV antihypertensives, lowering BP by about 25% over the first hours
MRI brain then lumbar puncture to measure opening pressure, before treating the BP
Oral amlodipine today and a referral to the medical outpatient clinic within 4 weeks
Intravitreal anti-VEGF injections to both eyes to clear the macular exudates quickly
mcq.e: Bilateral disc swelling with retinopathy and very high BP is **grade 4 (malignant) hypertensive retinopathy**. It is a hypertensive emergency with target-organ damage (here the kidney), so he needs **admission and controlled IV BP lowering**, roughly 25% over the first hours. An abrupt fall can cause ischaemia of the optic nerve head and brain, which have lost autoregulation, so the patient can go blind from the treatment itself. Note: the notes (p35) say 'severe intracranial hypertension'. The correct cause is severe **systemic** (malignant) hypertension.
w: Wrong - Dropping the BP to normal within an hour risks optic nerve and cerebral infarction. Short-acting sublingual nifedipine is no longer used.
Correct - Admit for gradual, monitored IV BP reduction (about 25% in the first hours) and screen for target-organ damage.
Wrong - The disc swelling here comes from malignant systemic hypertension. Delaying BP control for an LP is dangerous and does not address the cause.
Wrong - Grade 4 retinopathy with rising creatinine is an emergency. Outpatient oral therapy is far too slow.
Wrong - The macular star and haemorrhages resolve once BP is controlled. Anti-VEGF does not treat the cause and is not indicated.

mcq.stem:
A 63-year-old woman with 15 years of poorly controlled hypertension attends the eye clinic for review. VA is 6/9 in each eye. At several arteriovenous crossings in both eyes, the vein is pushed sideways where it passes under the thickened arteriole, changing direction to cross it almost at right angles. The vein calibre on either side of these crossings looks normal, and there is no venous dilatation beyond them.
Which crossing sign is being described?
o: Salus's sign
Gunn's sign
Bonnet's sign
Copper-wiring of the arteriole
Silver-wiring of the arteriole
mcq.e: At an AV crossing the arteriole and venule share an **adventitial sheath**, so a sclerosed arteriole distorts the vein in three named ways. **Salus** = deflection of the vein. **Gunn** = the vein tapers (seems to disappear) on either side of the crossing. **Bonnet** = banking (dilatation) of the vein distal to the crossing. Copper and silver wiring describe the **arteriolar light reflex**, not the vein at a crossing.
w: Correct - Salus's sign is deflection of the vein as it crosses the arteriole.
Wrong - Gunn's sign is tapering or apparent interruption of the vein on both sides of the crossing. Here the calibre is normal.
Wrong - Bonnet's sign is banking (distension) of the vein distal to the crossing, which is absent here.
Wrong - Copper-wiring is a broadened, coppery arteriolar light reflex in sclerosis. It is not a venous crossing sign.
Wrong - Silver-wiring is a fully opaque, white arteriolar reflex in advanced sclerosis. It does not describe venous deflection.

mcq.stem:
A 31-year-old woman with lupus nephritis is admitted with BP 220/130 mmHg and blurred vision. VA is 6/18 in both eyes. Fundoscopy shows bilateral disc swelling. In the mid-periphery there are several small pigmented patches, each with a pale yellow halo, and linear hyperpigmented streaks running along the course of the choroidal vessels. Shallow serous detachments involve both maculae.
What is the underlying mechanism of the patches and streaks?
o: Rupture of retinal capillary microaneurysms into the outer plexiform layer
Ischaemic infarction of the nerve fibre layer with axoplasmic stasis
Occlusion of the short posterior ciliary arteries at the optic nerve head
Fibrinoid necrosis of choroidal arterioles with focal choriocapillaris infarction
Breakdown of the inner blood-retinal barrier at the retinal capillary endothelium
mcq.e: This is **hypertensive choroidopathy**, seen in malignant hypertension and in young patients (pre-eclampsia, renal disease). Choroidal vessels have sympathetic innervation and no autoregulation, so very high BP causes **fibrinoid necrosis of choroidal arterioles**. The result is focal infarcts of the choriocapillaris and overlying RPE (**Elschnig spots**: pale yellow when acute, healing to a pigmented centre with a yellow halo), linear pigmentation along necrosed choroidal vessels (**Siegrist streaks**), and serous retinal detachment. Note: the notes (p35) describe Elschnig spots only as yellow. Healed spots are pigmented with a yellow halo.
w: Wrong - Microaneurysm leakage into the outer plexiform layer produces hard exudates and dot haemorrhages, not choroidal patches.
Wrong - Nerve fibre layer infarction with axoplasmic stasis is the mechanism of cotton-wool spots, which are retinal, not choroidal.
Wrong - Short posterior ciliary artery occlusion causes ischaemic optic neuropathy (AION), not mid-peripheral choroidal lesions.
Correct - Fibrinoid necrosis of choroidal arterioles infarcts the choriocapillaris and RPE, producing Elschnig spots and Siegrist streaks.
Wrong - Breakdown of the inner blood-retinal barrier explains retinal haemorrhages and exudates, not choroidopathy.

mcq.stem:
A 58-year-old non-diabetic man has fundoscopy in the medical clinic; BP is 182/108 mmHg. Close to the optic disc there are several small haemorrhages with feathered ends, lying along the course of the arcades. In the mid-periphery there are a few small round, dark-red haemorrhages with sharp edges.
Why do the peripapillary haemorrhages have a feathered shape?
o: The blood lies in the outer plexiform layer between vertically orientated fibres
The blood lies in the subhyaloid space and settles under gravity into a fluid level
The blood lies beneath the retinal pigment epithelium within Bruch membrane
The blood lies in the inner nuclear layer, arising from the deep capillary plexus
The blood tracks along horizontally running axons of the nerve fibre layer
mcq.e: The shape of a retinal haemorrhage tells you its depth. **Flame (splinter) haemorrhages** lie in the superficial **nerve fibre layer**, so blood spreads along the axons that run parallel to the surface, giving feathered edges. **Dot and blot haemorrhages** lie deeper, in the inner nuclear and outer plexiform layers, where vertically arranged cells hold the blood in a compact round shape. Note: the notes (p35) place dot-blot haemorrhages in the 'inner retinal layer'. They are in the deeper (middle) retina, as the DR section of the notes (p39) states.
w: Wrong - Blood in the outer plexiform layer is held by vertical fibres and forms round dot or blot haemorrhages. That describes the mid-peripheral lesions.
Wrong - Subhyaloid (preretinal) blood forms a boat-shaped haemorrhage with a flat upper fluid level, not feathered splinters.
Wrong - Sub-RPE blood looks dark grey-green and elevated, as in wet AMD. It does not form splinters.
Wrong - Inner nuclear layer blood from the deep capillary plexus forms dot or blot haemorrhages, not flame shapes.
Correct - Nerve fibre layer blood spreads along the horizontally running ganglion cell axons, giving a flame or splinter shape.

mcq.stem:
A 66-year-old man with treated hypertension (BP today 148/88 mmHg, HbA1c 5.6%) noticed blurred vision in his right eye on waking 5 days ago. VA is 6/36 right and 6/6 left, with a mild right RAPD. The right fundus shows a swollen disc, dilated tortuous veins, and flame and blot haemorrhages extending to the periphery in all four quadrants, with a few cotton-wool spots. The left fundus shows only mild arteriolar narrowing and AV nicking.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Keith-Wagener-Barker group 4 hypertensive retinopathy
Central retinal vein occlusion
Non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy
Diabetic papillopathy
Neuroretinitis
mcq.e: Hypertensive retinopathy is a **bilateral, roughly symmetrical** disease. A **unilateral** swollen disc with dilated tortuous veins and haemorrhages in all four quadrants out to the periphery is **CRVO**, and hypertension is its commonest risk factor. Moderate BP and a near-normal fellow eye argue strongly against malignant hypertension. The notes (p36) list CRVO, AION, diabetic papillopathy and neuroretinitis as the differentials of disc swelling.
w: Wrong - Grade 4 hypertensive retinopathy is bilateral with very high BP. Here the fellow eye shows only mild sclerosis and BP is 148/88.
Correct - A unilateral swollen disc with dilated tortuous veins and four-quadrant haemorrhages to the periphery ('blood and thunder') is CRVO.
Wrong - NAION gives sectoral disc swelling with a few peripapillary splinter haemorrhages, not dilated veins and haemorrhages throughout the retina.
Wrong - Diabetic papillopathy occurs in diabetics, often young type 1, with mild visual loss. He is not diabetic and the retina is flooded with haemorrhage.
Wrong - Neuroretinitis is disc swelling with a macular star, typically in a young patient after cat scratch. Widespread venous haemorrhage is not a feature.

mcq.stem:
A 27-year-old man is found to have BP 210/124 mmHg at a pre-employment check. He describes episodes of pounding headache, palpitations and drenching sweats over the past year. Fundoscopy shows bilateral flame haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and early disc swelling. Radial and femoral pulses are synchronous, and renal function and urinalysis are normal.
Which investigation is most likely to reveal the cause of his hypertension?
o: Plasma free or 24-hour urinary metanephrines
Fundus fluorescein angiography of both eyes
Echocardiogram to look for coarctation of the aorta
Carotid duplex ultrasound for atheromatous stenosis
MRI of the orbits and optic nerves with gadolinium
mcq.e: Severe retinopathy in a **young** hypertensive should always prompt a search for **secondary hypertension** (renal disease, renovascular, phaeochromocytoma, coarctation, hyperaldosteronism, pre-eclampsia). Paroxysms of headache, palpitations and sweating are the classic triad of **phaeochromocytoma**, so the first-line test is plasma free or urinary metanephrines. Synchronous radio-femoral pulses make coarctation unlikely. Ocular imaging describes the retinopathy but does not explain the BP.
w: Correct - Episodic headache, palpitations and sweating suggest phaeochromocytoma. Metanephrines are the screening test.
Wrong - FFA would show the retinal and choroidal damage but cannot identify the cause of the hypertension.
Wrong - Coarctation is reasonable to consider in young hypertensives, but synchronous radial and femoral pulses and paroxysmal symptoms point elsewhere.
Wrong - Carotid stenosis does not cause hypertension. It matters for unilateral ocular ischaemia and emboli in older patients.
Wrong - Orbital MRI is used for optic nerve disease. The disc swelling here comes from malignant systemic hypertension.

mcq.stem:
A 57-year-old woman is referred from a Klinik Kesihatan after a community health screening. She has no symptoms and no known illness. BP is 164/98 mmHg on repeated readings. VA is 6/6 in both eyes. Fundoscopy shows arteriolar narrowing, AV nicking, a few flame haemorrhages and two cotton-wool spots in each eye. The discs and maculae are normal.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Same-day admission for intravenous labetalol with hourly neurological observations
Urgent ophthalmology referral for pan-retinal laser photocoagulation to both eyes
Physician referral to treat BP, screen for diabetes and assess heart and kidneys
Fundus fluorescein angiography first, to grade retinal ischaemia before any treatment
Reassurance that these are age-related changes, with repeat fundoscopy in two years
mcq.e: This is **moderate** hypertensive retinopathy: exudative signs with **normal discs**, symptom-free, BP well below emergency levels. The notes (p36) advise **physician referral** to control BP, **exclude diabetes** (a cotton-wool spot or haemorrhage may be diabetic or mixed retinopathy) and look for cardiovascular and renal target-organ damage. Admission and IV therapy are for grade 4 disease or a hypertensive emergency. Laser has no role, because these changes regress once BP is controlled.
w: Wrong - IV antihypertensives and admission are for hypertensive emergencies (e.g. disc swelling, target-organ failure), not stable moderate retinopathy.
Wrong - PRP treats retinal neovascularisation (e.g. PDR, ischaemic CRVO). Hypertensive haemorrhages and cotton-wool spots resolve with BP control.
Correct - Moderate retinopathy needs physician care for BP control, diabetes screening and assessment of cardiovascular and renal target organs.
Wrong - FFA is not needed to manage hypertensive retinopathy and would only delay starting BP treatment.
Wrong - Haemorrhages and cotton-wool spots are not age-related. They show active hypertensive damage that needs treatment now.

mcq.stem:
A 44-year-old man was treated for accelerated hypertension 12 months ago, when he had bilateral disc swelling, flame haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and macular exudates. Since then his BP has been well controlled on three agents. He returns for review; VA is 6/6 in each eye.
Which fundus finding is most likely to still be present today?
o: Optic disc swelling with peripapillary splinter haemorrhages
Multiple fluffy cotton-wool spots near the disc
Flame-shaped nerve fibre layer haemorrhages
Shallow serous detachments at the maculae
Arteriolar wall thickening with AV nicking
mcq.e: Acute (vasoconstrictive and exudative) changes **regress** once BP is controlled. Haemorrhages and cotton-wool spots clear within weeks, disc swelling within weeks to months, and serous detachments settle. **Sclerotic** changes (thickened arteriolar walls, AV nicking, copper or silver wiring) are structural and **persist**, so they mark long-standing hypertension. Permanent visual loss, when it occurs, comes from optic atrophy after prolonged papilloedema or from pigmentary scarring after exudative detachment (notes p36).
w: Wrong - Disc swelling resolves over weeks to months with BP control. Persistent swelling a year later would need another explanation.
Wrong - Cotton-wool spots are acute nerve fibre layer infarcts that fade within weeks to a few months.
Wrong - Flame haemorrhages reabsorb within weeks once BP is controlled.
Wrong - Hypertensive serous detachments settle once choroidal perfusion recovers. Any lasting mark is RPE pigmentary change, not fluid.
Correct - Arteriolosclerosis and AV crossing changes are structural and remain despite good BP control.

mcq.stem:
A 29-year-old primigravida at 34 weeks’ gestation is admitted with BP 178/116 mmHg, 3+ proteinuria and headache. Over 2 days both eyes have become blurred. VA is 6/36 in each eye. Fundoscopy shows arteriolar narrowing, scattered pale yellow choroidal patches and bilateral bullous inferior serous retinal detachments. No retinal breaks are found on careful indentation.
What is the best management of the retinal detachments?
o: Urgent scleral buckling of both eyes within 24 hours
Pars plana vitrectomy with gas tamponade after delivery
360° barrier laser retinopexy around both detachments
BP control and planned delivery; no retinal surgery
Intravitreal triamcinolone to dry the subretinal fluid
mcq.e: Pre-eclampsia causes **hypertensive choroidopathy**: choroidal ischaemia damages the RPE pump and fluid collects under the retina as an **exudative (serous) detachment**, with no break. Exudative detachments are managed by treating the **cause**: control the BP and plan delivery with the obstetric team. The fluid usually absorbs within weeks with good visual recovery. Surgery for rhegmatogenous detachment (buckle, vitrectomy, retinopexy) has no role.
w: Wrong - Scleral buckling closes retinal breaks in rhegmatogenous detachment. There is no break here.
Wrong - Vitrectomy is for rhegmatogenous or tractional detachment. Serous detachment from pre-eclampsia resolves without it.
Wrong - Barrier laser stops a rhegmatogenous detachment from spreading. It does not remove choroidal exudation.
Correct - Exudative detachment from pre-eclampsia resolves once BP is controlled and the pregnancy is delivered.
Wrong - Intravitreal steroid does not treat hypertensive choroidopathy and adds risks (raised IOP, infection) without dealing with the cause.

mcq.stem:
A 49-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 6 years (HbA1c 7.4%, BP 128/78 mmHg, normal renal function) has two-field fundus photography at a Klinik Kesihatan screening clinic. VA is 6/6 in both eyes. Both eyes show microaneurysms, scattered dot and blot haemorrhages in two quadrants and a single cotton-wool spot. There is no venous beading, IRMA or new vessels, and no exudates or thickening within the macula.
According to the Malaysian CPG on screening for diabetic retinopathy, what should happen next?
o: Rescreen in 12-24 months at the Klinik Kesihatan
Rescreen in 6 months at the Klinik Kesihatan
Rescreen in 9-12 months at the Klinik Kesihatan
Refer to an ophthalmologist within 4 weeks
Refer to an ophthalmologist within 1 week
mcq.e: Haemorrhages and a cotton-wool spot beyond microaneurysms alone, but without any 4-2-1 feature, make this **moderate NPDR without maculopathy**. MOH CPG Table 3 schedules a review every **6 months** for that grade. Mild NPDR (microaneurysms only) is reviewed at 9-12 months and no DR at 12-24 months (annually if high risk). Referral is triggered by severe NPDR, any maculopathy or PDR. Note: the notes' table (p41) gives slightly different intervals (e.g. no DR 'yearly'). In Malaysia, follow the CPG.
w: Wrong - 12-24 months is the CPG interval for no retinopathy, not moderate NPDR.
Correct - Moderate NPDR without maculopathy is rescreened every 6 months (MOH CPG Table 3).
Wrong - 9-12 months is the interval for mild NPDR (microaneurysms only) without maculopathy.
Wrong - Referral within 4 weeks is for severe NPDR, any maculopathy or worsening DR. None are present.
Wrong - Referral within 1 week is for new vessels, preretinal or vitreous haemorrhage, or rubeosis.

mcq.stem:
A 61-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 14 years attends diabetic retinopathy screening. VA is 6/9 in both eyes. The right fundus shows definite venous beading in both the superotemporal and inferotemporal quadrants, scattered microaneurysms, and intraretinal haemorrhages that number fewer than 20 in each quadrant. There are no new vessels, no preretinal or vitreous haemorrhage, and no exudates or thickening at the macula.
What is the most appropriate action for the right eye?
o: Rescreen in 6 months as moderate NPDR
Rescreen in 3 months as moderate NPDR with high risk
Same-day emergency referral to the eye clinic
Refer to an ophthalmologist within 4 weeks
Refer to an ophthalmologist within 1 week
mcq.e: Severe NPDR follows the **4-2-1 rule**. Any ONE of: >20 intraretinal **haemorrhages** in each of 4 quadrants, definite **venous beading in 2 or more quadrants**, or prominent **IRMA in 1 or more quadrant**, with no new vessels. Venous beading in two quadrants alone qualifies, even with few haemorrhages. The MOH CPG says severe NPDR is **referred to an ophthalmologist within 4 weeks**. Note: the notes (p41) say 'microaneurysm (>20 intraretinal haemorrhage)'. The criterion is >20 intraretinal haemorrhages per quadrant, not microaneurysms.
w: Wrong - Venous beading in 2 quadrants meets the 4-2-1 rule, so this is severe NPDR, not moderate. Continuing 6-monthly screening is unsafe.
Wrong - The CPG has no 3-month rescreen for non-pregnant patients. Severe NPDR needs referral.
Wrong - Same-day referral is for sudden severe visual loss or signs of retinal detachment.
Correct - Severe NPDR (venous beading in 2 or more quadrants) is referred to an ophthalmologist within 4 weeks.
Wrong - One-week referral is reserved for proliferative signs: new vessels, preretinal or vitreous haemorrhage, rubeosis.

mcq.stem:
A 45-year-old man with poorly controlled type 1 diabetes has screening photographs at a Klinik Kesihatan. He has no visual symptoms. VA is 6/6 right and 6/9 left. The left image shows a frond of fine new vessels along the superotemporal arcade with a small boat-shaped haemorrhage lying in front of the retina beside it. The retina appears flat, and the right eye shows moderate NPDR.
According to the Malaysian CPG, how urgently should he be referred to an ophthalmologist?
o: Refer within one week
Refer on the same day as an emergency
Refer within 4 weeks
Refer within 3 months
Rescreen in 6 months instead
mcq.e: New vessels elsewhere (NVE) with a **preretinal (subhyaloid) haemorrhage** make this **PDR**, even though the patient has no symptoms and good acuity. MOH CPG Table 4 says new vessels, preretinal or vitreous haemorrhage, or rubeosis need referral **within 1 week**. **Same-day** referral is kept for sudden severe visual loss or signs of retinal detachment. **4 weeks** is for maculopathy, severe NPDR, unexplained VA drop or worsening DR. Good VA does not mean the eye is safe.
w: Correct - Retinal new vessels with preretinal haemorrhage are referred within 1 week (MOH CPG Table 4).
Wrong - Same-day referral is for sudden severe visual loss or signs of acute retinal detachment. The retina here is flat and VA is preserved.
Wrong - 4 weeks is the urgency for maculopathy or severe NPDR. Proliferative disease needs earlier review.
Wrong - A 3-month wait risks vitreous haemorrhage and traction from untreated new vessels.
Wrong - Rescreening is never appropriate once proliferative retinopathy is found. It must be referred.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes for 9 years is 10 weeks pregnant with her first child. Her HbA1c has fallen from 9.8% to 6.9% over the past 4 months. VA is 6/6 in both eyes. Dilated fundoscopy shows a few microaneurysms only in each eye, with no maculopathy.
According to the Malaysian CPG, what eye follow-up does she need during this pregnancy?
o: Rescreen in 9-12 months, as for mild NPDR outside pregnancy
A single further examination in the third trimester
Refer to an ophthalmologist within 4 weeks for laser
One examination at 6 weeks after delivery
Fundus examination every 3 months in pregnancy
mcq.e: Pregnancy accelerates DR, and so does the **rapid fall in HbA1c** she has just had. The MOH CPG schedule for pregnant women with **no DR or mild NPDR is every 3 months**. **Moderate NPDR or worse** in pregnancy means referral to an ophthalmologist. Women with pre-existing diabetes should ideally be examined **before conception**. Mild NPDR does not need laser.
w: Wrong - 9-12 months is the non-pregnant interval for mild NPDR. Pregnancy needs much closer surveillance.
Wrong - One third-trimester check could miss progression in the first and second trimesters.
Wrong - Mild NPDR does not need laser or referral. Referral in pregnancy starts at moderate NPDR or worse.
Wrong - A postpartum check alone ignores the risk of progression during pregnancy.
Correct - In pregnancy, no DR to mild NPDR is examined every 3 months (MOH CPG Table 3).

mcq.stem:
A 33-year-old woman has a normal booking OGTT at 12 weeks’ gestation. At 26 weeks a repeat OGTT confirms gestational diabetes, and the Klinik Kesihatan starts dietary advice and metformin. She has no visual symptoms and VA is 6/6 in each eye. She asks whether she needs eye checks like her sister, who has type 1 diabetes and was examined every few months in pregnancy.
According to the Malaysian CPG, what retinal screening does she need during this pregnancy?
o: Fundus examination every 3 months until delivery
Fundus examination once in each remaining trimester
No routine retinopathy screening is required
Fundus photography now and again at 36 weeks
Referral to an ophthalmologist within 4 weeks
mcq.e: The MOH CPG states that DR screening is **not required for gestational diabetes**. The exception is GDM **diagnosed in the first trimester**, which may be undiagnosed pre-existing diabetes and is screened like pre-existing DM. Other first-screening rules: adults with T2DM **at diagnosis**; adults with T1DM within 3-5 years (CPG recommendation: up to 3 years); pre-existing DM **before planned conception**; children with T1DM at age 9 with 5 years' duration or age 11 with 2 years' duration.
w: Wrong - 3-monthly review is for pregnant women with pre-existing diabetes and no or mild DR, not for second-trimester GDM.
Wrong - Trimester-based screening is not part of the CPG and is not needed for GDM found at 26 weeks.
Correct - GDM diagnosed after the first trimester does not need DR screening (MOH CPG).
Wrong - Repeated photography adds cost without benefit in late-onset GDM.
Wrong - She has no retinopathy or symptoms, so there is no indication for an ophthalmology referral.

mcq.stem:
A 52-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is reviewed in the eye clinic after a referral from screening. VA is 6/9 right. The right fundus shows new vessels on the disc covering about half of the disc area, with a small inferior vitreous haemorrhage. There is no tractional detachment, OCT shows no macular oedema, and the view is good enough for treatment.
What is the standard first-line treatment for the right eye?
o: Focal or grid macular laser to the posterior pole
Pars plana vitrectomy with endolaser
Pan-retinal (scatter) photocoagulation
Observation with 3-monthly fundus photographs
Intravitreal triamcinolone acetonide injection
mcq.e: High-risk **PDR** (NVD with vitreous haemorrhage) is treated with **pan-retinal photocoagulation**. Ablating the ischaemic peripheral retina lowers VEGF drive and makes the new vessels regress (notes p42; MOH CPG Table 5). Focal or grid laser treats macular oedema, which he does not have. Vitrectomy is for non-clearing vitreous haemorrhage or traction threatening the macula. Anti-VEGF is a useful adjunct, especially when haemorrhage or DME limits laser, but PRP remains the standard.
w: Wrong - Focal or grid laser treats leaking microaneurysms in macular oedema. It does not make new vessels regress.
Wrong - Vitrectomy is for persistent vitreous haemorrhage or tractional detachment involving the macula. Neither is present.
Correct - PRP is the standard treatment for PDR. It reduces the ischaemic VEGF drive so the new vessels regress.
Wrong - NVD with haemorrhage carries a high risk of severe visual loss if left alone. Treatment should not be delayed.
Wrong - Intravitreal steroid is a second-line option for refractory DME, not primary treatment for proliferative disease.

mcq.stem:
A 47-year-old taxi driver with proliferative diabetic retinopathy finished three sessions of pan-retinal photocoagulation to both eyes 2 months ago, and the new vessels have regressed. He now says he bumps into objects at his sides and struggles to see when driving at night. VA is 6/9 in each eye, the maculae are dry on OCT, the vitreous is clear and IOP is 15 mmHg in each eye.
What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
o: Loss of peripheral retina destroyed by the laser burns
Recurrent vitreous haemorrhage from persistent new vessels
Post-laser macular oedema lowering contrast sensitivity
Neovascular glaucoma with advanced arcuate field loss
Peripheral tractional retinal detachment after regression
mcq.e: PRP works by sacrificing peripheral retina, so its expected side effects are **constricted visual fields** and **poor night (dark-adapted) vision**. Rod-rich peripheral retina is destroyed (notes p42). Patients should be counselled beforehand, and those who drive for a living need a formal field test before they continue. A clear vitreous, dry maculae and normal IOP rule out the other options.
w: Correct - PRP burns destroy peripheral, rod-rich retina, which constricts the visual field and reduces night vision.
Wrong - Recurrent vitreous haemorrhage would give sudden floaters or blur, and the vitreous is clear.
Wrong - PRP can worsen macular oedema, but OCT shows dry maculae and the symptoms are peripheral.
Wrong - Neovascular glaucoma raises IOP, often painfully. IOP here is 15 mmHg.
Wrong - Traction would be visible on examination and usually gives a sectoral defect, not symmetrical night blindness.

mcq.stem:
A 64-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and poorly controlled hypercholesterolaemia has VA 6/12 in the left eye. Fundoscopy shows a circinate ring of sharply defined, waxy yellow deposits surrounding a cluster of microaneurysms temporal to the fovea. There are no new vessels.
What are these deposits composed of, and where do they lie?
o: Axoplasmic debris within ischaemic nerve fibre layer
Drusen between the RPE basal lamina and Bruch membrane
Cholesterol emboli lodged at retinal arteriolar branches
Leaked lipoprotein in the outer plexiform layer
Haemosiderin from old blot haemorrhages in the inner retina
mcq.e: These are **hard exudates**: **lipoprotein and lipid-laden macrophages** that collect in the **outer plexiform layer** after plasma leaks from microaneurysms. The water is reabsorbed and the lipid is left behind, often as a **circinate ring** around the leaking source (notes p39). Exudates near the fovea mean **diabetic maculopathy**, which needs referral, and high lipids make them worse. Cotton-wool spots, by contrast, are fluffy white nerve fibre layer infarcts.
w: Wrong - Axoplasmic debris in ischaemic nerve fibre layer forms cotton-wool spots: fluffy, white and ill-defined, not waxy rings.
Wrong - Drusen lie beneath the RPE in age-related maculopathy. They are not arranged around microaneurysms.
Wrong - Cholesterol (Hollenhorst) emboli are glinting plaques at arteriolar bifurcations from carotid atheroma.
Correct - Hard exudates are lipoprotein deposits in the outer plexiform layer, often forming a circinate ring around leaking microaneurysms.
Wrong - Haemosiderin from old haemorrhage leaves dull pigment, not sharply defined waxy yellow rings.

mcq.stem:
A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 12 years has had gradually blurred reading vision in his right eye for 2 months. VA is 6/18 right (no better with pinhole) and 6/6 left. The lens is clear. Fundoscopy shows a few hard exudates within one disc diameter of the fovea and a dull foveal reflex, with no new vessels.
Which investigation best confirms and quantifies centre-involving macular oedema and guides treatment?
o: Fundus fluorescein angiography
Optical coherence tomography of the macula
B-scan ultrasonography of the posterior segment
Humphrey 24-2 visual field test
Full-field electroretinography
mcq.e: Macular oedema is a **thickening** of the retina, which is hard to judge on a flat fundus view. **OCT** measures central retinal thickness non-invasively, shows whether the **centre** is involved, and is used to decide on and monitor **intravitreal anti-VEGF**, the first-line treatment for centre-involving DME in the MOH DME guideline. FFA shows leakage and ischaemia (useful for macular ischaemia or planning laser) but does not measure thickness. DME is the commonest cause of visual loss in diabetic retinopathy.
w: Wrong - FFA shows leakage and capillary non-perfusion but cannot measure retinal thickness. It is invasive, with a risk of dye reactions.
Correct - OCT measures retinal thickness, confirms centre involvement and guides and monitors anti-VEGF treatment.
Wrong - B-scan is for an opaque media (dense vitreous haemorrhage) to look for detachment. The view here is clear.
Wrong - Visual fields assess the optic nerve and peripheral retina, not macular thickness.
Wrong - ERG measures global retinal function and does not show or quantify focal macular oedema.

mcq.stem:
A 24-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes had moderate NPDR a year ago. After she started an insulin pump, her HbA1c fell from 12.8% to 6.8% within 4 months. She has no symptoms, but screening now shows new cotton-wool spots and IRMA in both eyes, with no new vessels. BP and renal function are normal.
What is the most likely explanation for the change?
o: Hypoglycaemic retinal infarction from excessive insulin
Superimposed hypertensive retinopathy not yet diagnosed
Retinal vein occlusion from raised blood viscosity
Natural progression unrelated to her glycaemic control
Early worsening from rapidly improved glucose control
mcq.e: A **rapid fall in HbA1c** can transiently worsen DR (**early worsening**), with new cotton-wool spots and IRMA. It is thought to be caused by reduced retinal blood flow and a VEGF surge in retina adapted to hyperglycaemia. It is commonest in long-standing poor control with pre-existing retinopathy, and pregnancy carries the same risk. Tight control still protects in the long term (DCCT), so **do not relax control**. Instead, increase the frequency of eye monitoring and refer if she reaches severe NPDR or PDR.
w: Wrong - Hypoglycaemia does not cause bilateral cotton-wool spots and IRMA. It is not a recognised cause of retinal infarction.
Wrong - Her BP is normal, and hypertensive retinopathy does not produce IRMA.
Wrong - Vein occlusion is usually unilateral, with dilated veins and haemorrhages in a sector or all four quadrants.
Wrong - The progression happened in step with a dramatic fall in HbA1c, the classic setting for early worsening.
Correct - Rapid improvement in glycaemic control can transiently worsen DR. Monitor more closely but keep control tight.

mcq.stem:
A 27-year-old female staff nurse attends the eye clinic with 4 days of blurred vision in her right eye and an ache behind the eye that is worse when she looks around. VA is 6/24 right and 6/6 left. There is a right RAPD; she reads 4/17 Ishihara plates with the right eye and says red objects look washed out. Confrontation testing shows a central scotoma. Both optic discs, maculae and retinal vessels look normal.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy
Functional visual loss
Papilloedema from raised intracranial pressure
Retrobulbar optic neuritis
Leber hereditary optic neuropathy
mcq.e: A young woman with subacute monocular loss, **pain on eye movement**, an **RAPD**, red desaturation and a central scotoma has optic nerve dysfunction. A **normal disc** places the inflammation behind the globe: **retrobulbar optic neuritis**, the commonest form in adults and strongly linked to MS. 'The patient sees nothing and the doctor sees nothing.' Note: the notes (p44) call optic neuritis 'painless'. Typical demyelinating optic neuritis is **painful**, especially on eye movement (~90%), as the notes themselves say on p45.
w: Wrong - NAION occurs over 50, is painless, and by definition shows a swollen (often sectoral) disc at onset.
Wrong - A definite RAPD and red desaturation are objective signs of optic nerve disease, so the loss is not functional.
Wrong - Papilloedema is bilateral disc swelling with preserved acuity early and no RAPD. Her discs are normal.
Correct - Painful subacute loss with RAPD, dyschromatopsia, a central scotoma and a normal disc is retrobulbar optic neuritis.
Wrong - LHON is painless, usually affects young men sequentially, and often shows disc hyperaemia with telangiectatic vessels.

mcq.stem:
A 31-year-old woman is recovering from a first episode of painful visual loss in her left eye 3 weeks ago. VA has improved from 6/36 to 6/12, there is still a left RAPD with red desaturation, and the left disc looked normal throughout. She has no other neurological symptoms or history, and examination is otherwise normal. She asks whether this means she will get multiple sclerosis.
Which investigation gives the best estimate of her risk of developing MS?
o: MRI brain with gadolinium contrast
Lumbar puncture for CSF oligoclonal bands
Visual evoked potentials of both eyes
CT brain and orbits with contrast
Serum ESR and C-reactive protein
mcq.e: The notes (p45) list LP, MRI and VEP for MS work-up, but **MRI brain** is the single best predictor after a first episode of optic neuritis. One or more typical **periventricular white matter lesions** carry roughly a **50-70% 15-year risk** of MS, compared with about 25% if the MRI is normal. MRI also fulfils dissemination criteria and steers referral for disease-modifying therapy. VEP confirms conduction delay, and oligoclonal bands add supportive evidence, but neither stratifies risk as well.
w: Correct - MRI brain white matter lesions are the strongest predictor of conversion to MS after optic neuritis.
Wrong - Oligoclonal bands support MS, but LP is invasive and predicts risk less well than MRI.
Wrong - VEP shows delayed conduction in the affected nerve but says little about future MS risk.
Wrong - CT is insensitive to demyelinating white matter lesions.
Wrong - ESR and CRP are for suspected GCA in older patients and do not predict MS.

mcq.stem:
A 29-year-old airline pilot has had painful loss of vision in his left eye for 5 days. VA is 6/60 left and 6/6 right, with a left RAPD and severe red desaturation; the left disc is mildly swollen. MRI brain shows two periventricular white matter lesions. Blood tests, including syphilis serology, are normal. He wants whatever will get his vision back fastest.
Which treatment is most appropriate?
o: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 14 days as the only treatment
Plasma exchange as first-line treatment within 48 hours
IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days, then an oral taper
Posterior sub-Tenon triamcinolone injection to the left eye
IV aciclovir until varicella zoster PCR results return
mcq.e: The Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial (ONTT) showed that **high-dose IV methylprednisolone** (about 1 g/day for 3 days, then an oral taper) **speeds visual recovery**, although it does not change final acuity. It also delayed MS onset over 2 years. **Standard-dose oral prednisolone alone increased recurrences** and should be avoided. Because MRI shows lesions, he should also see a neurologist about disease-modifying therapy. Plasma exchange is kept for severe, steroid-unresponsive disease (e.g. NMOSD).
w: Wrong - In the ONTT, standard-dose oral prednisolone alone gave no benefit and increased recurrences, so avoid it.
Wrong - Plasma exchange is second-line for severe steroid-refractory or NMOSD-related optic neuritis, not first-line for typical disease.
Correct - High-dose IV methylprednisolone followed by an oral taper speeds recovery (ONTT), which matters for his job.
Wrong - Local periocular steroid has no proven role in demyelinating optic neuritis.
Wrong - There is no rash, retinitis or immunosuppression to suggest viral optic neuritis, and this picture is typical demyelination.

mcq.stem:
A 26-year-old teacher was treated with IV methylprednisolone for typical demyelinating optic neuritis of the left eye. VA at presentation was 6/36 with a left RAPD and a normal disc; MRI brain was normal. At her 2-week review the pain has gone and she asks what to expect.
Which statement is the most accurate counselling?
o: The steroids will have improved her final acuity compared with no treatment
Most patients are left with acuity of 6/60 or worse in the affected eye
A normal MRI brain means she will not go on to develop multiple sclerosis
Vision usually keeps deteriorating for 2-3 months before it stabilises
About 9 in 10 patients recover to 6/12 or better over the next few months
mcq.e: Typical optic neuritis has a **good prognosis**. Vision worsens over days to about 2 weeks, starts improving within weeks, and ~**90% reach 6/12 or better** by a few months. Contrast, colour and brightness perception may stay subtly reduced, often with temporal disc pallor. Steroids speed recovery **without changing the final VA**. A normal MRI lowers but does not remove MS risk (~25% at 15 years). Poor recovery should prompt a search for NMOSD, MOG antibody disease, compression or another cause.
w: Wrong - The ONTT found that steroids speed recovery but do not change final visual acuity.
Wrong - Severe permanent loss is uncommon in typical optic neuritis. If it happens, suspect NMOSD or another cause.
Wrong - A normal MRI lowers the risk, but about 1 in 4 still develop MS within 15 years.
Wrong - Typical optic neuritis bottoms out within about 2 weeks. Loss that keeps progressing for months is atypical and needs re-investigation.
Correct - About 90% recover to 6/12 or better within months, although subtle colour and contrast deficits may persist.

mcq.stem:
A 19-year-old male student has had blurred vision in his right eye for a week. Two weeks earlier he had fever and a tender swollen axillary lymph node after his new kitten scratched his forearm. VA is 6/36 right with a mild RAPD. The right disc is swollen, and hard exudates radiate in a star pattern around the fovea. The left eye is normal and BP is 118/72 mmHg.
Which organism is most likely responsible?
o: Toxoplasma gondii
Bartonella henselae
Treponema pallidum
Borrelia burgdorferi
Toxocara canis
mcq.e: Disc swelling with a **macular star** in a young, normotensive patient is **neuroretinitis**. The commonest cause is **cat-scratch disease** (*Bartonella henselae*), inoculated by a cat scratch or bite with regional lymphadenopathy (notes p46). Neuroretinitis is rarely demyelinating, so it does not raise MS risk like retrobulbar neuritis. A bilateral macular star with disc swelling plus very high BP would point instead to malignant hypertension, so always check the BP.
w: Wrong - Toxoplasma causes focal necrotising retinochoroiditis next to a pigmented scar ('headlight in the fog'), not a disc-macular star picture after a scratch.
Correct - Bartonella henselae (cat-scratch disease) is the classic cause of neuroretinitis with a macular star.
Wrong - Syphilis can cause papillitis or neuroretinitis but would not explain a kitten scratch with regional lymphadenitis. Still test for it in atypical cases.
Wrong - Lyme disease (tick bite) can cause neuroretinitis, but the history points to a cat, and Lyme is rare in Malaysia.
Wrong - Toxocara (puppy exposure, children) usually forms a peripheral or posterior pole granuloma, not neuroretinitis.

mcq.stem:
A 46-year-old man on treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for 2 months) has had gradually blurred vision in both eyes over 3 weeks. He weighs 52 kg and has stage 3 chronic kidney disease. VA is 6/18 in both eyes with no RAPD. He misses most Ishihara plates with each eye and has bilateral central scotomas. Both discs look normal.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Stop ethambutol now, with the TB physician
IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days
Continue all drugs and add oral pyridoxine
Continue all drugs and review again in 3 months
Stop isoniazid and continue the other three drugs
mcq.e: Bilateral, symmetrical, painless loss with early **dyschromatopsia** and **central or caecocentral scotomas** in a patient on **ethambutol** is toxic optic neuropathy until proven otherwise. Symmetrical involvement explains why there is **no RAPD**. Ethambutol is renally cleared, so **CKD** and dose-per-kg errors raise the risk. Stop the drug **promptly** with the TB team (who will substitute another agent), because vision often recovers partially over months when it is stopped early. Prevent it with a baseline VA and colour test, then monthly checks.
w: Correct - Stop ethambutol promptly with the TB team. Early withdrawal gives the best chance of recovery.
Wrong - Steroids have no role in toxic optic neuropathy and would not remove the toxin.
Wrong - Pyridoxine prevents isoniazid peripheral neuropathy. It does not treat ethambutol optic neuropathy, and continuing the drug risks permanent loss.
Wrong - Continuing ethambutol for 3 months risks irreversible optic atrophy.
Wrong - Isoniazid is a rare cause of optic neuropathy. Ethambutol, especially with renal impairment, is the usual culprit.

mcq.stem:
A 22-year-old man noticed painless central blurring in his left eye 2 months ago, and this week his right eye has become similarly affected. VA is 6/60 right and CF left. Pupil reactions are fairly brisk for the degree of visual loss, and colour vision is severely reduced in both eyes. The right disc is mildly hyperaemic with tortuous peripapillary telangiectatic vessels that do not leak on fluorescein angiography. His mother's brother went blind in his twenties. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Bilateral demyelinating optic neuritis
Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder
Tobacco-alcohol nutritional optic neuropathy
Leber hereditary optic neuropathy
Papilloedema from idiopathic intracranial hypertension
mcq.e: **LHON** is a **mitochondrial** (maternally inherited) optic neuropathy, commonest in young men. It causes **painless, sequential** loss of central vision in both eyes, weeks to months apart. Classic acute signs are disc hyperaemia with **peripapillary telangiectatic microangiopathy that does not leak** on FFA. Pupils may be relatively spared, because the melanopsin ganglion cells survive. Smoking and alcohol are recognised triggers. Confirm with mtDNA testing (e.g. m.11778G>A) and counsel the maternal line.
w: Wrong - Demyelinating optic neuritis is painful, usually unilateral and recovers well. Sequential painless loss with a maternal family history fits LHON.
Wrong - NMOSD causes severe, often painful optic neuritis with myelitis or area postrema symptoms, not telangiectatic non-leaking discs.
Wrong - Nutritional or toxic optic neuropathy is simultaneous and symmetrical, with no disc telangiectasia and no maternal-line family history.
Correct - Painless sequential loss in a young man, non-leaking peripapillary telangiectasia and maternal-line blindness indicate LHON.
Wrong - Papilloedema preserves central acuity early, is bilateral at once, and the swollen discs leak on FFA.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old woman with a BMI of 38 kg/m² has had daily headaches for 6 weeks, worse when lying down and on waking, with brief greying-out of vision when she stands up. She takes doxycycline for acne. VA is 6/6 in both eyes, there is no RAPD and colour vision is normal. Both optic discs are swollen with blurred margins and absent spontaneous venous pulsation, and Humphrey fields show enlarged blind spots.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Lumbar puncture to measure opening pressure, then neuroimaging
Urgent neuroimaging (MRI with venography) before any lumbar puncture
IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days for bilateral papillitis
Start oral acetazolamide and review in the eye clinic in 3 months
Reassurance, as normal acuity and colour vision exclude a disc problem
mcq.e: Bilateral disc swelling with **preserved acuity and colour**, no RAPD, enlarged blind spots, transient visual obscurations and positional headache is **papilloedema**. Papilloedema means disc swelling from **raised intracranial pressure**. **Urgent neuroimaging** (MRI with MR venography, or CT/CTV) must come before LP, to exclude a mass lesion (risk of herniation) and venous sinus thrombosis. Only then is LP used to measure opening pressure (here likely IIH, with doxycycline as a contributor). Note: the notes (p44) say papilloedema is 'secondary to increased IOP'. The correct cause is raised **intracranial** pressure.
w: Wrong - LP before imaging risks coning if there is a space-occupying lesion. Image first.
Correct - Urgent MRI/MRV (or CT/CTV) before LP excludes a mass or venous sinus thrombosis as the cause of raised ICP.
Wrong - Papillitis causes reduced VA, RAPD and dyschromatopsia, and is usually unilateral. Steroids do not treat raised ICP.
Wrong - Acetazolamide may be used for IIH once the diagnosis is confirmed. Starting it blind and waiting 3 months misses dangerous causes.
Wrong - Early papilloedema typically spares acuity and colour vision. Normal function does not exclude raised ICP.

mcq.stem:
A 34-year-old Malay woman develops severe visual loss in both eyes over 5 days, with pain on eye movement. Three weeks earlier she was admitted for 10 days of intractable hiccups and vomiting with no cause found. VA is HM right and CF left, with poor colour vision in both eyes. MRI shows enhancement of a long segment of both optic nerves extending back to the chiasm, and a cervical cord lesion spanning four vertebral segments.
Which blood test is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
o: Antinuclear antibody and anti-dsDNA
Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme
Mitochondrial DNA testing for m.11778
Treponemal serology (TPHA)
Serum aquaporin-4 IgG antibody
mcq.e: Severe **bilateral** optic neuritis with **long-segment** optic nerve enhancement reaching the chiasm, **longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis** (3 or more vertebral segments) and an **area postrema syndrome** (intractable hiccups and vomiting) is **neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder**. It is relatively more common in Asian women than MS is. The confirmatory test is serum **AQP4-IgG** (MOG-IgG if negative). Recognition matters: NMOSD recovers poorly, needs early high-dose steroids ± plasma exchange and long-term immunosuppression, and some MS drugs worsen it.
w: Wrong - SLE can cause optic neuropathy, but the area postrema syndrome and LETM point specifically to NMOSD. The ANA may also be positive in NMOSD.
Wrong - ACE supports sarcoidosis, which can cause optic neuropathy but not this classic triad.
Wrong - mtDNA testing is for LHON, which is painless and sequential with no myelitis.
Wrong - Syphilis should be excluded in atypical optic neuritis, but it does not explain hiccups, vomiting and LETM.
Correct - Serum aquaporin-4 IgG confirms NMOSD in a patient with optic neuritis, LETM and area postrema syndrome.

mcq.stem:
A 32-year-old woman recovered to 6/6 after left optic neuritis 8 months ago. She now reports that vision in that eye dims for 10-20 minutes after jogging or a hot shower, then returns to normal. Between episodes VA is 6/6 left, there is a subtle residual left RAPD and the left disc shows temporal pallor. She has no new neurological symptoms.
What is the mechanism of her episodic symptoms?
o: Recurrent active demyelination with fresh optic nerve inflammation
Transient vasospasm of the short posterior ciliary arteries
Heat-induced conduction block in previously demyelinated axons
Exertional rise in intracranial pressure causing obscurations
Steroid-induced rise in intraocular pressure during exercise
mcq.e: This is **Uhthoff's phenomenon**. Demyelinated axons conduct with little safety margin, and a small rise in **body temperature** (exercise, hot bath, fever) causes **reversible conduction block**, so vision dims briefly and recovers on cooling. It does **not** mean a relapse and needs no steroid. A relapse would cause new, persistent loss lasting days, with pain. Temporal pallor and a residual RAPD are the expected scars of previous optic neuritis.
w: Wrong - A relapse causes loss that lasts days, usually with pain, not 10-20 minute dips that reverse on cooling.
Wrong - Ciliary artery vasospasm is not linked to heat. Ischaemia would cause NAION-like disc swelling, not stereotyped brief dimming.
Correct - Uhthoff's phenomenon: a rise in temperature causes temporary conduction block in demyelinated optic nerve fibres.
Wrong - Raised ICP obscurations last seconds, are bilateral, come with posture change, and need disc swelling, which she does not have.
Wrong - A steroid response raises IOP over weeks of treatment and causes no heat-triggered episodes. She is not on steroids now.

mcq.stem:
A 63-year-old man with hypertension and type 2 diabetes attends a district hospital eye clinic. On waking yesterday he noticed the lower half of the vision in his right eye was 'missing'. He has no pain, headache or jaw symptoms. VA is 6/12 right and 6/6 left with a right RAPD; Ishihara 12/15 right, 15/15 left. The right disc shows superior sectoral hyperaemic swelling with two peripapillary splinter haemorrhages; macula and vessels are normal. The left disc is small with no visible cup. ESR is 14 mm/h and CRP is normal.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Demyelinating papillitis with secondary splinter haemorrhages
Arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy from ciliary arteritis
Non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy of the right eye
Hemi-central retinal vein occlusion of the superior hemiretina
Early papilloedema with asymmetrical disc swelling
mcq.e: Sudden painless altitudinal loss on waking in a vasculopath, with HYPERAEMIC sectoral disc swelling, splinter haemorrhages, colour loss roughly proportional to VA and a crowded fellow disc, is classic **NAION**. Normal ESR/CRP and no GCA symptoms make arteritic AION unlikely. The trap is calling any swollen disc papillitis: optic neuritis is younger, painful on eye movement and gives colour loss out of proportion to VA.
w: Wrong - Optic neuritis typically affects 20-50-year-olds, hurts on eye movement and colour vision is worse than the VA suggests; here colour is only mildly reduced.
Wrong - Arteritic AION gives severe loss (often PL or worse) with a chalky white swollen disc and raised ESR/CRP; this disc is hyperaemic and the markers are normal.
Correct - Hyperaemic sectoral swelling with splinters, altitudinal loss on waking, vascular risk factors and a small cupless fellow disc (disc at risk) = NAION.
Wrong - A hemi-vein occlusion shows dilated veins and haemorrhages throughout half the retina, not a few peripapillary splinters with normal vessels.
Wrong - Papilloedema is bilateral, with normal VA and pupils early and an enlarged blind spot, not a unilateral RAPD with altitudinal loss.

mcq.stem:
A 76-year-old woman is referred from a Klinik Kesihatan with sudden loss of vision in her left eye this morning. For two weeks she has had brief episodes of that eye 'going black', with fatigue and poor appetite. Left VA is perception of light with a dense RAPD; right VA is 6/9. The left disc is swollen and strikingly pale, almost chalk-white; the right fundus is normal. ESR is 96 mm/h and CRP 64 mg/L. The physician is starting high-dose corticosteroids today.
What is the principal ophthalmic goal of starting treatment today?
o: To protect the right eye, which may infarct within days if untreated
To restore useful vision in the left eye by reperfusing the nerve head
To shrink the disc swelling and so prevent optic atrophy developing
To prevent neovascular glaucoma developing in the ischaemic left eye
To relieve her periocular pain while the biopsy is being arranged
mcq.e: Pale **chalky-white** disc swelling with PL vision, preceding amaurosis fugax, constitutional symptoms and very high ESR/CRP = **arteritic AION**. Vision in the infarcted eye is usually permanently lost (very rarely partial recovery); steroids are started immediately to protect the **fellow eye**, involved in about a third of untreated patients, usually within a week. Never wait for the biopsy before treating.
w: Correct - The index eye rarely recovers; the aim is to prevent bilateral blindness, as the fellow eye is often affected within days without steroids.
Wrong - Visual loss in arteritic AION is usually permanent; only very rarely does prompt steroid give partial recovery, so this is not a realistic aim.
Wrong - Optic atrophy follows over 1-2 months whatever is done; steroids are not given to prevent atrophy of an already infarcted nerve.
Wrong - Neovascular glaucoma follows retinal ischaemia (CRVO, PDR, ocular ischaemic syndrome), not optic nerve head infarction.
Wrong - Pain relief is welcome, but same-day treatment is about sight preservation; the biopsy can still be done within about 2 weeks of starting steroids.

mcq.stem:
A 52-year-old female teacher with treated hypertension presents to the eye clinic with blurred vision in the right eye for 4 days. She describes an ache behind the eye that is worse when she looks around, and colours look 'washed out'. VA is 6/9 right and 6/6 left, but she reads only 3/15 Ishihara plates with the right eye. There is a right RAPD and a central scotoma on confrontation. The right disc looks normal. ESR is 12 mm/h.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Non-arteritic ischaemic optic neuropathy
Posterior ischaemic optic neuropathy from hypertension
Central serous chorioretinopathy of the right macula
Leber hereditary optic neuropathy in a female carrier
Acute retrobulbar (demyelinating) optic neuritis
mcq.e: Pain on eye movement, colour vision far worse than the Snellen acuity (6/9 but 3/15 Ishihara), a central scotoma and a normal disc point to **retrobulbar optic neuritis**; age over 50 and hypertension are the distractors. In NAION colour loss is proportional to VA, the disc is swollen at onset (anterior by definition), the field loss is usually altitudinal and it is painless. Note: the notes (p44) list optic neuritis as painless; typical demyelinating optic neuritis is PAINFUL, especially on eye movement (about 90%), as p45 states.
w: Wrong - NAION is painless, the disc is swollen at presentation, the field loss is usually altitudinal and colour loss matches the VA.
Wrong - Posterior ION is rare (spinal surgery, massive blood loss, GCA), painless, and does not cause disproportionate colour loss with pain on eye movement.
Wrong - CSCR causes distortion and micropsia from a serous macular detachment; it does not cause an RAPD or marked dyschromatopsia.
Wrong - LHON mainly affects young men, is painless and gives sequential bilateral loss; pain on eye movement argues against it.
Correct - Pain on eye movement + colour loss out of proportion to VA + central scotoma + normal disc = retrobulbar optic neuritis.

mcq.stem:
A 58-year-old man wakes on the orthopaedic ward after 9 hours of prone lumbar spinal fusion complicated by 3 litres of blood loss and prolonged hypotension. He says he cannot see. VA is hand movements right and 6/60 left, with sluggish pupils and a right RAPD. Both optic discs, maculae and retinal vessels look completely normal and the red reflexes are clear. CT brain is normal.
What is the most likely cause of his visual loss?
o: Non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy in both eyes
Posterior ischaemic optic neuropathy affecting both nerves
Cortical blindness from bilateral occipital lobe infarction
Central retinal artery occlusion from headrest pressure on the globes
Retrobulbar optic neuritis triggered by surgical stress
mcq.e: Optic nerve dysfunction (poor VA, RAPD, sluggish pupils) with NORMAL discs straight after long prone surgery with major blood loss and hypotension is **posterior ischaemic optic neuropathy**: the retrobulbar nerve, supplied by pial vessels, infarcts without disc swelling. Anterior ION would show disc swelling, CRAO a white retina with cherry-red spot, and cortical blindness preserves pupil reactions. The discs turn pale weeks later; prognosis is poor.
w: Wrong - Anterior ION by definition involves the optic nerve head, so the discs would be swollen at onset.
Correct - Optic nerve signs with normal discs after prolonged prone surgery, anaemia and hypotension = posterior ION.
Wrong - Occipital (cortical) blindness spares the pupil reflexes and gives no RAPD; the normal CT also argues against it.
Wrong - Headrest compression CRAO gives retinal whitening, a cherry-red spot and often periorbital bruising; these retinae are normal.
Wrong - Optic neuritis is a disease of younger adults, painful on eye movement and not precipitated by anaesthesia or blood loss.

mcq.stem:
A 71-year-old woman with hypertension is seen in the eye clinic with painless loss of the lower half of the vision in her left eye, noticed on waking 2 days ago. She denies headache but, on direct questioning, mentions aching shoulders and stiffness for a month. VA is 6/18 left with a left RAPD. The left disc shows diffuse swelling with a splinter haemorrhage; its colour is hard to judge. The right disc is normal.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Prescribe aspirin 75 mg daily and review her visual fields in 6 weeks
Arrange MRI brain and orbits with gadolinium within the next month
Refer to neurology for lumbar puncture and CSF oligoclonal bands
Check ESR, CRP and platelet count today, before any other decision
Book carotid duplex ultrasound and echocardiography as an outpatient
mcq.e: Every patient over 50 with AION needs **same-day ESR and CRP (± platelets)**, because arteritic AION threatens the fellow eye within days and may occur without headache (occult GCA); her shoulder aching may be polymyalgia rheumatica. If markers or symptoms suggest GCA, steroids start at once and biopsy follows. Aspirin and vascular risk work-up come only after GCA has been excluded.
w: Wrong - Aspirin is reasonable for vascular protection in NAION, but starting it and waiting 6 weeks without excluding GCA risks the fellow eye.
Wrong - MRI looks for demyelination; it is not the priority in an elderly patient with ischaemic disc swelling and possible PMR.
Wrong - CSF oligoclonal bands support MS in optic neuritis; they are irrelevant to an ischaemic optic neuropathy at 71.
Correct - Same-day ESR/CRP/platelets screen for GCA, which must be excluded in every AION over 50, especially with PMR-type symptoms.
Wrong - Carotid and cardiac work-up suits embolic CRAO; NAION is a small-vessel (short posterior ciliary) problem and GCA must be excluded first.

mcq.stem:
A 60-year-old lorry driver with poorly controlled diabetes, hypertension and a BMI of 34 had right NAION diagnosed 1 week ago; ESR, CRP and platelets are normal and he has no GCA symptoms. His wife says he snores loudly and seems to stop breathing at night. Right VA is 6/24 with an inferior altitudinal defect; the left eye is normal. He asks what can be done.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily with a slow taper to speed recovery
Optimise vascular risk factors and refer for a sleep apnoea study
Optic nerve sheath decompression to relieve the compartment pressure
Start aspirin, explaining that it stops the left eye being affected
Intravitreal anti-VEGF to reduce the optic disc swelling
mcq.e: No treatment has been proven to restore vision in **NAION**; management is control of vascular risk factors (BP, glucose, lipids, smoking) and looking for contributors such as **obstructive sleep apnoea** and nocturnal hypotension. Optic nerve sheath decompression was ineffective and possibly harmful (IONDT). Aspirin is often given for systemic vascular protection but does not reduce fellow-eye involvement, so do not promise that; also check he still meets the driving visual standard.
w: Wrong - Systemic steroids have no proven benefit in NAION and would worsen his diabetes; high-dose steroids are for arteritic disease.
Correct - Treat the underlying risk factors; sleep apnoea (prolonged nocturnal hypoxia) is a recognised and treatable risk factor.
Wrong - The IONDT trial showed no benefit and possible harm from optic nerve sheath decompression; it has been abandoned.
Wrong - Aspirin reduces systemic vascular events but does not appear to protect the fellow eye; saying so would mislead him.
Wrong - Anti-VEGF is not an established NAION treatment; the swelling resolves by itself over 3-6 weeks, leaving pallor.

mcq.stem:
A 57-year-old businessman notices sudden painless loss of the lower field of his left eye on waking after a late business dinner. He has hypertension, type 2 diabetes and dyslipidaemia. Left VA is 6/9 with a left RAPD and superior sectoral hyperaemic disc swelling; the right disc is small and crowded. ESR and CRP are normal. His medicines are listed below.
Which medicine is it most important to advise him to stop?
o: Amlodipine 5 mg each morning
Atorvastatin 20 mg at night
Metformin 500 mg twice daily
Omeprazole 20 mg once daily
Sildenafil 50 mg as required
mcq.e: **PDE5 inhibitors** (sildenafil, tadalafil) are associated with NAION, probably via systemic hypotension in an eye with a crowded disc at risk; after one episode he should avoid them because the fellow eye is at risk. Amiodarone is another drug association. Antihypertensives must not be stopped, but bedtime dosing that causes nocturnal hypotension should be avoided; statins and metformin treat his vascular risk.
w: Wrong - Taken in the morning it does not cause nocturnal hypotension; good BP control is part of NAION management.
Wrong - Lipid control reduces vascular risk; statins have no association with NAION.
Wrong - Diabetic control is part of NAION management; metformin has no optic nerve toxicity.
Wrong - Omeprazole has no recognised link with ischaemic optic neuropathy.
Correct - PDE5 inhibitors are linked to NAION, especially with a crowded disc; the fellow eye remains at risk.

mcq.stem:
A 61-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is seen in the eye clinic 2 days after sudden painless loss of the upper field of his right eye. Right VA is 6/12 with a hyperaemic swollen disc; ESR and CRP are normal. You now examine his asymptomatic left eye with a 78D lens at the slit lamp.
Which left optic disc appearance is most likely, and explains his susceptibility?
o: A small disc with a tiny or absent cup and crowded nerve fibres
A large disc with a cup-disc ratio of 0.8 and inferior notching
A tilted myopic disc with a crescent of peripapillary atrophy
A hyperaemic disc with blurred margins and no venous pulsation
A normal-sized disc with temporal pallor from previous ischaemia
mcq.e: The **disc at risk** in NAION is small and crowded with a small or absent cup: axons squeeze through a narrow scleral canal, so mild ischaemic swelling starts a compartment-syndrome cycle of compression and further infarction. Finding it in the fellow eye supports NAION; a large glaucomatous cup is, if anything, protective. Optic disc drusen are another crowded-disc association in younger patients.
w: Correct - A small cupless crowded disc is the anatomical substrate of NAION and is usually present in both eyes.
Wrong - This is a glaucomatous disc; large cups are relatively protective against NAION.
Wrong - Tilted myopic discs with peripapillary atrophy usually have large canals and are not the typical NAION substrate.
Wrong - Hyperaemic swelling with absent venous pulsation suggests papilloedema, not the quiet fellow eye of NAION.
Wrong - Temporal pallor implies a previous optic neuropathy (e.g. optic neuritis); it does not explain susceptibility.

mcq.stem:
A 66-year-old retired teacher had sudden painless loss of vision in her right eye 2 weeks ago. Right VA is 6/36 with an inferior altitudinal defect, a hyperaemic swollen disc and splinter haemorrhages; ESR, CRP and temporal artery ultrasound are normal. She asks what is likely to happen to her right eye.
Which statement is the most accurate counselling?
o: Vision usually recovers fully within 6-8 weeks, as in optic neuritis
The disc swelling persists indefinitely, so pallor will never develop
Most patients have further painless loss in the same eye
Many eyes improve; about half reach 6/9 or better, some stay poor
The vision will inevitably fall to light perception in a few weeks
mcq.e: NAION prognosis (notes p48): improvement is common, about **50% reach 6/9 or better** but about 25% end at 6/60 or worse; recurrence in the same eye is uncommon (about 6%), and the fellow eye is affected in roughly 15% over 5 years (lecturer pearl). The swelling resolves over 3-6 weeks, leaving sectoral or diffuse pallor. Loss to PL or worse is the arteritic pattern, not NAION.
w: Wrong - Full recovery within weeks is typical of demyelinating optic neuritis (about 90% to 6/12 or better), not NAION.
Wrong - Swelling resolves within 3-6 weeks and is followed by sectoral or diffuse pallor (optic atrophy).
Wrong - Recurrence in the same eye is uncommon (about 6%); the fellow eye is the greater concern.
Correct - Partial improvement is common: about 50% reach 6/9 or better, while about 25% remain 6/60 or worse.
Wrong - Profound loss to PL or worse is the rule in arteritic AION, which her normal markers and ultrasound make unlikely.

mcq.stem:
A 69-year-old man is referred from the diabetic eye screening programme at his Klinik Kesihatan because his right optic disc looks swollen. He noticed something wrong with that eye 3 days ago but cannot describe it. Right VA is 6/9 with a right RAPD. The right disc shows hyperaemic swelling confined to its upper half with a splinter haemorrhage at 12 o'clock; the lower rim is flat with sharp margins.
Which defect is Humphrey perimetry of the right eye most likely to show?
o: A superior altitudinal defect respecting the horizontal meridian
A dense central scotoma with an otherwise full peripheral field
An inferior altitudinal defect respecting the horizontal meridian
An isolated enlarged blind spot with a full peripheral field of vision
A temporal hemianopia respecting the vertical meridian
mcq.e: The superior disc segment carries fibres from the superior retina, which sees the INFERIOR field (the retinal image is inverted), so superior sectoral swelling gives an **inferior altitudinal defect** respecting the horizontal meridian, the classic NAION field. The horizontal border reflects the nerve fibre arrangement around the horizontal raphe and separate upper and lower short posterior ciliary supply.
