A central scotoma suggests optic neuritis; an enlarged blind spot, papilloedema.
w: Wrong - A superior altitudinal defect would come from the INFERIOR disc segment; the trap is forgetting the field is inverted relative to the retina.
Wrong - A central scotoma is typical of optic neuritis or toxic/nutritional neuropathy, not sectoral disc ischaemia.
Correct - Superior disc swelling damages superior retinal fibres, producing an inferior altitudinal field defect.
Wrong - An enlarged blind spot alone suits papilloedema, where VA and pupils are normal early; this eye has an RAPD.
Wrong - Defects respecting the vertical meridian arise at or behind the chiasm, not from a single swollen disc.

mcq.stem:
A 74-year-old retired rubber tapper attends the eye clinic with 10 days of distortion in his left eye: door frames look bent and words have gaps in them. VA is 6/24 left and 6/9 right. The left macula shows a grey-green lesion beneath the retina with surrounding subretinal haemorrhage, hard exudates and a shallow fluid elevation; both maculae have multiple soft drusen. He is not diabetic.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Geographic atrophy (advanced atrophic macular degeneration)
Central serous chorioretinopathy with a serous detachment
Full-thickness macular hole with a surrounding fluid cuff
Choroidal neovascularisation from age-related macular degeneration
Branch retinal vein occlusion with secondary cystoid macular oedema
mcq.e: Distortion developing over days to weeks, with a grey-green subretinal membrane, subretinal blood, exudate and fluid on a background of soft drusen, is **neovascular (wet) AMD**: choroidal new vessels grow through Bruch membrane beneath the RPE and retina. Note: the notes (p50) list 'pre-retinal haemorrhage'; bleeding in wet AMD is SUBRETINAL or sub-RPE (it reaches the vitreous only when massive). Wet AMD is about 10% of AMD but causes most of the severe visual loss.
w: Wrong - Geographic atrophy is the dry end-stage: gradual over years, sharply demarcated atrophy with visible choroidal vessels and no blood or exudate.
Wrong - CSCR affects younger (often stressed or steroid-using) men and gives a clear serous blister without haemorrhage or drusen.
Wrong - A macular hole gives a round central defect and central scotoma; it does not bleed or produce exudates.
Correct - Subretinal membrane + subretinal blood + exudate + fluid over drusen with rapid metamorphopsia = wet AMD.
Wrong - BRVO gives flame haemorrhages in a sector drained by one vein beyond an AV crossing, not a subretinal membrane.

mcq.stem:
An 81-year-old woman is brought to a Klinik Kesihatan by her son because over 3 years she has gradually lost the ability to read and recognise faces, although she walks around the house without difficulty. She needs very bright light to read and takes a long time to see after coming indoors. VA is 6/36 in both eyes. Both maculae show sharply demarcated pale areas through which large choroidal vessels are visible, surrounded by drusen; there is no blood, exudate or fluid. She takes no regular medicines.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Bilateral disciform scars from old choroidal neovascularisation
Geographic atrophy from advanced dry (atrophic) AMD
Bull's-eye maculopathy from antimalarial drug toxicity
Stargardt macular dystrophy (fundus flavimaculatus)
Bilateral optic atrophy with secondary macular pallor
mcq.e: Slow bilateral central loss over years with preserved navigation, poor dark adaptation and sharply demarcated RPE atrophy exposing choroidal vessels is **geographic atrophy**, advanced dry AMD (about 90% of AMD). With no fluid or blood, anti-VEGF has no role; management is low-vision aids, good lighting, smoking cessation and Amsler monitoring for conversion to wet AMD. A disciform scar is the end-stage of wet AMD and is raised and fibrous.
w: Wrong - A disciform scar is a raised white-grey fibrovascular scar after wet AMD, usually after sudden distortion, not flat atrophic patches.
Correct - Gradual central loss over years with demarcated RPE atrophy showing choroidal vessels and no fluid = geographic atrophy.
Wrong - Chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine bull's-eye maculopathy needs a drug history; she takes no regular medicines.
Wrong - Stargardt disease is an inherited dystrophy presenting in childhood or young adulthood, not at 81.
Wrong - Optic atrophy gives a pale disc with RAPD and colour loss; here the pallor is at the macula with visible choroidal vessels.

mcq.stem:
A 69-year-old man is referred to an MOH hospital eye clinic with 1 week of wavy lines in his right eye. Right VA is 6/12. Fundoscopy shows soft drusen and a small spot of subretinal blood at the right fovea. The consultant wants the single test that best confirms the diagnosis today and that will also be repeated at each future treatment visit to decide whether to re-treat.
Which investigation is most appropriate?
o: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) of macula
Fundus fluorescein angiography of the macula
Indocyanine green angiography of the choroid
B-scan ultrasonography of the posterior segment
Humphrey 10-2 visual field test of the right eye
mcq.e: **OCT** is the key investigation in suspected wet AMD: quick, non-invasive cross-sectional imaging shows intraretinal and subretinal fluid, pigment epithelial detachment and the CNV complex, and it is repeated at every anti-VEGF visit (treat-and-extend decisions depend on whether the macula is dry). FFA (± ICG) confirms and classifies CNV when OCT is equivocal but needs IV dye and is not repeated each visit. Ultrasound is only for when the fundus cannot be seen.
w: Correct - Non-invasive OCT shows fluid and the CNV complex and is the monitoring tool at every injection visit.
Wrong - FFA confirms leakage and classifies CNV but is invasive (IV fluorescein, rare anaphylaxis) and is not repeated at every visit.
Wrong - ICG is reserved for suspected polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy (common in Asian patients) or occult CNV, not routine monitoring.
Wrong - B-scan is needed only when media opacity, such as dense vitreous haemorrhage, prevents a fundal view.
Wrong - Fields document the scotoma but do not show fluid, so they cannot guide re-treatment.

mcq.stem:
A 72-year-old woman has a subfoveal choroidal neovascular membrane in her left eye confirmed on OCT, with subretinal fluid and a small haemorrhage; her left VA has fallen from 6/9 to 6/24 over 3 weeks. The right eye has intermediate drusen. She is otherwise well and keen for treatment.
What is the most appropriate first-line treatment for the left eye?
o: Thermal argon laser photocoagulation applied to the subfoveal membrane
Verteporfin photodynamic therapy alone, repeated every 3 months
AREDS2 supplements, Amsler grid monitoring and review in 6 months
Intravitreal triamcinolone to reduce leakage
Intravitreal anti-VEGF, monthly loading then treat-and-extend
mcq.e: **Intravitreal anti-VEGF** (ranibizumab, aflibercept, faricimab or off-label bevacizumab) is first-line for active subfoveal CNV: monthly loading injections (usually 3) then treat-and-extend guided by OCT. Thermal laser destroys the overlying fovea and leaves an immediate permanent central scotoma; it suited only well-demarcated extrafoveal CNV (MPS). Note: the notes say PDT is activated by 'low light'; verteporfin is activated by a non-thermal 689 nm diode laser, and PDT is now used mainly for polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy or as an adjunct.
w: Wrong - Thermal laser to a subfoveal lesion burns the fovea, causing an immediate permanent scotoma; it was only for extrafoveal CNV.
Wrong - PDT (verteporfin activated by a non-thermal 689 nm laser) mainly slows further loss and needs repeated sessions; it is not first-line monotherapy.
Wrong - Supplements reduce progression in intermediate dry AMD but do not treat active neovascularisation; waiting loses vision.
Wrong - Intravitreal steroid is not first-line for CNV and causes cataract and raised IOP.
Correct - Anti-VEGF injections are first-line for active CNV and are the only option likely to improve vision.

mcq.stem:
A 70-year-old man who has smoked 20 cigarettes a day for 45 years attends for review. Both maculae show numerous large soft drusen with pigmentary change; VA is 6/9 in each eye with no distortion, and OCT shows no fluid. He has seen 'eye vitamins' advertised at the pharmacy and asks which to take.
Which advice is most appropriate?
o: Original AREDS formula with beta-carotene, vitamins C and E and zinc
No supplement, as they only benefit people who already have wet AMD
AREDS2 formula: vitamins C and E, zinc, copper, lutein, zeaxanthin
High-dose vitamin A capsules to support photoreceptors
Fish-oil omega-3 capsules alone, which are proven to halt progression
mcq.e: For intermediate AMD (large drusen) or advanced AMD in one eye, the **AREDS2 formula** (vitamin C, vitamin E, zinc, copper, lutein/zeaxanthin) reduces progression to advanced AMD by about 25% over 5 years. **Beta-carotene was removed** because it increased lung cancer in smokers and ex-smokers, which matters for this patient. Supplements do not help early AMD (a few small drusen) and do not treat active wet AMD; stopping smoking is still the most important step.
w: Wrong - Beta-carotene increases lung cancer risk in current and former smokers; this formula should be avoided in him.
Wrong - The proven benefit is in intermediate AMD and the fellow eye of unilateral advanced AMD, not only in wet AMD.
Correct - AREDS2 without beta-carotene is the evidence-based choice for intermediate AMD in a smoker.
Wrong - High-dose vitamin A has no proven role in AMD and risks toxicity; it is not part of either AREDS formula.
Wrong - AREDS2 found no added benefit from omega-3 fatty acids; they do not halt progression.

mcq.stem:
An 84-year-old widow with bilateral advanced AMD (VA 6/60 right, counting fingers left) tells you at clinic review that for 2 months she has seen small, brightly dressed people and flowers on the wallpaper, mostly in the evening. She knows they are not real and is not frightened, but worries she is 'going mad'. She is fully oriented, has no other neurological symptoms and takes only amlodipine.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Explain it is a benign result of her visual loss and reassure her
Start low-dose haloperidol at night to suppress the hallucinations
Refer urgently to psychiatry to assess for late-onset psychosis
Arrange an urgent CT brain to exclude an occipital mass lesion
Refer to neurology for an EEG to exclude occipital lobe seizures
mcq.e: Complex, well-formed visual hallucinations with retained insight in a visually impaired but cognitively intact person are **Charles Bonnet syndrome**: release hallucinations of a deafferented visual cortex, common in advanced AMD. The key step is explanation and reassurance (many patients fear dementia or psychosis and hide the symptom); coping tips include changing lighting, blinking or looking away, and maximising vision with low-vision aids. Investigate only if insight is lost, other sensory hallucinations occur or there are neurological signs.
w: Correct - Charles Bonnet syndrome is benign; explanation and reassurance are the main treatment.
Wrong - Antipsychotics are not needed when insight is preserved and carry risks (falls, stroke) in the elderly.
Wrong - Retained insight, no delusions or auditory hallucinations, and severe visual loss point away from psychosis.
Wrong - Imaging is reserved for focal neurological signs, loss of insight or atypical features; none are present.
Wrong - Seizure-related hallucinations are brief and stereotyped, often with other ictal features, unlike these.

mcq.stem:
A 77-year-old man with neovascular AMD in his right eye has just had his third monthly intravitreal ranibizumab injection. His VA has improved from 6/36 to 6/12 and OCT shows that the subretinal fluid has resolved. His daughter, a staff nurse, asks how the drug works.
Which explanation is correct?
o: It is a photosensitiser that closes new vessels when activated by laser
It stimulates angiogenesis so that the ischaemic macula is reperfused
It is a corticosteroid that suppresses inflammation in Bruch membrane
It binds and neutralises VEGF-A, reducing new vessel growth and leakage
It coagulates abnormal vessels by heating the retinal pigment epithelium
mcq.e: VEGF-A drives choroidal new vessel growth and makes the vessels leak; **ranibizumab** (antibody fragment), bevacizumab (full antibody) and aflibercept (decoy receptor) bind it, so leakage dries up (fluid resolves on OCT) and growth stops. Note: the notes (p50) say anti-VEGF 'stimulates angiogenesis and vascular permeability'; it is VEGF that does this, and anti-VEGF BLOCKS it. The effect wears off, so repeated injections are needed.
w: Wrong - This describes verteporfin PDT, activated by a non-thermal 689 nm laser.
Wrong - This is what VEGF itself does; the notes' wording confuses the drug with its target.
Wrong - Ranibizumab is a monoclonal antibody fragment, not a steroid.
Correct - Anti-VEGF neutralises VEGF-A, so new vessels stop growing and leaking.
Wrong - This describes thermal laser photocoagulation, which also destroys the overlying retina.

mcq.stem:
A 66-year-old Chinese man who has smoked for 40 years has a disciform scar in his right eye (VA counting fingers) and soft drusen in his left eye (VA 6/9). He also has hypertension, a BMI of 29 and raised cholesterol, and takes aspirin 75 mg daily after a TIA. He asks what single change would best protect his remaining good eye.
Which advice is most appropriate?
o: Wear blue-light-blocking spectacles whenever he uses a screen
Stop his daily low-dose aspirin, which promotes macular bleeding
Stop smoking completely, with help from a quit-smoking service
Reduce reading and close work to rest his remaining macula
Start a high-dose statin to dissolve the drusen already present
mcq.e: Smoking is the strongest **modifiable** risk factor for AMD (about twice the risk, notes p49), and stopping is the most important step for the fellow eye, which is at high risk once one eye has advanced AMD. Control of BP, weight and lipids is worthwhile, together with AREDS2 supplements (no beta-carotene in smokers) and Amsler monitoring. Aspirin given for a TIA should not be stopped on AMD grounds, and using the eyes does not wear out the macula.
w: Wrong - There is no good evidence that blue-light filters prevent AMD progression.
Wrong - Aspirin for secondary stroke prevention should not be stopped because of AMD; evidence of harm is weak.
Correct - Smoking cessation is the most effective modifiable step; offer referral to a quit-smoking service.
Wrong - Reading does not damage the macula; restricting it only reduces quality of life.
Wrong - Statins have no proven role in dissolving drusen; lipid control helps vascular health but is not the key AMD step.

mcq.stem:
A 73-year-old retired seamstress has intermediate dry AMD in both eyes (VA 6/9 each) and her older sister lost central vision to 'wet' macular disease. She is being discharged from the eye clinic to 6-monthly review and you give her an Amsler grid to use at home.
Which instruction about using the grid is most appropriate?
o: Look at it with both eyes open, from across the room, once a month
Use it only when her distance vision blurs, as distortion is unimportant
Take off her reading glasses so that blur does not hide any distortion
Look at the edges of the grid rather than the central dot while testing
Test each eye separately at reading distance, wearing reading glasses
mcq.e: The **Amsler grid** detects new metamorphopsia or a scotoma, the earliest sign of conversion to wet AMD. Each eye must be tested separately (with both open the good eye masks the bad), at about 30-40 cm with near correction, fixating the central dot; new wavy, missing or blurred lines mean she must be seen promptly (within about 1-2 weeks) for OCT, because early anti-VEGF gives the best outcome. Note: the notes list macropsia; micropsia is more typical, and metamorphopsia is the key symptom.
w: Wrong - With both eyes open the fellow eye fills in the defect, and the grid is designed for near viewing.
Wrong - Distortion (metamorphopsia) is THE key symptom of wet AMD; waiting for distance blur delays treatment.
Wrong - The grid is used with the near correction; uncorrected blur makes the test unreliable.
Wrong - She must fixate the central dot; distortion is then noticed in the surrounding lines.
Correct - One eye at a time, at near with reading glasses, fixating the centre, and report any new distortion promptly.

mcq.stem:
A 79-year-old man on warfarin for atrial fibrillation has known neovascular AMD in his left eye but defaulted his injections 6 months ago. He presents to the emergency department with sudden painless loss of vision in that eye to hand movements. The red reflex is dull and there is no fundal view. B-scan ultrasound shows diffuse vitreous echoes, an attached peripheral retina and a dome-shaped elevation at the posterior pole.
What is the most likely source of the bleeding?
o: A horseshoe retinal tear from an acute posterior vitreous detachment
Breakthrough bleeding from a submacular choroidal neovascular membrane
New vessels on the disc from undiagnosed proliferative diabetic retinopathy
Subarachnoid haemorrhage tracking into the vitreous (Terson syndrome)
Rupture of a retinal arterial macroaneurysm along the inferior arcade
mcq.e: A large submacular haemorrhage from CNV (more likely with anticoagulation and untreated disease) can **break through** the retina into the vitreous; this is the 'surgery for breakthrough vitreous haemorrhage' in the notes (p49). B-scan is mandatory when there is no fundal view: here it shows attached retina and a posterior pole dome of subretinal blood and CNV. Management is vitrectomy ± displacement of submacular blood with anti-VEGF, discussing anticoagulation with the physician (usually continued); visual prognosis is poor.
w: Wrong - A PVD-related tear gives flashes and floaters with peripheral pathology; here the lesion is at the macula of a known CNV eye.
Correct - Untreated CNV on warfarin with a posterior pole dome on B-scan = breakthrough submacular haemorrhage.
Wrong - He is not described as diabetic, and disc new vessels do not produce a dome-shaped macular elevation.
Wrong - Terson syndrome follows a sudden severe headache from subarachnoid haemorrhage and is often bilateral.
Wrong - Macroaneurysms arise along an arteriole, mostly in hypertensive women; with known untreated CNV the macular lesion is the likely source.
